**7.54.4**  Dry thunderbolts fell with crashing peals and lightning, and the earth trembled with its mountains, woods, and forests.

**7.54.5**  The oceans, abodes of sea-monsters, were churned into uproar, great king, and the rivers that flow to the sea began to run backward against their current.

**7.54.6**  Chariots, horses, men, and elephants were turned upside down, for the delight of the flesh-eaters and the swelling of Yama's realm.

**7.54.7**  The draught-animals let fall their dung and urine and wept aloud; and beholding all these dreadful, hair-raising portents—

**7.54.8**  —all your troops were filled with dismay, O bull of the Bhāratas, hearing the fierce vow of the mighty Savyasācin.

**7.54.9**  Then the mighty-armed son of the Chastiser of Pāka said to Kṛṣṇa: "Console your sister Subhadrā, and her daughter-in-law with her."

**7.54.10**  "Set the daughter-in-law and her mother-in-law, the blameless ones, free of grief, Mādhava; with gentle, true, and fitting words console them, O lord."

**7.54.11**  Then Vāsudeva, sore at heart, went to Arjuna's dwelling and consoled his grieving sister, stricken with sorrow for her son.

**7.54.12**  "Grieve not for the boy, daughter of the Vṛṣṇis, you and your daughter-in-law; for all living beings, O timid one, this is the end appointed by Time."

**7.54.13**  "For a hero born in a noble line, and most of all a Kṣatriya, such a death is befitting; grieve not for your son."

**7.54.14**  "By good fortune the heroic great warrior, equal in valor to his father, has by the law of the Kṣatriyas attained the goal that heroes long for."

**7.54.15**  "Having conquered foes in great numbers and sent them to their death, he has gone to the imperishable worlds of the doers of good, that yield every desire."

**7.54.16**  "That goal which the good seek through austerity, through chastity, through sacred learning and through wisdom—that goal your son has attained."

**7.54.17**  "You are the mother of a hero, the wife of a hero, kinswoman to heroic fathers-in-law; grieve not for your son, good lady, for he has gone to the highest goal."

**7.54.18**  "And that base Saindhava, the slayer of a boy, shall reap the fruit of his insolence, he together with his band of friends and kinsmen."

**7.54.19**  "When the night has passed, O fair-hipped one, that doer of evil deeds shall not escape Pārtha, even though he enter Amarāvatī itself."

**7.54.20**  "Tomorrow you shall hear that the head of that Saindhava has been struck off in battle, cast beyond Samantapañcaka. Be free of grief; weep not."

**7.54.21**  "Holding the law of the Kṣatriya foremost, the hero has gone to the goal of the good—the goal which we too may attain, and others who live by the sword."

**7.54.22**  "Broad-chested, mighty-armed, never turning back, humbler of the foremost foes—your son, O fair-hipped one, has gone to heaven. Cast off your fever of grief."

**7.54.23**  "Taking after his father and his mother's line, the valiant one, having slain enemies by the thousand, the heroic great warrior was himself slain."

**7.54.24**  "Console your daughter-in-law, O lady; grieve not so deeply, O Kṣatriya woman. Tomorrow, hearing tidings most welcome and great, you shall be free of grief, O joyful one."

**7.54.25**  "What Pārtha has vowed shall be so and not otherwise; for what your brother resolves to do can never come to nothing."

**7.54.26**  "Even if men and serpents, demons, night-rovers, and birds, gods and antigods, should rush to the side of the king of Sindhu in battle, he shall be no more, nor they with him, when morning comes."

**7.55.1**  Saṃjaya said: Having heard these words of the great-souled Keśava, Subhadrā, stricken with grief for her son and sorely afflicted, lamented aloud.

**7.55.2**  "Alas, my son! How is it that, going into battle, you who were equal to your father in valor have met your end, dear child, son of luckless me?"

**7.55.3**  "How is it that your face, dark as the blue lotus, with fine teeth and lovely eyes, is now seen, my darling, veiled in the dust of battle?"

**7.55.4**  "Surely they now look upon you, the hero fallen, who never turned back—fair of head, neck, arms, and shoulders, broad-chested, lean of belly—"

**7.55.5**  "—every limb beautifully formed, fair-eyed, strewn with weapon-wounds; surely the creatures gaze upon you as upon the risen moon."

**7.55.6**  "You whose couch was once spread with coverlets to be envied—how do you lie today upon the bare ground, flung down, you who were used to comfort?"

**7.55.7**  "The hero, mighty-armed, once waited upon by the loveliest of women—how is it that he, fallen in battle, is today waited upon by jackals?"

**7.55.8**  "He who was once praised by joyful bards, heralds, and minstrels is today attended by dreadful, howling packs of flesh-eaters."

**7.55.9**  "With the Pāṇḍavas for your protectors, O mighty one, and the heroes of the Vṛṣṇis and the heroes of the Pāñcālas—by whom were you slain, as though you had no protector at all?"

**7.55.10**  "Never sated with the sight of you, my blameless son, I, ill-fated, shall surely go today to the realm of Yama."

**7.55.11**  "Wide-eyed, fair-haired at the temples, sweet of speech and fragrant—when, my son, shall I look again upon your unwounded face?"

**7.55.12**  "A curse upon the strength of Bhīmasena, a curse upon Pārtha among the bowmen, a curse upon the prowess of the Vṛṣṇi heroes, and a curse upon the might of the Pāñcālas!"

**7.55.13**  "A curse upon the Kekayas, the Cedis, the Matsyas, and the Sṛñjayas, who knew not that you, the hero, had gone into the fray and been struck down."

**7.55.14**  "Today, not seeing Abhimanyu, with eyes troubled by grief, I behold the earth as if empty, its splendor put out."

**7.55.15**  "Sister's son of Vāsudeva, son of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva—how shall I look upon you, the hero, robbed of your chariot and brought down by others?"

**7.55.16**  "Alas, hero, seen and then lost, you are to me like wealth in a dream! Ah, how fleeting is human life, unsteady as a bubble on the water!"

**7.55.17**  "This your young wife, overwhelmed with grief for you—how shall I sustain her, like a cow bereft of her calf?"

**7.55.18**  "Ah, you have set forth out of season, my little son, forsaking me—who longed so to see you—at the very time of harvest."

**7.55.19**  "Surely the course of Fate is hard to fathom even for the wise, since you, with Keśava for your protector, were slain in battle as though protectorless."

**7.55.20**  "That goal which belongs to performers of sacrifice, to the charitable, to the Brāhmaṇas of perfected souls, to those who have kept the vow of chastity and have bathed at holy fords—"

**7.55.21**  "—to the grateful, the generous, those devoted to the service of their elders, and those who give the thousandfold sacrificial fee—that goal may you attain."

**7.55.22**  "That goal which belongs to heroes fighting on and never turning back, who slay their foes and are themselves slain in battle—to that goal go."

**7.55.23**  "That goal which is the givers' of a thousand cows and of the offerings of sacrifice, that blessed goal of those who bestow a cherished dwelling—"

**7.55.24**  "—that goal which sages of strict vows reach through chastity, and which faithful wives of a single husband reach—to that goal go, my little son."

**7.55.25**  "That everlasting goal which comes to kings by their good conduct, and to those of the four life-stages, purified and well-guarded by their meritorious deeds—"

**7.55.26**  "—that goal of those who pity the wretched, who ever share what they have, and who have turned away from slander—to that goal go, my little son."

**7.55.27**  "That goal of those true to their vows, of righteous nature, devoted to the service of their elders, who never turn a guest away in vain—to that goal go, my little son."

**7.55.28**  "That goal of the high-minded who go to their own wives only in the proper season and never resort to the wives of others—to that goal go, my little son."

**7.55.29**  "That goal of those, free from envy, who approach all beings with gentleness, who wound no one and are forbearing—that goal may you attain."

**7.55.30**  "That goal of those who abstain from wine and flesh, who have renounced pride, hypocrisy, and falsehood, and the tormenting of others—to that goal go, my little son."

**7.55.31**  "That goal which the good attain—the modest, the masters of all the scriptures, content in knowledge, with senses subdued—to that goal go, my little son."

**7.55.32**  As Subhadrā lamented thus, forlorn and wasted with grief, the Pāñcāla princess, together with Virāṭa's daughter, then came to her side.

**7.55.33**  Having wept their fill and lamented in deep distress, those women, like ones gone mad, fell senseless to the ground, O king.

**7.55.34**  But Kṛṣṇa, himself sorely grieved, tended to her in her sorrow, sprinkling water upon her and reviving her, speaking now this, now that, kindly word.

**7.55.35**  To his sister—well-nigh senseless, weeping, fallen prostrate and trembling—the lotus-eyed one spoke these words:

**7.55.36**  "Subhadrā, grieve not for your son; with the Pāñcāla princess console Uttarā. Abhimanyu, that bull among Kṣatriyas, has gone to the renowned goal."

**7.55.37**  "And whatever other men there are in our line, O fair-faced one—may they all attain the goal of the glorious Abhimanyu."

**7.55.38**  "May we, and our friends as well, perform such a deed as your son, the lone great warrior, has wrought this day."

**7.55.39**  Having thus consoled his sister, and Draupadī and Uttarā as well, the mighty-armed subduer of foes returned to Pārtha's side.

**7.55.40**  Then the lord Kṛṣṇa, taking leave of the kings and the kinsmen, entered the inner apartments, O king, while the others went each to his own quarters.

**7.56.1**  Saṃjaya said: Then the lotus-eyed lord entered Arjuna's peerless dwelling, and having touched water, spread upon an auspiciously marked patch of cleared ground a fair bed of darbha grasses that gleamed like beryl.

**7.56.2**  Then with garlands, duly with parched grain and sweet auspicious perfumes, he adorned that bed, ringing it about with the finest weapons.

**7.56.3**  Then the well-trained attendants showed to Pārtha, who had touched water, the customary nightly offering to Tryambaka.

**7.56.4**  Then Pārtha, glad of heart, adorning Mādhava with perfumes and garlands, presented to him that nightly offering.

**7.56.5**  Govinda, smiling, answered Phalguna: "Let us take our rest, Pārtha; blessings upon you. I go now to ensure your welfare."

**7.56.6**  Then, having posted doorkeepers and armed men as guards, the glorious one, followed by Dāruka, entered his own pavilion and lay down upon a spotless couch, pondering the many tasks at hand.

**7.56.7**  In the Pāṇḍavas' camp no one slept that night; wakefulness came over every one of them, O lord of peoples.

**7.56.8**  For the slaying of the king of Sindhu had been vowed in haste by the great-souled wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, overwhelmed with grief for his son.

**7.56.9**  "How then shall the mighty-armed son of Vāsava, slayer of enemy heroes, make his vow bear fruit?"—thus they pondered together.

**7.56.10**  "Grievous indeed is this that the great-souled Pāṇḍava has resolved upon; scorched by grief for his son, he has made a mighty vow."

**7.56.11**  "And the valiant brothers too, and the vast hosts—all this has been laid before Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son."

**7.56.12**  "May Dhanaṃjaya, when he has slain the Saindhava in battle, return again to us; and having vanquished the hosts of his foes, may Arjuna fulfill his vow."

**7.56.13**  "For if he does not slay the king of the Sindhus, he will enter the smoke-bannered fire; yet Pārtha Dhanaṃjaya is not one to let his word prove false."

**7.56.14**  "How shall the king, the son of Dharma, fare if Arjuna dies? For upon him alone has the Pāṇḍava rested the whole of his hope of victory."

**7.56.15**  "If we have done any good deed, if we have given gifts or made oblation, then by the fruit of all of that may Savyasācin conquer his enemies."

**7.56.16**  As they spoke thus, O lord, longing for his victory, the night passed away, O king, only with the greatest difficulty.

**7.56.17**  In the middle of that night Janārdana awoke, and remembering the vow of Pārtha, he spoke thus to Dāruka:

**7.56.18**  "Arjuna, stricken with grief at the slaying of his kinsman, has vowed, O Dāruka: 'I shall slay Jayadratha when tomorrow has come.'"

**7.56.19**  "When Duryodhana hears of this, he will take counsel with his ministers, so that Pārtha may not slay Jayadratha in the fight."

**7.56.20**  "All those armies in their full array will guard Jayadratha, and so too will Droṇa with his son, who is master of every science of arms."

**7.56.21**  "Even the thousand-eyed one, the lone hero who crushes the Daityas and Dānavas, could not bring himself to slay him in battle when he is guarded by Droṇa."

**7.56.22**  "Therefore tomorrow I shall so contrive it that Arjuna, the son of Kuntī, shall slay Jayadratha before the sun reaches its setting."

**7.56.23**  "For not my wives, nor friends, nor kinsmen, nor any other dearer to me than the son of Kuntī—none is there dearer to me than Arjuna."

**7.56.24**  "A world without Arjuna I could not bear to look upon even for a moment, O Dāruka; nor shall it ever come to be so."

**7.56.25**  "For Arjuna's sake I shall destroy the bannered hosts of the foe, with their horses, chariots, and elephants, together with Karṇa and Suyodhana themselves."

**7.56.26**  "Tomorrow let the three worlds behold my prowess in the great battle, O Dāruka, as I exert myself in the fray for the sake of Dhanaṃjaya."

**7.56.27**  "Tomorrow thousands of kings and hundreds of princes, with their horses, elephants, and chariots, shall flee before me in battle, O Dāruka."

**7.56.28**  "Tomorrow you shall see the host of kings crushed by my discus, struck down in battle by me in my wrath for the Pāṇḍava's sake."

**7.56.29**  "Tomorrow all the worlds, with their gods, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, shall know me to be the friend of Savyasācin."

**7.56.30**  "Whoever hates him hates me; whoever follows him follows me. Let it be understood with certainty in your mind: Arjuna is the half of my own body."

**7.56.31**  "While this night has not yet given way to dawn, do you, bound to your duty, make ready and bring forth my best of chariots according to the rule,"

**7.56.32**  "setting upon the chariot, O charioteer, the divine mace Kaumodakī, the spear, the discus, the bow and arrows, and all the other accoutrements as well."

**7.56.33**  "And having prepared upon the floor of the chariot a place for my banner—the heroic son of Vinatā, who graces the chariot in battle—"

**7.56.34**  "and the parasol with its nets of pure gold, bright as the sun and fire, fashioned by Viśvakarman, divine—and the horses, well adorned,"

**7.56.35**  "having yoked those best of steeds, Balāhaka, Meghapuṣpa, Saiṇya, and Sugrīva, stand ready and clad in armor, O Dāruka."

**7.56.36**  "And when you hear the terrible blast of Pāñcajanya, filled with a deep bull-like note, come swiftly to me."

**7.56.37**  "In a single day I shall sweep away all the indignation and all the sorrows of my cousin, the son of my father's sister, O Dāruka."

**7.56.38**  "By every means I shall strive so that Bībhatsu may slay Jayadratha in the battle before the very eyes of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."

**7.56.39**  "And against whomsoever Bībhatsu shall make his effort to slay, there, O charioteer, I am sure his victory is assured."

**7.56.40**  Dāruka said: "Victory indeed is assured to him—how could there ever be defeat for one whose charioteer you have become, O tiger among men?"

**7.56.41**  "And I shall do all this just as you command me, that this night may break in fair dawn for the victory of Vijaya."

**7.57.1**  Saṃjaya said: But the son of Kuntī, Dhanaṃjaya of inconceivable valor, even as he brooded upon that resolve and guarded his own vow, was overcome with bewilderment.

**7.57.2**  As he, the hero of the monkey banner, lay consumed with grief and lost in thought, the one of mighty splendor, he of the Garuḍa banner, came to him in a dream.

**7.57.3**  In every circumstance Dhanaṃjaya, righteous of soul, never failed in rising to greet Kṛṣṇa, always out of devotion and love.

**7.57.4**  And rising to greet Govinda, he gave him a seat; nor did Bībhatsu then set his own mind upon taking a seat himself.

**7.57.5**  Then Kṛṣṇa of great splendor, knowing the resolve of Pārtha, being seated, spoke these words to the son of Kuntī who stood before him:

**7.57.6**  "Set not your mind upon despair, O Pārtha; for Time is hard to conquer. Time draws all beings on, into the supreme ordinance."

**7.57.7**  "And why this despair of yours? Tell me, O best of speakers. The wise man should not grieve, for grief is the ruin of every undertaking."

**7.57.8**  "By grieving a man gladdens his enemies and wastes away his kinsmen, and is himself diminished. Therefore you ought not to grieve."

**7.57.9**  Thus addressed by Vāsudeva, the unconquered Bībhatsu, learned as he was, then spoke these meaningful words:

**7.57.10**  "A mighty vow has been made by me concerning the slaying of Jayadratha—that 'tomorrow I shall slay that evil-souled killer of my son,' O Keśava."

**7.57.11**  "To thwart my vow, O Acyuta, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will surely keep the Saindhava in the rear, guarded by all their great chariot-warriors."

**7.57.12**  "Eleven armies are theirs, O Kṛṣṇa, exceedingly hard to overcome; and should my vow fail, how could one such as I go on living?"

**7.57.13**  "My longing, O hero, turns toward a thing whose accomplishment is fraught with hardship, and the sun moves swiftly on—therefore I say this to you."

**7.57.14**  Having heard that ground of Pārtha's grief, Kṛṣṇa, whose emblem is the bird, touched water and then took his stand facing the east.

**7.57.15**  These words the lotus-eyed one of great splendor spoke, for the good of the son of Pāṇḍu, intent upon the slaying of the Saindhava:

**7.57.16**  "O Pārtha, there is the supreme and eternal weapon called Pāśupata, with which the god Maheśvara slew all the Daityas in battle."

**7.57.17**  "If that weapon be known to you today, you shall slay Jayadratha tomorrow. But if you would learn it, take refuge in your mind with the god of the bull banner."

**7.57.18**  "Meditating in your mind upon that god, remain in silence, O Dhanaṃjaya; then by his grace, being devoted, you shall obtain that mighty weapon."

**7.57.19**  Then, having heard the words of Kṛṣṇa, Dhanaṃjaya touched water and, seated upon the ground with single-pointed mind, went in thought to Bhava.

**7.57.20**  Then in the auspicious hour sacred to Brahmā, in that moment of fair omen, Arjuna beheld himself together with Keśava up in the sky.

**7.57.21**  And Pārtha, moving with the speed of the wind, together with Keśava, traversed the heaven, thronged with lights and frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.

**7.57.22**  Held by the mighty Keśava upon his right arm, gazing upon many a wondrous form, he passed on through sights marvelous to behold.

**7.57.23**  In the northern quarter the righteous one beheld the White Mountain, and in Kubera's pleasure-grove a lotus-pool adorned with blossoms.

**7.57.24**  And he gazed upon the Gaṅgā, best of rivers, abounding in waters, set about with trees ever in flower and fruit, her stones of crystal,

**7.57.25**  thronged with lions and tigers, teeming with herds of many kinds of deer, holy with hermitages, lovely, and frequented by charming birds.

**7.57.26**  And he beheld the regions of Mandara, resounding with the songs of Kiṃnaras, their peaks of gold and silver lit up by many healing herbs, and graced too with flowering coral trees.

**7.57.27**  He reached the Kāla mountain, dark as a heap of glistening collyrium, the holy foothills of the Himavat, and Mount Maṇimat, and Brahmatuṅga, and other rivers as well, and the lands of men.

**7.57.28**  And Suśṛṅga, and Śataśṛṅga, and the forest of Śaryāti, and the holy seat of the Horse's-Head, and the abode of Atharvaṇa.

**7.57.29**  And Vṛṣadaṃśa, lord of mountains, and great Mandara as well, thronged with Apsarases and made beautiful by Kiṃnaras.

**7.57.30**  And as he journeyed past those mountains, Pārtha, together with Keśava, gazed upon them, blessed with fair cascades and adorned with veins of gold.

**7.57.31**  He beheld the earth, her form gleaming as in moonbeams, garlanded with cities, and the oceans of wondrous aspect, abounding in rich stores of treasure.

**7.57.32**  Gazing on the firmament, the heaven, and the earth, journeying through Viṣṇu's step, filled with wonder, he sped on with Kṛṣṇa, swift as an arrow loosed.

**7.57.33**  Then Pārtha beheld a mountain blazing as it were, of a radiance equal to that of the planets, the stars, the moon, the sun, and fire.

**7.57.34**  And drawing near to that mountain, he beheld upon its summit the high-souled god of the bull banner, ever steadfast in austerity.

**7.57.35**  He blazed with his own splendor like a thousand suns, bearing the trident, his hair matted, fair of hue, clad in bark and hide.

**7.57.36**  With his thousands of eyes, his body of marvelous form, of mighty power—the god, together with Pārvatī and with shining hosts of spirits—

**7.57.37**  amid the swelling of song and instruments, attended by dance kept to the beat, by leaping and clapping and loud shouts, and served by holy fragrances.

**7.57.38**  He was being praised with divine hymns by sages who expound the Veda—the protector of all beings, bearer of the bow, the unfallen one.

**7.57.39**  But Vāsudeva, beholding him, touched the earth with his head, together with Pārtha, the righteous one chanting the eternal sacred verse,

**7.57.40**  hailing him as the origin of the worlds, the all-maker, the unborn, the lord, the imperishable, the supreme source of mind, the ether, the wind, the treasury of all lights,

**7.57.41**  the creator of the streams of water, the supreme primal nature of the earth, the fulfiller of gods, Dānavas, Yakṣas, and men,

**7.57.42**  the supreme Brahman of the yogins, made manifest, the treasure of those who know the Brahman, the creator of all that moves and is unmoving, and its destroyer too,

**7.57.43**  the great-souled one whose wrath is Time itself, in whom arise the powers of Śakra and Sūrya—him Kṛṣṇa then worshipped with word, mind, intellect, and deed.

**7.57.44**  To Bhava, the unborn, whose essence is the cause, whom the wise perceive who seek the subtle station of the inner Self—to him the two went for refuge.

**7.57.45**  And Arjuna too bowed before that god again and again, knowing him to be the one, the origin of what is and what shall be, the source of the becoming of all beings.

**7.57.46**  Then Śarva spoke to the two who had come, as though smiling: "Welcome to you both, O best of men. Rise up, your weariness gone. And what is the desire of your hearts, O heroes? Tell it quickly."

**7.57.47**  "Whatever the purpose for which you two have come, that I shall accomplish for you. Choose what is for your own good, and all of it I shall grant you."

**7.57.48**  Then, hearing that speech, Vāsudeva and Arjuna, the two of mighty mind, stood up with hands joined in reverence and praised Śarva:

**7.57.49**  "Homage to Bhava, to Śarva, to Rudra, and to the giver of boons; ever homage to the lord of beasts, to the fierce one, to him of the matted braid."

**7.57.50**  "To Mahādeva, to the terrible one, to the three-eyed, to Śambhu, to Īśāna, to the destroyer of Bhaga—homage be to the slayer of Andhaka."

**7.57.51**  Ever to the teacher of Kumāra, to the blue-throated, to the ordainer, to the deep-red one, to the smoke-hued, to the hunter, to the unvanquished.

**7.57.52**  Ever to the dark-crested one, to the bearer of the trident, to the one of divine sight, to the slayer, to the protector, to the three-eyed, to the hunter, to him whose seed is the Vasus.

**7.57.53**  To the inconceivable, to the husband of Ambikā, to him praised by all the gods, to him whose banner bears the bull, to the tawny one, to the matted-haired, to the chaste celibate.

**7.57.54**  To him who performs austerities within the waters, to the friend of the brahmans, to the unconquered, to the soul of the universe, to the maker of the universe, to him who stands enveloping all that is.

**7.57.55**  Homage, homage to you, the worshipful, ever the source of all beings, to him from whose mouth issues the Veda, to Śarva, to Śaṃkara, and to Śiva.

**7.57.56**  Homage be to the lord of speech; homage to the lord of creatures; homage to the lord of all that is; homage to the lord of the great ones.

**7.57.57**  Homage to the thousand-headed, to him whose thousand arms hold fury, to him of a thousand eyes and feet, homage to him whose deeds are beyond number.

**7.57.58**  Homage to the golden-hued, to him clad in golden armor, to him who ever shows compassion to his devotees: may our boon be granted, O Lord.

**7.57.59**  Having thus praised Mahādeva, Vāsudeva together with Arjuna then propitiated Bhava, that they might obtain the weapon.

**7.57.60**  Then Arjuna, his heart gladdened, bowed to him whose banner bears the bull; with eyes wide in wonder he beheld him, the whole treasury of all splendors.

**7.57.61**  And he saw, set before the three-eyed god, the nightly offering that was his own daily rite, presented there by Vāsudeva.

**7.57.62**  Then the Pāṇḍava, having worshipped Śarva and Kṛṣṇa in his mind, said to Śaṃkara, "I desire the divine weapon."

**7.57.63**  Then the Lord, the god, perceiving Pārtha's words spoken to seek the boon, addressed Vāsudeva and Arjuna with a smile.

**7.57.64**  "There is a divine lake of ambrosia close at hand, O slayers of foes; there long ago I placed that divine bow of mine, and the arrow.

**7.57.65**  With it I struck down in battle all the enemies of the gods. Let that supreme bow with its arrow be fetched from there, O you two Kṛṣṇas."

**7.57.66**  Saying "So be it" to Śarva, who stood among his attendants, the two heroes set out for that divine lake, ringed about by a hundred wondrous marvels.

**7.57.67**  To that holy lake which the bull-marked god had pointed out, accomplisher of every aim, the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa went, undismayed.

**7.57.68**  Then, reaching that lake which shone like the orb of the sun, Arjuna and Acyuta beheld a dreadful serpent within the waters.

**7.57.69**  And they beheld a second serpent, another excellent one with a thousand heads, vomiting forth vast flame and blazing like fire.

**7.57.70**  Then Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha touched the water and, with hands joined, approached those two serpents, doing homage to him whose banner bears the bull.

**7.57.71**  Learned in the Veda, the two reciting the immeasurable sacred hymn, the Śatarudriya, drew near and bowed to Bhava with their whole being.

**7.57.72**  Then, through the majesty of Rudra, those two mighty serpents cast off their forms, and that pair became a bow and an arrow, destroyers of foes.

**7.57.73**  Then the two great-souled ones, well pleased, took up the bow and the bright arrow, carried them back, and gave them to the great-souled god.

**7.57.74**  Then from the side of the bull-marked god there came forth a celibate ascetic, tawny-eyed, a very field of austerity, mighty, dark-red of hue.

**7.57.75**  Taking up that finest of bows, he stood in his stance with collected mind, and drew the supreme bow with its arrow according to the rule.

**7.57.76**  Marking his bowstring, his grip, and his stance, and hearing the spell spoken by Bhava, the Pāṇḍava of inconceivable valor grasped it all.

**7.57.77**  And into the lake itself the mighty lord loosed that arrow, and again the hero placed the bow back within that lake.

**7.57.78**  Then Arjuna, mindful and aware that Bhava was pleased, recalled in his heart the boon granted him in the forest and the vision of Śaṃkara, and thought, "May that come to fulfillment for me."

**7.57.79**  Knowing his intent, Bhava, well pleased, granted him the boon—that dread Pāśupata weapon, and the means to fulfill his vow.

**7.57.80**  Thrilled to the roots of his hair, the unassailable one deemed his task accomplished; and the two, full of joy, bowed their heads to Maheśvara.

**7.57.81**  Granted leave at that moment by Bhava, Arjuna and Keśava, those two heroes, reached their own camp filled with the highest joy, as glad as Indra and Viṣṇu eager to slay Jambha.

**7.58.1**  Saṃjaya said: While the two, Kṛṣṇa and Dāruka, were yet conversing, the night passed away, O king, and then the king awoke.

**7.58.2**  Hand-clapping musicians, bards of Magadha, those who bear the honeyed welcome-draught, panegyrists, and charioteer-minstrels recited and sang the praises of that bull among men.

**7.58.3**  Dancers too danced, and singers of sweet and ardent voice sang songs whose burden was the glory of the Kuru line.

**7.58.4**  Tabors, jharjharas, kettledrums, small drums and large drums and cow-horn pipes, war-drums and conch-shells and deep-voiced great drums—

**7.58.5**  all these, O Bhārata, and yet other instruments besides, were sounded with delight by skilled and well-trained players.

**7.58.6**  That great sound, roaring like a thundercloud, touched the heavens and roused the sleeping Yudhiṣṭhira, foremost of kings.

**7.58.7**  Awakened, having slept at ease upon his costly and excellent couch, he rose and went thence to the bath-house to perform his needful duties.

**7.58.8**  Then a hundred and eight young attendants for the bath, clad in white and freshly washed, drew near with golden jars filled with water.

**7.58.9**  Seated well upon an auspicious seat, wearing a light garment, he bathed in waters charged with sandal and hallowed by sacred chants.

**7.58.10**  He was rubbed with astringent paste by strong, well-trained men, and bathed with perfumed water steeped in sweet-scented herbs.

**7.58.11**  Having anointed his body with yellow sandal, the great-armed one, garlanded and clad in spotless raiment, stood facing east with hands joined in reverence.

**7.58.12**  The son of Kuntī murmured the prayer fit for muttering, following the path of the good, and then humbly entered the blazing chamber of the sacred fire.

**7.58.13**  Having worshipped the kindled fire with pure oblations hallowed by sacred formulas, he then came forth from the chamber.

**7.58.14**  Passing into the second courtyard, that tiger among men, the king, beheld there brahmans versed in the Veda, bulls among the twice-born.

**7.58.15**  Self-controlled, bathed in the vows of the Veda and in the final ablutions of sacrifice, devotees of the sun attended by thousands—eight thousand of them, and a thousand more.

**7.58.16**  Having had them pronounce blessings with whole grains and flowers, the great-armed one honored those twice-born with honey and clarified butter and with choice and auspicious fruits.

**7.58.17**  The Pāṇḍava gave to each brahman a golden coin, and a hundred caparisoned horses, garments, and the gifts they wished as sacrificial fees.

**7.58.18**  The son of Pāṇḍu likewise gave tawny milk-cows together with their bulls, their horns gilded and their hooves shod with silver, and walked round them in reverence.

**7.58.19**  Golden svastikas and vardhamānas and nandyāvarta emblems, garlands and water-jars, and the blazing fire that bears the oblations;

**7.58.20**  vessels filled with whole grains, ornaments and yellow pigment, and fair, well-adorned maidens bearing curds, ghee, honey, and water—

**7.58.21**  auspicious birds too, and whatever else is held holy—all these the son of Kuntī beheld and touched, and then passed on to the outer courtyard.

**7.58.22**  Then, as that great-armed one stood there, his attendants brought a golden throne, auspicious on every side, adorned with pearls and cat's-eye gems—

**7.58.23**  spread with priceless coverings, furnished with a canopy above, opulent and divine, fashioned by Viśvakarman—that finest of seats they brought forth.

**7.58.24**  When the great-souled one was seated there, the servants brought him costly ornaments, gleaming and bright in every part.

**7.58.25**  When the great-souled son of Kuntī was fitted with ornament and array, his form, O great king, was such as to swell the grief of his foes.

**7.58.26**  Fanned with white yak-tail whisks gleaming like moonbeams and set on golden handles, he shone like a rain-cloud lit by flashes of lightning.

**7.58.27**  Extolled by minstrels, lauded by panegyrists, and hymned by gandharvas, the joy of the Kurus sat enthroned.

**7.58.28**  Then, within a moment, there arose a great clamor of bards, the rumble of chariot-wheel rims, and the clatter of horses' hooves.

**7.58.29**  With the jangle of elephant-bells, the blare of conches, and the tread of men's feet, the very earth seemed to tremble.

**7.58.30**  Then a man, reaching the inner apartments, knelt with both knees upon the ground and bowed his head to that lord of men, worthy of homage.

**7.58.31**  A youth, earringed, his sword girded on, his armor fastened, a doorkeeper, bowing his head to the son of Dharma, announced to that great-souled one that Hṛṣīkeśa had arrived.

**7.58.32**  That tiger among men replied, "Welcome indeed to Mādhava! Let the guest-offering and a seat, held in highest honor, be given to him."

**7.58.33**  Then, having ushered in the Vārṣṇeya and seated him upon a noble seat, and having honored him and been honored by him in turn, Yudhiṣṭhira made inquiry.

**7.59.1**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: Has the night passed pleasantly for you, O slayer of Madhu? And are all your faculties serene, O Acyuta?

**7.59.2**  Saṃjaya said: Vāsudeva too made fitting inquiry of Yudhiṣṭhira in turn; then the chamberlain announced that the chief subjects had come and were waiting.

**7.59.3**  Granted leave by the king, he ushered in those people: Virāṭa and Bhīmasena, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Sātyaki,

**7.59.4**  Śikhaṇḍin and the twins, and Cekitāna and the Kekayas, and Yuyutsu of the Kuru line, and the Pāñcāla Uttamaujas.

**7.59.5**  These and many other warriors approached that great-souled bull among kṣatriyas and took their places upon the seats.

**7.59.6**  Upon a single seat sat two mighty heroes, Kṛṣṇa and Yuyudhāna, great-souled and of great splendor.

**7.59.7**  Then Yudhiṣṭhira, in the hearing of them all, addressed the lotus-eyed slayer of Madhu and spoke to him sweet words.

**7.59.8**  "Relying on you alone, as the immortals rely on the thousand-eyed Indra, we pray for victory in battle and for lasting happiness.

**7.59.9**  For you, Kṛṣṇa, know all our sufferings—the ruin of our kingdom, the humiliation at the hands of our foes, and our manifold afflictions.

**7.59.10**  In you, O lord of all, O lover of your devotees, the welfare of us all utterly depends, and our very course of action too, O slayer of Madhu.

**7.59.11**  Therefore act, O Vārṣṇeya, in accord with my trust in you, so that Arjuna's vow, which he longs to fulfill, may come true.

**7.59.12**  May you carry us across this vast ocean of sorrow and indignation; be this day our raft, O Mādhava, for we long to reach the farther shore.

**7.59.13**  For even a chariot-warrior the equal of Kārtavīrya cannot accomplish in battle, O Kṛṣṇa, what a charioteer who sets himself to the effort can accomplish."

**7.59.14**  Vāsudeva said: In all the worlds, even with their gods, there is no bowman of such a kind as Pārtha Dhanaṃjaya.

**7.59.15**  Valiant, accomplished in weapons, daring, of mighty strength, eager for battle, ever impatient of insult, in splendor the foremost of men—

**7.59.16**  that youth, bull-shouldered, long-armed, of mighty strength, with the gait of a lion and a bull, glorious—he shall slay your foes.

**7.59.17**  And I shall so contrive it that Arjuna, the son of Kuntī, shall burn up the armies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son as a blazing fire that has flared up.

**7.59.18**  This very day Arjuna shall hurl that vile-doing, base slayer of Subhadrā's son down the road from which there is no return.

**7.59.19**  Today vultures and hawks and herons and jackals, and whatever other man-eating creatures there are, shall feast upon his flesh.

**7.59.20**  Even if all the gods together with Indra were his protectors, yet this day, slain in the press of battle, he shall reach the royal city of Yama.

**7.59.21**  Having slain the lord of the Sindhus, the victorious one shall come back to you this very day. Be free of grief and free of fever, O king, and let prosperity attend you.

**7.60.1**  Saṃjaya said: As they were thus conversing, Dhanaṃjaya appeared, eager to behold the king, that best of the Bhāratas, surrounded by his band of friends.

**7.60.2**  When Arjuna had entered the fair enclosure and, having made obeisance, stood before him, that bull among the Pāṇḍavas rose up and embraced him with love.

**7.60.3**  Kissing him upon the head and folding him in his arms, and pronouncing the highest blessings, he spoke to him, smiling.

**7.60.4**  Plainly, O Arjuna, your great victory in battle is assured, for such is the radiance of your countenance, and Janārdana is well content.

**7.60.5**  Then the victorious one answered him: I have beheld a great and surpassing marvel, born of the grace of Keśava—blessings be upon you.

**7.60.6**  Then Dhanaṃjaya, to hearten his friends, related as he had witnessed it his meeting with the three-eyed god.

**7.60.7**  Then all of them, wonder-struck, touched the earth with their heads, and bowing to the god whose emblem is the bull, cried, "Well done, well done!"

**7.60.8**  Then all the friends, given leave by the son of Dharma, well girt and full of gladness, hastened forth to battle.

**7.60.9**  Having saluted the king, Yuyudhāna, Acyuta, and Arjuna went forth rejoicing from the dwelling of Yudhiṣṭhira.

**7.60.10**  On a single chariot the unassailable heroes Yuyudhāna and Janārdana went together to the encampment of Arjuna.

**7.60.11**  Having gone there, Hṛṣīkeśa, like a charioteer, made ready for the foremost of chariot-warriors that battle-car which bore the ensign of the bull-like ape.

**7.60.12**  That noble chariot, roaring like a thundercloud and gleaming with the splendor of refined gold, when made ready shone like the newborn sun.

**7.60.13**  Then that tiger among men, himself accoutred, going before, presented the equipped chariot to Pārtha, who had performed his daily rites.

**7.60.14**  And the Diademed One, the best of men in the world, clad in golden mail and bearing his bow and arrows, walked round that vehicle in reverent circuit.

**7.60.15**  Then, hymned with blessings of victory by men ripe in learning and in years, given to holy rites and masters of their senses, he mounted the great chariot.

**7.60.16**  That best of chariots had already been consecrated with martial, victory-bringing spells, and the radiant hero mounted it as the rising sun mounts the horizon.

**7.60.17**  That foremost of car-warriors, clad in gold, upon his golden chariot shone spotless and radiant, like the sun upon Mount Meru.

**7.60.18**  Yuyudhāna and Janārdana mounted up after Pārtha, as the two Aśvins follow the god Indra when he comes to the sacrifice of Śaryāti.

**7.60.19**  Then Govinda, best of those who hold the reins, took up the reins, as Mātali did for Vāsava when he set forth to slay Vṛtra.

**7.60.20**  Pārtha, mounted upon that noblest of chariots together with those two, was like the moon flanked by Mercury and Venus, dispelling the darkness.

**7.60.21**  Eager to slay the lord of the Sindhus, that destroyer of throngs of foes set forth, like Indra in the war against Tāraka, accompanied by Varuṇa, lord of waters, and by Mitra.

**7.60.22**  Then, as Arjuna went forth, bards and panegyrists praised him with the sound of instruments and with auspicious, holy hymns.

**7.60.23**  That sound of bards and minstrels, attended with blessings of victory and with proclamations of the holy day, joined to the music of instruments, became to them a thing of delight.

**7.60.24**  A pure breeze, bearing holy fragrances, blew gently after him, gladdening Pārtha and withering his foes.

**7.60.25**  Many omens appeared, foretelling victory for the Pāṇḍavas and, for your men, the contrary, O venerable one.

**7.60.26**  Seeing the favorable omens of victory, Arjuna spoke these words to Yuyudhāna, the mighty archer.

**7.60.27**  O Yuyudhāna, this day my victory in battle is plainly assured, for such are the signs that appear, O bull of Śini's line.

**7.60.28**  I shall go thither, where the king of the Sindhus, ready to depart for the realm of Yama, awaits my prowess.

**7.60.29**  As the slaying of the lord of the Sindhus is my highest task, even so is the guarding of the king of righteousness a most weighty task.

**7.60.30**  Therefore do you this day, O mighty-armed one, guard the king, so that he may be as well protected by you as he would be by me.

**7.60.31**  Trusting in you, or in Pradyumna that great car-warrior, I shall be able to slay the lord of the Sindhus free of all anxiety, O bull among men.

**7.60.32**  No concern need you have on my account in any way, O Sātvata; the king is your supreme charge, to be guarded by you with all your soul.

**7.60.33**  For where the mighty-armed Vāsudeva stands fixed, and where I am as well, there no harm can ever befall—of that be sure.

**7.60.34**  Thus addressed by Pārtha, Sātyaki, slayer of hostile heroes, said, "So be it," and went thither where King Yudhiṣṭhira was.

**7.61.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the next day came, what did they do, beset with grief and sorrow? When Abhimanyu had been slain there, which of my men gave battle?

**7.61.2**  Knowing the deeds of Savyasācin, how could my Kurus, having wrought that sin, remain unafraid? Tell me.

**7.61.3**  How did they look upon that tiger among men in battle as he came on, scorched with grief for his son and wrathful as death the ender?

**7.61.4**  Seeing in the fray the bearer of the ape-king ensign, brandishing his mighty bow and stricken with grief for his son, what did my men do?

**7.61.5**  What befell Duryodhana in the battle, O Saṃjaya? Here I hear only great lamentation, and no word of rejoicing.

**7.61.6**  Those sounds that once charmed the mind and brought delight to the ear are none of them heard this day in the encampment of the lord of the Sindhus.

**7.61.7**  In the camp of my sons no longer are heard, anywhere, the voices of the throngs of bards and panegyrists and dancers raised in praise.

**7.61.8**  Where once my ears were filled unceasingly with their sounds, today I no longer hear that sound raised up by men now sunk in misery.

**7.61.9**  In the dwelling of Somadatta of steadfast vow, O Saṃjaya, as I sat there once before, my son, I used to hear a most excellent sound.

**7.61.10**  But today, stripped of my merit, I mark the dwelling of my sons resounding with cries of anguish, its spirit broken.

**7.61.11**  From Viviṃśati, from Durmukha, from Citrasena and Vikarṇa, and from my other sons, no such sound is heard as before.

**7.61.12**  Around the son of Droṇa, the mighty archer, the refuge of my sons, brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and pupils used to gather in attendance—

**7.61.13**  he who delights day and night in disputations and discourses and conversations, in oblations, in petitions and praises, and in songs of many cherished kinds—

**7.61.14**  attended by many of the Kurus, Pāṇḍavas, and Sātvatas—O bard, in the abode of that son of Droṇa there is today no such sound as before.

**7.61.15**  The singers and dancers who used to wait in great numbers upon the son of Droṇa, that mighty archer—their voices are no longer heard.

**7.61.16**  That great clamor that of an evening was heard in the camp of Vinda and Anuvinda, and in the dwellings of the Kekayas, is not so heard today.

**7.61.17**  And that great sound of cymbals and song from the ever-merry companies as they danced—that din, my son, is not heard today.

**7.61.18**  The officiating priests who, spreading out the seven-threaded sacrifice, used to wait upon Somadatta's son, that treasury of sacred lore—their voices are not heard.

**7.61.19**  The twang of bowstrings, the chanting of the Vedas, the clatter of lances and swords and chariots that sounded ceaselessly in the abode of Droṇa—that I no longer hear.

**7.61.20**  That great sound of songs arising from many lands, and of instruments resounding, is not heard today.

**7.61.21**  From the time that Janārdana, the imperishable one, came from Upaplavya, desiring peace out of compassion for all beings—

**7.61.22**  then, O bard, I said to the foolish Duryodhana: "Through Vāsudeva as your worthy mediator, my son, make peace with the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.61.23**  I think this fitted to the hour. Do not, O Duryodhana, overstep the bounds. If you reject Keśava when he sues for peace and speaks for your good, then there can be no victory for you."

**7.61.24**  But he rebuffed that bull of the Dāśārhas, the foremost of all bowmen, as he spoke words deserving of compliance, and out of waywardness he would not yield.

**7.61.25**  Then, forsaking me, that evil-minded one, dragged on by Fate, followed the counsel of those two, Duḥśāsana and Karṇa.

**7.61.26**  For I myself did not desire the gambling; Vidura did not approve it; the lord of the Sindhus did not wish for the game; Bhīṣma did not wish for the game;

**7.61.27**  Śalya and Bhūriśravas, Purumitra and Jaya, Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and Droṇa—none of them desired the game, O Saṃjaya.

**7.61.28**  Had my boy but known the mind of these and acted upon it, he, with his kinsmen and his allies and his friends, would have lived long and free of affliction.

**7.61.29**  Gentle, sweet of speech, kindly-spoken among their kin, well-born, honored, and wise, the Pāṇḍavas shall surely attain happiness.

**7.61.30**  The man who ever has regard for righteousness gains happiness everywhere, and in the world to come attains blessedness and grace.

**7.61.31**  They, possessed of power and resource, deserve to enjoy half the earth; and theirs too is the sea-girt land, inherited from their fathers and forefathers.

**7.61.32**  If so directed, the Pāṇḍavas will keep to the path of righteousness; and we have kinsmen, my son, to whom the Pāṇḍavas will hearken—

**7.61.33**  to Śalya, to Somadatta, to the great-souled Bhīṣma, to Droṇa and Vikarṇa, to Bāhlika and Kṛpa,

**7.61.34**  and to the other aged, great-souled Bhāratas; when these speak for your good, my son, the Pāṇḍavas will heed their wholesome word.

**7.61.35**  Which of them do you suppose would counsel you otherwise than this? Kṛṣṇa would not abandon righteousness, and all those others follow your lead.

**7.61.36**  I too have spoken to those heroes a word in keeping with righteousness; they will not act otherwise, for the Pāṇḍavas are devoted to dharma.

**7.61.37**  Thus, O bard, lamenting, I spoke to my son again and again; yet the fool would not heed me. I deem it the turning of the wheel of Time.

**7.61.38**  Where Vṛkodara and Arjuna are, and Sātyaki, the Vṛṣṇi hero, and Uttamaujas the Pāñcāla, and Yudhāmanyu hard to conquer,

**7.61.39**  and the unassailable Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and the unvanquished Śikhaṇḍin, the Aśmakas and the Kekayas, and Kṣatradharman the son of the Somakas,

**7.61.40**  and the Caidya and Cekitāna, and Abhibhū the son of the king of Kāśi, the sons of Draupadī, Virāṭa and Drupada that great car-warrior, the twins, those tigers among men, and the slayer of Madhu for counselor—

**7.61.41**  who in this world that wished to live would ever do battle with these subduers of foes, who wield and let loose the celestial weapons?

**7.61.42**  Apart from Duryodhana, from Karṇa, and from Śakuni the son of Subala, with Duḥśāsana as the fourth—I can see no fifth man among them.

**7.61.43**  Those upon whose chariot Viṣvaksena stands with the reins in his hand, and who have Arjuna for their armored warrior—for them there is no defeat.

**7.61.44**  Duryodhana would not remember these laments of mine. Now you tell me that the two tigers among men, Bhīṣma and Droṇa, are slain.

**7.61.45**  Seeing this ripening of the fruit of those far-seeing words once spoken by Vidura, I think my little sons now grieve.

**7.61.46**  As at winter's end a great fire, driven by the wind, burns up the dry brushwood, so does that Dhanaṃjaya consume my army.

**7.61.47**  Tell us the whole of it, for you are skilled, Saṃjaya—what came about toward evening, the wrong done to Pārtha. When Abhimanyu was slain, my son, what then was the mood among you?

**7.61.48**  Never, my son, having done so great a wrong, will my people be able to withstand in battle the deeds of him who wields the Gāṇḍīva bow.

**7.61.49**  What did Duryodhana resolve to do? What did Karṇa, what did Duḥśāsana and the son of Subala say must be done, matters having gone thus, when all my sons were assembled together, Saṃjaya?

**7.61.50**  What came to pass in the battle, my son, through the grievous misdeeds of that dull-witted one—his mind warped by greed, his self deformed by wrath—

**7.61.51**  of that fool who craves the kingdom, whose understanding is undone by passion—whether it was ill-counseled or well-counseled, that tell me, Saṃjaya.

**7.62.1**  Saṃjaya said: Come then, I shall relate it all to you, for I saw it with my own eyes. Listen, and be steadfast—for great indeed is the misdeed that is yours.

**7.62.2**  As the building of a dam once the water has run off, such is this lament of yours—fruitless, O king. Grieve not, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.62.3**  This wondrous ordinance of Fate is not to be overstepped. Grieve not, O best of the Bhāratas—this was destined from of old.

**7.62.4**  Had you of old turned Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Kuntī, and your own sons, back from the dicing, this calamity would not have come upon you.

**7.62.5**  And again, when the time of war had come, had you even then turned back those who were inflamed, this calamity would not have come upon you.

**7.62.6**  And had you of old urged the Kurus, saying, 'Bind this unruly Duryodhana,' this calamity would not have come upon you.

**7.62.7**  This straying of your judgment the Pāṇḍavas will mark, and the Pāñcālas, and the Vṛṣṇis, and all the other great folk besides.

**7.62.8**  Had you, doing a father's duty and setting your son upon the good path, conducted yourself according to dharma, this calamity would not have come upon you.

**7.62.9**  But you, wisest of men in the world, forsaking the eternal dharma, followed the counsel of Duryodhana, of Karṇa, and of Śakuni.

**7.62.10**  All this lament of yours I have heard, O king—the lament of one who clings to his gain, like honey laced with poison.

**7.62.11**  Kṛṣṇa does not so esteem King Yudhiṣṭhira the Pāṇḍava of old, nor Bhīṣma, nor even Droṇa, as he esteems you, O king.

**7.62.12**  But from the moment he understood you to have fallen away from the king's duty, from then on Kṛṣṇa no longer holds you in such high regard.

**7.62.13**  And because you looked on indifferently while the sons of Pṛthā were addressed with harsh words, the consequence of that has overtaken you, who craved the kingdom for your sons.

**7.62.14**  The kingdom of your fathers and forefathers had then passed away from you, O blameless one; yet through the Pārthas you regained the whole earth they had conquered.

**7.62.15**  The kingdom won by Pāṇḍu, and the glory of the Kauravas—the Pāṇḍavas, walkers in dharma, made it yet greater than before.

**7.62.16**  That great work of theirs, coming to you, was rendered wholly fruitless, for by you, greedy for the spoil, they were cast out of their ancestral kingdom.

**7.62.17**  That now, in the time of war, you reproach your sons, O king, recounting their faults in many ways—this is not fitting today.

**7.62.18**  For kings who fight do not guard their lives in battle; plunging into the host of the Pārthas, those bulls among kṣatriyas do battle.

**7.62.19**  That army which Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, which Sātyaki and Vṛkodara guard—who could give battle to such a host, save the Kauravas?

**7.62.20**  They whose warrior is Guḍākeśa, whose counselor is Janārdana, whose protector is Sātyaki, whose protector is Vṛkodara—

**7.62.21**  what bowman of mortal nature could endure to fight them, save the Kauravas and those who follow in their train?

**7.62.22**  As much as can be done by devoted kings, by heroes given to the duty of the warrior caste, so much the Kauravas are doing.

**7.62.23**  Now how that most terrible battle of the Kurus, those tigers among men, was waged together with the Pāṇḍavas—hear it all in truth.

**7.63.1**  Saṃjaya said: When that night had passed into dawn, Droṇa, best of those who bear arms, set about marshaling all his own divisions into array.

**7.63.2**  From the roaring heroes, O king—wrathful, unforgiving, each seeking the other's death—were heard manifold cries.

**7.63.3**  Twanging their bows in the fray and stroking the bowstrings with their hands, breathing hard, they cried aloud, 'Where now is that Dhanaṃjaya?'

**7.63.4**  And some flung up their swords—unsheathed, fair-hilted, well-whetted, well-tempered, polished, gleaming like the sky.

**7.63.5**  Practicing the ways of the sword and the ways of the bow with skill, heroes whose minds were set on battle were seen there by the thousand.

**7.63.6**  And others, hung with bells, smeared with sandal, adorned with gold and diamond, raising up their maces, kept asking after the Pāṇḍava.

**7.63.7**  Others, drunk with the pride of strength, mighty of arm, crowded the very sky with their iron clubs, like upraised banners of Indra.

**7.63.8**  And others, bearing weapons of every kind, decked with garlands of varied hue, heroes whose minds were set on battle, took their stations here and there.

**7.63.9**  'Where is Arjuna? Where Govinda? Where the proud Vṛkodara? Where are those friends of theirs?'—so they called out then in the battle.

**7.63.10**  Then Droṇa, having blown his conch and himself urging on his horses, ranging here and there to set them in order, moved about at speed.

**7.63.11**  When all those divisions, rejoicing in battle, stood in their places, the son of Bharadvāja, O great king, then spoke to Jayadratha:

**7.63.12**  'You, and the son of Somadatta, and Karṇa the great chariot-warrior, and Aśvatthāman, and Śalya, and Vṛṣasena, and Kṛpa as well—'

**7.63.13**  'a hundred thousand horse, sixty thousand chariots, fourteen thousand rutting elephants in their must,'

**7.63.14**  'and one-and-twenty thousand mailed foot-soldiers—take your stand at a distance of three leagues from me, without coming near.'

**7.63.15**  'Standing there, not even the gods with Vāsava could prevail against you—how much less all the Pāṇḍavas. Take heart, O lord of the Sindhus.'

**7.63.16**  So addressed and reassured, Jayadratha the king of the Sindhus set forth with the Gāndhāras, surrounded by those great chariot-warriors, by mailed riders ready and resolute, lances in hand.

**7.63.17**  All crowned with yak-tail plumes and adorned with the gold of the Jambū river, the horses of Jayadratha, O lord of kings, ran true and well—seven thousand of them, and two thousand Sindhu steeds besides.

**7.63.18**  Of must-maddened elephants, mounted by skilled drivers—great beasts of terrible shape, armored, of dreadful deeds—

**7.63.19**  with fifteen hundred of these your son Durmarṣaṇa took his stand at the head of all the armies, ready to fight.

**7.63.20**  Then Duḥśāsana and Vikarṇa, those sons of yours, for the accomplishing of the Sindhu king's purpose, took their places in the foremost division.

**7.63.21**  Twelve leagues long, and in its rear half five leagues broad, that 'wheel-and-cart' array was fashioned by the son of Bharadvāja.

**7.63.22**  With sundry heroic kings stationed here and there, with floods of chariots, horse, elephants, and foot, it was disposed by Droṇa himself.

**7.63.23**  In its rear half was a lotus, an inner array hard to break through; and within the heart of the lotus a needle-formation, a hidden array, was again contrived.

**7.63.24**  Having marshaled this great array thus, Droṇa took his stand; and at the mouth of the needle the great archer Kṛtavarman was posted.

**7.63.25**  Next to him the Kāmboja and Jalasaṃdha, O sire; and immediately after them Duryodhana together with his counselors.

**7.63.26**  Then hundreds of thousands of warriors who would never turn back were all stationed in the cart-array, guarding the needle.

**7.63.27**  And behind them, O king, encompassed by a great force, Jayadratha then took his stand at the noose of the needle.

**7.63.28**  At the mouth of the cart, O lord of kings, stood the son of Bharadvāja; behind him was the Bhoja, who then guarded him himself.

**7.63.29**  In white armor, white robe, and white turban, broad-chested and mighty-armed, twanging his bow, Droṇa stood like the wrathful Ender of all.

**7.63.30**  Beholding Droṇa's chariot—pennoned, drawn by red horses, bearing for its standard an altar and a black antelope-skin—the Kurus grew glad.

**7.63.31**  A very great wonder arose among the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas as they beheld the array disposed by Droṇa, like a heaving ocean.

**7.63.32**  'This array would swallow up the whole earth, with its mountains, seas, and forests, thronged with its many peoples'—so thought the living beings.

**7.63.33**  Thronged with many chariots, men, horses, foot, and elephants, of fearful clamor and wondrous shape, rending the hearts of foes—beholding that vast cart-array thus made, the king rejoiced.

**7.64.1**  Saṃjaya said: Then, when the divisions had been marshaled and the war-cry raised, O sire, when the kettledrums were beaten and the tabors thundered,

**7.64.2**  amid the roar of the armies and the din of instruments, when the conches were sounded and the uproar was such as made the hair stand on end—

**7.64.3**  as the Bhāratas, eager for the fight, slowly advanced, and the dread hour came on, Savyasācin appeared.

**7.64.4**  Of herons and of crows, before Savyasācin, many thousands sported there, O Bhārata.

**7.64.5**  And beasts of dreadful cry, and jackals of ill-omened aspect, howled on the right hand of us as we marched forth.

**7.64.6**  Blazing meteors fell on every side with thunderous crashes, and the whole earth trembled as a dread terror arose.

**7.64.7**  Harsh winds raising thunderclaps and showering grit blew from every quarter as the son of Kuntī drew near and the battle was at hand.

**7.64.8**  Then Śatānīka the son of Nakula, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the grandson of Pṛṣata—those two prudent ones—marshaled the divisions of the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.64.9**  Then with a thousand chariots, a hundred elephants, three thousand horse, and hundreds upon hundreds of foot-soldiers,

**7.64.10**  with full fifteen hundred bows, your son Durmarṣaṇa, taking his stand at the head of all the armies, spoke thus:

**7.64.11**  'This day I will hold back the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, scorching and battle-mad, as the shore holds back the abode of the sea-monsters.'

**7.64.12**  'This day let them behold in battle the unforgiving Dhanaṃjaya, hard to assail, fastened upon me as a hammer of stone upon a stone.'

**7.64.13**  Speaking thus, O great king, that high-souled one of great mind, a mighty archer surrounded by mighty archers, took his stand, O king.

**7.64.14**  Then, like the wrathful Ender, like Vāsava bearing the thunderbolt, unbearable as Yama rod in hand—like Death itself driven on by Time—

**7.64.15**  Unshakable like the trident-bearer Śiva, like Varuṇa armed with his nooses, blazing like the fire at the end of an age about to burn up all creatures once more,

**7.64.16**  surging with the strength of wrath and indignation, the slayer of the Nivātakavacas, victory itself and the conqueror, firm in truth and resolved to carry his great vow through to its end,

**7.64.17**  his armor donned, his sword girt on, wearing a diadem of pure gold, clad in shining mail and raiment, with fair armlets and lovely earrings—

**7.64.18**  Nara, the follower of Nārāyaṇa, mounting his peerless chariot and brandishing the Gāṇḍīva in battle, shone like the risen sun.

**7.64.19**  Within bowshot of that great vanguard, the valiant Dhanaṃjaya, having drawn up his ready chariot, blew his conch.

**7.64.20**  Then Kṛṣṇa too, unflurried, together with Pārtha, O honored one, blew with all his might the Pāñcajanya, finest of conches.

**7.64.21**  At the blare of their conches, O lord of peoples, the men of your army bristled with horror, trembled, and lost their senses.

**7.64.22**  As all living things shudder at the crash of a thunderbolt, so at the blare of those conches your soldiers were seized with fear.

**7.64.23**  The beasts of burden everywhere let flow their dung and urine; thus the whole host, mounts and all, was thrown into turmoil.

**7.64.24**  The men sank down, O king, at the sound of the conch, O honored one; some fell senseless, and others, O king, were struck with terror.

**7.64.25**  Then the ape upon the banner, with the spirits that dwelt in it, raised a great roar with gaping jaws, terrifying your soldiers.

**7.64.26**  Then conches and kettledrums and tabors, together with the war-drums, were struck up once more to hearten your troops.

**7.64.27**  With the din of manifold instruments, with the tumult of shouts and the slapping of arms, with lions' roars mingled with music, the great chariot-warriors challenged one another.

**7.64.28**  Amid that wild uproar, which swelled the dread of cowards, the son of Indra, exceedingly elated, spoke to the Dāśārha:

**7.64.29**  "Drive on the horses, Hṛṣīkeśa, to where Durmarṣaṇa stands. Breaking through this elephant-host, I will plunge into the enemy's army."

**7.64.30**  Thus addressed by Savyasācin, mighty-armed Keśava urged the horses on to where Durmarṣaṇa stood.

**7.64.31**  Then there began a tumultuous and most terrible clash—between one man and many—a slaughter of chariots, elephants, and men.

**7.64.32**  Then Pārtha, with a downpour of arrows, like the rain-cloud Parjanya pouring water, drenched his foes as a cloud drenches the mountains.

**7.64.33**  And all those chariot-warriors too, swift and deft of hand, covered Kṛṣṇa and Dhanaṃjaya with nets of arrows.

**7.64.34**  Then the mighty-armed Pārtha, enraged, though held in check by his foes in the fight, struck the heads of the chariot-warriors from their bodies with his shafts.

**7.64.35**  The earth was strewn with handsome faces, their eyes rolling and their lips bitten, still wearing their earrings and helmets.

**7.64.36**  Scattered all about, the faces of the warriors gleamed like beds of white lotuses laid waste on every side.

**7.64.37**  Bright with golden ornaments and bathed in blood, they looked, O king, like masses of cloud lit by lightning.

**7.64.38**  The sound of the heads falling upon the ground, O king, was like that of ripe palmyra fruits dropping in their season.

**7.64.39**  Then here a headless trunk stood propped upon its bow, and there another stood with its sword drawn and raised aloft in its arm.

**7.64.40**  Those bulls among men did not even know their own heads had fallen to the earth—still unable to brook the son of Kuntī, still craving victory in the fight.

**7.64.41**  The earth was strewn with the heads of horses and the trunks of elephants, and with the arms and heads of heroes.

**7.64.42**  "Here is Pārtha! Where is Pārtha? This is Pārtha!"—so, O lord, among your troops it was as if the warriors saw nothing but Pārtha everywhere.

**7.64.43**  They even struck down one another, and some struck down themselves, deeming the whole world to have become Pārtha, deluded as they were by Time.

**7.64.44**  Many heroes lay there, moaning and bloodied, senseless and in sharp pain, calling out the names of their dear ones.

**7.64.45**  With slings and javelins, with lances, pikes, and battle-axes, with maces and swords, with bows and iron darts—

**7.64.46**  with arrows, armor, and ornaments, with clubs, still bearing their armlets in battle, arms like great serpents, like iron bludgeons,

**7.64.47**  writhed and twitched and curled in every direction, jerking in fury though severed by his keenest shafts.

**7.64.48**  Whatever man in the battle set himself in fury against Pārtha, upon that man's body an arrow crept like death itself.

**7.64.49**  As he danced along the chariot-tracks and bent his bow, not one there could spy in Pārtha even the smallest opening.

**7.64.50**  At the deftness with which the son of Pāṇḍu, striving hard, loosed his arrows so swiftly, the enemy host stood amazed.

**7.64.51**  Elephant and elephant-driver, horse and horseman alike, and chariot-warrior together with his charioteer—Phalguna pierced them all with his arrows.

**7.64.52**  Whoever wheeled about, whoever had turned away, whoever stood and fought, whoever stood before him in the van—there was none the Pāṇḍava did not slay.

**7.64.53**  As the rising sun in the sky dispels the great darkness, so did Arjuna destroy the elephant-host with his heron-feathered shafts.

**7.64.54**  With elephants fallen and shattered, your army looked like the earth at the end of time, strewn with mountains overthrown.

**7.64.55**  As the noonday sun is ever hard for living things to gaze upon, so was the wrathful Dhanaṃjaya hard for his foes to look upon in battle.

**7.64.56**  Thus, O scorcher of foes, was your son's army in the fight broken, routed, thrown into utter disorder, and grievously tormented by arrows.

**7.64.57**  That army, driven before him like a mass of clouds scattered by a mighty wind, could not so much as look upon him.

**7.64.58**  With goads and with the tips of their bows, with shouts and well-trained urging, with the lash and the strike of the heel, and with harsh words besides,

**7.64.59**  driving their horses on in haste, your men took to flight—riders, chariot-warriors, and foot-soldiers alike, tormented by Arjuna.

**7.64.60**  Others spurred their elephants on with heel and toe and goad, while still others, stupefied by his arrows, were borne straight toward him—your warriors then, their spirit broken and their minds awhirl.

**7.65.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When that vanguard of the army was broken and being slaughtered by the Diademed One, what heroes there in the battle went forth to meet Dhanaṃjaya?

**7.65.2**  Or had they, their resolve undone, withdrawn into the cart-array, taking refuge behind Droṇa as behind a rampart, free from any fear?

**7.65.3**  Saṃjaya said: When that host of yours had thus been shattered by Arjuna, its heroes slain, its spirit gone, watching only for the moment to flee,

**7.65.4**  as it was struck again and again by the son of Indra with his finest shafts, no one there in the fight was able even to look upon Arjuna.

**7.65.5**  Then your son Duḥśāsana, O king, seeing his army brought to such a pass, exceedingly enraged, advanced upon Arjuna to do battle.

**7.65.6**  Clad in armor wrought with gold, his helmet of pure gold, that hero of fierce prowess,

**7.65.7**  with a great host of elephants, as though devouring this very earth, Duḥśāsana, O great king, hemmed in Savyasācin.

**7.65.8**  With the clamor of the elephants' bells, with the blaring of conches, with the twang of bowstrings, and with the trumpeting of the tuskers,

**7.65.9**  the earth, the quarters, and the sky were filled with the din; and for a moment it grew dreadful and terrifying.

**7.65.10**  Seeing them rushing swiftly down, urged on by goads, their trunks swinging, furious, like winged mountains,

**7.65.11**  with a mighty lion's roar that man-lion Dhanaṃjaya scattered the elephant-host of his foes on every side with his arrows.

**7.65.12**  Into that elephant-host, heaving with great waves like a vast ocean stirred up by the wind, the Diademed One plunged like a sea-monster.

**7.65.13**  Like the sun blazing past its bounds at the dissolution of an age, Pārtha, conqueror of hostile cities, was seen in every quarter.

**7.65.14**  With the clatter of the horses' hooves and the rumble of the chariot-rims, with the uproar of shouting and the twang of the bowstring, with the blast of the Devadatta and the thunder of the Gāṇḍīva,

**7.65.15**  those elephants grew sluggish and lost their wits, pierced through by Savyasācin with shafts whose touch was that of venomous serpents.

**7.65.16**  Those elephants, struck in every limb by the sharp barbless shafts sped from the Gāṇḍīva in the fight, in their many hundreds of thousands,

**7.65.17**  raising a tremendous outcry as they were slain by the Diademed One, fell ceaselessly to the earth like mountains with their wings shorn off.

**7.65.18**  Other elephants, struck by arrows in their tusk-sockets, their frontal bosses, and their temples, cried out again and again like the krauñca bird.

**7.65.19**  And the heads of the men mounted upon the elephants' shoulders were lopped off by the Diademed One with his broad-headed, smooth-jointed shafts.

**7.65.20**  With the masses of heads, still wearing their earrings, that fell to the ground like clusters of lotuses, Pārtha made, as it were, his offering.

**7.65.21**  Lashed to their seats, stripped of armor, anguished with wounds and drenched in blood, men hung dangling upon the elephants as they wheeled about in the battle.

**7.65.22**  Some, two and three together, pierced through by a single well-loosed feathered shaft, fell to the ground.

**7.65.23**  Bowstring and bow and banner, yokes and poles alike, of the chariot-warriors he hewed to pieces with his broad-headed, smooth-jointed shafts.

**7.65.24**  Not nocking, not aiming, not loosing, not drawing out—Pārtha was seen dancing, his bow bent into one continuous circle.

**7.65.25**  And other elephants, pierced deep by his iron shafts, vomiting blood from their mouths, in a moment fell to the earth.

**7.65.26**  Countless headless trunks were seen rising up on every side, O great king, in that supreme melee.

**7.65.27**  Severed arms, still grasping bows, still in their finger-guards, still gripping swords, still wearing their armlets and adorned with golden ornaments, were seen upon the field.

**7.65.28**  With well-fitted frames and platforms, with poles, shafts, and chariot-floors, with wheels crushed and axles and yokes broken in many pieces,

**7.65.29**  with armor, bows, and arrows scattered here and there, with garlands, ornaments, and garments, and with great banners fallen down,

**7.65.30**  with elephants and horses slain and warriors struck down, the earth there appeared dreadful to behold.

**7.65.31**  Thus the army of Duḥśāsana, as it was being slaughtered by the Diademed One, fled away, O great king, sorely shaken, along with its leader.

**7.65.32**  Then Duḥśāsana, terrified, his force tormented by arrows, longing for Droṇa as his protector, made for the cart-array.

**7.66.1**  Saṃjaya said: Having struck down the host of Duḥśāsana, Savyasācin Dhanaṃjaya, eager to reach the king of the Sindhus, fell upon Droṇa's array.

**7.66.2**  Then, coming upon Droṇa stationed at the head of the formation, he folded his hands in salutation and, with Kṛṣṇa's assent, spoke these words:

**7.66.3**  Think upon me with kindness, O brāhmaṇa, and pronounce your blessing over me. By your grace I wish to penetrate this army that none can break.

**7.66.4**  You are to me as a father, and as the Dharmarāja as well, and even as Kṛṣṇa himself — this I tell you in truth.

**7.66.5**  As Aśvatthāman, dear sir, is one to be guarded by you, O sinless one, so too am I ever to be guarded by you, O best of the twice-born.

**7.66.6**  By your grace I wish to slay the king of the Sindhus in battle, O best of men; uphold my vow, O mighty one.

**7.66.7**  Thus addressed, the preceptor answered, as if smiling: "Without first conquering me, O Bībhatsu, Jayadratha cannot be conquered."

**7.66.8**  Having said only this much, Droṇa, laughing, covered him over with floods of sharp arrows — together with his chariot, horses, banner, and charioteer.

**7.66.9**  Then Arjuna, warding off Droṇa's floods of arrows with his own shafts, assailed Droṇa with arrows of dreadful form and greater might.

**7.66.10**  And in the battle, O lord of peoples, having first sought his leave and abiding by the law of the warrior, he pierced Droṇa again with nine shafts.

**7.66.11**  Cutting down his arrows with arrows of his own, Droṇa pierced them both — Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava — with shafts that blazed like poison and fire.

**7.66.12**  The Pāṇḍava sought to sever Droṇa's bow with his arrows; but while the great-souled Phalguna was still pondering thus, the valiant Droṇa, unflustered, swiftly cut the bowstring with his shafts.

**7.66.13**  And he pierced his horses, his banner, and his charioteer too, and, smiling, the hero covered Arjuna over with his shafts.

**7.66.14**  In that interval Pārtha, stringing his great bow afresh and bent on surpassing the preceptor, foremost of all who know the weapons, loosed six hundred arrows swiftly, as though he had taken but one.

**7.66.15**  Again he hurled seven hundred more, and a thousand unswerving shafts, and others by tens of thousands; and they slew that host of Droṇa's.

**7.66.16**  By those well-aimed weapons of that strong, skilled, and many-wiled fighter, men, horses, and elephants, pierced through, fell down with their lives gone.

**7.66.17**  And the chariot-warriors, their weapons and their lives cut short, fell scattered in the battle from their foremost cars, their horses with them, tormented by his arrows.

**7.66.18**  Like things pulverized, hurled down, and burnt by the thunderbolt, the wind, and the fire, the elephants fell, resembling the cloud-wreathed mansions upon mountain peaks.

**7.66.19**  Thousands of horses fell, struck down by Arjuna's arrows, like geese upon the ridge of Himavat beaten down by rain.

**7.66.20**  The floods of chariots, horses, elephants, and foot-soldiers, wondrous as floods of water, were slain by the Pāṇḍava's arrows that shone like the sun's rays at the end of an age.

**7.66.21**  That net of arrow-beams from the Pāṇḍava-sun, scorching the Kuru champions in the fight, the cloud that was Droṇa veiled over with the rush of its arrow-showers, as a cloud veils the rays of the sun.

**7.66.22**  Then with an iron shaft loosed with surpassing force, a feeder upon the lives of foes, Droṇa struck Dhanaṃjaya upon the breast.

**7.66.23**  His whole frame shaken, like a mountain in an earthquake, Bībhatsu, taking hold of his steadiness, pierced Droṇa with feathered shafts.

**7.66.24**  But Droṇa struck Vāsudeva with five arrows, and Arjuna with seventy-three, and his banner with three shafts.

**7.66.25**  And bent on outdoing his pupil, the valiant Droṇa, O king, made Arjuna invisible in the twinkling of an eye with showers of arrows.

**7.66.26**  We saw the shafts of Bhāradvāja falling in unbroken streams, and his bow, bent into a perfect circle, was a wondrous sight to behold.

**7.66.27**  They sped toward Vāsudeva and Dhanaṃjaya in the battle, O king — those very many shafts loosed by Droṇa, fledged with heron feathers.

**7.66.28**  Seeing such a combat then between Droṇa and the Pāṇḍava, Vāsudeva of great wisdom bethought himself of what must be done.

**7.66.29**  Then Vāsudeva spoke this word to Dhanaṃjaya: "Pārtha, Pārtha, O mighty-armed, let no waste of our time befall us.

**7.66.30**  Leaving Droṇa aside, let us go on; the task before us is far greater." And Pārtha too said to Kṛṣṇa, "As you wish, O Keśava."

**7.66.31**  Then the mighty-armed one, having circled Droṇa to the right, went on; and Bībhatsu, wheeling about, advanced, loosing his arrows.

**7.66.32**  Then Droṇa said, smiling: "Whither do you go, O Pāṇḍava? Surely you do not turn back without first conquering your foe in battle?"

**7.66.33**  Arjuna said: You are my teacher, not my foe; I am your pupil, like a son to you. Nor is there any man in this world who could vanquish you in battle.

**7.66.34**  Saṃjaya said: Speaking thus, Bībhatsu, eager for the slaying of Jayadratha, the mighty-armed one, in haste fell upon that host.

**7.66.35**  As he entered your forces, the two Pāñcāla guardians of his chariot-wheels, the great-souled Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, followed close behind him.

**7.66.36**  Then, O great king, Jaya and Kṛtavarman of the Sāttvatas, and the Kāmboja, and Śrutāyus, withstood Dhanaṃjaya.

**7.66.37**  In their following were ten thousand chariot-warriors — the Abhīṣāhas, the Śūrasenas, the Śibis, and the Vasātis,

**7.66.38**  the Mācellakas and the Lalitthas, the Kekayas and the Madrakas, the Nārāyaṇa cowherds, and those clans that are the Kāmbojas' —

**7.66.39**  all conquered before by Karṇa, honored as heroes in battle — placing Bhāradvāja at their head and casting away their lives, they advanced against Arjuna.

**7.66.40**  Burning with grief for his son, wrathful as death the all-ender, ready to lay down his life in the tumult, armored, a fighter of many wiles,

**7.66.41**  plunging through the ranks like the lord of an elephant herd, the great archer of surpassing valor, that tiger among men — him they withstood.

**7.66.42**  Then there arose a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end, between those warriors and Arjuna, each striving against the other.

**7.66.43**  As that bull among men came on, longing to slay Jayadratha, they together held him back, as remedies hold back a risen disease.

**7.67.1**  Saṃjaya said: Though held back by them, Pārtha of mighty strength and valor, foremost of chariot-warriors, was also pursued in haste by Droṇa.

**7.67.2**  Scattering volleys of sharp arrows, as the sun scatters its own rays, he tormented that host as a host of diseases torments the body.

**7.67.3**  Horses were pierced, banners cut down, elephants with their riders fell, parasols were struck away, and chariots were left without their wheels.

**7.67.4**  The armies, afflicted by arrows, fled in all directions; so tumultuous was the battle that nothing whatever could be made out.

**7.67.5**  As they strove against one another in the battle with straight-flying shafts, Arjuna, O king, made the banner-bearing host tremble again and again.

**7.67.6**  Seeking to make his vow come true, true to his pledges, the white-steeded one rushed upon that foremost chariot-warrior whose horses were red.

**7.67.7**  Droṇa the preceptor assailed that great archer, his own pupil, with twenty-five straight-flying shafts that pierced the vital parts.

**7.67.8**  Swiftly Bībhatsu, foremost of all bearers of weapons, charged him, hurling arrows that broke the force of his arrows.

**7.67.9**  As he swiftly cast his broad-headed shafts, the immeasurable one struck them back with broad-headed shafts of smooth joints, invoking the Brahmā weapon.

**7.67.10**  We beheld that wondrous mastery of Droṇa in the fight — that though the youthful Arjuna strove, he could not strike him back.

**7.67.11**  As a great cloud pours down its streams of water by the thousand, so the cloud that was Droṇa rained showers of arrows upon the mountain that was Pārtha.

**7.67.12**  That rain of arrows, O sire, the radiant Arjuna received with the Brahmā weapon itself, scattering arrows with arrows.

**7.67.13**  But Droṇa afflicted the white-steeded one with twenty-five swift shafts, and Vāsudeva with seventy, upon the arms and the breast.
