**7.77.33**  Beholding thus the joyful Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava, those warriors, stricken with fear, cried out, "The king is slain, the king is slain!"

**7.77.34**  But Duryodhana, hearing the clamor of the host, said: "Let your fear depart; I shall send the two Kṛṣṇas to death."

**7.77.35**  Having so spoken to all his soldiers, that lord of men, looking for victory, addressed Pārtha and in his fury uttered these words:

**7.77.36**  "O Pārtha, whatever weapon you have learned, divine or human, show it on me at once — if indeed you were begotten of Pāṇḍu.

**7.77.37**  Whatever strength and valor are yours, and Keśava's as well, exert it on me at once — let us see your manhood.

**7.77.38**  Out of our sight, men tell of deeds you are said to have done, deeds meant to win your master's favor — show those very deeds here."

**7.78.1**  Saṃjaya said: Having so spoken to Arjuna, the king pierced him in return with three arrows that pierced the vitals, and with four swift shafts struck his four horses.

**7.78.2**  And he pierced Vāsudeva with ten arrows between the breasts, and cutting his goad with a broad-headed shaft, cast it to the ground.

**7.78.3**  Him Pārtha, unflurried, swiftly pierced with fourteen stone-whetted shafts of gaily feathered shanks; but they glanced off from his armor.

**7.78.4**  Seeing them fall fruitless, he loosed again fourteen more sharp arrows; and these too glanced off from his armor.

**7.78.5**  Seeing those twenty-eight shafts that he had shot fall in vain, Kṛṣṇa, slayer of hostile heroes, spoke these words to Arjuna:

**7.78.6**  "A thing never seen before I now behold — your arrows creep away like stones. The feathered shafts you send, O Pārtha, accomplish nothing.

**7.78.7**  Is the life of the Gāṇḍīva still the same, O bull of the Bhāratas? Is your grip as of old, and the strength of your two arms?

**7.78.8**  If this be not the last hour decreed by fate, come today for you and for this foe — then tell me, who ask you.

**7.78.9**  Great is my wonder, O Pārtha, to see these arrows of yours fall vainly in battle against Duryodhana's chariot.

**7.78.10**  Your arrows, terrible as the thunderbolt and the lightning, cleavers of an enemy's body, accomplish nothing — what mockery is this today, O Pārtha?"

**7.78.11**  Arjuna said: This device, O Kṛṣṇa, was set by Droṇa upon the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; this fitting of armor is the last of the lore of weapons.

**7.78.12**  In this armor, O Kṛṣṇa, even the three worlds lie hidden and warded; Droṇa alone knows this art, and I from that best of men.

**7.78.13**  This armor cannot be pierced by arrows in any wise, O Govinda — no, not by the thunderbolt itself in the hand of Maghavat in battle.

**7.78.14**  Knowing all this, O Kṛṣṇa, why do you seek to bewilder me? Whatever has passed in the three worlds, and whatever now comes to pass, O Keśava,

**7.78.15**  and whatever shall be — all of it is known to you; nor does any other know it as you do, O slayer of Madhu.

**7.78.16**  This Duryodhana, O Kṛṣṇa, wearing this armor wrought by Droṇa, stands fearless in the battle.

**7.78.17**  But the rite that must here accompany it he does not know, O Mādhava; like a woman he wears this well-fitted armor in vain.

**7.78.18**  Behold the might of my arms and of my bow, O Janārdana; I shall overcome the Kaurava, guarded by his armor though he be.

**7.78.19**  This shining armor the Lord of the gods once gave to Aṅgiras; and again the lord of the gods gave to me that armor together with its mystic rite.

**7.78.20**  Though this armor of his be divine, or fashioned by Brahmā himself, it shall not save that fool today, smitten by my arrows.

**7.78.21**  Saṃjaya said: Having so spoken, Arjuna, charging his arrows with sacred spells, drew them back; but as he drew those shafts set at the middle of the bow, the son of Droṇa cut them apart with his weapon that destroys all weapons.

**7.78.22**  Seeing those arrows cut down from afar by that knower of the sacred word, the white-steeded warrior, amazed, made it known to Keśava:

**7.78.23**  "This weapon I cannot loose a second time, O Janārdana, for the weapon would then turn and slay me; yet behold today my strength."

**7.78.24**  Then Duryodhana, O king, pierced the two Kṛṣṇas in battle with nine smooth-jointed arrows like venomous serpents, and again rained his shafts upon Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava in the fray.

**7.78.25**  At that great rain of arrows your men rejoiced, and raised the din of instruments and roars like lions.

**7.78.26**  Then Pārtha, enraged in battle, licking the corners of his mouth, looked but could find no limb of his that was not guarded by the armor.

**7.78.27**  Then with sharp arrows, well loosed and like Death himself, he made his horses lifeless, and both his flank-charioteers as well.

**7.78.28**  The valiant one cut his gaily-wrought bow and his hand-guard, and the Ambidextrous Archer set about to splinter his chariot to pieces.

**7.78.29**  And Duryodhana, now bereft of his chariot, Arjuna then pierced in both palms of his hands with two keen arrows.

**7.78.30**  Seeing him fallen into so dire a strait, tormented by Dhanaṃjaya's shafts, the foremost bowmen rushed up, eager to rescue him.

**7.78.31**  With chariots by the many thousands, with elephants and horses arrayed, and with raging floods of foot-soldiers, they hemmed in Dhanaṃjaya.

**7.78.32**  Then neither Arjuna nor Govinda, nor even their chariot, could be seen, so enveloped were they by the great rain of weapons and the throngs of men.

**7.78.33**  Then Arjuna, by the might of his weapons, smote that host; there, maimed by the hundred, fell the chariots and the elephants.

**7.78.34**  Slain and being slain, they yet hemmed in that noblest of chariots; halted in its course, it stood there, ringed about for a krośa on every side.

**7.78.35**  Then the hero of the Vṛṣṇis swiftly said to Arjuna: "Twang your bow with all your might, and I shall blow my conch."

**7.78.36**  Then, twanging the Gāṇḍīva mightily, Arjuna smote his foes with a great rain of arrows and with the clap of his bowstring on his palm.

**7.78.37**  And Keśava blew the Pāñcajanya loud and shrill, the edges of his eyelashes clogged with dust, his face streaming heavily with sweat.

**7.78.38**  At the blast of that conch and the twang of that bow, the men, both the spiritless and the stout-hearted, fell then to the earth.

**7.78.39**  Freed of them, the chariot shone like a cloud driven on by the wind; thereupon the guardians of Jayadratha, with their followers, were thrown into turmoil.

**7.78.40**  But the guardians of the lord of the Sindhus, seeing Pārtha suddenly upon them, raised cries of many kinds, making the earth tremble.

**7.78.41**  Those great-souled warriors sent forth fierce twangings of arrows mingled with the blare of conches, and roars like lions as well.

**7.78.42**  Hearing that terrible din arisen from your men, Vāsudeva and Dhanaṃjaya then blew their conches.

**7.78.43**  By that mighty blast this earth was filled, with its mountains, its sea-girt isles, and its nether realms, O lord of peoples.

**7.78.44**  That sound, O best of the Bhāratas, spreading through all the ten directions, echoed back upon the very hosts of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.78.45**  Beholding Kṛṣṇa and Dhanaṃjaya there, your car-warriors, the great chariot-fighters, were seized with the utmost fury and hastened forward.

**7.78.46**  Then your warriors, seeing the two illustrious Kṛṣṇas clad in their armor, rushed against them in wrath, and that was a wondrous thing to behold.

**7.79.1**  Saṃjaya said: But your men, the moment they caught sight of the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas and Kurus, pressed forward eager to slay them; and even so did Vijaya, eager to slay his foes.

**7.79.2**  With their great chariots gleaming with gold and clothed in tiger-skins, resounding as they rolled, they lit up all the directions as though with blazing fires.

**7.79.3**  With their bows gold-backed and hard to gaze upon, O lord of the earth, twanging forth incomparable notes like enraged serpents,

**7.79.4**  Bhūriśravas, Śala, Karṇa, Vṛṣasena, Jayadratha, Kṛpa, the king of the Madras, and the son of Droṇa, foremost of car-warriors —

**7.79.5**  those eight great chariot-warriors, seeming as if to drink up the sky with their steeds, made the ten directions resplendent with their tiger-skin coverings adorned with golden orbs.

**7.79.6**  Armored and furious, with their chariots rumbling like masses of clouds, they covered all the directions, and Pārtha as well, with their sharp shafts.

**7.79.7**  The spirited horses of the Kulūta breed, dappled and swift, bearing those great car-warriors, shone forth then, lighting up the ten directions.

**7.79.8**  With steeds of noble lineage and great speed, sprung from many lands — mountain-bred, river-born, and of the Sindhu country, the finest of horses —

**7.79.9**  the foremost of the Kuru warriors, O king, longing to protect your son, swiftly assailed the chariot of Dhanaṃjaya from every side.

**7.79.10**  Those best of men, taking up their great conches, blew them, filling heaven, O king, and the earth with its seas.

**7.79.11**  In like manner Vāsudeva and Dhanaṃjaya, the foremost of all beings, blew their two conches, the best of all conches on earth — the son of Kuntī his Devadatta, and Keśava his Pāñcajanya.

**7.79.12**  The sound of Devadatta, sent forth by Dhanaṃjaya, filled the earth, the firmament, and all the directions.

**7.79.13**  So too the Pāñcajanya, sounded by Vāsudeva, surpassing all other sounds, filled heaven and earth.

**7.79.14**  While that terrible tumult of clamor raged on, striking terror into the timid and swelling the joy of the brave,

**7.79.15**  while kettledrums, jharjharas, tabors, and tom-toms were beaten, O lord of kings, sounding forth in countless number,

**7.79.16**  those renowned as mighty car-warriors, the well-wishers of Duryodhana, unable to brook that sound, the wrathful and supreme bowmen, kings of many lands, guardians of their own troops,

**7.79.17**  those heroes, the great chariot-warriors, in their indignation blew their great conches, resolved to answer the deed of Keśava and Arjuna.

**7.79.18**  That army of yours, stirred by the blasts of the conches, with its chariots, elephants, and horses thrown into agitation, seemed, O lord, as though disquieted.

**7.79.19**  The sky, as it were, set ringing by the heroes with the blare of conches, became greatly troubled, as though resounding with thunderclaps.

**7.79.20**  That mighty sound, O king, made all the directions resound and terrified that army, gathering like the doom of the world's end.

**7.79.21**  Then Duryodhana and those eight kings, the great car-warriors, surrounded the son of Pāṇḍu for the protection of Jayadratha.

**7.79.22**  Then the son of Droṇa struck Vāsudeva with seventy-three arrows, and Arjuna with three broad-headed shafts, his banner and his horses with five.

**7.79.23**  Arjuna, exceedingly enraged because Janārdana had been struck, smote him in turn with six hundred arrows.

**7.79.24**  Piercing Karṇa with twelve arrows and Vṛṣasena with three, the valiant one cut asunder, at the grip, the bow of Śalya together with its arrow.

**7.79.25**  Taking up another bow, Śalya pierced the son of Pāṇḍu; and Bhūriśravas struck him with three arrows, gold-feathered and whetted on stone.

**7.79.26**  Karṇa with thirty-two, Vṛṣasena with five, Jayadratha with seventy-three, Kṛpa with ten arrows, and the king of the Madras with ten — all pierced Phalguna in the battle.

**7.79.27**  Then the son of Droṇa covered Pārtha with sixty arrows, Vāsudeva with seventy, and Pārtha again with five.

**7.79.28**  But that tiger among men, of the white steeds and with Kṛṣṇa for his charioteer, laughing, pierced them all in return, displaying the swiftness of his hand.

**7.79.29**  Piercing Karṇa with twelve and Vṛṣasena with three arrows, he cut off Śalya's bow at the place of the grip in the fight.

**7.79.30**  Piercing the son of Somadatta with three arrows and Śalya with ten sharp shafts shaped like tongues of flame, he struck the son of Droṇa with eight.

**7.79.31**  He smote Gautama with twenty-five, the ruler of the Sindhus with a hundred, and the son of Droṇa again with seventy arrows.

**7.79.32**  But Bhūriśravas, greatly enraged, cut off the goad of Hari and struck Arjuna with seventy-three arrows.

**7.79.33**  Then he of the white steeds, wrathful, swiftly checked those foes with hundreds of sharp arrows, as a mighty wind scatters the clouds.

**7.80.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Of the banners of many shapes, gleaming with surpassing splendor, both of the sons of Pṛthā and of my own men — tell me of those, Saṃjaya.

**7.80.2**  Saṃjaya said: Hear of the banners of many shapes belonging to those high-souled ones; learn from me their forms, their colors, and their names.

**7.80.3**  Upon the chariots of those who rode therein, O lord of kings, divers banners were seen, blazing like fires.

**7.80.4**  Golden they were, with golden crests, adorned with golden wreaths, like the golden peaks of the great golden mountain.

**7.80.5**  Those banners of theirs, wrapped about on every side with pennants of varied and brilliant hues, shone forth, encompassed all around.

**7.80.6**  And those pennants, stirred by the wind, were seen dancing, like graceful courtesans amid the dancing-ground.

**7.80.7**  The pennants, glowing with the hues of Indra's bow, O bull of the Bhāratas, fluttering, lent beauty to those great car-warriors.

**7.80.8**  With its lion's tail and fierce mouth, the banner bearing the sign of the ape — Dhanaṃjaya's, terrible to behold — we beheld in the battle.

**7.80.9**  That foremost of apes, O king, adorned with pennants — the banner of the wielder of Gāṇḍīva — struck terror into that army.

**7.80.10**  In like manner, O Bhārata, we beheld the lion's-tail crest atop the banner of Droṇa's son, radiant as the rising sun.

**7.80.11**  Golden, tossed by the wind, splendid as the banner of Śakra, gladdening the lords of the Kurus, the emblem of Droṇa's son was raised on high.

**7.80.12**  And again, a golden elephant-girth was upon the banner of the son of Adhiratha, which in the battle, O great king, seemed to fill the very sky.

**7.80.13**  Decked with pennants and golden wreaths, the banner of Karṇa in the fight seemed to dance upon the chariot-platform, stirred by the wind.

**7.80.14**  And the preceptor of the Pāṇḍus, the illustrious Brāhmaṇa Gautama, Kṛpa, bore a bull most finely wrought.

**7.80.15**  With that bull, O king, the great car-warrior shone, even as the chariot of the destroyer of Tripura is resplendent with its bull.

**7.80.16**  Vṛṣasena's peacock, golden and set with gems and jewels, stood as if about to cry out, lending beauty even to the van of the host.

**7.80.17**  With that peacock the chariot of that high-souled one shone, O lord of kings, even as Skanda's is resplendent with its glittering peacock.

**7.80.18**  Atop the banner of Śalya, king of the Madras, we beheld a golden plough-furrow, peerless and fair, like a tongue of flame.

**7.80.19**  That furrow shone, set upon his chariot, O sire, as a furrow sprung up with every kind of seed, encompassed with splendor.

**7.80.20**  The boar of the king of the Sindhus, of silver, gleamed atop his banner, bright as the unreddened sun and wrought with a net of gold.

**7.80.21**  With that silver standard Jayadratha shone forth, even as Pūṣan of old shone in the war of the gods and the asuras.

**7.80.22**  Again, the banner of the son of Somadatta — that wise one devoted to sacrifice — bore a sacrificial post that shone like the sun, and upon it the moon could be seen.

**7.80.23**  That golden sacrificial post of the son of Somadatta was resplendent, O king, like the post raised aloft at the Rājasūya, the foremost of sacrifices.

**7.80.24**  And Śala's standard, O great king, was a great silver elephant, adorned with peacocks whose limbs were variegated with gold.

**7.80.25**  That standard lent beauty to your army, O bull of the Bhāratas, even as the great white elephant graces the host of the king of the gods.

**7.80.26**  The king's banner was an elephant fashioned of gems, sheathed in gold, ringing with a hundred little bells, shining upon his splendid and excellent chariot.

**7.80.27**  Your son shone forth exceedingly, O king, O lord of peoples, with that mighty banner in the battle — that bull among the Kurus.

**7.80.28**  These nine supreme banners, raised aloft in your host, lit up the army, resembling the suns of the world's end.

**7.80.29**  But the tenth was Arjuna's — that one mighty ape alone — by which Arjuna blazed forth like the Himālaya wrapped in fire.

**7.80.30**  Then those great car-warriors, scorchers of foes, swiftly took up their bows — variegated, bright, and very great — for the sake of opposing Arjuna.

**7.80.31**  And so too Pārtha, the destroyer of foes, of divine deeds, drew his Gāṇḍīva, O king — all owing to your evil counsel.

**7.80.32**  For through your fault many men, summoned from every quarter, were slain in the battle, together with their horses, their chariots, and their elephants.

**7.80.33**  There arose a fierce exchange of blows among them, as they roared at one another — those led by Duryodhana and that bull among the sons of Pāṇḍu.

**7.80.34**  There the son of Kuntī, with Kṛṣṇa for his charioteer, wrought a supreme marvel, in that, alone, he closed fearlessly with many.

**7.80.35**  The mighty-armed one shone as he wielded the Gāṇḍīva bow, eager to vanquish those tigers among men and to slay Jayadratha.

**7.80.36**  There Arjuna, O great king, the tormentor of foes, with arrows loosed by the thousand, made your warriors invisible.

**7.80.37**  Then those tigers among men too, all the great car-warriors, made Pārtha invisible in the battle with floods of arrows from every side.

**7.80.38**  When Arjuna, that bull among the Kurus, was thus enveloped by those lions among men, a mighty uproar arose from that army.

**7.81.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When Arjuna had reached the ruler of the Sindhus, what did the Pāñcālas, hemmed in by the son of Bharadvāja together with the Kurus, do, Saṃjaya?

**7.81.2**  Saṃjaya said: In the afternoon, O great king, amid the hair-raising combat, a gambling-match was waged between the Pāñcālas and the Kurus over Droṇa.

**7.81.3**  For the Pāñcālas, eager to slay Droṇa, with hearts elated, poured down showers of arrows, roaring, O sire.

**7.81.4**  Then a most tumultuous and wondrous battle was waged between them, between the Pāñcālas and the Kurus, terrible and like the war of the gods and the asuras.

**7.81.5**  All the Pāñcālas, together with the sons of Pāṇḍu, reaching the chariot of Droṇa and seeking to pierce that division, displayed their great weapons.

**7.81.6**  The car-warriors, mounted upon their chariots, advanced right up to the chariot of Droṇa, making it tremble, pressing on at a moderate speed.

**7.81.7**  Against him advanced Bṛhatkṣatra, the great chariot-warrior of the Kekayas, sowing whetted arrows that resembled the thunderbolt of mighty Indra.

**7.81.8**  But the illustrious Kṣemadhūrti swiftly rose to meet him, loosing whetted arrows by the hundred and by the thousand.

**7.81.9**  And Dhṛṣṭaketu, the bull of the Cedis, risen up in surpassing strength, rushed in haste upon Droṇa as great Indra upon Śambara.

**7.81.10**  As he bore down all at once, like Death with gaping jaws, the mighty archer Vīradhanvan hastened forth to confront him.

**7.81.11**  Then, O great king, the valiant Droṇa held back Yudhiṣṭhira, who stood firm with his host, eager for victory.

**7.81.12**  Your valiant son Vikarṇa, O lord, went forth against Nakula, skilled and prowess-filled in battle, as he came on.

**7.81.13**  And as Sahadeva likewise advanced, Durmukha, the harrier of foes, overwhelmed him with many thousands of swift-flying shafts.

**7.81.14**  Vyāghradatta held off Sātyaki, that tiger among men, with keen and sharpened arrows, shaking him again and again.

**7.81.15**  Saumadatti held back the sons of Draupadī, those tigers among men, foremost of chariot-warriors, who in their fury loosed their finest shafts.

**7.81.16**  And the great chariot-warrior Ārṣyaśṛṅgi, dreadful and fearsome in form, withstood the wrathful Bhīmasena as he came on.

**7.81.17**  A battle arose between the two of them on the field, that man and that rākṣasa, O king, even such as once took place between Rāma and Rāvaṇa.

**7.81.18**  Then Yudhiṣṭhira struck Droṇa with ninety smooth-jointed arrows in all his vital parts, O best of the Bhāratas, O Bhārata.

**7.81.19**  Droṇa, enraged by the illustrious son of Kuntī, struck him in turn between the breasts with twenty-five shafts, O best of the Bhāratas.

**7.81.20**  And once more Droṇa covered him over with a score of arrows, together with his horses, charioteer, and banner, before the eyes of all the bowmen.

**7.81.21**  But the righteous son of Pāṇḍu warded off those arrows loosed by Droṇa with a shower of his own, displaying the swiftness of his hand.

**7.81.22**  Then Droṇa the bowman, exceedingly wroth, suddenly cut asunder in the fray the bow of that high-souled king of righteousness.

**7.81.23**  And as his bow was severed, the great chariot-warrior in haste covered him over on every side with many thousands of arrows.

**7.81.24**  Seeing the king made invisible by the shafts of Bharadvāja's son, all beings thought Yudhiṣṭhira already slain.

**7.81.25**  Some thought him thus turned away in flight: "The king is carried off," O lord of kings, "by the illustrious brāhmaṇa."

**7.81.26**  The king of righteousness, Yudhiṣṭhira, fallen into the utmost extremity, cast aside that bow cut down by Bharadvāja's son in the fray and took up another, a celestial bow, burden-crushing and swifter still.

**7.81.27**  Then the hero cut to pieces in the battle all those arrows loosed by Droṇa by the thousand, and it was as a marvel to behold.

**7.81.28**  And having cut those shafts apart, the king, his eyes red with wrath, seized in the battle a spear that could rend even mountains, gold-shafted, most terrible, hung with eight bells, and dread to behold.

**7.81.29**  And raising it aloft in his joy, the mighty one roared with a great roar, as if terrifying all beings with that cry, O Bhārata.

**7.81.30**  Seeing the spear uplifted by the king of righteousness in the fray, all beings cried out at once, "Hail to Droṇa! May it be well with Droṇa!"

**7.81.31**  Loosed from the king's arm, like a serpent that has cast its slough, blazing across the sky and the quarters and the intermediate quarters, it drew near to Droṇa like a flaming-mouthed she-snake.

**7.81.32**  Seeing it bearing down upon him all at once, O lord of peoples, Droṇa, the best of those versed in weapons, brought forth the brāhma weapon.

**7.81.33**  That weapon reduced to ashes the spear of dreadful aspect and sped swiftly toward the chariot of the illustrious son of Pāṇḍu.

**7.81.34**  Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, exceedingly wise, quelled that uplifted weapon of Droṇa with the brahma weapon itself, O Bhārata.

**7.81.35**  And he pierced Droṇa in the fight with five smooth-jointed shafts, and with a sharp razor-headed arrow cut asunder his great bow.

**7.81.36**  Casting aside that severed bow, Droṇa, the crusher of kṣatriyas, suddenly hurled a mace at the son of Dharma, O worthy one.

**7.81.37**  Seeing that mace bearing down on him all at once, Yudhiṣṭhira, scorcher of foes, in his wrath seized a mace of his own and hurled it.

**7.81.38**  Those two maces, suddenly loosed, met each other and, striking out fire from their collision, came together upon the ground.

**7.81.39**  Then Droṇa, exceedingly enraged, O worthy one, slew the horses of the king of righteousness with four keen and sharpened, choicest shafts.

**7.81.40**  With a single arrow he cut his bow, and with one he severed his banner that rose like Indra's standard, and with three he tormented the son of Pāṇḍu.

**7.81.41**  Leaping down swiftly from his chariot with its slain horses, King Yudhiṣṭhira stood with arms upraised, weaponless, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.81.42**  Beholding him bereft of his chariot and weaponless besides, Droṇa threw the foes and all their armies into confusion, O lord.

**7.81.43**  Loosing volleys of sharp arrows, swift of hand and firm of vow, he rushed upon the king as a fierce lion upon a deer.

**7.81.44**  Seeing him thus assailed by Droṇa, the slayer of foes, a sudden cry of "Alas! Alas!" arose all at once among the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.81.45**  "The king is carried off, the king is carried off by Bharadvāja's son!" O worthy one, such was the mighty clamor that rose on every side from the army of the sons of Pāṇḍu.

**7.81.46**  Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, swiftly mounting Sahadeva's chariot, withdrew with its fleet horses.

**7.82.1**  Saṃjaya said: As Bṛhatkṣatra the Kekaya, firm in valor, came on, Kṣemadhūrti, O great king, pierced him in the breast with arrows.

**7.82.2**  But King Bṛhatkṣatra, eager in the fight to breach Droṇa's array, swiftly struck him with ninety smooth-jointed shafts.

**7.82.3**  But Kṣemadhūrti, greatly enraged, cut asunder the bow of the high-souled Kekaya with a sharp, yellow-burnished broad-headed arrow.

**7.82.4**  And as his bow was severed, he swiftly pierced in the heart with a smooth-jointed shaft that foremost of all the bowmen.

**7.82.5**  Then taking up another bow, Bṛhatkṣatra, as if with a smile, stripped the great chariot-warrior Kṣemadhūrti of his horses, charioteer, and banner.

**7.82.6**  Then with another sharp, yellow-burnished broad-headed arrow he severed from the king's body his head with its blazing earrings.

**7.82.7**  That head of his, suddenly severed, with its curling locks and its diadem, falling to the earth, shone like a star fallen from the sky.

**7.82.8**  Having slain him in battle, the great chariot-warrior Bṛhatkṣatra, exultant, fell suddenly upon your host for the sake of the sons of Pṛthā.

**7.82.9**  And as Dhṛṣṭaketu came on, the valiant mighty archer Vīradhanvan held him back for Droṇa's sake, O Bhārata.

**7.82.10**  Closing with each other, those two swift warriors, their teeth as arrows, struck one another with many thousands of shafts.

**7.82.11**  Those two tigers among men fought with each other like two leader-elephants of the herd, fierce with rut, in a great forest.

**7.82.12**  Like two enraged tigers met within a mountain cavern, those two mighty heroes fought, each seeking to slay the other.

**7.82.13**  That battle was tumultuous and worth the beholding, O lord of peoples, a marvelous and wondrous sight for the throngs of Siddhas and Cāraṇas.

**7.82.14**  Then Vīradhanvan, enraged, cut Dhṛṣṭaketu's bow in two with a broad-headed arrow, as if with a laugh, O Bhārata.

**7.82.15**  Casting aside that severed bow, the great chariot-warrior, king of the Cedis, seized a broad spear, gold-shafted and wrought of iron.

**7.82.16**  Drawing back that mighty spear with both arms, O Bhārata, he hurled it all at once, with full effort, against the chariot of Vīradhanvan.

**7.82.17**  Struck hard by that hero-slaying spear, his heart pierced through, he swiftly fell from his chariot to the earth.

**7.82.18**  When that hero, the great chariot-warrior of the Trigartas, was slain, your force was broken on every side by the Pāṇḍavas, O lord.

**7.82.19**  Then Durmukha cast sixty arrows at Sahadeva and roared a great roar, threatening the son of Pāṇḍu in the fray.

**7.82.20**  Then the son of Mādrī, enraged, pierced the oncoming Durmukha with ten arrows, brother piercing brother, as if with a laugh.

**7.82.21**  Seeing the mighty Sahadeva impetuous in battle, Durmukha smote him with nine arrows, O Bhārata.

**7.82.22**  But the mighty Sahadeva, having cut down Durmukha's banner with a broad-headed arrow, slew his four steeds with four whetted shafts.

**7.82.23**  And with another sharp, yellow-burnished broad-headed arrow he severed from the charioteer's body his head with its blazing earrings.

**7.82.24**  And with a sharp razor-headed arrow Sahadeva cut asunder in the fight the great bow of the Kaurava and pierced him with five shafts.

**7.82.25**  Then Durmukha, dejected, abandoning his chariot with its slain horses, mounted the chariot of Niramitra, O king, O Bhārata.

**7.82.26**  Then Sahadeva, the slayer of hostile heroes, in his wrath struck down Niramitra in the great battle, in the midst of the host, with a broad-headed arrow.

**7.82.27**  Niramitra, lord of men, son of the king of the Trigartas, fell from the floor of his chariot, troubling your host as he fell.

**7.82.28**  Having slain him, the mighty-armed Sahadeva shone forth as Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, when he had slain the mighty Khara.

**7.82.29**  A great cry of dismay arose among the Trigartas, O lord of men, when they saw the mighty prince Niramitra slain.

**7.82.30**  Nakula, O king, overcame your son Vikarṇa of the large eyes in battle within a moment, and it was as a marvel.

**7.82.31**  But Vyāghradatta made Sātyaki, together with his horses, charioteer, and banner, invisible amid the host with smooth-jointed arrows.

**7.82.32**  Warding off those arrows, the hero, the grandson of Śini, with the skill of a master hand, brought down Vyāghradatta with his shafts, together with his horses, charioteer, and banner.

**7.82.33**  When that prince, the son of the king of Magadha, was slain, O lord, the men of Magadha, straining on every side, rushed upon Yuyudhāna.

**7.82.34**  Hurling by the thousand arrows and lances, slings and javelins, maces and pestles as well,

**7.82.35**  those heroes did battle in the fray with the Sātvata, mad for combat; but the mighty Sātyaki, himself mad for combat, vanquished them all without great trouble, as if with a laugh, O bull among men.

**7.82.36**  Seeing the men of Magadha, those who survived the slaughter, fleeing on every side, your force, tormented by the arrows of Yuyudhāna, was broken, O lord.

**7.82.37**  Having destroyed your host in the fight, the illustrious chief of the Mādhavas shone forth, brandishing his excellent bow.

**7.82.38**  The force being broken, O king, by the high-souled Sātvata, terrified by the long-armed hero, did not turn back to the battle.

**7.82.39**  Then Droṇa, exceedingly enraged, his eyes suddenly rolling, himself rushed upon Sātyaki of the truthful deeds.

**7.83.1**  Saṃjaya said: The illustrious Saumadatti, having pierced each of the mighty-archer sons of Draupadī with five arrows, pierced them again with seven.

**7.83.2**  Sorely pressed by that fierce warrior all at once, O lord, they were so dazed that they could not tell what was to be done in the fray.

**7.83.3**  But Śatānīka, Nakula's son, that scorcher of foes, having pierced Saumadatti, that bull among men, with two arrows, roared aloud in delight.

**7.83.4**  And the others too, steadfast in the battle, swiftly pierced the wrathful Saumadatti, each with three straight-flying shafts.

**7.83.5**  Against them, O great king, that warrior of high renown hurled five arrows, striking each one of them in the heart with a single shaft.

**7.83.6**  Then the five brothers, pierced by the shafts of that great-souled one, surrounded the hero with their chariots and pierced him sorely with their arrows.

**7.83.7**  But the son of Arjuna, filled with wrath, dispatched his horses to the abode of Yama with four whetted shafts.

**7.83.8**  The son of Bhīmasena, having cut the bow of the great-souled Saumadatti, roared a mighty roar and pierced him with sharpened arrows.

**7.83.9**  The son of Yudhiṣṭhira, cutting down his banner, brought it to the ground, while Nakula's son swept the charioteer from the chariot-box.

**7.83.10**  But the high-minded son of Sahadeva, perceiving him turned aside by his brothers, severed his head, O king, with a razor-headed shaft.

**7.83.11**  That head, adorned with refined gold, fell to the earth, lighting up that quarter of the battlefield, radiant as the rising sun.

**7.83.12**  Seeing the head of the great-souled Saumadatti falling, your warriors, O king, took fright and fled in many directions.

**7.83.13**  But Alambusa, full of wrath, fought in battle with the mighty Bhīmasena, as the son of Rāvaṇa fought with Lakṣmaṇa.

**7.83.14**  Seeing those two, the man and the rākṣasa, locked together in combat, wonder and delight then arose in all beings.

**7.83.15**  Then Bhīma, laughing, O king, pierced the son of Ṛśyaśṛṅga, that wrathful lord of rākṣasas, with nine whetted shafts.

**7.83.16**  That rākṣasa, pierced in the fight, raised a terrifying roar and rushed upon Bhīma, together with those who followed in his train.

**7.83.17**  Having pierced Bhīma with five smooth-jointed arrows, that subduer of foes swiftly slew thirty chariots of Bhīma's followers, and again, after slaying four hundred, he pierced Bhīma with a feathered shaft.

**7.83.18**  Then the mighty Bhīma, deeply pierced by the rākṣasa, sank down upon the floor of his chariot, overwhelmed by a swoon.

**7.83.19**  Regaining his senses, the son of the Wind-god, beside himself with rage, drew his dreadful bow, that supreme weapon of heavy work, and tormented Alambusa on every side with keen arrows.

**7.83.20**  Pierced by many shafts, that rākṣasa, dark as a heap of black collyrium, shone all over, O king, like a kiṃśuka tree in full blossom.

**7.83.21**  As he was being struck in the fight by the arrows loosed from Bhīma's bow, he remembered the slaying of his brother by the great-souled son of Pāṇḍu.

**7.83.22**  Then, assuming a fearsome form, he addressed Bhīmasena: "Stand now in the battle, O son of Pṛthā, and behold this day my prowess."

**7.83.23**  "There was one named Baka, O fool, a mighty chief among rākṣasas; out of my sight that deed was done, when my brother was slain by you."

**7.83.24**  Having spoken thus, then, vanishing from sight, he covered Bhīma utterly with a mighty downpour of arrows.

**7.83.25**  But Bhīma in the battle, O king, when the rākṣasa had become invisible, filled the sky with his smooth-jointed shafts.

**7.83.26**  Struck by Bhīma, that vile one, in the twinkling of an eye, now mounting his chariot, now reaching the earth, and now suddenly springing into the sky.

**7.83.27**  He took on many forms, high and low, and uttered on every side voices loud and faint.

**7.83.28**  By him the elephants of the Pāṇḍava army were crushed in the fight, and many horses too, O king, and foot-soldiers as well; and the chariot-warriors, struck by his arrows, fell from their chariots.

**7.83.29**  With blood for its water, chariots for its whirlpools, thronged with elephants for its crocodiles, parasols for its swans, mire for its silt, and crowded with severed arms for its snakes—

**7.83.30**  —he set flowing a river teeming with hosts of rākṣasas, bearing along in many places, O king, the Cedis, the Pāñcālas, and the Sṛñjayas.

**7.83.31**  As he ranged thus fearlessly through the battle, O king, the Pāṇḍavas, deeply troubled, beheld his prowess.

**7.83.32**  But among your troops great delight arose, and there rose a fierce and mighty din of instruments that made the hair stand on end.

**7.83.33**  Hearing that dreadful clamor of your host, the son of Pāṇḍu could not brook it, even as an elephant cannot brook the clapping of hands.

**7.83.34**  Then, his eyes red with wrath and scorching like a blazing fire, he fitted the weapon of Tvaṣṭṛ, himself like Tvaṣṭṛ in person, O sire.

**7.83.35**  Then thousands of arrows appeared on every side, and by those arrows a great rout of your army was wrought.

**7.83.36**  That weapon, loosed by Bhīmasena in the encounter, after destroying the great magic of the rākṣasa, tormented the rākṣasa himself.

**7.83.37**  That rākṣasa, struck in many ways by Bhīmasena, abandoning Bhīma in the encounter, ran toward the division of Droṇa.

**7.83.38**  When that lord of rākṣasas had been vanquished by the great-souled one, O king, the Pāṇḍavas made all the quarters resound with their lion-roars.

**7.83.39**  And, filled with joy, they honored the mighty son of the Wind-god, as the hosts of the Maruts honored Śakra when he had vanquished Prahlāda in battle.

**7.84.1**  Saṃjaya said: As Alambusa ranged thus fearlessly through the battle, the son of Hiḍimbā advanced swiftly upon him and pierced him with sharpened arrows.

**7.84.2**  Terrible was the combat of those two lions among rākṣasas, as they wrought their manifold illusions, like that of Śakra and Śambara.

**7.84.3**  Alambusa, exceedingly wrathful, struck Ghaṭotkaca; but Ghaṭotkaca, having pierced Alambusa between the breasts with twenty iron shafts, roared again and again like a lion.

**7.84.4**  In the same way Alambusa, O king, piercing again and again the son of Hiḍimbā, that warrior maddened with battle, roared in delight, filling the sky on every side.

**7.84.5**  Thus those two mighty lords of rākṣasas, exceedingly enraged, fought each other without distinction by means of their illusions.

**7.84.6**  Sending forth a hundred illusions, proud, bewildering each other, well skilled in the warfare of illusion, they fought a battle of illusion.

**7.84.7**  Whatever illusion Ghaṭotkaca displayed in the fight, O king, that very illusion Alambusa, O monarch, destroyed by illusion in turn.

**7.84.8**  Seeing Alambusa, that lord of rākṣasas, fighting thus and skilled in the warfare of illusion, the Pāṇḍavas grew wroth.

**7.84.9**  Greatly enraged, those foremost warriors, Bhīmasena and the rest, O king, rushed upon him in their wrath from every side with their chariots.

**7.84.10**  Hemming him in with the array of their chariots, O sire, they showered him from all sides with arrows, as men beset an elephant with firebrands.

**7.84.11**  Having warded off the force of their weapons by the magic of his own weapons, he broke free from that ring of chariots like an elephant escaping a forest fire.

**7.84.12**  Twanging his dreadful bow, whose sound was like the thunderbolt of Indra, he pierced the son of the Wind-god with twenty-five shafts, the son of Bhīmasena with five, Yudhiṣṭhira with three, and Sahadeva with seven.

**7.84.13**  And having pierced Nakula with seventy-three shafts and the sons of Drupada each with five, O sire, he uttered a dreadful roar.

**7.84.14**  Bhīmasena pierced that rākṣasa in return with nine shafts, Sahadeva with five, Yudhiṣṭhira with a hundred, Nakula with sixty-four, and the sons of Draupadī each with three.

**7.84.15**  The son of Hiḍimbā, having pierced that rākṣasa in the fight with fifty arrows, pierced him again with seventy, and the mighty one roared aloud.

**7.84.16**  That mighty bowman, deeply pierced on all sides by those great chariot-warriors, pierced them all in return, each with five shafts.

**7.84.17**  That rākṣasa, the son of Hiḍimbā, O best of the Bhāratas, enraged in turn against the enraged rākṣasa in the fight, pierced him with seven arrows.

**7.84.18**  That mighty lord of rākṣasas, deeply pierced by the strong one, swiftly loosed arrows feathered with gold and whetted on stone.

**7.84.19**  Those smooth-jointed arrows then entered the rākṣasa as fierce and mighty serpents in their fury enter a mountain.

**7.84.20**  Then those Pāṇḍavas, O king, troubled, dispatched sharpened arrows from all sides, and so did Ghaṭotkaca, the son of Hiḍimbā.

**7.84.21**  As he was being struck in the battle by the Pāṇḍavas flushed with victory, he seized that rākṣasa—like the scorched peak of a mountain, like a riven heap of black collyrium—

**7.84.22**  —and lifting him up with both arms and whirling him round again and again, he swiftly dashed him upon the earth, as one dashes a full pitcher against a rock.

**7.84.23**  Endowed with strength and dexterity, and endowed with prowess as well, the son of Bhīmasena, wrathful in the fight, struck terror into all the troops.

**7.84.24**  With all his limbs shattered and the ornaments of his bones ground to powder, that rākṣasa Sālakaṭaṅkaṭa was slain by the hero Ghaṭotkaca.

**7.84.25**  Then the sons of Pṛthā, joyful at heart when that night-ranger was slain, raised lion-roars and waved their garments.

**7.84.26**  And your troops, O bull of the Bhāratas, seeing that mighty lord of rākṣasas, Alambusa of fearsome form, slain like a mountain crumbled to ruin, raised a cry of woe.

**7.84.27**  And the people beheld that rākṣasa, filled with wonder, fallen by chance to the earth like the planet Mars.

**7.84.28**  And Ghaṭotkaca, having slain that rākṣasa, foremost among the mighty, let forth a powerful roar, as Vāsava did when he had slain Bala.

**7.84.29**  Honored by his fathers and kinsmen for that hard deed accomplished, Ghaṭotkaca then, having slain his foe, rejoiced indeed, having taken Alambusa as one gathers a ripe āḍambusa fruit.

**7.84.30**  Then a great clamor arose, mingled with conch-blasts and the din of arrows of every kind; and hearing it the Kauravas roared in answer, and that sound thereupon touched the very world with its might.

**7.85.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: How did Yuyudhāna withstand the son of Bharadvāja in the battle? Tell me truly, Saṃjaya, for great is my curiosity.

**7.85.2**  Saṃjaya said: Hear, O king of great wisdom, of the hair-raising battle of Droṇa with the Pāṇḍavas, led on by Yuyudhāna.

**7.85.3**  Seeing his force being struck down by Yuyudhāna, O sire, Droṇa himself rushed upon Sātyaki of unfailing prowess.

**7.85.4**  As that great chariot-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, came swiftly on, Sātyaki met him with twenty-five small arrows.

**7.85.5**  Droṇa too, valiant in the fight and intent, swiftly pierced Yuyudhāna with five gold-feathered arrows whetted on stone.

**7.85.6**  Those shafts, feeders on the flesh of foes, having pierced his stout armor, entered the earth, O king, hissing like serpents.

**7.85.7**  The long-armed warrior, enraged like an elephant goaded by the hook, pierced Droṇa with fifty iron shafts resembling fire.

**7.85.8**  The son of Bharadvāja, swiftly pierced in the battle by Yuyudhāna, pierced in return the striving Sātyaki with many arrows.

**7.85.9**  Then that mighty bowman of great strength, enraged once more, oppressed the Sātvata with a hundred smooth-jointed shafts.

**7.85.10**  Sātyaki, being struck down in the battle by the son of Bharadvāja, could find nothing whatever that should be done, O lord of peoples.

**7.85.11**  And Yuyudhāna, O king, grew downcast of countenance, seeing the son of Bharadvāja in the battle loosing his sharpened arrows.

**7.85.12**  Beholding him thus, O lord of peoples, your sons and your soldiers, their hearts filled with joy, roared again and again like lions.

**7.85.13**  Hearing that terrible roar, and that Mādhava was being hard pressed, Yudhiṣṭhira, O king, addressed all his armies, O descendant of Bharata.

**7.85.14**  Yonder the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis, the hero Sātyaki, doer of true deeds, is being devoured in battle by a hero as the sun is devoured by Rāhu. Charge, hasten to where Sātyaki is fighting!

**7.85.15**  And the lord of men spoke thus to Dhṛṣṭadyumna of the Pāñcālas: "Charge swiftly upon Droṇa! Why do you stand idle, O son of Pṛṣata? Do you not see the terrible peril that has come upon us from Droṇa?"

**7.85.16**  That mighty bowman Droṇa toys with Yuyudhāna in the battle as a child toys with a bird bound by a string.

**7.85.17**  Let all the chariot-warriors, with Bhīmasena at their head, joined with you and resolute, go there toward Yuyudhāna's chariot.

**7.85.18**  I myself, with my troops, shall follow behind you. Deliver Sātyaki today, who has passed between the very fangs of Yama.

**7.85.19**  Having spoken thus, the king, the son of Pāṇḍu, then charged upon Droṇa in battle with all his army for Yuyudhāna's sake.

**7.85.20**  Then there arose a mighty uproar—blessings upon you!—from the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas on every side, all eager to do battle with Droṇa alone.

**7.85.21**  Those tigers among men, closing in, rained down upon the great chariot-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, sharp arrows fledged with the feathers of heron and peacock.

**7.85.22**  But Droṇa, smiling, received those heroes himself, as one receives guests arrived, with water and a seat.

**7.85.23**  They were gratified by the arrows of that bowman, the son of Bharadvāja, O king, as guests are gratified on reaching a hospitable house.

**7.85.24**  And none of them could so much as look upon the son of Bharadvāja, O lord, who was like the thousand-rayed sun arrived at midday.

**7.85.25**  And Droṇa, foremost of weapon-bearers, scorched all those mighty bowmen with showers of arrows, as the sun scorches with its rays.

**7.85.26**  Slain in the battle, O king, the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas alike found no deliverer, like elephants sunk in the mire.

**7.85.27**  And Droṇa's great arrows were seen darting forth, blazing on every side like the rays of the sun.

**7.85.28**  In that fight twenty-five Pāñcālas were slain by Droṇa, men renowned as great chariot-warriors and esteemed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

**7.85.29**  Throughout all the armies of the Pāṇḍus and of the Pāñcālas alike, they beheld the valiant Droṇa striking down their best warriors one after another.

**7.85.30**  Having slain a hundred of the Kekayas and driven them off on every side, Droṇa stood, O great king, like Death with gaping jaws.

**7.85.31**  The mighty-armed Droṇa vanquished the Pāñcālas, the Sṛñjayas, the Matsyas, the Kekayas, and the Pāṇḍavas too, by the hundreds and by the thousands.

**7.85.32**  From them, as they were slain by Droṇa's arrows, arose a clamor like that of forest-dwellers being burned in the woods by the fire.

**7.85.33**  Thereupon the gods, the Gandharvas, and the ancestors said, O king: "Yonder the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas flee with their troops."

**7.85.34**  As Droṇa thus struck down the Somakas in the fray, some would not advance against him at all, and others did not even pierce him.

**7.85.35**  As that fearful slaughter of the foremost heroes was thus proceeding, Pārtha of a sudden heard the blast of the Pāñcajanya.

**7.85.36**  Filled with breath by Vāsudeva, the king of conches sounded loud, while the heroes who guarded the Saindhava fought on, and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra roared against the chariot of the victorious one.

**7.85.37**  And as the twang of the Gāṇḍīva died away utterly on every side, the king, the son of Pāṇḍu, smitten with dismay, fell to brooding.

**7.85.38**  "Surely it is not well with Pārtha, the way the king of conches blares, and the way the Kauravas roar exultantly again and again."

**7.85.39**  Having pondered thus, with his inmost soul in turmoil, Ajātaśatru, the son of Kuntī, spoke to the Sātvata.

**7.85.40**  In a voice choked with tears, faltering again and again, looking to what must next be done, he addressed the grandson of Śini, that bull of Śini's line.

**7.85.41**  "That eternal duty which the good of old beheld, O grandson of Śini—the service a friend renders in the hour of crisis—the time for it has now come.

**7.85.42**  Reflecting upon all the warriors, O bull of Śini's line, I can recognize none a dearer friend than you, O Sātyaki.

**7.85.43**  For he who is ever loving of heart, and who is ever devoted—it is my conviction that such a one is to be appointed to a task in a time of crisis.

**7.85.44**  As Keśava is ever the refuge of the Pāṇḍavas, so too are you, O Vārṣṇeya, equal to Kṛṣṇa in prowess.

**7.85.45**  Therefore I shall lay this burden upon you; it is for you to bear it. And my wish you ought never to render vain.

**7.85.46**  So do you, O bull among men, render aid in this peril to my brother Arjuna in the battle—your friend and your teacher as well.

**7.85.47**  For you are vowed to truth, a hero, a giver of fearlessness to friends; you are renowned in the world, O hero, by your deeds as a man of true word.

**7.85.48**  For he who, fighting for a friend's sake, O grandson of Śini, lays down his body, and he who gives the whole earth to the twice-born—the two are equal.

**7.85.49**  And we have heard of many kings who went to heaven, having given this whole earth to the Brāhmaṇas according to the ordinance.

**7.85.50**  So I too beseech you, O righteous one, with joined palms: the reward shall be equal to the gift of the earth, or even greater, O mighty one.

**7.85.51**  Kṛṣṇa alone has ever been a giver of fearlessness to friends, ready to lay down his life in battle—and you, O Sātyaki, are the second such.

**7.85.52**  For a valiant hero who seeks glory in battle, only a brave man can be a fit companion—not some other, common fellow.

**7.85.53**  And in such a crushing onslaught as is now under way, O Mādhava, there is no protector of the victorious one in battle other than you.

**7.85.54**  For the son of Pāṇḍu, praising your deeds a hundredfold and kindling joy in me, recounted them again and again:

**7.85.55**  "Swift of hand with weapons, fighting in dazzling fashion, nimble in valor, wise, knowing every weapon, a hero—he is never bewildered in battle.

**7.85.56**  Broad of shoulder, broad of chest, mighty-armed, wielder of a great bow, of great strength and great might, that great-souled one is a great chariot-warrior.

**7.85.57**  My pupil and my friend as well—I am dear to him and he is dear to me. Yuyudhāna, my ally, will crush the Kauravas.

**7.85.58**  And, O lord of kings, were Keśava to arm himself for our sake, or Rāma, or Aniruddha, or Pradyumna the great chariot-warrior,

**7.85.59**  or Gada, or Sāraṇa, or Sāmba together with the Vṛṣṇis, to lend their aid, O great king, at the forefront of the great battle—

**7.85.60**  even then I would appoint to that aid the grandson of Śini, that tiger among men of true valor; for I have no other equal to him."

**7.85.61**  Thus, dear one, in the Dvaita forest, Dhanaṃjaya spoke to me, recounting your true qualities in your absence, in the assembly of the noble.

**7.85.62**  You ought not, O Vārṣṇeya, to render vain such a resolve of his—of Dhanaṃjaya, and of myself and Bhīma, both of us.

**7.85.63**  And when, journeying on pilgrimage to the holy fords, I went toward Dvārakā, there too I beheld your devotion toward Arjuna.

**7.85.64**  Such friendship as you show us, dwelling at Upaplavya, I have marked in none other, O grandson of Śini.

**7.85.65**  Therefore, for the sake of your noble birth and your devotion, for friendship's sake and the sake of your tutelage, for affection and valor and high lineage, O Mādhava,

**7.85.66**  and for the sake of truth, O mighty-armed one, and out of compassion as well—it is for you, O great bowman, to do a deed befitting all this.

**7.85.67**  For Duryodhana has swiftly gone forth, armed, with Droṇa; and the great chariot-warriors of the Kauravas had set out before him.

**7.85.68**  And a very great roar is heard against the victorious one. Therefore, O grandson of Śini, O Mādhava, it is for you to go there with all speed.

**7.85.69**  Bhīmasena and I myself, made ready with our troops, will hold off Droṇa, should he move against you.

**7.85.70**  Behold, O grandson of Śini, the armies fleeing in the battle, and the mighty din in the fray, and the host of the Bhāratas being torn asunder—

**7.85.71**  the force of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons, dear one, scattered by Savyasācin as the sea is by the rush of a great wind at the turning of the moon.

**7.85.72**  With chariots dashing about in all directions, and with men and with horses, this army, wrapped in the dust it has raised, whirls round and round.

**7.85.73**  Phalguna, the slayer of enemy heroes, is hemmed in by the men of Sindhu and Sauvīra, warriors fighting with claw-like spears and javelins, valiant and ever honored.

**7.85.74**  Without first turning back this host, Jayadratha cannot be slain; for all these have laid down their lives for the Saindhava's sake.

**7.85.75**  Behold this army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons, a forest of arrows, spears, and banners, thronged with horses and elephants, exceedingly hard to assail.

**7.85.76**  Hear the thunder of the kettledrums, and the abundant blasts of conches, and the lion-roars, and likewise the rumble of chariot-wheels.

**7.85.77**  Hear too the noise of the elephants, and of the foot-soldiers by the thousands, and hear the horsemen as they charge, making the earth tremble.

**7.85.78**  In front is the Saindhava's host, and at the rear the host of Droṇa; by its very numbers, O tiger among men, it could press hard even upon the lord of the gods.

**7.85.79**  Sunk within that boundless host, he might lay down his very life; and were he slain in that battle, how could one like me go on living? In every way, alas, my life has come to a most grievous pass.

**7.85.80**  Dark of hue, youthful, with thick locks, fair to look upon—the son of Pāṇḍu, swift of hand and dazzling in fight, has plunged, dear one, into the host of the Bhāratas.

**7.85.81**  At sunrise the mighty-armed one went forth, and now the day is wearing away; whether he lives or not, O Vārṣṇeya, I do not know. And that army of the Kurus is vast, like the very ocean.

**7.85.82**  And Bībhatsu, the mighty-armed, has plunged alone, dear one, into the host of the Bhāratas, unassailable even by the gods, in that great battle.

**7.85.83**  And today my mind cannot rest at all upon the battle; Droṇa too, fierce in the fray, presses hard upon my force—before your very eyes, O mighty-armed one, you see how that twice-born one ranges.

**7.85.84**  And you are skilled in tasks that crowd upon you all at once; it is for you, O Mādhava, to do the great thing, joined with swiftness.

**7.85.85**  Of all my purposes, this has ever been the purpose I hold supreme: that the rescue of Arjuna must be accomplished in the battle.

**7.85.86**  I do not grieve for the Dāśārha, the protector of the world, its lord; for he, dear one, is able in battle to conquer even the three worlds when they stand together.

**7.85.87**  This I tell you in truth, O tiger among men—how much the more, then, this army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, which is so very weak.

**7.85.88**  But Arjuna himself, O Vārṣṇeya, pressed hard by many in the fight, might yield up his life in the battle—and therefore I am seized with dismay.

**7.85.89**  Go you upon his track, as those like you ought to go, urged on by one like me at such a time on behalf of such a one as he.

**7.85.90**  Of the foremost heroes of the Vṛṣṇis, two only are reckoned supreme chariot-warriors in battle: the mighty-armed Pradyumna, and you, O renowned Sātvata.

**7.85.91**  In weapons you are the equal of Nārāyaṇa, in strength the equal of Saṃkarṣaṇa, and in heroism, O tiger among men, you are indeed the equal of Dhanaṃjaya.

**7.85.92**  Passing over Bhīṣma and Droṇa, the good in the world today proclaim you, O tiger among men, the most skilled in all warfare.

**7.85.93**  In this world there is nothing Sātyaki cannot achieve, O Mādhava; therefore do that which I am about to ask of you, O mighty-armed one.

**7.85.94**  The world's high regard rests upon both you and Pārtha alike; it must not be otherwise, O mighty-armed one—you must make it good here and now.

**7.85.95**  Forsaking your own dear life, range across the battlefield like a hero; for the Dāśārhas, O Śaineya, do not guard their lives in war.

**7.85.96**  To refuse to fight, to falter, to flee from the field—this is the path of cowards and base men; it is not the way the Dāśārhas walk.

**7.85.97**  Arjuna, righteous of soul, is your teacher, dear child, O bull of the Śinis, and Vāsudeva too is the teacher both of you and of the wise Pārtha.

**7.85.98**  Knowing these two grounds, I have spoken to you thus; do not scorn my word, for I am the teacher even of your teacher.

**7.85.99**  This is the will of Vāsudeva, and mine, and Arjuna's as well; what I have told you is the truth. Go now to where Dhanaṃjaya is.

**7.85.100**  Heeding this word of mine, O you of true valor, break into this army of the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, dear child.

**7.85.101**  And having entered as is fitting, and closed with the great chariot-warriors, show forth in battle the deeds worthy of yourself, O Sātvata.

**7.86.1**  Saṃjaya said: That speech—affectionate and heartfelt, sweet of syllable, timely and finely turned, and spoken with his own native grace—

**7.86.2**  having heard that speech of the King of Righteousness, Sātyaki, the bull of the Śinis, O best of the Bhāratas, answered Yudhiṣṭhira thus.

**7.86.3**  I have heard all of this speech of yours as you uttered it, O unshaken one—just and finely framed, and glorious in its purpose for Phalguna's sake.

**7.86.4**  At such a moment as this, O lord of kings, having regarded one esteemed like me, it is right that you should speak to me even as to Pārtha himself.

**7.86.5**  For Dhanaṃjaya's sake my own life is in no wise to be guarded; and once dispatched by you, what would I not do in the great battle?

**7.86.6**  At your command I would do battle with the three worlds, gods, asuras, and men together, O lord of men—how much more, then, with this feeble host?

**7.86.7**  This day I shall give battle on every side to Suyodhana's army, and I shall conquer it in the field, O king; this I tell you for truth.

**7.86.8**  Safe and well I shall reach Dhanaṃjaya, safe and well, and once Jayadratha is slain, O king, I shall return again to your side.

**7.86.9**  Yet of necessity I must make all of this known to you, O ruler of men—the word of Vāsudeva and of the wise Phalguna.

**7.86.10**  For I was firmly bound by Arjuna, again and again, in the midst of the whole army, while Vāsudeva listened.

**7.86.11**  "This day, O Mādhava, watch over the king vigilantly, holding firm to your noble resolve in the fighting, until I slay Jayadratha."

**7.86.12**  "Having entrusted the king to you, O mighty-armed one, or to the great chariot-warrior Pradyumna, I would go untroubled against Jayadratha."

**7.86.13**  "For you know Droṇa to be impetuous in battle and held the foremost of all, and you have ever heard, O Mādhava, of Droṇa's vow."

**7.86.14**  "The son of Bharadvāja longs to capture the King of Righteousness, and Droṇa is indeed able in battle to seize Yudhiṣṭhira."

**7.86.15**  "Having thus committed the King of Righteousness, that best of men, into your charge, I shall set out this day to slay the lord of the Sindhus."

**7.86.16**  "Having slain Jayadratha I shall surely return, O Mādhava—lest Droṇa should seize the King of Righteousness by force in the field."

**7.86.17**  "For if that best of men were captured by the son of Bharadvāja, O Mādhava, the slaying of the Saindhava would avail nothing, and so my joy would turn to grief."

**7.86.18**  "In such a case, O best of men—should the truth-speaking Pāṇḍava be taken—it is clear that we should have to go once more into the forest."

**7.86.19**  "And so my victory would plainly come to nothing, if Droṇa, wrathful in battle, should seize Yudhiṣṭhira."

**7.86.20**  "Therefore this day, O mighty-armed Mādhava, for my sake, and for victory, and for honor, guard the king in the battle."

**7.86.21**  You, my lord, have been laid upon me as a sacred trust by Savyasācin, who ever foresees danger to you from the son of Bharadvāja.

**7.86.22**  And he too, O mighty-armed lord, ever sees in the fray no other fit to oppose the wise son of Bharadvāja in combat, save the son of Rukmiṇī—or else myself.

**7.86.23**  And so I cannot bring myself to set aside that honor and the teacher's charge, nor to abandon you, O lord of the earth.

**7.86.24**  For the teacher, by the swiftness of his hand and clad in armor none can pierce, would, once he found you in battle, toy with you as a child toys with a bird.

**7.86.25**  If the son of Kṛṣṇa, bow in hand and bearing the sea-monster banner, were here, to him I would commit you, and he would guard you even as Arjuna would.

**7.86.26**  See to your own protection: who shall be your guardian once I am gone—one who could withstand Droṇa in battle—while I go to the Pāṇḍava?

**7.86.27**  And let there be no fear in you this day, O king, on Arjuna's account; never does that mighty-armed one falter once he has taken up his burden.

**7.86.28**  The warriors of the Sauvīras, and the men of Sindhu and of Pūru, the northerners and the southerners, and whatever other great chariot-warriors there are—

**7.86.29**  and those eminent chariot-warriors renowned with Karṇa at their head, O king—all these are not worth a sixteenth part of the wrathful Arjuna.

**7.86.30**  Though the whole earth should rise up in arms, with gods, asuras, and men, with the hosts of the rākṣasas, O king, with kiṃnaras and great serpents,

**7.86.31**  all that moves together with all that stands still—none of it is a match for Pārtha in combat. Knowing this, O great king, let your fear for Dhanaṃjaya depart.

**7.86.32**  Where the two heroes, those mighty archers, the two Kṛṣṇas of true valor, are present, there no mischance to the undertaking can ever come to be.

**7.86.33**  Call to mind your brother's destiny, his mastery of weapons, his discipline, his unrelenting wrath in war, his gratitude, and his compassion.

**7.86.34**  And when I have departed, gone forth toward Arjuna, bear in mind too, O king, Droṇa's wondrous skill with weapons in the fray.

**7.86.35**  For the teacher, O king, hungers keenly to take you captive, guarding his own vow and resolved to make it good, O Bhārata.

**7.86.36**  See this day to your own protection: who shall be your guardian once I am gone, O Pārtha—one in whom I might trust as I set out toward Phalguna?

**7.86.37**  For never, O great king, shall I go anywhere in this great battle without first entrusting you to safe keeping, O Kaurava; this I tell you for truth.

**7.86.38**  Having weighed this many times with your mind, O best of the wise, and discerned with judgment the highest good, then, O king, command me.

**7.86.39**  Yudhiṣṭhira said: It is even so, O mighty-armed Mādhava, as you say; yet my heart is not at ease concerning him of the white horses, O worthy one.

**7.86.40**  I shall make the utmost effort for my own protection; go, then, with my leave, to where Dhanaṃjaya has gone.

**7.86.41**  My own safety in battle and your going toward Arjuna—having weighed these two with reason, I judge your going there the better course.

**7.86.42**  So make ready then for the journey to where Dhanaṃjaya has gone; the mighty Bhīma will see to my protection.

**7.86.43**  The son of Pṛṣata with his brothers, and the mighty kings, and the sons of Draupadī will guard me, dear child—of that there is no doubt.

**7.86.44**  The five Kekaya brothers, and the rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca, Virāṭa and Drupada, and Śikhaṇḍin the great chariot-warrior—

**7.86.45**  and the mighty Dhṛṣṭaketu, and Kuntibhoja, O worthy one, Nakula and Sahadeva, and the Pāñcālas and the Sṛñjayas—all these, intent and ready, will guard me, dear child, without doubt.

**7.86.46**  Droṇa, together with his army, and Kṛtavarman as well, will not be able to reach me in the fray, nor shall they overpower me.

**7.86.47**  And Dhṛṣṭadyumna, scorcher of foes, will boldly hold off the wrathful Droṇa in battle, as the shore holds back the abode of sea-monsters.

**7.86.48**  Wherever in the battle the son of Pṛṣata, slayer of enemy heroes, takes his stand, there Droṇa's mighty host can in no way advance.

**7.86.49**  He sprang from the sacrificial fire for the destruction of Droṇa—armored, bearing arrows, sword, and bow, and adorned with splendid ornaments.

**7.86.50**  Go with confidence, O Śaineya; have no anxiety on my account. Dhṛṣṭadyumna, wrathful in battle, will hold Droṇa at bay.

**7.87.1**  Saṃjaya said: Having heard that speech of the King of Righteousness, the bull of the Śinis, fearing both peril from Pārtha and the charge of abandoning the king,

**7.87.2**  and guarding himself above all from the world's reproach—lest, as he went toward Phalguna, men should say of him, "He is afraid"—

**7.87.3**  having thus resolved the matter in many ways, that Sātyaki, drunk with the lust for battle, spoke this word to the King of Righteousness, O bull among men.

**7.87.4**  If you deem your protection assured, may it be well with you, O lord of peoples; I shall follow after Bībhatsu and carry out your bidding.

**7.87.5**  For in the three worlds there is none dearer to me than the Pāṇḍava, O king; this I tell you for truth.

**7.87.6**  I shall go upon his track at your command, O giver of honor; for your sake there is nothing whatsoever I would leave undone.

**7.87.7**  For just as my teacher's word stands high with me, O best of two-footed beings, so your word too stands even higher with me.

**7.87.8**  For the two brothers, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava, abide in your love; and know me too, O bull among kings, to stand within the love of those two.

**7.87.9**  Taking your command upon my head, for the Pāṇḍava's sake, O lord, I shall break through this army that none can break and go forth, O best of men.

**7.87.10**  Even now, in my wrath, I enter Droṇa's host as a great fish enters the ocean; there I shall go, where that king Jayadratha is, O king.

**7.87.11**  where, sheltered behind the army, he stands in dread of the Pāṇḍava, guarded by the foremost of great chariot-warriors—Droṇa's son, Karṇa, Kṛpa, and the rest.

**7.87.12**  I reckon that road from here to be three yojanas, O lord of peoples—to where Pārtha stands bent upon the slaying of Jayadratha.

**7.87.13**  Though he has gone three yojanas away, I shall follow his footsteps, O king, with a steadfast inner resolve, until the lord of the Sindhus is slain.

**7.87.14**  What man, unbidden by his teacher, would do battle? But once bidden by you, O king, what man like me would not fight? I know well that ground whither I shall go, O lord.

**7.87.15**  That ocean of an army—dense with shields, spears, maces, javelins, swords, bucklers, lances, and pikes, thronged with arrows and the finest weapons—I shall set churning.

**7.87.16**  That host of elephants, a thousand strong, which you behold yonder—those mighty beasts are of the lineage called Añjanaka.

**7.87.17**  Mounted by many barbarians, battle-hardened and fierce in the strike, those elephants are like clouds, O king, raining down like rain-clouds in their rut.

**7.87.18**  Never would these turn back once urged on by their riders; save by death alone, O king, there is no defeating them.

**7.87.19**  And those chariot-warriors whom you see on every side, O king—these are the princes called the Rukmarathas, great chariot-warriors all.

**7.87.20**  Skilled in chariots, in weapons, and in elephants, O lord of peoples, masters who have reached the far shore of the science of archery, and adept in fist-fighting,

**7.87.21**  expert in the special arts of mace-combat and skilled likewise in close grappling, practiced in the wielding of the sword and in the clash of blade and shield.

**7.87.22**  They are heroes, masters of their craft, and they vie with one another; ever, O king, do they long to conquer their fellow men in battle.

**7.87.23**  Subdued by Karṇa, O king, they are devoted followers of Duḥśāsana; even Vāsudeva praises these noble chariot-warriors.

**7.87.24**  Always eager to please, they stand under Karṇa's command; it was at his word, O king, that they turned back from him whose steeds are white.

**7.87.25**  Unwounded and unwearied, with sturdy armor and bows, they wait now on my account, surely by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son.

**7.87.26**  Crushing these in battle for your pleasure, O Kaurava, I shall afterward set out upon the track of Savyasācin.

**7.87.27**  And those others you behold, O king—seven hundred elephants sheathed in armor, mounted by Kirātas—

**7.87.28**  these the king of the Kirātas, taken captive by Savyasācin, gave as servants, well adorned, desiring to keep his own life.

**7.87.29**  Formerly, O king, these were your steadfast servants; today they are eager to fight against you. Behold the turning of time!

**7.87.30**  Their mahouts are these Kirātas, frenzied for battle, skilled in the lore of elephants, and all of them sprung from fire.

**7.87.31**  All these were vanquished in battle by Savyasācin; today, arrayed against me, they follow the will of Duryodhana.

**7.87.32**  Having shattered these battle-maddened Kirātas with my arrows, O king, I shall follow the Pāṇḍava, intent on the slaying of the Saindhava.

**7.87.33**  And those mighty elephants born of the line of Añjana—rugged yet well trained, their cheeks and trunks streaming with rut—

**7.87.34**  all richly adorned with armor of pure gold, unerring of aim in battle, O king, the equals of Airāvaṇa in war—

**7.87.35**  these, from the northern mountain, are ridden by fierce marauders, rugged and matchless warriors clad in coats of black iron.

**7.87.36**  Among them are some of cattle-born stock and some of monkey-born stock, and others of manifold origin, and some of human origin as well.

**7.87.37**  Smoke-colored, this host of the wicked rises up—of Mlecchas, doers of evil, dwellers in the fastnesses of Himavat.

**7.87.38**  Having gained this whole circle of elephants, Duryodhana, driven by his doom, holds in contempt Kṛpa, the son of Somadatta, Droṇa best of chariot-warriors,

**7.87.39**  the king of the Sindhus, and Karṇa too, and disdains the Pāṇḍavas, and reckons his own purpose already accomplished.

**7.87.40**  And all these, once come within range of my iron shafts, shall not escape, O son of Kuntī, even were they swift as thought.

**7.87.41**  Ever favored by him who lives upon the valor of others, they shall go to their destruction, beaten down by the floods of my arrows.

**7.87.42**  And those chariot-warriors you see, O king, with banners of gold—these are the Kāmbojas called Durvāraṇa, if you have heard of them.

**7.87.43**  Heroes, masters of their craft, accomplished in the science of the bow, tightly knit together, each seeking the welfare of the others.

**7.87.44**  Whole armies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, roused to fury, O Bhārata, stand ready on my account, guarded round by the Kuru heroes.

**7.87.45**  Vigilant, O great king, they have ranged themselves against me; yet I shall consume them as fire consumes blades of grass.

**7.87.46**  Therefore, O king, let the chariot-fitters set in proper order upon my car all the quivers and all the equipment.

**7.87.47**  In this battle indeed weapons of many kinds must be taken up; as the teachers have prescribed, the chariot must be fivefold furnished.

**7.87.48**  For I shall meet the Kāmbojas, enraged and like venomous serpents, masters of many missiles, warriors of manifold weapons.

**7.87.49**  And I shall meet the Kirātas, smiters like poison, ever cherished by the king and seeking Duryodhana's good.

**7.87.50**  And I shall meet the Śakas too, in prowess the equals of Śakra, like fire itself, unassailable, blazing as kindled flames.

**7.87.51**  And with many other warriors of every kind, like Death itself and hard to withstand, I shall close in battle, O king—with hosts of them, frenzied for war.

**7.87.52**  Therefore let my chief horses, rested and of auspicious marks, watered and given drink, be yoked again to my chariot.

**7.87.53**  For him the king had set upon the chariot all the quivers and all the equipment and weapons of many kinds.

**7.87.54**  Then the men, unyoking on every side the four fine steeds, gave them a savory draught to drink, a brew that quickened their spirit.

**7.87.55**  The four horses, watered and turned out, bathed, fed with grain, well adorned, their thorns and burrs removed, garlanded with gold,

**7.87.56**  these, ready and gleaming gold of hue, well broken, swift of foot, glad of heart and unflustered—they yoked to the chariot duly made ready,

**7.87.57**  a chariot crowned with a great lion-standard maned in gold, hung about with golden ensigns inlaid with gems and coral, and adorned with banners bright as pale clouds,

**7.87.58**  a chariot with a parasol raised on a golden staff and arrayed with many weapons—to it they yoked them duly, decked in golden trappings.

**7.87.59**  Dāruka's younger brother, his charioteer and dear friend, announced the yoked chariot, as Mātali does to Vāsava.

**7.87.60**  Then, bathed and made pure, the rites of good omen performed, Sātyaki, best of the glorious, caused golden coins to be given to a thousand graduate Brahmins, and was enfolded in their blessings.

**7.87.61**  Then, worthy of the honey-offering, having drunk the mead of Kailāvata, the red-eyed one shone there, his eyes swimming with its potency.

**7.87.62**  Touching the hero's bowl, filled with great gladness, his splendor redoubled, blazing like fire, the best of chariot-warriors took up upon his lap his bow with its arrows,

**7.87.63**  the rites of blessing done for him by the Brahmins—armored, well adorned, greeted with parched grain, fragrances, and garlands, and by maidens.

**7.87.64**  Having saluted the feet of Yudhiṣṭhira with joined palms, and kissed by him upon the head, he mounted his great chariot.

**7.87.65**  Then those Saindhava steeds, glad and well nourished, swift as the wind and unconquerable, drew that conqueror along, prancing as they went.

**7.87.66**  Then Sātyaki, his every limb flooded with joy, said to Bhīma: "Do you, Bhīma, guard the king; that is the foremost of your duties.

**7.87.67**  I shall break through and enter this host now ripened for doom; both for the time to come and for the present, the guarding of the king is the greater good."

**7.87.68**  "You know my valor, and I yours, O scourge of foes; therefore, Bhīma, turn back, if you wish me well."

**7.87.69**  So addressed, he said to Sātyaki: "Go you to the accomplishing of your task; I shall keep guard over the king, O best of men."

**7.87.70**  Thus addressed, that Mādhava replied to Bhīmasena: "Go, go swiftly, O Pārtha; sure is my victory this day.

**7.87.71**  For you, loving and devoted, stand today obedient to me, and the omens speak of good fortune to me, O Bhīma.

**7.87.72**  When the wicked Saindhava is slain by the great-souled Pāṇḍava, I shall embrace the king, that soul of righteousness—of this there is no doubt."

**7.87.73**  Having said this much to Bhīma and taken his leave of him, the great-spirited one surveyed your army as a tiger surveys the herds of deer.

**7.87.74**  Seeing him about to enter, O lord of men, your army was bewildered yet more and trembled exceedingly.

**7.87.75**  Then Sātyaki advanced at once against your host, longing to behold Arjuna, O king, at the command of the Dharma King.

**7.88.1**  Saṃjaya said: When Yuyudhāna had advanced against your army in his eagerness for battle, the Dharma King, O great king, encircled by his own troops, set forth behind Yuyudhāna, seeking to reach Droṇa's chariot.

**7.88.2**  Then the son of the Pāñcāla king, frenzied in battle, and the prince Vasudāna cried aloud within the Pāṇḍava host:

**7.88.3**  "Come on, strike, run swiftly hither and yon, so that Sātyaki, frenzied for battle, may pass through with ease.

**7.88.4**  For many great chariot-warriors will strive for his defeat." So saying, they fell with fury upon your host.

**7.88.5**  We, seeking to overcome them, rushed against them there; then a mighty din arose about Yuyudhāna's chariot.

**7.88.6**  The great army of your son, shaken by the Sātvata, O great king, was rent asunder a hundredfold.

**7.88.7**  As it was being torn apart, the grandson of Śini, that great chariot-warrior, crushed seven heroic, mighty archers in the forefront of the host.

**7.88.8**  Terrified, ground down and swept away by the long-armed one, those heroes abandoned the field of battle, seeing him more than human.

**7.88.9**  With chariots whose axles were broken and whose frames were shattered, O sire, with wheels crushed and split, and banners cast down,

**7.88.10**  with chariot-poles, pennants, golden helmets, and arms smeared with sandal and braced with armlets, O lord of the people,

**7.88.11**  and with the thighs of men, like the trunks of elephants, like the coils of serpents, was the earth strewn over, O best of men.

**7.88.12**  With the fallen faces of bull-eyed men, faces like the moon and adorned with lovely earrings, the earth shone, O Bhārata.

**7.88.13**  And with elephants hewn in many pieces, lying like mountains, the ground gleamed exceedingly, as though strewn with shattered hills.

**7.88.14**  With harness of bright gold, decked with nets of pearl, and with bright-figured breast-plates, the horses gleamed—lifeless now, fallen to the earth, swept down by the long-armed one.

**7.88.15**  Having slain your troops of many kinds, the Sātvata pierced deep into your host, and put your army to violent flight.

**7.88.16**  Then Sātyaki sought to go by that very road by which Dhanaṃjaya had passed; but he was checked by Droṇa.

**7.88.17**  Coming upon the son of Bharadvāja, Yuyudhāna, O sire, though enraged, advanced no farther—as the sea does not pass its shore.

**7.88.18**  Having stayed in battle Yuyudhāna, that great chariot-warrior, Droṇa pierced him with five sharp, vital-rending arrows.

**7.88.19**  But Sātyaki in the fight pierced Droṇa, O king, with seven shafts of golden notch, whetted on stone, fledged with heron and peacock feathers.

**7.88.20**  With six arrows Droṇa struck him, together with his horses and his driver; but Yuyudhāna, that great chariot-warrior, would not brook this from Droṇa.

**7.88.21**  Then, with a lion's roar, Sātyaki pierced Droṇa with ten arrows, and with six others, and with eight again.

**7.88.22**  Yuyudhāna pierced Droṇa once more with ten arrows, and his charioteer with one, and his four horses with four, and with a single shaft he pierced his banner in the fight, O sire.

**7.88.23**  Him, with his horses and driver, his chariot and banner, Droṇa swiftly covered with his fleet arrows, as with swarms of locusts.

**7.88.24**  And in the same way Yuyudhāna too, unflinching, covered Droṇa with many fleet arrows; then Droṇa spoke:

**7.88.25**  "Your teacher has left the battle and gone, like a coward; for he forsook me while I fought, and turned aside, keeping me on his right.

**7.88.26**  You shall not escape me with your life today while I do battle, O Mādhava—unless you too forsake me in the fight and flee in haste, as your teacher did."

**7.88.27**  Sātyaki said: At the command of the Dharma-king I am following the track of Dhanaṃjaya. Fare you well, O brāhmaṇa—let no time of mine be lost.

**7.88.28**  Saṃjaya said: Having said only this much, O king, the grandson of Śini avoided the preceptor and swiftly drove on, and he spoke thus to his charioteer:

**7.88.29**  Droṇa will make every effort to bar my way. Drive on with care in the battle, O charioteer, and hear besides this further word of mine.

**7.88.30**  There is seen the army of the Āvantyas, of great splendour; and next to it that mighty host of the southerners.

**7.88.31**  And next to that is this great force of the Bāhlīkas; and close beside the Bāhlīkas, joined with them, is also the mighty host of Karṇa.

**7.88.32**  These armies, though distinct one from another, O charioteer, lean each upon the other and will not abandon the field of battle.

**7.88.33**  Reaching the gap between them, urge on the horses gladly; holding a middling pace, carry me through there, O charioteer.

**7.88.34**  There where the Bāhlīkas are seen, raising their varied weapons, and the many southerners with the Sūta's son at their head—
