**7.88.35**  and that division which is seen thronged with elephants, horses, and chariots, and beset with foot-soldiers risen from many lands—

**7.88.36**  Having said this much to his driver, and shunning the brāhmaṇa, he passed on to where stood the fierce and exceeding mighty force of Karṇa.

**7.88.37**  Wrathful, Droṇa pursued him, scattering many shafts—Yuyudhāna the mighty-armed, who advanced and would not turn back.

**7.88.38**  Having struck Karṇa's great host with his sharp arrows, that Sātyaki entered the boundless Bhārata army.

**7.88.39**  When Yuyudhāna had entered and the soldiers had fled, the unforbearing Kṛtavarman moved to hem Sātyaki in on every side.

**7.88.40**  As he rushed upon him, the valiant Sātyaki struck him with six shafts and swiftly smote his four horses with four arrows.

**7.88.41**  Then again, with sixteen swift, smooth-jointed arrows, Sātyaki pierced Kṛtavarman in the centre of the chest.

**7.88.42**  Tormented by the Sātvata with many shafts of keen point, O great king, Kṛtavarman could not endure it.

**7.88.43**  Fitting a calf-tooth arrow, like a fire that flies aslant, and drawing it back to his ear, O king, he pierced Sātyaki in the breast.

**7.88.44**  That arrow, feathered to its butt, having cleft the armour that guarded his body and his body too, entered the earth, drenched with blood.

**7.88.45**  Then Kṛtavarman, master of the highest weapons, with many arrows cut asunder Sātyaki's bow, O king, together with its arrow and its string.

**7.88.46**  And in fury, O king, he pierced Sātyaki of true valour in the centre of the chest with ten keen shafts in that battle.

**7.88.47**  Then, his bow being shattered, Sātyaki, foremost of the mighty, struck Kṛtavarman's right arm with a spear.

**7.88.48**  Then the hero Sātyaki, taking up another very stout bow, quickly loosed his shafts by hundreds and by thousands.

**7.88.49**  That Sātyaki covered Kṛtavarman together with his chariot on every side, and screened the son of Hṛdika utterly in the battle.

**7.88.50**  Then with a broad-headed shaft he severed the head of his charioteer; slain, the driver of the son of Hṛdika fell from that great car, and, the driver being slain, the horses bolted wildly.

**7.88.51**  But the Bhoja chief, unflustered, himself reined in the horses and stood, arrows and bow in hand—and the armies honoured him for it.

**7.88.52**  Having recovered breath for a moment, he urged on his good horses; free of fear, he carried great terror into the foes. Sātyaki passed on from him, while Kṛtavarman rushed upon Bhīma.

**7.88.53**  Yuyudhāna too, O lord of kings, having issued forth from Droṇa's division, sped swiftly and at once toward the great host of the Kāmbojas.

**7.88.54**  Though there hemmed in by many heroic great car-warriors, Sātyaki of true valour did not waver then, O king.

**7.88.55**  And Droṇa, having marshalled his division and laid the burden of it upon the Bhoja, pursued Yuyudhāna in battle with intent to fight, full of care.

**7.88.56**  As he thus pursued, following at Yuyudhāna's back, the mightiest warriors in the Pāṇḍava army, greatly enraged, held him off.

**7.88.57**  But the Pāñcālas, with Bhīmasena at their head, having closed with the son of Hṛdika—foremost car among cars—lost their ardour; for though they showed their prowess, they were held back, O king, by the hero Kṛtavarman.

**7.88.58**  All of them, striving on yet somewhat bereft of their senses, their mounts grown weary, he warded off on every side with floods of arrows.

**7.88.59**  Checked by the Bhoja, those heroes who longed to break through the Bhoja division stood their ground in battle like noblemen, seeking great renown.

**7.89.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: An army so manifold, so excellently arrayed, so marshalled in due order, and so vast, O Saṃjaya—

**7.89.2**  ever honoured by us and ever well-disposed toward us, mature, of most wondrous aspect, and steadfast in valour in the van—

**7.89.3**  neither too old nor too young, neither lean nor over-stout, nimble and long of wind, sturdy of limb and free of sickness—

**7.89.4**  furnished with donned armour, equipped with manifold weapons, and perfected in the many arts of wielding arms—

**7.89.5**  skilled in mounting and in leaping down, in charging and in vaulting across, in striking truly, in advancing and in withdrawing—

**7.89.6**  tested again and again upon elephants, horses, and chariots, and, once duly tested, provided with its wages—

**7.89.7**  in my army there was none who came uninvited, none unpaid—not through mere fellowship, nor flattery, nor by reason of kinship.

**7.89.8**  manned by high-born and honourable folk, contented and well-nourished, unarrogant, shown honour and good service, glorious and high of spirit—

**7.89.9**  and guarded, my son, by other chief counsellors—many of them, doers of foremost deeds, like the guardians of the worlds, those best of men—

**7.89.10**  protected by many kings who sought to do us pleasure, who had come to us of their own desire with their forces and their followers—

**7.89.11**  full like the great ocean filled on every side by rivers, encompassed by chariots and horses that, though wingless, were like winged birds—

**7.89.12**  a fearsome sea whose inexhaustible waters were its warriors, whose surging waves were its mounts, teeming as with fishes with slings, swords, maces, lances, arrows, and javelins—

**7.89.13**  thronged with banners and ornaments, heaped with bands of jewels, and stirred to trembling, as by the speed of the wind, by its onrushing mounts—

**7.89.14**  with Droṇa for its deep abyss, Kṛtavarman for its great whirlpool, Jalasaṃdha for its mighty shark, and roused high by Karṇa as by the moon's rising—

**7.89.15**  when the bull of the Pāṇḍavas had gone, cleaving through that ocean of my host by his swiftness, O Saṃjaya, and Yuyudhāna too, with but a single chariot—

**7.89.16**  once Savyasācin had entered, and the high-souled Sātvata car-warrior, I see no remnant of my army there, O Saṃjaya.

**7.89.17**  Seeing those two impetuous and fearless warriors break clean through, and beholding the king of the Sindhus within the range of Gāṇḍīva's arrows—

**7.89.18**  what task did the Kurus then set themselves, driven on by fate? And how did they bear themselves in that dread and narrow pass of time?

**7.89.19**  For I think the Kauravas are seized, my son, gripped close by death; for their prowess in battle no longer shows itself today as it once did.

**7.89.20**  Unhurt, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava have penetrated into that battle, and there is no one here to bar them, O Saṃjaya.

**7.89.21**  And many warriors were maintained, great car-warriors taken on only after testing, with fitting pay—and others with kindly words.

**7.89.22**  In my army, my son, there is none kept on without cause; for the wages of a retainer are earned by service that befits them.

**7.89.23**  And there was not, O Saṃjaya, a single warrior in my army maintained on scant gifts, my son, nor any man hired with paltry goods.

**7.89.24**  For they were honoured to my utmost means with gifts, with respect, and with seats of rank—by me, and by my sons, my son, and by my kinsmen and their relations alike.

**7.89.25**  Yet these very men, when they met them in battle, were vanquished by Savyasācin and overwhelmed by the grandson of Śini. What is this but the work of destiny?

**7.89.26**  He who is guarded in battle, O Saṃjaya, and those who are his guardians—one common road lies before the guarded and his guards alike.

**7.89.27**  Seeing Arjuna stationed in battle before the Saindhava, what course did my son, sorely bewildered, resolve upon?

**7.89.28**  And seeing Sātyaki entering the battle fearlessly, what task fit for the hour did Duryodhana then deem to be his?

**7.89.29**  Seeing those two best of car-warriors, surpassing all in arms, enter the army, what firmness in the fight did my people muster?

**7.89.30**  Beholding Kṛṣṇa the Dāśārha set there for Arjuna's sake, and the bull of the Śinis as well, I think my poor sons are grieving.

**7.89.31**  Seeing the army broken through by the Sātvata and by Arjuna, and the Kurus in flight, I think my poor sons are grieving.

**7.89.32**  Seeing the car-warriors scattered, void of zeal to conquer the foe and bent all their zeal upon flight, I think my poor sons are grieving.

**7.89.33**  Beholding the chariot-platforms emptied by the Sātvata and by Arjuna, and the warriors slain, I think my poor sons are grieving.

**7.89.34**  Seeing heroes there by the thousand, stripped of horses, elephants, and chariots, running distraught about the field, I think my poor sons are grieving.

**7.89.35**  Seeing the horses left riderless and the men left chariotless there by Sātyaki and Pārtha, I think my poor sons are grieving.

**7.89.36**  Seeing the bands of foot-soldiers running every which way in the battle, all of them despairing of victory, I think my poor sons are grieving.

**7.89.37**  Seeing those two unconquered heroes break clean through Droṇa's division in an instant, I think my poor sons are grieving.

**7.89.38**  I am sorely bewildered, my son, to hear that Kṛṣṇa and Dhanaṃjaya, together with the Sātvata, those unfaltering ones, have entered my army.

**7.89.39**  When that foremost car-warrior of the Śinis had entered the host and broken through the Bhoja division, how then fared the Kauravas?

**7.89.40**  And when the Pāṇḍavas were held in check by Droṇa in the battle, how did the fighting go there? Tell me that, O Saṃjaya.

**7.89.41**  For Droṇa is strong, a hero, accomplished in arms, and firm in valour; how did the Pāñcālas fight against that great archer in the battle?

**7.89.42**  They had sworn a bitter feud with Droṇa and sought the Dharma-king's victory; and the great car-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, had likewise sworn enmity against them.

**7.89.43**  And whatever Arjuna did toward the slaying of the king of the Sindhus, tell me all of that, O Saṃjaya, for you are skilled in the telling.

**7.90.1**  Saṃjaya said: This calamity has arisen from your own offence, O bull of the Bhāratas; having met with it, O hero, you ought not to grieve like a common man.

**7.90.2**  Knowing your want of virtue, your partiality toward your sons, your double-mindedness in matters of duty, your spite against the Pāṇḍavas, and your many wails of distress, O best of rulers of men—

**7.90.3**  Vāsudeva, the lord who knows the truth of all the worlds, the teacher of all the worlds, thereupon brought about this great war of the Kurus.

**7.90.4**  From your own offence has this exceedingly vast destruction come upon you; for no good deed of yours is seen at the beginning, nor in the middle, nor at the end, O Bhārata—the defeat has its root in you alone.

**7.90.5**  Therefore now, holding yourself steady and grasping the world's appointed end, hear how the battle was waged—terrible, like the war of gods and demons.

**7.90.6**  When the Śaineya of true valor had entered your army, the sons of Pṛthā with Bhīmasena at their head advanced against your host.

**7.90.7**  As they came on suddenly, wrathful in aspect and with their followers, Kṛtavarman the great chariot-warrior alone held back the Pāṇḍavas in battle.

**7.90.8**  As the shore holds back the surging ocean of waters, so in the fray did the son of Hṛdika hold back the Pāṇḍava army.

**7.90.9**  There they deemed it a marvel, the prowess of the son of Hṛdika, that the sons of Pṛthā united could not overpass him in the battle.

**7.90.10**  Then Bhīma, having pierced Kṛtavarman with three iron shafts, the mighty-armed one blew his conch, gladdening all the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.90.11**  Sahadeva with twenty, the King of Righteousness with five, and Nakula too with a hundred shafts pierced the son of Hṛdika.

**7.90.12**  The sons of Draupadī with seventy-three, Ghaṭotkaca with seven, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna with three afflicted Kṛtavarman; Virāṭa and Drupada, and the son of Yājñasenī, each with five.

**7.90.13**  And Śikhaṇḍin too, having pierced the son of Hṛdika with five swift arrows, struck him again with twenty shafts, as though laughing.

**7.90.14**  Then, O King, Kṛtavarman, piercing each one of those great chariot-warriors all about with five shafts apiece, struck Bhīma with seven; and, intent, he cast his bow and his banner from the chariot down to the earth.

**7.90.15**  Then upon him whose bow was severed, the great chariot-warrior in haste and wrath struck him on the chest with seventy sharpened shafts.

**7.90.16**  Deeply wounded by the son of Hṛdika's finest shafts, the mighty one, standing in the midst of his chariot, swayed like a mountain in an earthquake.

**7.90.17**  Seeing Bhīmasena thus, those led by the King of Righteousness, loosing terrible shafts, afflicted Kṛtavarman.

**7.90.18**  Having thus penned him in with a wall of chariots, O honored one, they joyfully pierced him with shafts to protect the son of the Wind-god in the fray.

**7.90.19**  Then, having regained his senses, Bhīmasena of mighty strength seized in battle a golden-shafted iron spear and swiftly hurled it from his chariot at the chariot of Kṛtavarman.

**7.90.20**  Released from Bhīma's arm, like a serpent that has cast its slough, dreadful, it blazed up all about Kṛtavarman.

**7.90.21**  As it fell suddenly upon him, gleaming like the fire at the end of an age, the son of Hṛdika then cut it in two with a pair of shafts.

**7.90.22**  Severed, the gold-adorned spear fell to the earth, lighting up the quarters, O King, like a great meteor fallen from the sky; and seeing the spear struck down, Bhīma grew exceedingly wrathful.

**7.90.23**  Then, taking up another bow, swift and of mighty twang, Bhīmasena, wrathful in the battle, beset the son of Hṛdika.

**7.90.24**  Then Bhīma of terrible strength struck him with five arrows between the breasts, O King—and all by your ill counsel.

**7.90.25**  The Bhoja, every limb wounded by Bhīmasena, O honored one, shone upon the field of battle like a red aśoka tree in full bloom.

**7.90.26**  Then in wrath, as though laughing, he struck Bhīmasena hard with three arrows in the fight, and shot back at all of them.

**7.90.27**  The mighty archer struck those striving great chariot-warriors with three shafts each, and they in turn pierced him back with seven shafts apiece.

**7.90.28**  Then the great chariot-warrior, wrathful, with a razor-tipped shaft cut Śikhaṇḍin's bow in the battle, as though laughing, O Bhārata.

**7.90.29**  Then Śikhaṇḍin, wrathful at his bow being cut, quickly seized in the battle a sword and a gleaming hundred-mooned shield.

**7.90.30**  Whirling his great gold-adorned shield, he sent that sword flying toward the chariot of Kṛtavarman.

**7.90.31**  That great sword, having cut his bow together with the arrow upon it in the fray, fell to the earth, O King, like a star fallen from the heavens.

**7.90.32**  At that very moment the great chariot-warriors, hastening, pierced Kṛtavarman deeply with shafts in the battle.

**7.90.33**  Then, casting aside that great shattered bow and taking up another, the son of Hṛdika, slayer of enemy heroes, O best of the Bhāratas,

**7.90.34**  pierced the Pāṇḍavas in the fight with three straight-flying shafts each, and pierced Śikhaṇḍin with three and then with five.

**7.90.35**  But Śikhaṇḍin of great renown, taking up another bow, held back the son of Hṛdika with swift tortoise-nailed shafts.

**7.90.36**  Then, wrathful in the battle, O King, the son sprung from Hṛdika rushed swiftly upon the son of Yājñasenī, that great chariot-warrior,

**7.90.37**  upon him who in battle was the cause of high-souled Bhīṣma's death, O King—the hero displaying his strength like a tiger against an elephant.

**7.90.38**  Those two, like the elephants of the quarters, blazing like flames, those two tamers of foes, closed upon each other with masses of arrows.

**7.90.39**  Shaking their splendid bows, nocking their shafts, and loosing them by the hundred like two suns sending forth their rays,

**7.90.40**  scorching each other with sharp shafts, those two great chariot-warriors, those heroes like the end of an age, shone like two suns.

**7.90.41**  But Kṛtavarman, fiercely piercing the son of Yājñasenī, that great chariot-warrior, with seventy-three arrows, struck him again with seven.

**7.90.42**  Deeply wounded and distressed, he sank down upon the floor of his chariot, letting fall his bow with its arrow, overwhelmed by a swoon.

**7.90.43**  Seeing him sunk down in his chariot, your men, O bull of the Bhāratas, honored the son of Hṛdika and waved their garments aloft.

**7.90.44**  Knowing Śikhaṇḍin thus tormented by the son of Hṛdika's shafts, his charioteer in haste bore the great chariot-warrior away from the battle.

**7.90.45**  But seeing Śikhaṇḍin laid low upon the floor of his chariot, the sons of Pṛthā swiftly hemmed in Kṛtavarman with their chariots in the battle.

**7.90.46**  There Kṛtavarman the great chariot-warrior wrought a surpassing marvel, in that alone in battle he held back the sons of Pṛthā with their followers.

**7.90.47**  Having vanquished the sons of Pṛthā, Kṛtavarman the great chariot-warrior overcame the Cedis, the Pāñcālas, and the Sṛñjayas too, and the mighty Kekayas.

**7.90.48**  The Pāṇḍavas, being struck down in battle by the son of Hṛdika, running this way and that, could find no firmness in the fray.

**7.90.49**  Having vanquished the sons of Pāṇḍu in the fight, those led by Bhīmasena, the son of Hṛdika stood in the battle like a smokeless fire.

**7.90.50**  Those great chariot-warriors, driven off in the battle by the son of Hṛdika and afflicted by his showers of arrows, were turned to flight.

**7.91.1**  Saṃjaya said: Hear with single mind, O King, that which you ask of me, when that host was being driven off by the high-souled son of Hṛdika.

**7.91.2**  And while your men rejoiced and the Pāṇḍavas were bowed down with shame, he who had been an island to them as they sought a foothold in fathomless depths—

**7.91.3**  hearing the terrible roar of your men in the great battle, the Śaineya in haste, O King, advanced upon Kṛtavarman.

**7.91.4**  But Kṛtavarman, son of Hṛdika, in great wrath covered the Śaineya with sharpened shafts; thereat Sātyaki grew wrathful.

**7.91.5**  Then the Śaineya sent a well-sharpened broad-headed shaft at Kṛtavarman in the battle, and four other arrows besides.

**7.91.6**  They slew his horses; with a broad-headed shaft he severed his bow, and he pierced the rear-guard and the charioteer too with sharpened shafts.

**7.91.7**  Then, having made him chariotless, Sātyaki of true valor afflicted his army with smooth-jointed shafts.

**7.91.8**  Then that host, tormented by the Śaineya's shafts, broke apart; and Sātyaki of true valor pressed swiftly onward.

**7.91.9**  Hear, O King, what that valiant one did among your troops, when, O great King, he had passed beyond the great ocean that was Droṇa's host.

**7.91.10**  And the hero, gladdened at having vanquished Kṛtavarman in the battle, said calmly and without flurry to his charioteer, "Go on slowly."

**7.91.11**  But beholding that army of yours, thronged with chariots, horses, and elephants and filled with foot-soldiers, he spoke again to his charioteer:

**7.91.12**  "That vast elephant-division, dark like a cloud, to the left of Droṇa's host, whose front is the warrior of the golden chariot—

**7.91.13**  these many, O charioteer, are hard to ward off in battle—commanded by Duryodhana, having given up their lives for my sake, princes and mighty archers, all of them warriors of daring valor.

**7.91.14**  The noble chariot-warriors of the Trigartas, with banners wrought of gold, those heroes stand drawn up facing me alone, ready to fight.

**7.91.15**  Bring me there quickly; urge on the horses, O charioteer—I shall fight with the Trigartas before the very eyes of the son of Bharadvāja."

**7.91.16**  Then the charioteer, abiding by the Sātvata's wish, advanced slowly with the chariot sun-hued, gleaming, and bannered.

**7.91.17**  Obedient to the charioteer, prancing, the excellent horses bore him, swift as the wind in battle, gleaming like jasmine, the moon, and silver.

**7.91.18**  As that chariot rushed on with its conch-hued excellent horses, the heroes then hemmed it in on every side with an elephant-division, scattering various sharp, swift-piercing shafts.

**7.91.19**  The Sātvata too with whetted arrows assailed the elephant-division, as a great cloud assails the mountains with rain at the end of the hot season.

**7.91.20**  Struck by arrows whose touch was like the thunderbolt and lightning, sped by the strength of Śini's line, the elephants fled, abandoning the battle.

**7.91.21**  Their tusks broken, bleeding, the bony swellings of their heads burst open, ears, mouths, and trunks torn, bereft of drivers and banners,

**7.91.22**  their armor and bells shattered, their great standards cut down, their riders slain and their housings fallen, they fled, O King, in all directions.

**7.91.23**  Bellowing manifold cries, with a din like that of clouds, they were torn open by the Sātvata with iron shafts and calf-tooth arrows.

**7.91.24**  When that elephant-division was put to flight, Jalasaṃdha the great chariot-warrior, intent, brought his elephant toward the silver-horsed chariot.

**7.91.25**  The hero, gold-hued of hand, with armlets of refined gold, pure, wearing earrings, a crown, and a conch-armlet, smeared with red sandal,

**7.91.26**  bearing on his head a blazing garland wrought of refined gold, bearing on his breast a golden ornament and a gleaming neck-chain,

**7.91.27**  and brandishing a bow wrought with gold upon the elephant's head, shone, O great King, like a rain-cloud charged with lightning.

**7.91.28**  As the Magadha king's noble elephant rushed suddenly on, Sātyaki held it back as the shore holds the surging sea.

**7.91.29**  Seeing his elephant held back by the Śaineya's finest shafts, Jalasaṃdha of mighty strength grew wrathful in the battle, O King.

**7.91.30**  Then the wrathful mighty archer Jalasaṃdha pierced the grandson of Śini upon the broad chest with shafts that bear a heavy work.

**7.91.31**  Then with another broad-headed shaft, yellow and sharpened, he cut asunder the bow of the Vṛṣṇi hero as he was shooting.

**7.91.32**  At Sātyaki, whose bow was severed, as though laughing, O Bhārata, the Magadha hero shot, striking him with five sharpened shafts.

**7.91.33**  Though pierced by many arrows from Jalasaṃdha, the valiant, mighty-armed one did not waver—and that was as it were a marvel.

**7.91.34**  Heeding the arrows not at all, the mighty one, without much flurry, took up another bow and said, "Stand, stand!"

**7.91.35**  Having spoken thus, the grandson of Śini pierced Jalasaṃdha full in his broad chest with sixty arrows, driving them home with force, as though laughing the while.

**7.91.36**  And with a yellow razor-edged shaft he cut through Jalasaṃdha's great bow at the grip, and struck him with three more arrows.

**7.91.37**  But Jalasaṃdha, casting aside that bow with its arrow, swiftly hurled a lance at Sātyaki, O honoured one.

**7.91.38**  Having pierced through the left arm of the Mādhava in that great battle, the dreadful weapon plunged into the earth, hissing like a mighty serpent.

**7.91.39**  Though his left arm was pierced through, Sātyaki of true valour smote Jalasaṃdha with thirty sharp shafts.

**7.91.40**  Then mighty Jalasaṃdha, seizing a sword and a great bull's-hide shield adorned with a hundred moons, and whirling that sword, flung it at the Sātvata.

**7.91.41**  That sword, having cut through the bow of the grandson of Śini, fell to the earth, and lying upon the ground it gleamed like a whirling circle of firebrand.

**7.91.42**  Then, taking up another bow that could tear through any body, like the trunk of a śāla tree, twanging like Indra's thunderbolt, the wrathful one drew it and pierced Jalasaṃdha with an arrow.

**7.91.43**  Then with two razor-shafts the foremost of the Mādhavas, as though laughing, cut off both of Jalasaṃdha's arms, still bearing their ornaments and armlets.

**7.91.44**  Those two arms, like iron bludgeons, fell from that finest of elephants, dropping from him who bore them earthward, like a pair of five-hooded serpents.

**7.91.45**  Then with a third razor-shaft Sātyaki severed his head, fine of tooth and jaw, with comely earrings and a lifted nose.

**7.91.46**  That headless, armless trunk, terrible to behold, drenched Jalasaṃdha's elephant with its blood.

**7.91.47**  Having slain Jalasaṃdha in the fray, the Sātvata in haste struck down the Niṣāda prince too from the elephant's shoulders, O lord of peoples.

**7.91.48**  Jalasaṃdha's elephant, its limbs bathed in blood, bore upon it the splendid seat hanging askew and clinging fast to its back.

**7.91.49**  Tormented by the Sātvata's arrows, the great elephant, trampling its own ranks and uttering a dreadful cry of anguish, fled away.

**7.91.50**  A great cry of woe arose among your troops, O honoured one, when they saw Jalasaṃdha slain by that bull of the Vṛṣṇis.

**7.91.51**  Your warriors, turning their faces away, fled on every side, eager now for flight and without heart to vanquish the foe.

**7.91.52**  At that moment, O king, Droṇa, foremost of those who bear arms, advanced with swift horses upon Yuyudhāna, the great chariot-warrior.

**7.91.53**  Seeing the grandson of Śini thus raging, the bulls of the Kurus, wrathful, together with Droṇa hemmed Sātyaki in on all sides.

**7.91.54**  Then there broke out a battle between the Kurus and the Sātvata, and between Droṇa and him in that fray, O king — dreadful, like the war of gods and demons.

**7.92.1**  Saṃjaya said: All those striking warriors, straining to the utmost and showering volleys of arrows, fought Yuyudhāna in haste, O great king.

**7.92.2**  Droṇa struck him with seventy-seven sharp arrows, Durmarṣaṇa with twelve, and Duḥsaha with ten shafts.

**7.92.3**  And Vikarṇa pierced him with thirty sharp heron-feathered arrows in the left flank, and in the space between his breasts.

**7.92.4**  Durmukha struck the grandson of Śini with ten arrows, Duḥśāsana with eight, and Citrasena with two, O honoured one.

**7.92.5**  And Duryodhana with a great rain of arrows beset the Mādhava in the battle, O king, as did other heroic great chariot-warriors.

**7.92.6**  Though pierced on every side by your sons, those great chariot-warriors, the grandson of Śini struck back at each of them severally with straight-flying shafts.

**7.92.7**  He struck the son of Bharadvāja with three arrows, Duḥsaha with nine, Vikarṇa with twenty-five, and Citrasena with seven.

**7.92.8**  He struck Durmarṣaṇa with twelve, Viviṃśati with four, Satyavrata with nine, and Vijaya with ten arrows.

**7.92.9**  Then, brandishing his gold-banded bow, the great chariot-warrior Sātyaki swiftly advanced upon your son, that great chariot-warrior.

**7.92.10**  He smote with deep-driven arrows that king of all the world, that best of all who bear weapons; then there arose a battle between the two.

**7.92.11**  Loosing sharp arrows and fitting fresh shafts to string, those two great chariot-warriors made each other invisible in the battle.

**7.92.12**  Sātyaki, pierced deep by the king of the Kurus, shone resplendent, the blood flowing freely from him like sap from a sandal tree.

**7.92.13**  And your son, pierced through by the floods of the Sātvata's arrows, gleamed like a tall sacrificial post crowned with a golden wreath.

**7.92.14**  But the Mādhava in that fray, O king, swiftly cut through the bow of the Kuru king, that bowman, with a razor-shaft, as though laughing; and then, his bow severed, he covered him with many arrows.

**7.92.15**  Pierced by the arrows of that swift-acting foe, the king could not endure in battle this mark of his enemy's triumph.

**7.92.16**  Then, taking up another bow, gold-backed and hard to withstand, he swiftly pierced Sātyaki with a hundred shafts.

**7.92.17**  Sorely pierced by your mighty son, that bowman, and overcome with fury, he beset your son in turn.

**7.92.18**  Seeing the king hard pressed, your sons, those great chariot-warriors, at once covered the Sātvata with a rain of arrows.

**7.92.19**  Covered by your many sons, those great chariot-warriors, he pierced each of them with five arrows and then struck them again with seven.

**7.92.20**  And swiftly he pierced Duryodhana with eight fleet shafts, and laughing, he cut through his bow that struck terror in foes.

**7.92.21**  With his arrows he brought down the jewelled serpent-banner, and slaying the four horses with four sharp shafts, the illustrious one struck down the charioteer with a razor-shaft.

**7.92.22**  And at that same moment, exulting, he overwhelmed the Kuru king, that great chariot-warrior, with many arrows that pierce the vital parts.

**7.92.23**  Struck down in the fray by the finest arrows of the grandson of Śini, your son Duryodhana suddenly fled, O king, and leapt up into the chariot of Citrasena the bowman.

**7.92.24**  The whole world cried out in dismay to see the king in that battle being devoured by Sātyaki, as the moon in the sky is devoured by Rāhu.

**7.92.25**  Hearing that great clamour, Kṛtavarman, the great chariot-warrior, rushed at once to the place where the lordly Mādhava stood.

**7.92.26**  Brandishing his excellent bow, urging on his horses, and fiercely chiding his charioteer, he cried in haste, "On, on!"

**7.92.27**  Beholding him bearing down like Death with gaping jaws, Yuyudhāna, O great king, spoke thus to his driver:

**7.92.28**  "Kṛtavarman, armed with arrows, comes swiftly upon us in his chariot. Drive forward to meet him, this foremost of all bowmen."

**7.92.29**  Then, with horses urged to full speed and his chariot duly arrayed, he closed in battle with the Bhoja, the very measure of all archers.

**7.92.30**  Then those two tigers among men, blazing in utmost wrath like two fires, came together like two swift and furious tigers.

**7.92.31**  Kṛtavarman assailed the grandson of Śini with twenty-six sharp, keen shafts, and his charioteer with seven.

**7.92.32**  And with four excellent arrows he struck the four noble horses of the Sātvata, those well-trained steeds of the Sindhu breed.

**7.92.33**  He of the golden banner, the golden armlets, and the golden mail, twanging his great gold-backed bow, poured forth gold-feathered arrows.

**7.92.34**  Then the grandson of Śini, intent and eager to behold Dhanaṃjaya, swiftly sped eighty shafts at Kṛtavarman.

**7.92.35**  Sorely pierced by his mighty foe, that scorcher of foes, unassailable though he was, trembled as a mountain trembles in an earthquake.

**7.92.36**  With sixty-three sharp arrows Sātyaki swiftly pierced Kṛtavarman's four horses, and his charioteer with seven.

**7.92.37**  Fitting a gold-feathered shaft to his bow, Sātyaki loosed it, blazing with great flame like an enraged serpent.

**7.92.38**  That arrow, like the rod of Yama, entered Kṛtavarman, and piercing through his shining armour wrought of gold, it plunged fierce into the earth, drenched with blood.

**7.92.39**  Bleeding in the fray and tormented by the Sātvata's arrows, he reeled, and letting fall his bow, sank down upon his splendid chariot.

**7.92.40**  That bull among men, lion-toothed and of measureless valour, tormented by Sātyaki's arrows, fell to his knees upon the floor of his chariot.

**7.92.41**  Having checked Kṛtavarman — peer of the thousand-armed Arjuna, unshakable as the ocean — Sātyaki then passed onward.

**7.92.42**  Strewn with swords, spears, and bows, thronged with elephants, horses, and chariots, made to flow with rivers of dread blood by hundreds of bulls among the warriors —

**7.92.43**  — through the midst of that host the bull of the Śinis broke, before the eyes of all the troops, cleaving the army as the slayer of Vṛtra cleaves the demon array.

**7.92.44**  And the son of Hṛdika, having recovered himself and taken up another great bow, stood his ground there, mighty as he was, holding back the Pāṇḍavas in the fight.

**7.93.1**  Saṃjaya said: As the troops were being driven hither and thither by the grandson of Śini, the son of Bharadvāja overwhelmed him with great showers of arrows.

**7.93.2**  Tumultuous grew that combat between Droṇa and the Sātvata, before the eyes of all the troops, like the strife of Bali and Vāsava.

**7.93.3**  Then Droṇa pierced the grandson of Śini in the forehead with three bright all-iron arrows shaped like venomous snakes.

**7.93.4**  With those straight-flying arrows fixed in his forehead, Yuyudhāna shone, O great king, like a three-peaked mountain.

**7.93.5**  Then the son of Bharadvāja, watching for his opening, sped at him still more arrows that rang like Indra's thunderbolt in the fray.

**7.93.6**  Those arrows loosed from Droṇa's bow as they came flying, the Dāśārha, that master of supreme weapons, cut down two by two with well-feathered shafts.

**7.93.7**  Beholding that nimbleness of his, O lord of peoples, Droṇa laughed and suddenly pierced the bull of the Śinis with twenty arrows.

**7.93.8**  Again he assailed him with fifty arrows and then with a hundred, surpassing Yuyudhāna's nimbleness with his own swiftness of hand.

**7.93.9**  As angry great serpents dart up from an anthill, so, O king, did the body-cleaving shafts dart up from Droṇa's chariot.

**7.93.10**  And in like manner the arrows loosed by Yuyudhāna in their hundreds and thousands, those blood-drinking shafts, rained down upon Droṇa's chariot.

**7.93.11**  Between the swiftness of hand of that foremost of brāhmaṇas and of the Sātvata, O honoured one, we could mark no difference: those two bulls among men were equal.

**7.93.12**  Then Sātyaki, sorely wroth, smote Droṇa with nine smooth-jointed arrows, and his banner with sharp shafts, and his charioteer with a full hundred, while the son of Bharadvāja looked on.

**7.93.13**  Seeing Yuyudhāna's swiftness of hand, Droṇa, the great chariot-warrior, pierced Sātyaki with seventy arrows, his horses with three apiece, and with a single shaft struck the banner standing on the Mādhava's chariot.

**7.93.14**  Then with another gold-feathered, broad-headed winged shaft he cut through, in the battle, the bow of the high-souled Mādhava.

**7.93.15**  Then Sātyaki, that great chariot-warrior, wroth, cast aside his bow, seized a mighty mace, and hurled it at the son of Bharadvāja.

**7.93.16**  That iron mace bound about with cloth, as it came hurtling on, Droṇa warded off with many arrows of manifold forms.

**7.93.17**  Then Sātyaki, whose valor was unfailing, took up another bow and pierced the hero, the son of Bharadvāja, with many shafts whetted on stone.

**7.93.18**  Having wounded Droṇa in the battle, he let loose a lion's roar; but Droṇa, foremost of all who bear arms, would not endure it.

**7.93.19**  Then, taking up a spear of iron with a golden shaft, he hurled it with force toward the chariot of the Mādhava.

**7.93.20**  But that spear, like unto Death, failing to reach the grandson of Śini, cleaved through the chariot and, fierce and dreadful in its sound, plunged into the earth.

**7.93.21**  Then, O king, the grandson of Śini pierced Droṇa with a winged shaft, striking his right arm and afflicting him sorely, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.93.22**  Droṇa too, O king, in the battle severed the great bow of the Mādhava with a crescent-headed arrow, and struck down his charioteer with a chariot-lance.

**7.93.23**  His charioteer, smitten by the chariot-lance, swooned away; sinking down into the floor of the car, he sat there senseless for a while.

**7.93.24**  Then Sātyaki, O king, performed there a more than human feat, for he both fought against Droṇa and himself took up the reins.

**7.93.25**  Then the great car-warrior Yuyudhāna, his face glad with joy, O lord of peoples, pierced the brāhmaṇa in the battle with a hundred shafts.

**7.93.26**  Droṇa sent against him five arrows, O Bhārata; piercing his armor, they drank his blood in the fray.

**7.93.27**  Sorely pierced by those dreadful shafts, Sātyaki grew exceedingly wrathful, and the hero loosed his arrows against the golden-charioted one.

**7.93.28**  Then, having felled Droṇa's driver to the ground with a single arrow, with his shafts he drove off the horses of that high-souled one, now bereft of their charioteer.

**7.93.29**  That chariot, careering through the battle, traced circles by the thousand, O king, shining like the radiant sun.

**7.93.30**  "Charge! Seize Droṇa's horses! Run!" — thus did all the princes, together with their kings, cry out.

**7.93.31**  Setting Sātyaki aside in haste, O king, those great car-warriors all at once rushed forward to wherever Droṇa was.

**7.93.32**  Seeing them all in flight, tormented by the arrows of the Sātvata, your army, broken once more, fell again into confusion.

**7.93.33**  Having gone again to the gate of the battle-array, Droṇa took his stand there, carried thither by those horses that ran like the wind, sorely afflicted by the shafts of the Vṛṣṇi.

**7.93.34**  Beholding his array shattered by the Pāṇḍavas and the Pāñcālas, the valiant one made no further effort against the grandson of Śini, but turned to the guarding of the array itself.

**7.93.35**  Driving back the Pāṇḍavas and Pāñcālas, Droṇa, like a fire consuming all, stood there blazing with the fire of his wrath, like the sun of doom risen high.

**7.94.1**  Saṃjaya said: That foremost of men, the hero of Śini's line, having vanquished Droṇa and likewise your warriors led by the son of Hṛdika, laughed and spoke these words to his charioteer, O chief among the bulls of the Kurus.

**7.94.2**  "We are but the instrument here, O charioteer; the foes have been consumed by Keśava and Phalguna. Here we but slay the already slain — through that bull among men, sprung from the very self of the lord of the gods."

**7.94.3**  Having spoken thus, that bull of Śini's line, the foremost bowman, the slayer of foes, the mighty one, scattering his shafts on every side at once in that great battle, swooped down as a hawk upon its prey.

**7.94.4**  As he advanced, borne by horses of the hue of the moon and the conch, plunging into the host, that foremost of men, that chief of warriors, equal to the rays of the sun, they could not on any side hold him back.

**7.94.5**  Him of irresistible prowess and undaunted spirit, hard to withstand, O Bhārata, all those companies found unbearable — equal in might to the thousand-eyed one, like the sun in the sky when the clouds have passed.

**7.94.6**  But Sudarśana, that best of kings, filled with wrath, a wondrously skilled fighter, a great bowman clad in golden mail, by main force checked the onrushing Sātyaki.

**7.94.7**  Then there arose between the two, O Bhārata, a most terrible encounter, which both your warriors and the Somakas applauded, even as the hosts of the immortals praised the combat of Vṛtra and Indra.

**7.94.8**  With keen shafts by the hundred Sudarśana pierced the chief of the Sātvatas in the battle; but that bull of Śini's line cut those arrows asunder with his own shafts before ever they reached him.

**7.94.9**  In like manner, the arrows that Sātyaki, the peer of Śakra, hurled at Sudarśana, Sudarśana, mounted on his excellent car, split into two and into three with his choicest shafts.

**7.94.10**  Beholding his arrows then struck down by the force of Sātyaki's shafts, Sudarśana, of fierce energy, as though about to consume him in his wrath, loosed arrows bright as burnished gold.

**7.94.11**  Again, with three arrows like unto fire, drawn back to the ear, keen and well-feathered, he pierced him; breaking through his body-armor, they entered Sātyaki's flesh.

**7.94.12**  Then likewise the king's son, fixing other blazing arrows to the string, struck by main force, with four shafts, those four horses bright as silver.

**7.94.13**  Thus smitten by him, the swift grandson of Śini, whose valor was equal to Indra's, swiftly slew Sudarśana's horses with his keen volleys of arrows and sounded a roar.

**7.94.14**  Then, having cut off the head of his charioteer with a broad-headed shaft like the thunderbolt of Indra, the hero of Śini's line by main force severed the head of Sudarśana himself with a razor-edged arrow.

**7.94.15**  That radiant face, decked with earrings and bright as the full moon, he struck from the body, even as of old the wielder of the thunderbolt by force struck off the head of the exceedingly mighty Bala in battle, O king.

**7.94.16**  Having slain in battle that son and grandson of kings, the swift bull of the Yadus, that high-souled one, filled with the highest joy, shone forth, O king, like the king of the gods.

**7.94.17**  Then, holding back your host with floods of arrows, that hero among men set forth toward Arjuna, riding on a chariot yoked with goodly steeds, as if to fill the worlds with wonder as he went.

**7.94.18**  That supreme and marvelous deed of his the assembled foremost warriors honored — that he consumed with his shafts the foes who came within the range of his arrows, even as the fire-god devours all.

**7.95.1**  Saṃjaya said: Then that wise and high-souled Sātyaki, the bull of the Vṛṣṇis, having slain Sudarśana in the battle, spoke thus to his charioteer:

**7.95.2**  "Choked with chariots, horses, and elephants, garlanded with waves of arrows and spears, with swords for its fishes and maces for its sea-monsters, loud with the din of the weapons of heroes;

**7.95.3**  life-stealing and terrible, resounding with the clamor of war-instruments, painful to the touch of warriors, unassailable to those who longed to conquer it —

**7.95.4**  we have crossed, dear friend, that hard-to-cross great ocean which is Droṇa's army, beset in battle by the force of Jalasandha as if by man-eating demons.

**7.95.5**  The remnant of the host beyond this I deem but a paltry rivulet, fordable and shallow of water; urge on the horses, untroubled.

**7.95.6**  Now that I have vanquished in battle the irresistible Droṇa together with his followers, I count Savyasācin as good as reached by my hand.

**7.95.7**  Having overcome the son of Hṛdika, that best of warriors, I count Dhanaṃjaya as reached; for no fear arises in me at the sight of these manifold hosts, which are to me like dry grass and reeds before a blazing fire in summer.

**7.95.8**  Behold the ground traversed by the diademed chief of the Pāṇḍavas, made rough with the fallen masses of foot-soldiers, horses, chariots, and elephants.

**7.95.9**  I deem him near at hand — him of the white steeds, whose charioteer is Kṛṣṇa; for there, lo, is heard the sound of Gāṇḍīva of boundless might.

**7.95.10**  By such omens as appear to me, before the sun has set Arjuna shall slay the ruler of the Sindhus.

**7.95.11**  Soothing the horses gently, drive on with care against the enemy's host, to where these warriors clad in armor stand, led by Suyodhana —

**7.95.12**  the mailed Kāmbojas of cruel deeds, frenzied for battle, bearers of arrows and bows, and the Yavanas, hard smiters,

**7.95.13**  the Śakas, Kirātas, Daradas, Barbaras, and the men of Tāmralipta, and many other barbarians, weapons of every kind in hand — all stand facing me, eager for the fight.

**7.95.14**  Once I have slain these in battle, with their chariots, elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers, know this dread and most terrible stronghold to be already crossed.

**7.95.15**  The charioteer said: No agitation is in me, O scion of the Vṛṣṇis, O thou of unfailing valor, even were the wrathful son of Jamadagni to stand before us;

**7.95.16**  or Droṇa, the best of car-warriors, or Kṛpa, or even the lord of the Madras — still no agitation would there be, leaning upon thee, O mighty-armed one.

**7.95.17**  Very many hast thou vanquished in battle, O slayer of foes, and never before has any agitation come upon me at any time — how much less now, O hero, on meeting this mere cow's-hoofprint of a fight?

**7.95.18**  O long-lived one, by which way shall I bring thee to Dhanaṃjaya? Against whom art thou wrathful, O scion of the Vṛṣṇis? For whom has death drawn near? Whose minds are eager today to go to the city of Yama?

**7.95.19**  Who, beholding thee in battle ranging in thy prowess, like Yama the ender at the time of doom, endowed with valor, shall flee in the fray? Of whom does king Vaivasvata think today, O mighty-armed one?

**7.95.20**  Sātyaki said: These shaven-headed ones I shall slay, as Vāsava slew the Dānavas; I shall fulfill my vow. Bear me straight against the Kāmbojas; having wrought their slaughter today, swiftly shall I go to the Pāṇḍava.

**7.95.21**  Today shall the Kauravas with Suyodhana behold my valor, O charioteer, when the host of the shaven-headed ones, and all the armies, are slain again and again.

**7.95.22**  Today, hearing the manifold outcry of the Kaurava host as it is rent asunder in the battle, Suyodhana shall be consumed with grief.

**7.95.23**  Today, in the battle, I shall display the path of mastery taught me by my teacher — the high-souled chief of the Pāṇḍavas, him of the white steeds.

**7.95.24**  Today, beholding the foremost warriors slain by my shafts in their thousands, king Duryodhana shall fall into remorse.

**7.95.25**  Today the Kauravas shall behold my bow, as I let fly my choicest arrows with swift hand, like a wheel of blazing firebrands.

**7.95.26**  Beholding the slaughter of the soldiers, their limbs studded with my shafts and streaming much blood, Suyodhana shall be consumed with grief.

**7.95.27**  Today, as I strike down the best of the best in my form of wrath, that Suyodhana shall deem this world to hold a second Arjuna.

**7.95.28**  Today, beholding kings by the thousand slain by me in the battle, king Duryodhana shall be consumed with grief in that great encounter.

**7.95.29**  Today, slaying kings by the thousand, I shall show forth among the kings my love and my devotion to the high-souled Pāṇḍavas.

**7.95.30**  Saṃjaya said: Thus addressed, the charioteer then urged on sharply the well-trained, smoothly-bearing steeds, white as the moon.

**7.95.31**  Those excellent horses, swift as thought and wind, as if drinking up the sky, bore Yuyudhāna swiftly to the Yavanas.

**7.95.32**  Coming upon Sātyaki, who never turned back in battle, many of them, light of hand, covered him with showers of arrows.

**7.95.33**  But their arrows and their weapons Sātyaki cut down with swift, smooth-jointed shafts, O king, and those arrows of theirs did not reach him.

**7.95.34**  With keen, straight-flying shafts, gold-nocked and winged with vulture-feathers, the fierce one struck off the heads of the Yavanas, and their arms as well.

**7.95.35**  Cleaving on every side their armor of wrought iron and of bronze, and likewise their bodies, his arrows passed on into the surface of the earth.

**7.95.36**  Those barbarians, smitten by the hero Sātyaki in the battle, fell there by the hundred, lifeless, upon the bosom of the earth.

**7.95.37**  With shafts loosed from a fully-drawn bow, falling unbroken and close-clustered, he pierced the Yavanas five, six, seven, and eight at a time.

**7.95.38**  With the thousands of the Kāmbojas and of the Śakas, O lord of peoples, of the Śabaras, the Kirātas, and the Barbaras as well,

**7.95.39**  the grandson of Śini made the earth there impassable to look upon, a mire of flesh and blood, as he wasted away your host.

**7.95.40**  With the helmeted heads of the marauders, their locks shorn off, the earth was strewn here and there, as if with plumeless birds.

**7.95.41**  Covered all over with those headless trunks, every limb sprinkled with blood, that battlefield shone like the sky overspread with coppery clouds.

**7.95.42**  Slain by his well-jointed, straight-flying shafts, whose touch was as the thunderbolt and the lightning, they, together with their horses and chariots, lay covering the earth.

**7.95.43**  Few left remaining, broken, their lives barely clinging, bereft of sense — thus, O great king, were the mailed warriors vanquished in battle by Yuyudhāna.

**7.95.44**  Goading their horses with heels and whips, the warriors took to their swiftest pace and fled in terror in every direction.

**7.95.45**  Having routed the Kāmboja host, hard to vanquish in battle, O Bhārata, and the army of the Yavanas and the great force of the Śakas,

**7.95.46**  that tiger among men, Sātyaki of true valour, having joyfully conquered your troops, urged his charioteer, saying, 'Drive on!'

**7.95.47**  As he rode on, the guardian of Arjuna's rear, O lord of peoples, the Cāraṇas beheld him with delight, and even your own warriors paid him honour.

**7.96.1**  Saṃjaya said: Having conquered the Yavanas and the Kāmbojas, Yuyudhāna, that foremost of chariot-warriors, then advanced toward Arjuna through the midst of your army.

**7.96.2**  That tiger among men, sharp-fanged and gleaming in his many-coloured armour, terrified your army as a tiger sniffing out deer strikes fear into them.

**7.96.3**  Coursing along the paths in his chariot, he whirled his bow with great force—a bow gold-backed, mighty in might, studded with golden crescents.

**7.96.4**  With golden armlets and golden helm, encased in golden mail, that hero of the splendid golden banner shone like a peak of Meru.

**7.96.5**  His drawn bow bent into a circle in the fray, radiant with beams of brilliant lustre, that sun among men blazed forth like the autumn sun newly risen.

**7.96.6**  Striding with shoulders like a bull's, bull-eyed, that bull among men shone amid your troops as a bull amid the cattle.

**7.96.7**  Resembling a rutting elephant, moving with the gait of a rutting elephant, standing like a must elephant with temples streaming in the midst of his herd—your men, like tigers bent on the kill, rushed upon him in battle.

**7.96.8**  He had passed through Droṇa's division and the Bhoja division, hard to cross, and had crossed the ocean-like array and the host of the Kāmbojas as one fords a flood-swollen sea.

**7.96.9**  As he won free of that sea of soldiers, with Hārdikya for its sea-monster, and crossed it, your chariot-warriors in great wrath encircled Sātyaki.

**7.96.10**  Duryodhana, Citrasena, Duḥśāsana and Viviṃśati, Śakuni and Duḥsaha, the youth Durmarṣaṇa, and Krātha—

**7.96.11**  and many other heroes, weapon-bearing and unassailable, gave chase, enraged, to Sātyaki as he rode ahead of them.

**7.96.12**  Then there arose a mighty din from your army, O sire, like that of the sea whipped to fury by the wind on the day of the full moon.

**7.96.13**  Beholding them all rushing upon him, that bull of Śini's line said to his charioteer, smiling, as it were, 'Drive on, but slowly.'

**7.96.14**  'See how the host of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son comes surging on, straight and swift against me, with its elephants, horse, chariots, and foot.'

**7.96.15**  'It makes all the quarters resound with the rumble of its chariots, O charioteer, and makes the earth and the sky tremble, and the very seas besides.'

**7.96.16**  'This ocean of armies, my friend, I shall stem in the great battle, as the shore stems the swollen waters on the night of the full moon.'

**7.96.17**  'Behold my prowess in the great fray, O charioteer, like that of Indra; see, I scatter the armies of the foe with my whetted shafts.'

**7.96.18**  'Behold foot, horse, chariots, and elephants slain in battle by my shafts, bright as fire, robbed of their lives by the thousand.'

**7.96.19**  As Sātyaki of measureless might spoke thus, your soldiers, eager for the fight, swiftly closed upon him, crying, 'Strike! Charge! Stand fast! Look there, look there!'

**7.96.20**  As those heroes shouted thus, Sātyaki with his keen shafts slew three hundred of their horses and four hundred of their elephants.

**7.96.21**  That tumultuous clash between him and those bowmen, like the war of gods and demons, set in motion a great slaughter of men.

**7.96.22**  The grandson of Śini received the army of your son, dense as a mass of clouds, O sire, with shafts that were like venomous serpents.

**7.96.23**  Though veiled over in the battle by nets of arrows, that valiant one, unflustered, O great king, slew many of your warriors.

**7.96.24**  A very great marvel did I behold there, O lord of kings: not one shaft of Sātyaki's, O lord, fell in vain.

**7.96.25**  Thick with chariots, elephants, and horses, churning with waves of foot-soldiers, that vast ocean of an army, reaching the shore that was the scion of Śini, came to a halt.

**7.96.26**  With its men, elephants, and horses thrown into confusion, it wheeled about again and again; that army, smitten on every side by his arrows, milled hither and thither like cattle tormented by the cold.

**7.96.27**  Footman, chariot, elephant, horseman, and horse alike—not one did I see there unpierced by the shafts of Yuyudhāna.

**7.96.28**  Not such havoc, O king, did Phalguna work there as the destruction Sātyaki wrought among the divisions; the grandson of Śini fought surpassing even Arjuna, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.96.29**  Then King Duryodhana pierced the charioteer of the Sātvata with three keen shafts, and with four more his four horses.

**7.96.30**  Having struck Sātyaki with three shafts, he pierced him again with eight, while Duḥśāsana pierced that bull of Śini's line with sixteen.

**7.96.31**  Śakuni with twenty-five, Citrasena with five, and Duḥsaha with fifteen pierced Sātyaki in the breast.

**7.96.32**  That tiger of the Vṛṣṇis, smiling though thus smitten with arrows, pierced every one of them, O great king, with three shafts apiece.

**7.96.33**  Having pierced his foes deeply with those exceedingly sharp arrows, the scion of Śini ranged through the battle like a hawk, swift and nimble in his movements.

**7.96.34**  Having cut Saubala's bow and severed his leather hand-guard, he struck Duryodhana with three arrows between the breasts.

**7.96.35**  That bull of Śini's line pierced Citrasena with a hundred shafts, Duḥsaha with ten, and Duḥśāsana with twenty.

**7.96.36**  Then your brother-in-law, taking up another bow, O lord of peoples, pierced Sātyaki with eight shafts and again with five.

**7.96.37**  And Duḥśāsana with ten, Duḥsaha with three shafts, and Durmukha with twelve, O king, pierced Sātyaki.

**7.96.38**  Duryodhana, O Bhārata, having pierced the Mādhava with seventy-three shafts, then struck his charioteer with three keen arrows.

**7.96.39**  All those heroes together, those mighty car-warriors straining their utmost, Sātyaki pierced again, each with five arrows.

**7.96.40**  Then that foremost of chariot-warriors swiftly struck the charioteer of your son with a broad-headed shaft, and the slain man fell to the ground.

**7.96.41**  When that charioteer was struck down, the chariot of your son, O lord, was carried off from the field by those horses that ran like the wind.

**7.96.42**  Then your sons, O king, and the soldiers, O lord of peoples, beholding the king's chariot borne away, fled by the hundreds.

**7.96.43**  Seeing that army in flight, O Bhārata, Sātyaki overwhelmed it with sharp arrows, gold-feathered and whetted on stone.

**7.96.44**  Having routed all your troops on every side, Sātyaki went on, O king, toward the chariot of him whose steeds were white.

**7.96.45**  As he took up his arrows, guarded his charioteer, and delivered his own self from peril, your warriors paid him honour.

**7.97.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the scion of Śini, having crushed that great army, was going on toward Arjuna, what did my shameless sons do then, O Saṃjaya?

**7.97.2**  And how, in such a battle, could there be any firmness left in those doomed men, when they had seen the scion of Śini bear himself like Savyasācin himself?

**7.97.3**  What will they say of their warriorhood, vanquished there in the midst of the host? And how did Sātyaki of great renown pass them by in the battle?

**7.97.4**  And how, while my sons yet lived, did the scion of Śini press on there in the fight, O Saṃjaya? Tell me that truly.

**7.97.5**  Most wondrous is this that I hear from you, my son—the battle of one man against many foes, all of them mighty car-warriors.

**7.97.6**  I deem it an ill omen turned against my luckless sons, that they should be cut down in battle by the high-souled Sātvata.

**7.97.7**  For my whole army is not a match for that one man, O Saṃjaya—for Yuyudhāna in his wrath; let all the Pāṇḍavas stand aside!

**7.97.8**  Having vanquished in battle Droṇa, the skilled, the unconquerable in war, he slays my sons as a lion slays a herd of beasts.

**7.97.9**  By Kṛtavarman and the many other heroes, striving hard in the fray, Yuyudhāna, that bull among men, could not be slain.

**7.97.10**  Not such a fight did Phalguna wage there as the fight that the grandson of Śini, of great renown, has waged.

**7.97.11**  Saṃjaya said: This is the fruit of your ill counsel, O king, and of Duryodhana's deeds. Listen attentively to what I shall tell you, O Bhārata.

**7.97.12**  They turned back once more, binding themselves to one another as sworn warriors, setting their hearts firmly upon battle, at the command of your son.

**7.97.13**  Three thousand horsemen, with Duryodhana at their head—Śakas, Kāmbojas, Bāhlīkas, Yavanas, and Pāradas as well—

**7.97.14**  Kuṇindas, Taṅgaṇas, Ambaṣṭhas, and the Paiśācas together with the Mandaras—rushed upon the scion of Śini as locusts rush upon a flame.

**7.97.15**  And the harnessed chariots of the highlanders who fight with stones, five hundred heroes strong, O king, charged upon the scion of Śini.

**7.97.16**  Then with a thousand chariots and a hundred mighty car-warriors, with a thousand elephants and two thousand horses,

**7.97.17**  those great car-warriors, loosing showers of arrows of every kind, rushed upon the scion of Śini, together with footmen past counting.

**7.97.18**  Urging them all on with the cry 'Slay him!', O Bhārata, Duḥśāsana, O great king, hemmed Sātyaki round about.

**7.97.19**  There we beheld the great and wondrous feat of the scion of Śini—that he alone fought, unflinching, against so many.

**7.97.20**  He slew the chariot-division and that force of elephants, and all the horsemen, and the barbarians too, every one of them.

**7.97.21**  There, with wheels crushed and the finest weapons shattered, with axles broken in many places, and shafts, poles, and chariot-frames,

**7.97.22**  with splintered chariot-poles and banners struck down, with coats of mail and yak-tail whisks, the earth lay all bestrewn.

**7.97.23**  With garlands, ornaments, garments, and chariot-trappings, O sire, the earth was covered over there, as the sky is covered with planets, O Bhārata.

**7.97.24**  And lordly elephants, mountain-like in form, lay fallen—born of the line of Añjana and of Vāmana, O Bhārata, born of the line of Supratīka and of the line of Mahāpadma as well,

**7.97.25**  and of the line of Airāvaṇa, and of yet other lines as well—those choicest of tuskers, O king, lay there slain in great numbers.

**7.97.26**  Horses of the finest breed—from Vanāyu, from the hill-country, from Kāmboja, Āraṭṭa, and Bāhlika—Sātyaki slew there, O king.

**7.97.27**  And footmen sprung from many lands and of many races the scion of Śini slew there by the hundreds and by the thousands.

**7.97.28**  As they were being driven before him, Duḥśāsana said to the barbarians, 'Turn back, you who know no law! Fight on! What good is your fleeing?'

**7.97.29**  And looking upon them all, your son Duḥśāsana spurred on the highland heroes who fought with stones.

**7.97.30**  'You are skilled in battle with stones; this Sātyaki knows it not. He knows not stone-warfare—slay him, this man so eager for the fight!'

**7.97.31**  'Just so, none of the Kurus are versed in battle with stones. Charge on, fear not! Sātyaki shall not overtake you.'

**7.97.32**  Then the mountain-dwellers, taking up boulders as large as young elephants, stood facing Yuyudhāna, longing for death.

**7.97.33**  Others too, hurling missiles and seeking the death of the Sātvata, urged on by your son, hemmed him in from every side.

**7.97.34**  As they rushed upon him, eager to wage war with stones, Sātyaki took aim and let fly thirty arrows.

**7.97.35**  That tumultuous rain of stones, loosed by the mountaineers, the bull of Śini's line shattered with iron shafts like serpents.

**7.97.36**  By the splinters of stone, blazing like swarms of fireflies, the troops for the most part were struck down, crying out in dismay, O honored one.

**7.97.37**  Then five hundred warriors, their great stones raised aloft, their arms severed, O king, fell to the surface of the earth.

**7.97.38**  He slew many thousands of those stone-fighting warriors who stood their ground and struggled on; and that seemed a marvel.

**7.97.39**  Then once more, on every side, a rain of stones was cast by the goat-faced ones, by the Ayohastas, the spear-wielders, the Daradas, and the throngs of Khaśas.

**7.97.40**  As the Ambaṣṭhas and the Kuṇindas hurled them again and again, the mighty Sātyaki, watching keenly, pierced each in turn with iron arrows.

**7.97.41**  As the boulders were split in mid-air by his sharp arrows, at that din, O king, the elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers fled.

**7.97.42**  Covered over with stone-dust, both men and birds were unable to hold their ground, as though stung by bees.

**7.97.43**  The elephants that survived the slaughter, streaming blood, their temple-bosses split open, turned away from the path of Yuyudhāna's chariot.

**7.97.44**  Then there arose from your army, tormented by the Mādhava, a din terrible as the roar of the ocean, O honored one.

**7.97.45**  Hearing that tumultuous din, Droṇa said to his charioteer: "Yonder, O charioteer, is the wrathful great warrior of the Sātvatas in battle.

**7.97.46**  Rending the host in many places, he ranges over the field like Death itself. Where that tumultuous din is heard, there, O charioteer, drive the chariot.

**7.97.47**  Surely Yuyudhāna has clashed with the stone-fighters, for all our chariot-warriors are being borne away by their bolting horses.

**7.97.48**  Stripped of weapons and armor, shattered, they fall here and there, and the drivers cannot rein in their horses amid the tumult."

**7.97.49**  As the wise son of Bharadvāja spoke thus, O king, the charioteer then answered Droṇa, foremost of weapon-bearers:

**7.97.50**  "O long-lived one, the Kaurava host is fleeing on every side. Behold the warriors broken in battle, running this way and that.

**7.97.51**  And these heroic Pāñcālas, united with the Pāṇḍavas, seeking to slay you yourself, are rushing forward from all sides.

**7.97.52**  Determine here what the moment demands, O tamer of foes—whether to stand fast or to advance; for Sātyaki has gone far afield."

**7.97.53**  Even as the son of Bharadvāja was speaking thus, O honored one, the scion of Śini came into view, striking down chariots of every kind.

**7.97.54**  Your men, being slaughtered in battle by Yuyudhāna, abandoned Yuyudhāna's chariot and fled toward Droṇa's division.

**7.97.55**  And those chariots with which Duḥśāsana had earlier turned to the fight—all of them, terrified, ran toward Droṇa's chariot.

**7.98.1**  Saṃjaya said: Seeing Duḥśāsana's chariot drawn up close at hand, the son of Bharadvāja then spoke these words to Duḥśāsana:

**7.98.2**  "Duḥśāsana, why have all these chariots fled away? Is it well with the king? Does the lord of the Sindhus yet live?

**7.98.3**  You are here a king's son, a king's brother, a great chariot-warrior who has attained the rank of crown prince. Why then do you flee from the battle?

**7.98.4**  Having yourself stirred up this great enmity with the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas, how is it that on meeting Sātyaki alone you are afraid in battle?

**7.98.5**  Long ago, while you grasped the dice in the gaming hall, you did not know that these arrows would come to be, cruel as venomous serpents.

**7.98.6**  The speaking of harsh words to the Pāṇḍavas in particular, and the affliction of Draupadī—of these you alone were the root, long ago.

**7.98.7**  Where now is your pride and your arrogance? Where, O hero, is that roaring of yours? Having enraged the Pārthas, who are like venomous serpents, where will you go?

**7.98.8**  Pitiable is this army of the Bhāratas, and pitiable is King Suyodhana, whose hard-hearted brother you are—you who are bent on flight.

**7.98.9**  Surely, O hero, this host being torn apart and stricken with fear ought to have been guarded by you, relying on the might of your own arms; yet you this day, forsaking the battle in your terror, gladden the foe.

**7.98.10**  When you, the leader of the host, have fled, O slayer of foes, who else will stand his ground in battle, the fearful taking refuge in one already afraid?

**7.98.11**  Today, fighting against the Sātvata alone, O blameless one, your mind turns to flight from the battle.

**7.98.12**  When you behold in battle the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, and Bhīmasena, O Kaurava, and the twins, then what will you do?

**7.98.13**  Not equal to Phalguna's arrows in battle, whose splendor is like the sun and fire, are these shafts of Sātyaki from which you flee in terror.

**7.98.14**  If indeed your mind is set on flight, then let the earth be given over to the King of Righteousness, and so make peace.

**7.98.15**  While Phalguna's iron shafts, like serpents loosed from their slough, have not yet entered your body, make your peace with the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.98.16**  While the high-souled Pārthas, having slain your hundred brothers in battle, have not yet seized the earth, make your peace with the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.98.17**  While King Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma, is not yet wrathful, nor Kṛṣṇa who glories in battle, make your peace with the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.98.18**  While mighty-armed Bhīma, plunging into the great host, has not yet crushed your own brothers, make your peace with the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.98.19**  Long ago your brother Suyodhana was told by Bhīṣma: 'The Pāṇḍavas are unconquerable in war, O gentle one; make your peace with the Pāṇḍavas.' Yet that dull-witted brother of yours, Suyodhana, did not do so.

**7.98.20**  Now, summoning steadfastness in battle, fight on with effort against the Pāṇḍavas. Go swiftly by chariot to where Sātyaki stands.

**7.98.21**  This host, bereft of you, will scatter, O Bhārata. For your own sake, give battle in the field to Sātyaki of true valor."

**7.98.22**  Thus addressed, your son answered not a word, but, treating what he had heard as though unheard, set out toward where Sātyaki was.

**7.98.23**  Joined with a great host of unyielding Mlecchas, and reaching the field, he strove and gave battle to Yuyudhāna.

**7.98.24**  Droṇa too, foremost of chariot-warriors, in great wrath rushed upon the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas, holding to a measured speed.

**7.98.25**  And entering the array of the Pāñcālas in battle, Droṇa put their warriors to flight by hundreds and by thousands.

**7.98.26**  Then Droṇa, O great king, proclaiming his name aloud in the battle, wrought a great slaughter among the Pāṇḍavas, Pāñcālas, and Matsyas.

**7.98.27**  As the son of Bharadvāja was conquering the divisions on every side, the radiant Vīraketu, son of the Pāñcāla king, advanced against him.

**7.98.28**  He pierced Droṇa with five arrows of well-smoothed joints, struck his standard with one, and his charioteer with seven.

**7.98.29**  There, O great king, I beheld a marvel in the battle: that Droṇa did not at once move against the impetuous Pāñcāla prince in the fight.

**7.98.30**  Seeing Droṇa held in check in the battle, O honored one, the Pāñcālas, desiring the victory of Dharma's son, surrounded him on every side, O king.

**7.98.31**  With arrows like fire, with costly lances, and with weapons of every kind, O king, they overwhelmed Droṇa alone.

**7.98.32**  Droṇa struck down those swarms of arrows on every side, O king, as the wind sweeping the sky scatters great rain-clouds.

**7.98.33**  Then the slayer of enemy heroes fitted to his bow a most dreadful arrow, like the sun and fire, aimed at Vīraketu's chariot.

**7.98.34**  That arrow, O king, piercing the Pāñcāla prince, the delight of his line, swiftly entered the earth, wet with blood and blazing as it went.

**7.98.35**  Then the Pāñcāla prince, the delight of his line, fell swiftly from his chariot, like a great campaka tree from a mountain peak, beaten down by the wind.

**7.98.36**  When that mighty-armed prince, a great archer, was slain, the Pāñcālas in haste surrounded Droṇa on every side.

**7.98.37**  Citraketu and Sudhanvan, and Citravarman, O Bhārata, and Citraratha as well, racked by grief at their brother's ruin,

**7.98.38**  rushed together upon the son of Bharadvāja, eager to fight, loosing showers of arrows like rain-clouds at the close of the hot season.

**7.98.39**  Assailed in many ways by those princely great chariot-warriors, he, enraged in battle, stripped those youths of their horses, charioteers, and cars.

**7.98.40**  And with other keen-edged broad arrows, the illustrious one struck down their heads, as though plucking flowers.

**7.98.41**  Slain, those splendid warriors fell from their chariots to the earth, O king, as the Daiteyas and Dānavas fell of old in the war of the gods and demons.

**7.98.42**  Having slain them in battle, O king, the valiant son of Bharadvāja whirled his unassailable, gold-backed bow.

**7.98.43**  Seeing the godlike Pāñcāla great chariot-warriors slain, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, exceedingly wrathful, letting tears fall from his eyes, advanced in his fury toward Droṇa's chariot in the battle.

**7.98.44**  Then of a sudden a cry of "Alas! Alas!" arose, O king, when men saw Droṇa hemmed in by the arrows of the Pāñcāla prince in the battle.

**7.98.45**  Though covered over in many ways by the high-souled grandson of Pṛṣata, Droṇa did not waver, but fought on, even smiling.

**7.98.46**  Then the Pāñcāla prince, O great king, beside himself with rage, struck Droṇa upon the chest in his wrath with ninety arrows of bent joints.

**7.98.47**  Deeply wounded by that strong warrior, the illustrious son of Bharadvāja sank down upon the floor of his chariot and fell into a swoon.

**7.98.48**  Seeing him brought to such a pass, the valiant, heroic Dhṛṣṭadyumna swiftly cast aside his bow and seized his sword.

**7.98.49**  Leaping down from his chariot, that great warrior in haste swiftly mounted the chariot of the son of Bharadvāja, O honored one, his eyes red with wrath, longing to sever the head from his body.

**7.98.50**  Then the mighty Droṇa, recovering, took up his bow and, with span-long arrows ever fit for close fighting, O king, gave battle in the field to the great chariot-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

**7.98.51**  Those arrows called span-long, made for fighting at close quarters and well known to Droṇa, O king, beat Dhṛṣṭadyumna back.

**7.98.52**  Assailed by those many shafts, that mighty and valiant one, his onset broken, leaped swiftly down from the chariot.

**7.98.53**  Mounting his own chariot, the hero, the great warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna, took up his mighty bow and pierced Droṇa in the battle.

**7.98.54**  That marvelous combat between the two the hosts of beings hailed with praise, and the kṣatriyas too, O great king, and whatever other soldiers were there.

**7.98.55**  "Droṇa, now joined in combat with Dhṛṣṭadyumna, will surely fall into the power of our king"—so the Pāñcālas cried aloud.

**7.98.56**  But Droṇa, swift in battle, struck off the head of Dhṛṣṭadyumna's charioteer, as one knocks a ripe fruit from a tree; and thereupon the horses of that high-souled one bolted away, O king.

**7.98.57**  As they fled in rout, Droṇa, valorous everywhere upon the field, drove off the Pāñcālas and the Sṛñjayas in the battle.

**7.98.58**  Having vanquished the Pāṇḍavas and Pāñcālas, the majestic son of Bharadvāja, that subduer of foes, took his stand once more within his own array and stood unshaken; nor did the Pāṇḍavas dare to conquer him in battle, O lord.

**7.99.1**  Saṃjaya said: Then, O king, Duḥśāsana rushed upon Śaineya, scattering arrows by the thousand like a rain-laden thundercloud.

**7.99.2**  Though he pierced Sātyaki with sixty arrows and then with sixteen more, he could not make him waver, who stood firm in the fight like Maināka, the mountain.

**7.99.3**  But that hero covered Duḥśāsana thickly with his shafts, as a spider, with its web, enmeshes a gnat that has blundered into it.

**7.99.4**  Seeing Duḥśāsana so studded with a hundred arrows, the king urged on the Trigartas against the chariot of Yuyudhāna.

**7.99.5**  Those doers of cruel deeds drew near to Yuyudhāna—three thousand chariot-warriors of the Trigartas, skilled in battle.

**7.99.6**  They surrounded him with a vast host of chariots, having steadied their resolve for the fight, bound to one another as sworn confederates unto death.

**7.99.7**  As they strove in the fight and loosed their showers of arrows, he crushed five hundred of their foremost warriors in the front of the array.

**7.99.8**  Swiftly slain by the shafts of the chief of the Śinis, they fell like great trees shattered by the force of a mighty gale.

**7.99.9**  With chariots broken in many parts, with banners, O lord of peoples, and with horses adorned in gold all fallen there, the earth was strewn.

**7.99.10**  With those mangled by Śaineya's arrows and drenched in floods of blood, the field shone, O great king, as though with kiṃśuka trees in full flower.

**7.99.11**  Slaughtered in battle by Yuyudhāna, your men found no deliverer, like elephants sunk fast in the mire.

**7.99.12**  Then they all turned back toward Droṇa's chariot, as great serpents flee to their holes in dread of the king of birds.

**7.99.13**  Having slain five hundred warriors with arrows like venomous serpents, that hero advanced slowly toward the chariot of Dhanaṃjaya.

**7.99.14**  As that best of men went forward, your son Duḥśāsana swiftly pierced him with nine arrows of smooth-jointed shafts.

**7.99.15**  But that mighty bowman pierced him in turn with five whetted arrows, gold-feathered, fledged with vulture-plumes, and flying straight.

**7.99.16**  And Duḥśāsana, as if laughing, O great king, O Bhārata, having struck Sātyaki with three arrows, pierced him again with five.

**7.99.17**  But Śaineya, having struck your son with five swift arrows and severed his bow in the fight, went on toward Arjuna, leaving him astonished.

**7.99.18**  Then Duḥśāsana, enraged, hurled at the departing hero of the Vṛṣṇis an all-steel javelin, eager to slay him.

**7.99.19**  But that dreadful javelin of your son Sātyaki cut into a hundred pieces, O king, with whetted heron-feathered shafts.

**7.99.20**  Then your son, O lord of men, taking up another bow and piercing Sātyaki with ten arrows, roared aloud like a lion.

**7.99.21**  But Sātyaki, enraged in battle, having bewildered your son, smote him upon the breast with arrows shaped like tongues of fire, and pierced him again with eight all-iron, keen-pointed shafts.

**7.99.22**  Duḥśāsana then pierced Sātyaki in turn with twenty arrows; and the Sātvata too, O great king, struck him upon the breast with three smooth-jointed shafts of mighty speed.

**7.99.23**  Then that great chariot-warrior, sorely enraged, slew his steeds with sharp arrows, and his charioteer too with smooth-jointed shafts.

**7.99.24**  With one broad-headed shaft that master of the highest weapons cut his bow, with five his hand-guard, with two more his banner and his chariot-lance, and with keen arrows both his flanking charioteers as well.

**7.99.25**  His bow cut, his chariot wrecked, his horses and charioteer slain, he was borne away upon his own chariot by the commander of the Trigarta host.

**7.99.26**  Though Śaineya rushed upon him, for a moment, O Bhārata, that mighty-armed one did not slay him, remembering the words of Bhīmasena.

**7.99.27**  For Bhīmasena had vowed, O Bhārata, in the midst of the assembly, the slaying of all your sons in battle.

**7.99.28**  And so, having conquered Duḥśāsana in the fight, O lord, Sātyaki went swiftly, O king, in the direction whither Dhanaṃjaya had gone.

**7.100.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Were there in that army of mine no great chariot-warriors at all, who neither slew nor even checked Sātyaki as he went on his way?

**7.100.2**  For alone he wrought his deeds in the battle, that hero of true valor, equal in might to Śakra, as great Indra among the Dānavas.

**7.100.3**  Or was that path empty by which Sātyaki passed—he, a bull among men, crushing alone the teeming armies?

**7.100.4**  And how did Śaineya, one against many, pass out from the midst of those great-souled warriors as they fought? Tell me this, Saṃjaya.

**7.100.5**  Saṃjaya said: O king, the muster of your armies—with chariots, elephants, horse, and foot—grew tumultuous, like the ending of an age.

**7.100.6**  Among the daily-gathered hosts of your army, O giver of honor, there was, I think, no muster in the world to equal it.

**7.100.7**  There the gods, and the cāraṇas assembled together, were saying: 'Surely the hosts upon this earth shall have their ending here.'

**7.100.8**  And never was there such an array, O lord of peoples, as the one Droṇa had ordered at the slaying-quest of Jayadratha.

**7.100.9**  Like the roar of oceans lashed by a furious gale was the din in the battle of those floods of troops as they rushed upon one another.

**7.100.10**  Of the assembled kings, O best of men, there were many—in your host and in the Pāṇḍavas'—thousands and hundreds.

**7.100.11**  Of those furious champions, steadfast in their deeds in battle, there arose a vast and turbulent uproar that made the hair stand on end.

**7.100.12**  Then Bhīmasena cried aloud, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O sire, and Nakula and Sahadeva and the Pāṇḍava, the king of righteousness.

**7.100.13**  'Come on! Strike! Range about with all your might! For the two heroes, the Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava, have entered the host of the foe.'

**7.100.14**  'So contrive it swiftly that those two may pass with ease toward the slaying of Jayadratha'—thus he urged on the armies; 'were they to fail, the Kurus would gain their end, and we be conquered.'

**7.100.15**  'Therefore do you, joined together and swift, churn up at once that ocean of troops, even as the high-rushing winds churn the sea.'

**7.100.16**  Urged on by Bhīmasena, O king, and by the prince of Pāñcāla, they smote the Kauravas in the fray, casting away their own dear lives.

**7.100.17**  Desiring death in battle, those men of surpassing splendor, for the sake of heaven and for their friends' cause, did not guard their lives with their weapons.

**7.100.18**  Even so your men, O king, longing for great renown and fixing their minds upon the noble resolve in battle, drew up only for the fight.

**7.100.19**  And while that turbulent and dreadful battle was raging, Sātyaki, having cut down all the troops, went on toward Arjuna.

**7.100.20**  There the gleams of the armor, made dazzling by the rays of the sun, smote the eyes of the soldiers in the battle on every side.

**7.100.21**  While the Pāṇḍavas were thus striving, Duryodhana, fearless, O great king, plunged into that vast host.

**7.100.22**  That tumultuous clash between them and him, O Bhārata, became a great undoing of all the armies.

**7.100.23**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: With the armies in such a plight, and himself fallen into hardship, did not Duryodhana, O sūta, wage the battle from the front rather than turn his back?
