**7.100.24**  This clash of one against the many in that great battle, and a king at that, seems to me a grievously unequal thing.

**7.100.25**  He who was reared in the height of comfort, lord of fortune and of the world—encountering many alone, did he not turn his face away?

**7.100.26**  Saṃjaya said: O king, O Bhārata, hear of the wondrous combat of your son, one against the many—a marvel, as I relate it.

**7.100.27**  By Duryodhana, of a sudden, the Pāṇḍava host in battle was thrown into confusion on every side, as a lotus-pool is churned up by an elephant.

**7.100.28**  Seeing the army thus made by your son, O Kaurava, the Pāñcālas, with Bhīmasena at their head, rushed upon him.

**7.100.29**  He pierced Bhīmasena with ten arrows, the two sons of Mādrī with three apiece, Virāṭa and Drupada with six, and Śikhaṇḍin with a hundred.

**7.100.30**  And piercing Dhṛṣṭadyumna with twenty arrows, the son of Dharma with seven, the Kekayas with ten, and the sons of Draupadī with three apiece,

**7.100.31**  with fierce arrows in the battle he hewed down hundreds of other warriors and their chariots with their elephants, enraged like Death amid living beings.

**7.100.32**  Whether nocking or loosing, he could not be seen, his bow bent into a circle, as he smote the foe by his training and the power of his weapons.

**7.100.33**  As he smote the foe, the eldest Pāṇḍava with two broad-headed shafts cut his great gold-backed bow into three pieces, O sire.

**7.100.34**  And he pierced him with many keen arrows well aimed; but striking his mail at once they broke and sank into the earth.

**7.100.35**  Then the rejoicing Pārthas gathered round Yudhiṣṭhira, as at the slaying of Vṛtra the gods, with the great seers, in their joy gathered round Śakra.

**7.100.36**  Then King Duryodhana, taking up a stout bow and crying 'Stand! Stand!' to the king, advanced upon the Pāṇḍava.

**7.100.37**  As your son, that great chariot-warrior, spoke thus, O king, the Pāñcālas, rejoicing and greedy for victory, went forth to meet him.

**7.100.38**  These Droṇa held in check, seeking to win the Pāṇḍava in the fight, as a mountain holds the water-laden clouds driven up by a raging wind.

**7.100.39**  There, O king, was a great combat that swelled vastly, like the playground of Rudra, a destruction of all embodied beings.

**7.101.1**  Saṃjaya said: In the afternoon, O great king, the combat broke out anew, loud as a thundercloud, between Droṇa and the Somakas.

**7.101.2**  Mounting his chariot drawn by red steeds, that hero among men, composed, rushed in the battle upon the Pāṇḍavas at a moderate speed.

**7.101.3**  Devoted to your welfare and weal, that mighty bowman of great strength, born from the noblest of pitchers, with whetted arrows of variegated feathers—

**7.101.4**  singling out, as it were, the choicest among the warriors, O Bhārata—the majestic son of Bharadvāja, O king, sported in the battle.

**7.101.5**  Against him came Bṛhatkṣatra, the great chariot-warrior of the Kekayas, eldest of five heroic brothers, hardened in battle.

**7.101.6**  Loosing keen arrows and thickly covering the preceptor, as a great cloud loosing rain upon Gandhamādana.

**7.101.7**  At him Droṇa, O great king, in fury sent seventeen gold-feathered shafts whetted upon stone.

**7.101.8**  But those dread shafts loosed from Droṇa's bow, like venomous serpents, he cut each one with ten arrows in the fight, as though delighting in it.

**7.101.9**  Seeing that deftness of his, the best of the twice-born, smiling, sent eight smooth-jointed arrows.

**7.101.10**  Seeing those arrows sped from Droṇa's bow swiftly descending, he warded them off with just as many sharp and stout arrows.

**7.101.11**  Then, O great king, there came wonder upon your army, beholding that most arduous feat performed by Bṛhatkṣatra.

**7.101.12**  Then, O great king, Droṇa of mighty austerities, singling out the Kekaya prince, brought forth in battle the divine Brāhma weapon.

**7.101.13**  That weapon, O king, the unshaken Kaikeya of mighty arms warded off in the fray, countering it with the very Brahmā weapon as it was launched.

**7.101.14**  Having beaten back that weapon of the son of Bharadvāja in the encounter, he pierced the brāhmaṇa with sixty stone-whetted shafts feathered with gold.

**7.101.15**  Droṇa, foremost among men, answered him with an iron arrow, which, cleaving his armour, sank into the surface of the earth.

**7.101.16**  As a black serpent set loose enters an anthill, O best of kings, so did that arrow, having pierced the Kaikeya in the fight, enter the earth.

**7.101.17**  Sorely pierced, O great king, by Droṇa the master of weapons, and seized with a mighty wrath, he rolled his fair eyes.

**7.101.18**  He pierced Droṇa with seventy stone-whetted shafts feathered with gold, and struck his charioteer with a broad-headed arrow upon the arms and breast.

**7.101.19**  But Droṇa, pierced in many places by Bṛhatkṣatra, O noble one, let fly sharp arrows toward the Kekaya's chariot.

**7.101.20**  Having thrown Bṛhatkṣatra, that great car-warrior, into confusion, Droṇa loosed a keen arrow toward the Kekaya, O descendant of Bharata.

**7.101.21**  Deeply pierced by it at once between the breasts, O great king, that tiger among men, his heart cleft asunder, fell from his chariot.

**7.101.22**  When Bṛhatkṣatra, the great car-warrior of the Kekayas, was slain, O king, the son of Śiśupāla, greatly enraged, spoke thus to his driver:

**7.101.23**  "Charioteer, drive to where this mailed Droṇa stands, slaughtering all the Kekayas and the host of the Pāñcālas."

**7.101.24**  Hearing those words of his, the charioteer bore that foremost of car-warriors toward Droṇa with swift Kāmboja steeds.

**7.101.25**  And Dhṛṣṭaketu, the bull among the Cedis, of surpassing might, fell suddenly upon Droṇa as a moth falls upon the flame.

**7.101.26**  He pierced Droṇa, with his horses, car, and standard, with sixty arrows, and again with other keen shafts, as one prodding a sleeping tiger.

**7.101.27**  Droṇa, with a sharp razor-headed arrow, cut asunder in the middle the bow of that mighty king as he strove in the encounter.

**7.101.28**  Then the son of Śiśupāla, that great car-warrior, taking up another bow, pierced Droṇa again with sharp and sturdy arrows.

**7.101.29**  Droṇa of mighty strength, having slain his horses and his charioteer, then assailed him with twenty-five arrows.

**7.101.30**  Deprived of his car and bereft of his bow, the king of the Cedis too, enraged in the fray, hurled his mace toward the chariot of the son of Bharadvāja.

**7.101.31**  That mace, rushing down in sudden onset—of terrible form and fearsome, heavy, made of iron and adorned with gold—the son of Bharadvāja brought to the ground with many thousands of arrows.

**7.101.32**  That mace, struck down by the son of Bharadvāja, fell to the earth, decked with red garlands and cloth, like a star falling from the floor of heaven.

**7.101.33**  Seeing his mace struck down, the wrathful Dhṛṣṭaketu swiftly let fly a lance and a gold-gleaming spear.

**7.101.34**  But Droṇa, deft of hand and of mighty strength, cleaving the lance with three arrows in that great battle, sundered the spear at once.

**7.101.35**  Then the glorious son of Bharadvāja, bent on his death, sent against him in battle a sharp arrow to slay him.

**7.101.36**  That arrow, cleaving the armour and the heart of him of measureless might, entered the earth as a wild goose enters a lotus-pool.

**7.101.37**  As a hungry blue jay, O king, devours a moth, so did the heroic Droṇa devour Dhṛṣṭaketu in that great battle.

**7.101.38**  When the king of the Cedis was slain, his son, a master of the highest weapons, overcome by wrath, took his stand in his father's portion of the field.

**7.101.39**  Him too Droṇa, smiling, sent with his arrows to the abode of Yama, as a mighty tiger in the great forest carries off a fawn.

**7.101.40**  As the warriors of the Pāṇḍava side were being thus destroyed, O descendant of Bharata, the heroic son of Jarāsaṃdha himself rushed against Droṇa.

**7.101.41**  And he, O great king, veiling Droṇa with sharp arrows, swiftly made him unseen, as a rain-cloud veils the sun.

**7.101.42**  Beholding that lightness of hand, Droṇa, the crusher of warriors, swiftly loosed his arrows by the hundred and the thousand.

**7.101.43**  Having covered him over in battle, Droṇa then slew the son of Jarāsaṃdha, that foremost of car-warriors standing in his car, before the eyes of all the bowmen.

**7.101.44**  Whoever closed with Droṇa, him Droṇa, like the Ender himself, took away, as the Ender at the appointed hour takes away all living beings.

**7.101.45**  Then Droṇa, the mighty archer, proclaiming his name aloud in the battle, bewildered the warriors of the Pāṇḍava side with many thousands of arrows.

**7.101.46**  Then the arrows that bore Droṇa's mark, gold-feathered and stone-whetted, struck down men, elephants, and horses on every side in the battle.

**7.101.47**  Slaughtered by Droṇa as the great asuras by Śakra, the Pāñcālas trembled like cattle tormented by the cold.

**7.101.48**  Then a terrible wailing arose among the Pāṇḍavas as their troops were being slain by Droṇa, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.101.49**  Bewildered by the arrow-shower of the son of Bharadvāja in the fight, the great car-warriors of the Pāñcālas were as if seized by a cramp in the thighs.

**7.101.50**  And the Cedis, O great king, and the Sṛñjayas and the Somakas, eager and exultant, rushed upon the son of Bharadvāja with longing for battle.

**7.101.51**  "Slay Droṇa, slay Droṇa!" crying thus, those tigers among men advanced upon Droṇa, striving with all their might, seeking in battle to send that one of great splendour to the abode of Yama.

**7.101.52**  But those striving heroes the son of Bharadvāja sent on to Yama with his shafts, the chiefs of the Cedis above all.

**7.101.53**  As those chiefs of the Cedis were being destroyed, O descendant of Bharata, the Pāñcālas, sorely pressed by Droṇa's arrows, trembled.

**7.101.54**  Seeing such deeds of Droṇa, O noble one, they cried out to Bhīmasena and toward the chariot of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

**7.101.55**  "Surely this brāhmaṇa has performed some mighty penance, hard to perform, that he so prevails in battle and consumes the bulls among the warriors."

**7.101.56**  "War is the duty of the warrior, but austerity the highest calling of the brāhmaṇa; an ascetic accomplished in learning could burn up a foe with a mere glance."

**7.101.57**  Into Droṇa's weapon, whose touch is like fire, many bulls among the warriors have entered, O descendant of Bharata, and there, beyond crossing and terrible, have been consumed.

**7.101.58**  "Each according to his strength, his zeal, his courage—Droṇa of great splendour, confounding all beings, slays our forces."

**7.101.59**  Hearing those words of theirs, Kṣatradharman, taking his stand, cut off with a crescent-headed arrow Droṇa's bow together with the shaft set upon it.

**7.101.60**  Grown the more furious thereat, Droṇa, the crusher of warriors, took up another bow, shining and of swifter force.

**7.101.61**  Fitting to it a keen arrow, burden-destroying, bright and firm, the mighty preceptor drew it to the ear and let it fly.

**7.101.62**  That arrow, having slain Kṣatradharman, passed on into the surface of the earth; and he, his heart cleft, fell from his car upon the ground.

**7.101.63**  Then, when the son of Dhṛṣṭadyumna was slain, the armies trembled; and the great car-warrior Cekitāna closed upon Droṇa.

**7.101.64**  He pierced Droṇa with ten arrows between the breasts, his charioteer with four, and his four horses with four.

**7.101.65**  The preceptor pierced his right arm with sixteen arrows, his standard with sixteen, and his driver with seven.

**7.101.66**  When his charioteer was slain, those horses, enwrapped in the arrows of the son of Bharadvāja, bolted in the battle, dragging the car away, O noble one.

**7.101.67**  Seeing Cekitāna's car bolting with its charioteer slain, a great fear came over the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas alike.

**7.101.68**  Routing on every side those gathered heroes in the battle—the Cedis, the Pāñcālas, and the Sṛñjayas—Droṇa shone forth in great splendour, O noble one.

**7.101.69**  Grey to the ears and dark of hue, past eighty years of age, the aged Droṇa ranged through the battle like a youth of sixteen.

**7.101.70**  And his foes, O great king, deemed Droṇa, the slayer of foes, ranging fearlessly, to be Indra himself with the thunderbolt in his hand.

**7.101.71**  Then, O great king, the wise Drupada spoke, O monarch: "This greedy man slays the warriors as a tiger slays small game."

**7.101.72**  "The wicked, evil-minded Duryodhana shall come to grievous realms—he through whose greed the bulls among the warriors are slain in battle."

**7.101.73**  "By the hundred they lie upon the earth, cut down like bulls, their limbs bathed in blood, made food for dogs and jackals."

**7.101.74**  Having spoken thus, O great king, Drupada, lord of an army, placing the sons of Pṛthā at the front, swiftly rushed upon Droṇa in battle.

**7.102.1**  Saṃjaya said: As the battle-arrays of the Pāṇḍavas were thrown into turmoil here and there, the sons of Pṛthā, the Pāñcālas, and the Somakas pursued the foe far afield.

**7.102.2**  While that fierce battle, hair-raising, raged on in the dire destruction of the world, as at the ending of an age, O descendant of Bharata—

**7.102.3**  —while Droṇa pressed valiantly in the fight, roaring again and again, and the Pāñcālas dwindled and the Pāṇḍavas were being slain—

**7.102.4**  Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of righteousness, saw no refuge anywhere, and pondered, O lord of kings: "How shall this end?"

**7.102.5**  Looking then in every direction with a longing to behold Savyasācin, Yudhiṣṭhira saw neither the son of Pṛthā nor the descendant of Madhu.

**7.102.6**  Not seeing that tiger among men marked by the standard of the bull among monkeys, and not hearing the twang of the Gāṇḍīva, his senses were stricken with distress.

**7.102.7**  Nor seeing Sātyaki either, that foremost car-warrior of the Vṛṣṇis, the king of righteousness Yudhiṣṭhira, his whole frame overcome with anxiety, found then no peace, beholding not those two bulls among men.

**7.102.8**  From fear of the world's reproach, the greatly renowned king of righteousness, of mighty arms, fell to musing concerning the chariot of the grandson of Śini.

**7.102.9**  "By me has the grandson of Śini, the true Sātyaki, giver of fearlessness to his friends, been sent upon the track of Phalguna in the battle."

**7.102.10**  "What was once a single care has now become twofold for me this day: for I must look both to Sātyaki and to the Pāṇḍava Dhanaṃjaya."

**7.102.11**  "Having sent Sātyaki to follow upon the track of the Pāṇḍava, whom now shall I send in the battle to follow upon the track of the Sātvata as well?"

**7.102.12**  "If with all effort I make search for my brother, yet seek not after Yuyudhāna, the world will censure me."

**7.102.13**  "'In searching for his brother, Yudhiṣṭhira the king of righteousness has forsaken the Vṛṣṇi Sātyaki of true valour'—so will they say."

**7.102.14**  "From fear of the world's blame, I shall therefore send the son of Pṛthā, Vṛkodara, upon the track of the high-souled descendant of Madhu."

**7.102.15**  "For even as is my love for Arjuna, the slayer of foes, so too is it for that Vṛṣṇi hero, the Sātvata, fierce and unrelenting in battle."

**7.102.16**  "To an overwhelming burden have I appointed the joy of Śini's line; and he, mighty in strength, out of regard for his friends and out of reverence, has entered the Bhārata host as a sea-monster plunges into the ocean."

**7.102.17**  "For yonder is heard the clamour of warriors who turn not back, locked in mutual combat with the wise hero of the Vṛṣṇis."

**7.102.18**  Having weighed the matter many times over and judged it most fitting to the hour, it seems best to me that Bhīmasena the bowman, the son of Pāṇḍu, should go to that very place where the two great car-warriors have gone.

**7.102.19**  There is nothing on earth that Bhīma cannot endure; relying on the strength of his own arms, he is able with ease to hold at bay in battle all the bowmen of the earth, however resolute they stand.

**7.102.20**  Leaning upon the might of that great-souled one's arms, we all returned from our dwelling in the forest, and in our battles we were never overcome.

**7.102.21**  If Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava goes from here toward the Sātvata, then in the fight the Sātvata and Phalguna will both have a protector at hand.

**7.102.22**  To be sure, the Sātvata and Phalguna need not be grieved over in battle, for they are guarded by Vāsudeva himself, and are themselves masters of every weapon.

**7.102.23**  Yet I must surely do something to dispel my own grief; therefore I shall appoint Bhīma to follow upon the Sātvata's track. By this I think the measure on behalf of Sātyaki will be fulfilled.

**7.102.24**  Having resolved thus in his mind, O king, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Dharma said to his charioteer, "Drive me toward Bhīma."

**7.102.25**  Hearing the word of the Dharma-king, the charioteer skilled with horses brought the gold-adorned car near to Bhīma.

**7.102.26**  Having reached Bhīmasena, and calling to mind what the hour demanded, the king sank into despondency even as he gave him many commands.

**7.102.27**  "He who, alone upon his car, conquered the gods together with the Gandharvas and the Daityas — of him, your younger brother Bhīmasena, I see no sign."

**7.102.28**  Then Bhīmasena said to the Dharma-king, who had come to him in such a state, "Never have I seen nor heard such despondency in you."

**7.102.29**  "In days past, when we were torn by sorrows, it was you who were our refuge. Rise up, rise up, lord of kings; command me — what shall I do for you?"

**7.102.30**  "There is nothing impossible for me, nor anything I will not do, O giver of honor. Give the order, best of the Kurus, and do not set your mind upon grief."

**7.102.31**  To him the king, his eyes brimming with tears, hissing like a black serpent, his face withered, spoke these words to Bhīmasena:

**7.102.32**  "As the blast of the conch Pāñcajanya is heard, blown by the glorious Vāsudeva in his fury, surely your brother Dhanaṃjaya lies slain this day."

**7.102.33**  "He being struck down, Janārdana himself surely fights on now — he, by whose valor, mighty in spirit, the Pāṇḍavas live."

**7.102.34**  "To whom in times of peril we resort as the immortals resort to the thousand-eyed one — that hero, seeking the ruler of the Sindhus, followed after the Bhārata host."

**7.102.35**  "Of his going, Bhīma, we know; of his return we have no word — that dark, youthful one, Guḍākeśa, fair to look upon, mighty-armed,"

**7.102.36**  "broad-chested, great-shouldered, with the stride of a rutting elephant, eyes like the cakora bird, copper-hued of eye, swelling the woes of his foes."

**7.102.37**  "This, then — blessings upon you, crusher of foes — is the ground of my grief: for Arjuna's sake, O mighty-armed one, and on the Sātvata's account."

**7.102.38**  "It grows as fire kindled with oblation grows, blazing up again and again. Of him I see no sign, and so I am overcome with despondency."

**7.102.39**  "Know too that tiger among men, the Sātvata, the great car-warrior: he followed afterward upon the track of that great car-warrior, your younger brother. Not seeing that mighty-armed one, I am sunk in despondency."

**7.102.40**  "Therefore Kṛṣṇa, skilled in war, surely now fights on in battle — he by whose valor, mighty in might, the Pāṇḍavas live."

**7.102.41**  "Go you there, son of Kuntī, where Dhanaṃjaya has gone, and Sātyaki of great valor — if you hold my word fit to be obeyed, O knower of dharma, for I am your eldest brother."

**7.102.42**  "You need not be so concerned for Arjuna as you must be for Sātyaki, O Pārtha, who, wishing to do me a kindness, set out along Savyasācin's path — hard to traverse, terrible, impassable to the unschooled in soul."

**7.102.43**  Bhīmasena said: "The car that of old bore Brahmā, Īśāna, Indra, and Varuṇa — mounted upon that, the two Kṛṣṇas have gone; for them there is no fear."

**7.102.44**  "Yet bearing your command upon my head, here I go — grieve not. Having met those tigers among men, I shall send you tidings."

**7.102.45**  Saṃjaya said: Having spoken thus much, the mighty one set forth, entrusting Yudhiṣṭhira again and again to Dhṛṣṭadyumna and to his friends; and Bhīmasena of great strength said this to Dhṛṣṭadyumna:

**7.102.46**  "You know, mighty-armed one, how Droṇa the great car-warrior bends every means toward the capture of the Dharma-king."

**7.102.47**  "No duty in my going, O son of Pṛṣata, weighs upon me as does the guarding of the king; for that is our most pressing task."

**7.102.48**  "Thus has Pārtha bidden me, and I cannot gainsay it; I shall go there where the Saindhava, doomed to die, has taken his stand. By the word of the Dharma-king one must stand without misgiving."

**7.102.49**  "So this day, intent in battle, guard Pārtha Yudhiṣṭhira; for this is, of all our charges, the highest task in the fray."

**7.102.50**  To him, O great king, Dhṛṣṭadyumna said to Vṛkodara, "Go, mighty-armed one, as you desire, untroubled in heart, O Pārtha."

**7.102.51**  "Not until in battle he has slain Dhṛṣṭadyumna will Droṇa ever in the encounter lay hold of the Dharma-king."

**7.102.52**  Then the Pāṇḍava, committing the king to Dhṛṣṭadyumna and saluting his elder, his guide, set forth to where Phalguna was.

**7.102.53**  The son of Kuntī, O Bhārata, was embraced by the Dharma-king, kissed upon the head, and given fair blessings to hear.

**7.102.54**  Bhīmasena, the mighty-armed, mailed, with bright earrings, with armlets, with cuirass, with arrows — the foremost of car-warriors —

**7.102.55**  his armor of black iron, figured with gold and richly wrought, shone like a lightning-laced rain-cloud clinging to a mountain.

**7.102.56**  Well-wrapped in cloths of yellow, red, black, and white, and with his throat-guard, he gleamed like a cloud spanned by Indra's bow.

**7.102.57**  When Bhīmasena had set forth eager for battle against your army, again, O lord of peoples, there rose the terrible blast of the Pāñcajanya.

**7.102.58**  Hearing that terrible roar, vast and terrifying to the three worlds, the mighty-armed son of Dharma again spoke to Bhīma:

**7.102.59**  "This king of conches, the water-born, blown hard by the Vṛṣṇi hero, makes earth and the mid-air resound."

**7.102.60**  "Surely, some great calamity having befallen Savyasācin, the bearer of discus and mace fights now against all the Kurus."

**7.102.61**  "Surely the noble Kuntī, and Draupadī, and Subhadrā behold this day, together with their kinsfolk, the showing of a great evil."

**7.102.62**  "So, Bhīma, set with haste, go where Dhanaṃjaya is; for all the quarters and their sub-quarters seem to swim before me, O Pārtha, out of longing to see Dhanaṃjaya, and on the Sātvata's account."

**7.102.63**  "Go, go," he said again to Bhīmasena. Urged on hard by his brother, that brother who did his brother's pleasure, Bhīma struck the war-drum and blew the conch again and again,

**7.102.64**  and roaring his lion's roar, drawing the bowstring again and again, showing forth his terrible self, he rushed suddenly upon the foe.

**7.102.65**  Him the swift, well-broken, prancing best of horses bore on, harnessed by Viśoka, fleet as mind and wind.

**7.102.66**  Shattering and crushing, drawing the bowstring with his hand, Pārtha, dragging it down and drawing it back, churned up the vanguard of the host.

**7.102.67**  As he went on, that mighty-armed one, the Pāñcālas together with the Somakas, heroes, followed behind him as the immortals follow Maghavan.

**7.102.68**  Him, O great king, your sons born of one womb hemmed in with their troops — Duḥśalā and Citrasena and Kuṇḍabhedī and Viviṃśati,

**7.102.69**  Durmukha and Duḥsaha, and Vikarṇa, and Śala too, Vinda and Anuvinda, Sumukha, Dīrghabāhu, Sudarśana,

**7.102.70**  Vṛndāraka and Suhasta, Suṣeṇa, Dīrghalocana, Abhaya and Raudrakarman, Suvarman and Durvimocana —

**7.102.71**  these foremost of car-warriors, with their varied troops and their followers, girt for battle, the heroes, rushed upon Bhīmasena.

**7.102.72**  Beholding them, the son of Kuntī, valiant Bhīmasena, turned upon them with speed, as a lion upon lesser beasts.

**7.102.73**  There those heroes displayed great celestial weapons, holding off Bhīma with their arrows as clouds hold off the risen sun.

**7.102.74**  Passing them by with speed, he rushed upon Droṇa's division, and the elephant-host before him he overwhelmed with showers of arrows.

**7.102.75**  In but a little while the son of the Wind, sweeping his swift shafts in every direction, scattered that elephant-host.

**7.102.76**  As beasts in the forest are frightened by the roar of the śarabha, all those elephants fled, bellowing dreadful cries.

**7.102.77**  And again, passing on with speed, he rushed upon Droṇa's division; the preceptor held him back as the shore holds back the swollen sea.

**7.102.78**  He struck him on the forehead with an iron shaft, smiling as it were; and the Pāṇḍava shone there like the sun with rays upraised.

**7.102.79**  And the preceptor, supposing that Bhīma would do him honor as Phalguna would, said to Vṛkodara:

**7.102.80**  "Bhīmasena, you cannot pierce into the enemy's host without first conquering me in battle, O mighty one, here amid the foes."

**7.102.81**  "If that younger brother of yours, and Kṛṣṇa, entered with my leave, yet this array, sir, cannot be entered here by you."

**7.102.82**  Then Bhīma, fearless, hearing that word of the teacher, wrathful, his eyes red as copper, hissing with breath, spoke to Droṇa:

**7.102.83**  "Not by your leave, O wretch of a brahmin, did Arjuna enter the field of war; for he, unassailable, could pierce even the host of Śakra."

**7.102.84**  "By him, doing you the highest honor, you have indeed been honored; but I am no Arjuna full of compassion, Droṇa — I am Bhīmasena, your enemy."

**7.102.85**  "You are our father, our teacher, our kinsman, and we are your sons — so we all hold you, and stand before you bowed."

**7.102.86**  "But this day the contrary of that is seen in you as you speak to us. If you hold yourself our enemy, then so be it here; behold, I, Bhīma, do unto you the deed befitting a foe."

**7.102.87**  Then whirling his mace like Death wielding the rod of Time, Bhīma hurled it at Droṇa, O king; and he leaped down from his car.

**7.102.88**  Then it crushed Droṇa's vehicle together with horses, driver, and banner, and ground down many warriors, as the wind grinds trees by its force.

**7.102.89**  Then again your sons surrounded that best of cars; and Droṇa, foremost of strikers, mounting another car —

**7.102.90**  Then, O great king, the wrathful and valiant Bhīmasena overwhelmed the chariot-host before him with showers of arrows.

**7.102.91**  Being struck down in the battle, your sons, the great car-warriors, fought against Bhīma of terrible strength in the fight, seeking victory.

**7.102.92**  Then Duḥśāsana, enraged, hurled a chariot-lance, all of steel and keen, eager to slay the son of Pāṇḍu.

**7.102.93**  That great lance flying upon him, sped by your son, Bhīma cleft in two; and that seemed a wondrous thing.

**7.102.94**  Then, enraged, with other whetted arrows the mighty one slew with three shafts the three — Kuṇḍabhedī, Suṣeṇa, and Dīrghanetra.

**7.102.95**  Then he slew again Vṛndāraka, the hero, the increaser of the Kurus' fame, one of your valiant sons as they fought.

**7.102.96**  Abhaya and Raudrakarman, and Durvimocana too — these three sons of yours Bhīma slew again with three shafts.

**7.102.97**  Being slain, O great king, by that stronger one, your sons hemmed in on every side Bhīma, the foremost of strikers.

**7.102.98**  Vinda and Anuvinda together, and your son Suvarman as well — the son of Kuntī, as though smiling, dispatched them all with his arrows to the abode of Yama.

**7.102.99**  Then, O bull of the Bhāratas, he swiftly pierced your heroic son Sudarśana in the battle, and that one fell and died.

**7.102.100**  In but a little while the son of Pāṇḍu, scattering them with his swift shafts in every direction, shattered that division of chariots.

**7.102.101**  Then, O lord of peoples, like deer at the thunder of his chariot's roar, your sons, slaughtered in the battle and afflicted with dread of Bhīmasena, all fled away together with their chariots.

**7.102.102**  But the son of Kuntī, pursuing the great host of your sons, O king, pierced the Kauravas on every side in the battle.

**7.102.103**  Being slaughtered by Bhīmasena, O great king, your men abandoned Bhīma in the fight and fled, urging on their finest horses.

**7.102.104**  Having vanquished them in the battle, the mighty Bhīmasena, son of Pāṇḍu, let loose a lion's roar and clapped his arms in challenge.

**7.102.105**  And making a great resounding clap of his palms, the mighty Bhīma, leaving the chariot-warriors behind, charged upon Droṇa's division.

**7.103.1**  Saṃjaya said: As he emerged from that division of chariots like the sun from darkness, the preceptor, seeking to hold him back, overwhelmed him with showers of arrows.

**7.103.2**  As though drinking up those floods of shafts loosed from the foremost bow of Droṇa, he advanced against his brothers, bewildering the host with his cunning.

**7.103.3**  Putting forth their utmost speed in the fray, those mighty archers, urged on by your sons, surrounded him on every side.

**7.103.4**  Thus hemmed in, Bhīma, as though laughing, O Bhārata, raised against them that terrible mace and, roaring like a lion, hurled it among them with force, and the mighty one crushed them.

**7.103.5**  Like the thunderbolt hurled by Indra with a steadfast aim, O king, filling the earth as it were with its mighty din, blazing with splendor and terrible, it struck terror into your sons.

**7.103.6**  Seeing that mace of tremendous speed descending, wreathed in splendor, your men all fled, uttering frightful cries.

**7.103.7**  And marking that unbearable sound of it, O sir, the men there, the chariot-warriors, fell down then from their chariots.

**7.103.8**  Having put his foes to flight in the battle, the unassailable son of Kuntī, swift as Suparṇa the king of birds, passed beyond the host.

**7.103.9**  As Bhīmasena, that leader among the leaders of chariot-troops, was thus working havoc, the son of Bharadvāja, O great king, advanced against him.

**7.103.10**  But Droṇa, having checked Bhīma in the battle with waves of arrows, suddenly raised a shout, striking dread into the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.103.11**  That fight between Droṇa and the great-souled Bhīma, O great king, was vast and terrible, like the war of gods and demons.

**7.103.12**  When the warriors were being slain in the battle by hundreds and by thousands by the keen shafts loosed from Droṇa's bow,

**7.103.13**  then the son of Pāṇḍu, leaping down from his chariot and gathering his speed, closing his eyes, O king, advanced on foot against Droṇa.

**7.103.14**  Just as a bull receives the rain at his ease, so Bhīma, that tiger among men, took upon himself the shower of arrows.

**7.103.15**  Though thus assailed in the battle, the mighty one, O sir, seized Droṇa's chariot by the shaft-pole with his hand and flung it away.

**7.103.16**  But Droṇa, hurled aside by Bhīma in the fight, O king, swiftly mounted another chariot and made his way to the gateway of the battle-array.

**7.103.17**  In that instant Bhīmasena's charioteer swiftly urged on his horses, O Kaurava, and that was a wondrous thing to behold.

**7.103.18**  Then, having mounted his own chariot, the mighty Bhīmasena charged with speed against the host of your son.

**7.103.19**  Crushing the warriors in the fray like a raging wind that crushes trees, he went on, cleaving the army like a river's current rending its banks.

**7.103.20**  Reaching the Bhoja division, guarded by the son of Hṛdika, Bhīmasena, having broken it utterly, O king, pressed onward.

**7.103.21**  Terrifying the troops with the clap of his palms, O sir, he overcame all the armies as a tiger overcomes bulls.

**7.103.22**  Passing beyond the Bhoja division and the host of the Kāmbojas, and likewise many other bands of barbarians skilled in warfare,

**7.103.23**  and beholding Sātyaki too, that bull among men, fighting, the son of Kuntī, intent in his chariot, then sped onward swiftly.

**7.103.24**  Bhīmasena, O great king, the son of Pāṇḍu, longing to behold Dhanaṃjaya, passed beyond your warriors in the battle.

**7.103.25**  That valiant one beheld Arjuna there, that bull among men, fighting and striving valiantly for the slaying of the lord of the Sindhus.

**7.103.26**  Seeing Arjuna there, he then sent forth mighty roars, and the son of Pṛthā heard that great shout of his as he roared.

**7.103.27**  Then the son of Pṛthā, uttering a great shout, and Mādhava as well, advanced, O great king, both roaring like bulls.

**7.103.28**  Vāsudeva and Arjuna, hearing the roar of that impetuous one, cried out again and again, longing to behold Vṛkodara.

**7.103.29**  Hearing the roar of Bhīmasena and of Phalguna the archer, the son of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira, rejoiced, O great king.

**7.103.30**  The king became free of sorrow on hearing that mighty roar, and the lord hoped for Dhanaṃjaya's victory in the battle.

**7.103.31**  As Bhīmasena thus roared, fierce in the fray, the mighty-armed son of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira, smiled,

**7.103.32**  and that best of the upholders of righteousness, reflecting, spoke within his heart: 'You have given the signal, Bhīma, and so have fulfilled your elder's word.'

**7.103.33**  'There is no victory in war for those whose enemy you are, O son of Pāṇḍu. By good fortune, Dhanaṃjaya the ambidextrous archer yet lives in the battle.'

**7.103.34**  'By good fortune the hero Sātyaki, of true valor, is safe; by good fortune I hear Vāsudeva and Dhanaṃjaya roaring.'

**7.103.35**  'He by whom, after vanquishing Śakra in battle, the bearer of oblations was gratified — that slayer of foes in the fight, Phalguna, by good fortune lives.'

**7.103.36**  'He upon the strength of whose arms we all depend for our lives — that destroyer of enemy hosts, Phalguna, by good fortune lives.'

**7.103.37**  'He by whom, a single chariot-warrior, the Nivātakavacas, hard for even the gods to conquer, were overcome — by good fortune that son of Pṛthā lives.'

**7.103.38**  'He who vanquished all the Kauravas gathered together for the seizing of the cattle at the city of the Matsyas — by good fortune that son of Pṛthā lives.'

**7.103.39**  'He who slew fourteen thousand Kālakeyas in the great battle by the might of his arms — by good fortune that son of Pṛthā lives.'

**7.103.40**  'He who, on account of Duryodhana's plight, vanquished by the power of his weapons the mighty king of the Gandharvas — by good fortune that son of Pṛthā lives.'

**7.103.41**  'The mighty one crowned with the diadem, with white steeds and Kṛṣṇa for charioteer, ever dear to me — by good fortune Phalguna lives.'

**7.103.42**  'He who, burning with grief for his son and resolved to accomplish a hard deed, seeking the slaying of Jayadratha, took an oath — will that Dhanaṃjaya, I wonder, slay the lord of the Sindhus in battle?'

**7.103.43**  'Shall I, I wonder, meet Arjuna before the sun has set — Arjuna with his vow fulfilled, guarded by Vāsudeva?'

**7.103.44**  'Shall the king of the Sindhus, who delights in Duryodhana's welfare, struck down by Phalguna, gladden our foes — or not?'

**7.103.45**  'Will King Duryodhana, on seeing the lord of the Sindhus laid low in battle by Phalguna, make peace with us?'

**7.103.46**  'On seeing his brothers slain by Bhīmasena in the fight, will the foolish Duryodhana make peace with us?'

**7.103.47**  'And on seeing many other warriors cast down upon the earth, will the foolish Duryodhana feel remorse?'

**7.103.48**  'Shall our enmity be appeased through Bhīṣma alone, and will Suyodhana make a treaty for the protection of those who remain?'

**7.103.49**  As he pondered thus in many ways, O king, overcome with compassion, the terrible battle raged on.

**7.104.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: As the mighty Bhīmasena thus roared with a din like the thunder of clouds, what heroes surrounded him?

**7.104.2**  For I do not see anyone, Saṃjaya, in the three worlds who could stand before the enraged Bhīmasena in battle.

**7.104.3**  As he lifts his mace in the great fray like Death himself, I do not see, my child, who could stand his ground on the field of battle.

**7.104.4**  He who would smash a chariot with a chariot and an elephant with an elephant — who could withstand him in battle, even Śatakratu in person?

**7.104.5**  When the enraged Bhīmasena sought to slay my sons, who, devoted to Duryodhana's good, stood up before him?

**7.104.6**  When the wildfire that is Bhīmasena was about to burn up my sons like grass and reeds at the front of the battle, what heroes stood in his way?

**7.104.7**  Seeing my sons driven off by Bhīma in the fight, as all creatures are by Time, who surrounded Bhīma?

**7.104.8**  When the blazing fire of Bhīma sought to consume my sons, what brave men turned to face him? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.

**7.104.9**  Saṃjaya said: As that great chariot-warrior Bhīmasena thus roared, the mighty Karṇa too rushed upon him with a tumultuous shout.

**7.104.10**  Drawing his powerful bow to its utmost, the impatient and mighty Karṇa, eager for the fight, made ready to display his strength.

**7.104.11**  At the meeting of Karṇa and Bhīma, the limbs of the chariot-warriors and the horsemen alike trembled, as they heard the clap of the two heroes' palms.

**7.104.12**  Hearing the terrible roar of Bhīmasena on the field of battle, the foremost of warriors fancied that sky and earth had become one.

**7.104.13**  At another terrible roar of the great-souled son of Pāṇḍu, the bows of all the warriors in the battle fell to the ground.

**7.104.14**  All the beasts of burden, terrified, let flow their dung and urine, O great king, and lost their senses.

**7.104.15**  Many dreadful portents appeared, O king, at that tumultuous encounter of Bhīma and Karṇa.

**7.104.16**  Then Karṇa wounded Bhīma with a score of arrows, and swiftly pierced his charioteer with five swift shafts.

**7.104.17**  But Bhīmasena, laughing, the mighty one quick of hand, repaid Karṇa in the fight with sixty-four arrows.

**7.104.18**  Karṇa, the great archer, hurled four arrows at him; but Bhīma, before they reached him, cut them to many pieces with his smooth-jointed shafts, O king, displaying the deftness of his hand.

**7.104.19**  Karṇa covered him over with multitudes of arrows again and again, and the son of Pāṇḍu was thus enveloped by Karṇa on every side.

**7.104.20**  The great chariot-warrior cut Karṇa's bow at the grip, and pierced him with many smooth-jointed shafts.

**7.104.21**  Then the son of the charioteer, taking up another bow and stringing it, that great chariot-warrior of terrible deeds, pierced Bhīma in the battle.

**7.104.22**  At this Bhīma, exceedingly enraged and impelled with force, then drove three smooth-jointed shafts deep into the breast of the charioteer's son.

**7.104.23**  With those arrows lodged in the midst of his chest, Karṇa then shone forth, O bull of the Bhāratas, like a lofty three-peaked mountain.

**7.104.24**  And the blood streamed from him, pierced as he was by those mightiest of shafts, as streaks of red ochre run down from a mountain that oozes its mineral ores.

**7.104.25**  Shaken a little, Karṇa, sorely afflicted by that well-aimed blow, set arrow to bow and pierced Bhīma, O sire, and loosed his shafts again by the hundreds and the thousands.

**7.104.26**  Overwhelmed all at once by Karṇa, that firm-bowed archer, the son of Pāṇḍu, smiling, swiftly cut through his bowstring.

**7.104.27**  With a broad-headed shaft he dispatched his charioteer to the abode of Yama, and in the battle that great car-warrior made his four horses lifeless.

**7.104.28**  Then from that chariot whose horses were slain Karṇa leapt down, O lord of peoples, and the great car-warrior mounted the chariot of Vṛṣasena.

**7.104.29**  Having vanquished Karṇa in battle, the valiant Bhīmasena roared a mighty roar like the thunder of a storm-cloud.

**7.104.30**  Hearing that roar of his, Yudhiṣṭhira was filled with joy, deeming Karṇa vanquished by Bhīmasena, O Bhārata.

**7.104.31**  On every side the host of Pāṇḍu then raised the blare of conches; and hearing the clamour of the enemy's army your men too sent up their cries. Pārtha twanged the Gāṇḍīva, and Kṛṣṇa sounded his conch Pāñcajanya.

**7.104.32**  Drowning out that din, the roar of Bhīma as he bellowed was heard, O great king, throughout all the armies, O Bhārata.

**7.104.33**  Then those two tamers of foes contended each apart with their weapons: Rādheya gently at first, and the son of Pāṇḍu with full force.

**7.105.1**  Saṃjaya said: When that host was thrown into confusion, with Arjuna gone toward the Saindhava, and the Sātvata and Bhīmasena as well, your son hastened up to Droṇa upon his single chariot, pondering the many things that must be done.

**7.105.2**  That chariot of your son, urged with the utmost speed, swift as thought and as the wind, rushed straight upon Droṇa.

**7.105.3**  And your son, his eyes red with agitation, said to him: "Arjuna and Bhīmasena and the unvanquished Sātyaki—

**7.105.4**  these great car-warriors, having overcome our vast armies, those grinders of foes, have reached the neighbourhood of the king of the Sindhus; and there too they all contend, every one of them unvanquished.

**7.105.5**  If indeed Pārtha, that great car-warrior, has passed you by in battle, how is it that you have been passed by Sātyaki and Bhīma as well, O bestower of honour?

**7.105.6**  It is held a marvel in this world, like the drying up of the ocean, that you, O foremost of brāhmaṇas, should be overcome by the Sātvata and by Arjuna.

**7.105.7**  And by Bhīmasena likewise—so all the world keeps saying in wonder: how was Droṇa, that master of the whole science of archery, conquered in battle?

**7.105.8**  Surely it is my own ruin in this war—luckless that I am—when three car-warriors have passed beyond you, O tiger among men.

**7.105.9**  Things having come to this pass, tell me what you would say. What is gone is gone; consider now what remains, O bestower of honour.

**7.105.10**  Whatever must be done at once for the king of the Sindhus, now that the moment has come—let your honour speak it quickly, and let it be well arranged."

**7.105.11**  Droṇa said: Much, O great king, is the work to be pondered there; hear my mind upon it. Three great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas have broken through; as great is the danger behind them as before them.

**7.105.12**  That side I deem the weightier where Kṛṣṇa and Dhanaṃjaya are; for the Bhārata host is now hemmed in both before and behind.

**7.105.13**  In this case I judge the task to be the guarding of the Saindhava; he, my son, is most to be protected by us, terrified as he is of the wrathful Dhanaṃjaya.

**7.105.14**  For the heroes Yuyudhāna and Vṛkodara have gone against the Saindhava; now is come upon us that very gambling-match which sprang from Śakuni's cunning.

**7.105.15**  In the assembly-hall there was neither true victory nor defeat; but here, my son, as we throw our stakes today, victory and defeat are at hand.

**7.105.16**  Those dread dice that Śakuni cast in the Kuru assembly—reckoning them mere dice—they were in truth unconquerable arrows.

**7.105.17**  Where your many Kurus stand arrayed, my son, know the army for the gaming-board and the arrows for the dice, O lord of peoples.

**7.105.18**  And the Saindhava is the stake, O king; herein lies the issue of this game; for upon the Saindhava the great gambling with the foe is now joined.

**7.105.19**  Here, O great king, all of us, laying down our very lives, must duly make the protection of the Saindhava in the fight; for there, my son, as we cast our stakes, victory and defeat are certain to fall.

**7.105.20**  Where your mighty archers stand intent, guarding the Saindhava—go there yourself with all speed, and protect those very protectors.

**7.105.21**  But I myself shall remain right here, and I will send others, and will hold off the Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍus and the Sṛñjayas.

**7.105.22**  Then Duryodhana set forth at once at the teacher's command, rousing himself for the fierce deed, with his train of followers behind him.

**7.105.23**  But the two Pāñcālas, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, guards of Arjuna's wheels, having come round the army by an outer path, made their way to Savyasācin.

**7.105.24**  For those two, O great king, had earlier been held off by Kṛtavarman when Arjuna, O king, had entered your host in his eagerness to fight.

**7.105.25**  With those two the mighty Bhārata Duryodhana joined a surpassing combat—swift against the swift, the brothers and he.

**7.105.26**  Both of them, bows uplifted, rushed upon him—those two renowned as great car-warriors, foremost of kṣatriyas in battle.

**7.105.27**  Yudhāmanyu, blazing with wrath, in haste loosed thirty steel shafts into your son's breast.

**7.105.28**  Duryodhana too, O lord of kings, slew the four horses of Uttamaujas the Pāñcāla and both his flanking charioteers.

**7.105.29**  Uttamaujas, his horses slain and his driver slain in the fight, made haste and mounted the chariot of his brother Yudhāmanyu.

**7.105.30**  Having gained his brother's chariot, he struck Duryodhana's horses with many shafts; slain, they fell to the ground.

**7.105.31**  His horses fallen, Yudhāmanyu with a choice shaft swiftly cut Duryodhana's bow and his quiver in the battle.

**7.105.32**  Leaping down from that chariot whose horses and driver were slain, your son, the great car-warrior, took up his mace and rushed at the two Pāñcālas.

**7.105.33**  Beholding him bearing down upon them in fury—that conqueror of hostile cities—Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas sprang down from their chariot's seat.

**7.105.34**  Then, mace in hand, he shattered with his mace that splendid car bright with gold, horses, driver, banner and all, in the fray.

**7.105.35**  Having destroyed it, your son—his own horses slain and his driver slain—that scorcher of foes swiftly mounted the chariot of the king of the Madras.

**7.105.36**  And the two princes, foremost of the Pāñcālas and mighty in strength, mounting another chariot, went on toward Dhanaṃjaya.

**7.106.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Those two mighty ones, Karṇa and Bhīma, locked in combat near Arjuna's chariot—what manner of battle did it become?

**7.106.2**  For Karṇa had earlier been vanquished by Bhīmasena in the fight; how did Rādheya, that great car-warrior, come once more against Bhīma?

**7.106.3**  Or how did Bhīma go forth in battle to meet the son of the sūta, that man renowned as a great car-warrior, the foremost chariot-fighter on earth?

**7.106.4**  Passing over Bhīṣma and Droṇa, the son of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira, took no fear from any other save Karṇa the bowman.

**7.106.5**  Out of fear he never sleeps, ever brooding on that great car-warrior; how then did Bhīma fight that son of the sūta in battle?

**7.106.6**  How did Bhīma do battle with Karṇa—reverent of brāhmaṇas, endowed with valour, never turning back in fights, the best of warriors?

**7.106.7**  Those two heroes who came together near Arjuna's chariot—how indeed did they fight, the son of the sūta and Vṛkodara?

**7.106.8**  Brotherhood had been shown to him before, and that son of the sūta is compassionate too; how did he fight with Bhīma, remembering Kuntī's words?

**7.106.9**  Or how did the hero Bhīma, recalling the enmity wrought of old, do battle with the son of the sūta, with Karṇa, in the fight?

**7.106.10**  And ever, O sūta, does my son Duryodhana cherish the hope, "Karṇa will conquer the assembled Pāṇḍavas in the war."

**7.106.11**  He on whom rests the hope of victory of my dull-witted son in the war—how did he do battle with Bhīmasena of terrible deeds?

**7.106.12**  He, leaning upon whom my sons, the great car-warriors, made this feud—how, my son, did Bhīma fight that son of the sūta?

**7.106.13**  Recalling the many insults that had sprung from the son of the sūta, how did Bhīma do battle with the sūta's offspring?

**7.106.14**  He who, valiant, conquered the whole earth with a single chariot—how did Bhīma fight that son of the sūta in battle?

**7.106.15**  He who was born together with his earrings and his armour—how did Bhīma fight that son of the sūta in the encounter?

**7.106.16**  How the battle between those two went, and which of the two was victorious—tell me that truly, for you are skilled in such telling, Saṃjaya.

**7.106.17**  Saṃjaya said: But Bhīmasena, leaving aside Rādheya, that best of car-warriors, sought to go to where the heroes Kṛṣṇa and Dhanaṃjaya stood.

**7.106.18**  As he set off, Rādheya rushed after him and rained upon him heron-feathered shafts, O great king, as a cloud rains upon a mountain.

**7.106.19**  His face, with its smile, like a blooming lotus, the mighty son of Adhiratha then hailed Bhīma in challenge as he went on through the battle.

**7.106.20**  Bhīmasena could not brook that challenge from Karṇa in the fight; wheeling round in a half-circle, he engaged the son of the sūta in battle.

**7.106.21**  With straight-flying arrows of mighty iron he rained upon him in that single combat—upon that mailed and resolute one, the best of all who bear arms.

**7.106.22**  Wishing to make an end of the quarrel, eager to slay Karṇa, the mighty one wore him down, longing, once he had killed him, to slay all the rest.

**7.106.23**  Against him that scorcher of foes, the wrathful, impatient son of Pāṇḍu, loosed fierce showers of arrows of every kind, O sire.

**7.106.24**  Those arrow-showers of his, who moved with the gait of a rutting elephant, the son of the sūta of mighty fame swallowed up by his magic art of weapons.

**7.106.25**  Thus, O great king, that great archer Karṇa, well honoured by his learning as is fitting, moved through the battle like a master.

**7.106.26**  As Bhīmasena fought with vehemence, Rādheya, as if smiling, the impatient one, bore down upon that Vṛkodara.

**7.106.27**  That smile of Karṇa in the encounter the son of Kuntī could not endure, while the heroes fought and looked on from every side.

**7.106.28**  As Karṇa drew near, the mighty Bhīmasena, in wrath, pierced him in the breast with calf-tooth shafts, as one goads a great elephant with the hook.

**7.106.29**  And the bright-armoured charioteer of the son of the sūta he pierced with thrice seven keen, fair-feathered, well-loosed shafts.

**7.106.30**  The hero Karṇa pierced Bhīma's horses, swift as the wind and covered with nets of gold, with five arrows and five more apiece.

**7.106.31**  Then a net wrought of arrows, fashioned by Karṇa against Bhīmasena's chariot, appeared, O king, in half the wink of an eye.

**7.106.32**  There the son of Pāṇḍu, with his chariot, his banner and his driver, was wholly covered over, O great king, by the shafts sped from Karṇa's bow.

**7.106.33**  Karṇa with sixty-four shafts shattered Bhīma's stout armour, and in his wrath smote him in the side with iron arrows that pierced the vitals.

**7.106.34**  Then, heedless of those swift shafts sped from Karṇa's bow, Vṛkodara, unshaken, closed in upon the son of the sūta.

**7.106.35**  Bearing the arrows loosed from Karṇa's bow, O great king—shafts like venomous serpents—Bhīma felt no flinch of distress in the battle.

**7.106.36**  Then with thirty-two whetted, keen-pointed broad-headed arrows the valorous Bhīmasena pierced Karṇa in the fight.

**7.106.37**  With no effort at all Karṇa overwhelmed with his shafts the mighty-armed Bhīmasena, who sought the death of the Saindhava.

**7.106.38**  Rādheya fought Bhīma in the battle gently at first, while Bhīma, recalling their old enmity, fought him in wrath.

**7.106.39**  Bhīmasena, intolerant of insult, would not endure the slight; that conqueror of foes swiftly let loose a rain of arrows upon him.

**7.106.40**  Those arrows sped by Bhīmasena in the fray, O king, fearsome and falling on every side, screamed like birds in flight.

**7.106.41**  Gold-feathered, O great king, sped from Bhīmasena's bow, they rushed upon Rādheya as wolves upon a lesser beast.

**7.106.42**  But Karṇa, foremost of chariot-warriors, covered on every side, O king, loosed in turn his own fierce showers of arrows in the fight.

**7.106.43**  Those shafts of his, like thunderbolts, splendid in battle, Vṛkodara cut down with many broad-headed arrows before they reached him.

**7.106.44**  And again, O Bhārata, Karṇa Vaikartana covered the great chariot-warrior Bhīmasena with a rain of arrows in the fight.

**7.106.45**  There, O Bhārata, we beheld Bhīma in the battle, his body bristling with arrows like a porcupine with its quills.

**7.106.46**  Gold-feathered, stone-whetted shafts sped from Karṇa's bow the hero bore in battle, as the sun bears its own rays.

**7.106.47**  His every limb drenched with blood, Bhīmasena shone like a palāśa tree in the forest with its blossoms bright as gold.

**7.106.48**  But Bhīma, O great king, that mighty archer, did not endure this deed of Karṇa's in the battle, and in his wrath he rolled his eyes.

**7.106.49**  He struck Karṇa with twenty-five iron shafts—as one strikes a white mountain—shafts whose barbs lay hidden and whose touch was venomous.

**7.106.50**  Then Bhīma, valiant as a god, pierced the son of the charioteer once more, with six and then with eight shafts in his vital points in that great battle.

**7.106.51**  Then the valorous Bhīmasena, full of fury, swiftly cut to pieces Karṇa's bow and all its fittings.

**7.106.52**  In haste he slew his four horses and his charioteer with arrows, and with iron shafts bright as the sun's rays he pierced Karṇa in the breast.

**7.106.53**  All those shafts, having pierced Karṇa through, sank into the earth, O sir, as the rays of the sun pass through and beyond a cloud, O king.

**7.106.54**  Reduced to great helplessness, his bow severed and tormented by arrows, that proud man, full of manhood as he was, withdrew to another chariot.

**7.107.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: He in whom my sons forever placed their hope of victory, Saṃjaya—seeing him turned away from the battle, what then did Duryodhana say, and what, my son, did Karṇa do next in the fight?

**7.107.2**  Saṃjaya said: Beholding Bhīmasena in the battle blazing like fire, Karṇa mounted another chariot duly equipped and rushed again upon the Pāṇḍava, like the ocean lashed by the wind.

**7.107.3**  Seeing the son of Adhiratha enraged, O lord of peoples, your sons reckoned Bhīmasena as already offered into the mouth of the son of Vivasvat.

**7.107.4**  Making a great twang of his bow and a terrible slap of his palm, Rādheya bore down upon Bhīmasena's chariot.

**7.107.5**  Then once more, O king, there arose a great and most dreadful clash between the son of the charioteer and Bhīma, O lord of peoples.

**7.107.6**  For those two mighty-armed warriors, enraged and each seeking the other's death, gazed upon one another as though they would burn each other with their eyes.

**7.107.7**  Their eyes red with wrath, both enraged and breathing hard, those great chariot-warriors, those tamers of foes, closing on each other in the fight, hewed at one another.

**7.107.8**  Furious as two tigers, swift as two hawks, raging as two śarabhas, they fought with one another.

**7.107.9**  Then Bhīma, that tamer of foes, recalled the torments suffered at the dice-game and in the forest too, and the misery endured in the city of Virāṭa.

**7.107.10**  And the seizing of their kingdoms, rich in jewels, by your sons, and the unending torments inflicted by you together with your son—

**7.107.11**  How you sought to burn Kuntī, guiltless, together with her sons, and the abuse of Kṛṣṇā in the midst of the assembly by those wicked men—

**7.107.12**  "Seek another husband; your husbands are no more; the Pārthas are all fallen into hell, like seeds of sesame without kernel."

**7.107.13**  What the Kurus said then before your eyes, O Kaurava, when your sons desired to use Kṛṣṇā as a bondwoman to be enjoyed—

**7.107.14**  And the harsh words Karṇa spoke against them as they set forth into exile, clothed in black antelope-skins, there in the assembly, in your presence—

**7.107.15**  And how, counting the Pārthas as so much straw, your son had exulted—he, secure himself, over them in their distress, his wits gone in his fury—

**7.107.16**  Brooding on these sorrows from his childhood on, that slayer of foes, the righteous Vṛkodara, grew weary of his very life.

**7.107.17**  Then, drawing his great gold-backed and unassailable bow, that tiger of the Bhāratas, careless of his own life, rushed upon Karṇa.

**7.107.18**  With nets of arrows, gleaming and stone-whetted, Bhīma cloaked Karṇa's chariot and veiled the very radiance of the sun.

**7.107.19**  Then the son of Adhiratha, laughing, swiftly hurling his keen shafts, scattered Bhīmasena's nets of arrows with his own feathered ones.

**7.107.20**  The great chariot-warrior, mighty-armed and mighty in strength, the son of Adhiratha, pierced Bhīma with nine swift and whetted arrows.

**7.107.21**  Like an elephant goaded with hooks, held back by those winged shafts, Vṛkodara, undismayed, charged at the son of the charioteer.

**7.107.22**  As that bull of the Pāṇḍavas rushed on swift and impetuous, Karṇa advanced to meet him in combat, as one rutting elephant meets another.

**7.107.23**  Then, his conch blown and a hundred kettledrums resounding, the host was stirred with joy, like the ocean upheaved.

**7.107.24**  Seeing that host upheaved, with its chariots, elephants, horses, and foot, Bhīma closed with Karṇa and covered him with arrows.

**7.107.25**  Karṇa, his horses the color of the antelope, mingled them in battle with the swan-white steeds of the Pāṇḍava as he covered him with shafts.

**7.107.26**  Seeing the antelope-hued horses mingled with the white ones, swift as the wind, the host of your sons broke into cries of dismay.

**7.107.27**  Those horses, swift as the wind, mingled together, shone in their multitude, white and dark, O great king, like clouds in the sky.

**7.107.28**  Beholding Karṇa and Vṛkodara enraged, their eyes copper-red with wrath, the great chariot-warriors of your side trembled in terror.

**7.107.29**  The battlefield of those two was terrible as the realm of Yama, hard to look upon, O best of the Bhāratas, like the city of the king of the dead.

**7.107.30**  Watching that wondrous spectacle as if it were a festival, the great chariot-warriors could not clearly discern victory for either in the warding off of the other.

**7.107.31**  They watched the clash of those two, their great weapons drawn close, a clash born of your ill counsel, O king, yours and your son's, O lord of peoples.

**7.107.32**  Those two slayers of foes, covering one another with keen arrows, made the sky veiled with nets of shafts by their showers of arrows.

**7.107.33**  Those two great chariot-warriors, each striving to slay the other with sharp arrows, were a most beautiful sight, like two rain-laden clouds pouring down.

**7.107.34**  Loosing arrows wrought with gold, those two tamers of foes made the sky blaze as if with falling meteors of fire, O lord.

**7.107.35**  Loosed by the two, the shafts fledged with heron and peacock feathers shone in their rows, like flights of exultant cranes in the autumn sky.

**7.107.36**  Seeing Bhīma, that tamer of foes, locked in combat with the son of the charioteer, Kṛṣṇa and Dhanaṃjaya thought the burden upon Bhīma too great.

**7.107.37**  There, struck hard by the arrows loosed by the son of Adhiratha and by Bhīma, horses, men, and elephants fell beyond even the range of the shafts.

**7.107.38**  By the many falling and fallen, lifeless beyond number, a great slaughter was wrought, O great king, among the people of your sons.

**7.107.39**  In an instant the earth was covered over with the lifeless bodies of men, horses, and elephants, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.108.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Most wondrous I deem the prowess of Bhīmasena, in that he made Karṇa, deft and swift in battle, give fight to him.

**7.108.2**  That Karṇa, who in battle could hold off even the thirty gods arrayed for war and bearing every weapon, together with yakṣas, asuras, and men—

**7.108.3**  How could he not overcome the Pāṇḍava in the fight, who shone as if with glory in the battle? Tell me that, my son Saṃjaya.

**7.108.4**  And how did the battle between those two unfold once more, that desperate gamble for life? On this, I think, hangs victory or defeat.

**7.108.5**  Having Karṇa in the battle, O charioteer, my son Suyodhana dares to hope he can conquer the Pārthas, together with Govinda and the Sātvatas.

**7.108.6**  But hearing that Karṇa was vanquished, and not once only, by Bhīmasena of dreadful deeds in the battle, a daze well-nigh overcomes me.

**7.108.7**  Undone I deem the Kauravas through the misrule of my son; for Karṇa will not vanquish the Pārthas, those mighty archers, O Saṃjaya.

**7.108.8**  In all the battles Karṇa has waged with the sons of Pāṇḍu, everywhere the Pāṇḍavas have defeated Karṇa on the field of war.

**7.108.9**  Unconquerable are the Pāṇḍavas, my son, even by the gods with Vāsava among them; yet my dull-witted son Duryodhana does not perceive it.

**7.108.10**  Having seized the wealth of Pārtha as one might seize the wealth of the lord of riches, my foolish son, like a man greedy for honey, does not see the fall before him.

**7.108.11**  Skilled in fraud, having stolen by fraud the kingdom of those great-souled ones, and reckoning them already conquered, he holds the Pāṇḍavas in contempt.

**7.108.12**  And by me too, overborne by love for my son and undisciplined in soul, were the great-souled sons of Pāṇḍu, steadfast in dharma, wronged.

**7.108.13**  Pārtha Yudhiṣṭhira, ever desiring peace and far-sighted, was spurned by my sons, who reckoned him powerless.

**7.108.14**  Taking all those manifold sorrows and outrages to heart, the mighty-armed Bhīma fought the son of the charioteer.

**7.108.15**  Therefore tell me, Saṃjaya, how Karṇa and Bhīma, those two foremost in war, fought in the battle, each seeking the other's death.

**7.108.16**  Saṃjaya said: Hear, O king, how the combat unfolded between Karṇa and Bhīma, each seeking the other's death, like two elephants in the forest.

**7.108.17**  O king, Vaikartana, enraged, advancing in valor upon Bhīma the tamer of foes—enraged and valiant in turn—pierced him with thirty arrows.

**7.108.18**  With swift, bright-pointed arrows adorned with gold, Vaikartana struck Bhīma, O best of the Bhāratas.

**7.108.19**  As he loosed his shafts, Bhīma cut his bow with three whetted arrows, and with a broad-headed shaft struck his driver down from the chariot-seat to the ground.

**7.108.20**  Then Vaikartana, that bull among men, longing for Bhīmasena's death, laid hold of a spear with a shaft bright with gold and lapis.

**7.108.21**  Grasping that great spear, like a second spear of Death, the mighty Rādheya raised it, took his aim, and hurled it at Bhīmasena, as though to make an end of his life.

**7.108.22**  Having hurled the spear as Puraṃdara hurls the thunderbolt, the mighty son of the sūta, Rādheya, roared a tremendous roar; and hearing that roar your sons were filled with joy.

**7.108.23**  That spear loosed from Karṇa's arm, blazing like the sun and like fire, Bhīma cut to pieces in mid-air with seven swift arrows.

**7.108.24**  Having shattered that spear, which resembled a serpent freed from its slough, Bhīma then, O venerable one, as though seeking out the very life-breath of the son of the sūta,

**7.108.25**  in his fury sent forth in battle nine arrows fledged with peacock plumes, gold-shafted, whetted upon stone, like to the rod of Yama.

**7.108.26**  Karṇa too, taking up another bow, gold-backed and hard to withstand, and drawing it, that mighty-splendored one let fly nine shafts.

**7.108.27**  Those the son of Pāṇḍu cut apart with nine smooth-jointed shafts; and having severed the nine great arrows loosed by Vasuṣeṇa, O great king, Bhīma roared as a lion roars.

**7.108.28**  The two mighty ones, bellowing like bulls over a cow in heat, roared exceedingly at one another like two tigers.

**7.108.29**  Each longing to strike the other, each watching for the other's opening, they glared at one another like two great bulls in the cattle-pens.

**7.108.30**  Closing like two great elephants goring each other with the tips of their tusks, they smote one another with arrows loosed from bows drawn to the full.

**7.108.31**  Scorching each other, O great king, with showers of arrows, they glared at one another, their eyes wide open in wrath.

**7.108.32**  Laughing at one another and taunting each other again and again, sounding their conches the while, they fought together.

**7.108.33**  Once more Bhīma cut his bow asunder at the grip, O venerable one, and with his arrows sent his conch-white horses to the abode of Yama.

**7.108.34**  Seeing Karṇa thus brought to straits, King Duryodhana, trembling as it were with rage, then gave command to Durjaya:

**7.108.35**  "Go, Durjaya, before the Pāṇḍava devours Rādheya; swiftly slay this hornless one and lend your strength to Karṇa."

**7.108.36**  Thus addressed, your son answered "So be it," and rushed upon Bhīmasena, who was engaged elsewhere, scattering arrows as he came.

**7.108.37**  He afflicted Bhīma with nine arrows, his horses with eight, his driver with six, his standard with three, and Bhīma again with seven.

**7.108.38**  Bhīmasena too, greatly enraged, with his swift shafts pierced Durjaya in his vitals and, horses and charioteer with him, sent him to the dwelling of Yama.

**7.108.39**  As your richly adorned son lay crushed upon the earth, writhing like a serpent, Karṇa, weeping and stricken with grief, made a reverent circuit about him.

**7.108.40**  But Bhīma, having stripped his bitter foe of his chariot, smiling, covered him over with masses of arrows as a śataghnī is studded with spikes.

**7.108.41**  Yet even so the mighty car-warrior Karṇa, that scorcher of foes, though pierced through by the shafts, did not abandon the wrathful-visaged Bhīma in the fight.

**7.109.1**  Saṃjaya said: Karṇa, thus deprived of his chariot and again vanquished by Bhīma, mounting another car, straightway pierced the Pāṇḍava.

**7.109.2**  Closing like two great elephants goring each other with the tips of their tusks, they smote one another with arrows loosed from bows drawn to the full.

**7.109.3**  Then Karṇa afflicted Bhīma sorely with multitudes of arrows, roared a mighty roar, and again pierced him in the chest.

**7.109.4**  Bhīma pierced him back with ten straight-flying arrows, and pierced him again with twenty smooth-jointed shafts.

**7.109.5**  But Karṇa, O king, having pierced Bhīma with nine arrows between the breasts, pierced his standard with a single keen shaft.

**7.109.6**  Then the son of Pṛthā pierced him in return with sixty-three shafts, as a great elephant is goaded with hooks, or a horse with whips.

**7.109.7**  Sorely pierced, O great king, by the illustrious Pāṇḍava, that hero, licking the corners of his mouth, his eyes red with wrath,

**7.109.8**  then, O great king, loosed at Bhīmasena an arrow that could rend any body, as Indra hurls the thunderbolt against the Daityas.

**7.109.9**  That gaily-feathered shaft, loosed from the sūta's son's bow, having pierced the son of Pṛthā in battle, passed on and split the ground.

**7.109.10**  Without hesitation Bhīma hurled at the sūta's son a heavy mace, wholly of iron, four cubits long, banded with gold and six-edged.

**7.109.11**  With that mace the wrathful Bhārata slew the goodly, well-trained steeds of the son of Adhiratha, as Indra slew the Asuras with the thunderbolt.

**7.109.12**  Then the mighty-armed Bhīma, O bull of the Bhāratas, with two razor-edged arrows cut down the standard of Adhiratha's son and struck down his charioteer.

**7.109.13**  Forsaking the car whose horses and driver were slain and whose standard had fallen, Karṇa, twanging his bow, stood there, O Bhārata, downcast in heart.

**7.109.14**  There we beheld a wondrous feat of Rādheya's prowess: bereft of his chariot, that best of car-warriors yet held his enemy at bay.

**7.109.15**  Seeing the son of Adhiratha, that foremost of car-warriors, deprived of his car in the battle, Duryodhana then, O king, spoke to Durmukha:

**7.109.16**  "This Rādheya, O Durmukha, has been stripped of his chariot by Bhīma; furnish that best of men, that mighty car-warrior, with a car."

**7.109.17**  Hearing Duryodhana's word, O Bhārata, Durmukha hastened to Karṇa and held Bhīma off with arrows.

**7.109.18**  Beholding Durmukha in the fray hastening to the side of the sūta's son, the son of Vāyu rejoiced, licking the corners of his mouth.

**7.109.19**  Then, O great king, having warded off Karṇa with his arrows, the Pāṇḍava swiftly drove his car toward Durmukha.

**7.109.20**  In that instant, O great king, with nine well-feathered, smooth-jointed shafts Bhīma sent Durmukha to the abode of Yama.

**7.109.21**  Then, Durmukha being slain, the son of Adhiratha mounted that very car and shone, O king, like the radiant sun.

**7.109.22**  Seeing Durmukha lying with his vitals pierced and bathed in blood, Karṇa, his eyes filled with tears, for a moment did not advance.

**7.109.23**  Passing by the lifeless one and making a reverent circuit about him, the hero Karṇa, sighing long and hot, could do nothing at all.

**7.109.24**  In that opening, O king, Bhīmasena loosed at the sūta's son fourteen iron arrows fledged with vulture-feathers.

**7.109.25**  Those gold-shafted, exceedingly powerful arrows, splendidly wrought with gold, O great king, having pierced his armor, lit up the ten directions,

**7.109.26**  and, feeding upon blood, drank the blood of the sūta's son, O lord of men, like enraged serpents urged on by Death.

**7.109.27**  Gliding upon the earth, those shafts shone forth as, half-entered into their holes, great serpents furiously dart.

**7.109.28**  Rādheya pierced him in return, without hesitation, with fourteen exceedingly fierce iron arrows adorned with gold.

**7.109.29**  Those terrible winged shafts, having pierced through Bhīmasena's left arm, entered the earth as birds plunge into the Krauñca mountain.

**7.109.30**  Those iron arrows, entering the earth, shone like the blazing rays of the day-maker as he goes to his setting.

**7.109.31**  Bhīma, pierced in battle by those vital-rending iron arrows, streamed forth blood in abundance as a mountain pours down water.

**7.109.32**  That Bhīma, stretched to his utmost, pierced the sūta's son with three winged shafts swift as Suparṇa, and his charioteer with seven.

**7.109.33**  Reeling, O great king, and sore afflicted by Bhīma's might, the illustrious Karṇa abandoned the battle and fled away with his swift horses.

**7.109.34**  But Bhīmasena, twanging his gold-decked bow, that mighty car-warrior stood in the battle blazing like the fire that devours offerings.

**7.110.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Fate, I deem, is supreme; fie upon human effort, that comes to naught, since the son of Adhiratha, straining his utmost, could not overcome the Pāṇḍava in battle.

**7.110.2**  "Karṇa is able to conquer the sons of Pṛthā together with Govinda in battle, and I see no warrior in the world equal to Karṇa" — thus did I hear Duryodhana prate again and again.

**7.110.3**  "For Karṇa is mighty, a hero, firm of bow, conqueror of fatigue" — thus the foolish Duryodhana spoke to me of old, O sūta.

**7.110.4**  "With Vasuṣeṇa for my ally, not even the gods are a match for me in war, O king — how much less the sons of Pāṇḍu, drained of strength and bereft of sense."

**7.110.5**  Now, seeing Karṇa there vanquished, like a serpent drained of its venom, withdrawn from the fight — what, pray, did Duryodhana say?

**7.110.6**  Alas, in his bewilderment he sent Durmukha alone, unskilled in warfare, into the battle, as a moth is sent into the fire.

**7.110.7**  Aśvatthāman, the king of the Madras, Kṛpa, and Karṇa, even joined together, are surely unable to stand before Bhīma, O Saṃjaya.

**7.110.8**  They too, knowing his most terrible strength, like that of ten thousand elephants, and the cruel resolve of that one whose splendor is the Wind's,

**7.110.9**  why, knowing his might, his fury, and his valor, would they provoke in battle that one of cruel deeds, who is like Yama, Time, and the Ender?

**7.110.10**  Yet Karṇa alone, the mighty-armed son of the sūta, relying on the strength of his own arms, made light of Bhīmasena and fought him in battle.

**7.110.11**  He who vanquished Karṇa in battle as Puraṃdara vanquished the Asura — that son of Pāṇḍu can be conquered by none in the fight.

**7.110.12**  Bhīma, who, crushing Droṇa, alone penetrated my host in search of Dhanaṃjaya — who that wished to live would withstand him?

**7.110.13**  For who, O Saṃjaya, would dare to stand before Bhīma, as a Dānava before great Indra with his thunderbolt upraised?

**7.110.14**  A man might come even to the city of the king of the dead and return, but having come upon Bhīmasena he would never return.

**7.110.15**  Like moths into the fire those dull-witted ones plunged, who in their bewilderment rushed against the wrathful Bhīmasena.

**7.110.16**  That oath which Bhīma swore in the assembly, touching the slaughter of my sons, the fierce and furious one, in the hearing of the Kurus then —

**7.110.17**  surely remembering that, and seeing Karṇa vanquished, Duḥśāsana with his brother drew back from Bhīma out of fear.

**7.110.18**  And he of evil mind, O Saṃjaya, who said again and again in the council, "Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and I shall conquer the Pāṇḍavas in battle" —

**7.110.19**  he, surely, seeing Karṇa stripped of his car and vanquished by Bhīma, and recalling his rejection of Kṛṣṇa, grieves bitterly, O Saṃjaya.

**7.110.20**  Seeing his mailed brothers slain in battle by Bhīmasena, my little son, surely, grieves exceedingly for his own transgression.

**7.110.21**  For who that wished to live would advance against the Pāṇḍava Bhīma, of terrible weapons, enraged, standing there like Death made manifest?

**7.110.22**  A man set in the midst of the mare-mouthed fire beneath the sea might yet escape, but one who has come within Bhīma's reach cannot escape — such is my conviction.

**7.110.23**  Neither the Pāṇḍavas, nor the Pāñcālas, nor Keśava and Sātyaki, when roused in battle, know how to guard their lives.

**7.110.24**  Saṃjaya said: That you grieve, O Kaurava, now that the slaughter of folk is upon us — you yourself are the root of this world's destruction, there is no doubt.

**7.110.25**  Having yourself stirred up this great enmity, and abiding by the word of your sons, though counseled you would not take the counsel, as a dying man refuses wholesome medicine.

**7.110.26**  Having yourself drunk down, O great king, the Kālakūṭa poison so hard to digest, now reap its fruit in full, O best of men.

**7.110.27**  As for your reviling of the warriors who fought with all their strength, I shall now describe to you how the battle truly unfolded.

**7.110.28**  When they saw Karṇa worsted by Bhīmasena, your five sons, born of the same mother and mighty archers, could not endure it, O honored one.

**7.110.29**  Durmarṣaṇa, Duḥsaha, Durmada, Durdhara, and Jaya, splendid in their armor, rushed against that son of Pāṇḍu to oppose him.

**7.110.30**  Surrounding the mighty-armed Vṛkodara on every side, they veiled the quarters with arrows, as though with swarms of locusts.

**7.110.31**  As those princes, fair as the gods, came swiftly on, Bhīmasena received them in battle as though with a laugh.

**7.110.32**  But seeing your sons drawn close to Bhīmasena, Rādheya advanced against the mighty Bhīmasena.

**7.110.33**  Loosing shafts with golden nocks, whetted on stone, O king, he came on; and Bhīma rushed at him at once, though held back by your sons.

**7.110.34**  Then the Kurus, encircling Karṇa on all sides, covered Bhīmasena with arrows of smooth-jointed shafts.

**7.110.35**  With twenty-five arrows, O king, Bhīma of the fearsome bow sent those bull-like men, together with their horses and charioteers, to the abode of Yama.

**7.110.36**  Lifeless, they fell from their chariots together with their charioteers, like great flowering trees laden with bright blossoms, broken by the wind.

**7.110.37**  There we beheld the wondrous valor of Bhīmasena, who, while warding off the son of Adhiratha with his arrows, yet slew your sons.

**7.110.38**  Though held off on every side by Bhīma's sharp arrows, the son of the sūta, O great king, kept his gaze fixed upon Bhīmasena.

**7.110.39**  And Bhīmasena, in his fury, his eyes red with wrath, drawing his vast bow taut, gazed again and again upon Karṇa.

**7.111.1**  Saṃjaya said: When valiant Karṇa saw your sons fallen, he was seized with a great wrath and grew weary of his own life.

**7.111.2**  The son of Adhiratha then deemed himself an offender, as it were; and in his anger he rushed upon Bhīmasena in haste.

**7.111.3**  Rādheya, having pierced Bhīma with five shafts as though with a smile, struck him again with seventy arrows golden-nocked and whetted on stone.

**7.111.4**  But Vṛkodara, son of Pṛthā, would not brook that mockery, and pierced Rādheya in turn with a hundred smooth-jointed shafts.

**7.111.5**  And again, having pierced him with five swift, keen arrows, he cut asunder the bow of the sūta's son with a broad-headed shaft, O honored one.

**7.111.6**  Then Karṇa, taking up another bow, O Bhārata, sore at heart, covered Bhīmasena on every side with his arrows.

**7.111.7**  But Bhīma, having slain his horses and struck down his charioteer, laughed a great laugh, the deed repaid once more.

**7.111.8**  And that bull among men cut his bow apart with arrows; it fell, O great king, gold-backed and loud-resounding.

**7.111.9**  Then Karṇa, that mighty car-warrior, descended from his chariot, and seizing a mace, hurled it at Bhīmasena in the fray.

**7.111.10**  Seeing that mace come hurtling suddenly upon him, Vṛkodara warded it off with his arrows, O king, in the sight of the whole army.

**7.111.11**  Then the valiant son of Pāṇḍu, eager to slay the sūta's son, sent forth in haste thousands of arrows.

**7.111.12**  Warding off those shafts with his own arrows in that great battle, Karṇa with his darts struck down the armor of Bhīmasena.

**7.111.13**  Then he pierced him with twenty-five small arrows; and to all beings who beheld it, that seemed a wondrous thing.

**7.111.14**  Then Bhīma, O great king, in his wrath sent against the sūta's son in battle nine smooth-jointed shafts, O honored one.

**7.111.15**  Piercing his armor and his right arm, those keen shafts entered the earth like serpents entering an anthill.

**7.111.16**  But seeing Rādheya standing on foot in the battle, sore beset by Bhīmasena, King Duryodhana said: 'Make haste, all of you, intent and ready, to bring a chariot to Rādheya.'
