**7.111.17**  Then your sons, O king, hearing their brother's word, swiftly advanced against the son of Pāṇḍu in battle, loosing keen arrows.

**7.111.18**  Citra, Upacitra, Citrākṣa, Cārucitra, Śarāsana, Citrāyudha, and Citravarman—warriors of wondrous skill in battle.

**7.111.19**  As they came on swiftly, Bhīma, that mighty car-warrior, O king, struck them down in the fray together with their horses, charioteers, and standards; slain, they fell to the earth like trees felled by the wind.

**7.111.20**  Seeing your sons, those mighty car-warriors, slain, O king, Karṇa, his face full of tears, fell into a swoon of grief.

**7.111.21**  Mounting another chariot duly equipped, the valiant one again advanced in haste against the son of Pāṇḍu in battle.

**7.111.22**  Piercing each other with arrows golden-nocked and whetted on stone, the two shone, O great king, like a pair of kiṃśuka trees in flower.

**7.111.23**  Then the son of Pāṇḍu, in his wrath, with thirty-six sharp broad-headed shafts of fierce point, shattered the armor of the sūta's son.

**7.111.24**  Their limbs as if smeared with red sandal, deeply wounded by arrows and bathed in blood, the two shone like twin suns of the world's end newly risen.

**7.111.25**  With their bodies drenched in blood, their armor riven by arrows, the two, stripped of mail, shone like serpents that had cast their slough.

**7.111.26**  Like two tigers tearing each other with their fangs, those tamers of foes, those tigers among men, brandishing arrows for fangs, rent one another.

**7.111.27**  Locked together like two elephants, they shone in the midst of the field, striking each other with keen shafts, in prowess like rutting elephants.

**7.111.28**  Covering each other in battle with nets of arrows, and making all the quarters resound with their chariots, the two ranged about.

**7.111.29**  With their chariots, O great king, in wheeling rounds and like maneuvers, those two high-souled ones shone like Vṛtra and the wielder of the thunderbolt.

**7.111.30**  Drawing his bow with arms adorned with bracelets, Bhīma shone in the battle like a thunderhead lit with lightning.

**7.111.31**  Thundering with the roar of his bow, that great rain-cloud of arrow-showers, the dread cloud that was Bhīma, O great king, advanced upon the mountain that was Karṇa.

**7.111.32**  Then with a thousand arrows loosed from his bow, O Bhārata, the son of Pāṇḍu covered Karṇa as a cloud covers a mountain with its rains.

**7.111.33**  There your sons beheld the valor of Bhīmasena, who covered Karṇa with shafts fair-nocked and fledged with heron's feathers.

**7.111.34**  Gladdening the son of Pṛthā in battle, and the glorious Keśava, and Sātyaki and the two guardians of the wheels, Bhīma fought against Karṇa.

**7.111.35**  The prowess of his arms, the valor and the steadfastness of that self-possessed hero—your sons, O great king, beheld it all in the son of Pāṇḍu.

**7.112.1**  Saṃjaya said: When Rādheya heard the twang of Bhīmasena's bowstring and the slap of his palm, he brooked it no more, as a rutting elephant brooks not the trumpeting of a rival.

**7.112.2**  Withdrawing for a moment from the range of Bhīma's arrows, the son of Adhiratha beheld your sons fallen from their chariots.

**7.112.3**  Slain by Bhīmasena, they lay there; downcast and grieved, sighing long and hot, he again advanced upon the son of Pāṇḍu.

**7.112.4**  His eyes red as copper with wrath, hissing like a great serpent, Karṇa, loosing his arrows, blazed like the radiant sun shedding its beams.

**7.112.5**  As if by the spreading webs of the sun's rays, O bull of the Bhāratas, Vṛkodara was overspread by the arrows loosed from Karṇa's bow.

**7.112.6**  The bright arrows fledged with peacock-feathers, loosed from Karṇa's bow, entered the son of Pṛthā from every side, as birds settle upon a tree to roost.

**7.112.7**  The golden-nocked arrows loosed from Karṇa's bow, flying hither and thither, shone like wild geese ranged in rows.

**7.112.8**  Springing forth, as it seemed, from his bow, his banner, and the gear of his car, from his parasol, from the shaft-end of the pole, and from the yoke, the arrows of Adhiratha's son were seen, O king.

**7.112.9**  Filling the sky, the son of Adhiratha let fly his arrows of great speed, sky-coursing and feather-fledged, bright and wrought with gold.

**7.112.10**  As he bore down like Death himself strained for the kill, Vṛkodara, with his own life held cheap and burning with wrath, pierced him with nine arrows.

**7.112.11**  Seeing the unbearable onslaught of Karṇa and those great floods of arrows, the valiant son of Pāṇḍu was not in the least dismayed.

**7.112.12**  Then, scattering the nets of arrows of Adhiratha's son, the son of Pāṇḍu pierced Karṇa with twenty more keen shafts.

**7.112.13**  Even as the son of Pṛthā had been covered with arrows by the sūta's son, so too did the son of Pāṇḍu cover Karṇa in the battle.

**7.112.14**  Beholding the valor of Bhīmasena in battle, O Bhārata, your own people and the celestial bards rejoiced and applauded with delight.

**7.112.15**  Bhūriśravas, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, the king of the Madras, Jayadratha, Uttamaujas, Yudhāmanyu, Sātyaki, Keśava, and Arjuna—

**7.112.16**  these ten foremost mighty car-warriors among the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, O king, crying 'Well done! Well done!' raised forthwith a mighty lion's roar.

**7.112.17**  While that tumultuous, hair-raising clamor arose, O king, Duryodhana hastily addressed your sons.

**7.112.18**  To the kings and the princes, and his own brothers especially: 'Go to Karṇa—good fortune to you—seeking to deliver him from Vṛkodara.'

**7.112.19**  'Before the arrows loosed from Bhīma's bow strike down Rādheya, exert yourselves, O great archers, to guard the sūta's son.'

**7.112.20**  At Duryodhana's command, seven of his brothers, O honored one, rushed furiously upon Bhīmasena and surrounded him.

**7.112.21**  Closing in upon the son of Kuntī, they enveloped him with showers of arrows, as rain-clouds in the wet season enwrap a mountain with their torrents.

**7.112.22**  Those seven mighty car-warriors in their wrath beset Bhīmasena, O king, as the seven planets beset the moon at the time of the dissolution of beings.

**7.112.23**  Then the son of Kuntī, the son of Pāṇḍu, gripping his bow tightly in his firm left fist, O king—that well-wrought bow—

**7.112.24**  and judging them but men like himself, fitted seven arrows like the sun's own beams, and the mighty one, drawing them taut, loosed them upon those foes.

**7.112.25**  As if casting forth the very life-breaths from the bodies of your sons, Bhīmasena, O great king, remembered the old enmity.

**7.112.26**  Those arrows hurled by Bhīmasena, O Bhārata, golden-nocked and whetted on stone, having pierced the Bhāratas, sprang up into the sky.

**7.112.27**  Having rent open their hearts, those gold-adorned arrows shone, O great king, like sky-coursing eagles.

**7.112.28**  Their feathered tips smeared with blood, those seven gold-wrought shafts, O lord of kings, sprang up again, having drunk the blood of your sons.

**7.112.29**  Their vital parts pierced by the arrows, they fell from their chariots to the earth, like great trees grown on mountain ridges, broken by an elephant.

**7.112.30**  Śatruṃjaya, Śatrusaha, Citra, Citrāyudha, Dṛḍha, Citrasena, and Vikarṇa—these seven were laid low.

**7.112.31**  Having slain them, the mighty-armed son of Pāṇḍu, before the very eyes of Rādheya, sent forth a terrible roar like a lion's.

**7.112.32**  That roar of the hero, O Bhārata, seemed to proclaim to the King of Righteousness that battle and his own great victory.

**7.112.33**  Hearing that mighty roar of Bhīmasena the bowman, the Dharmarāja was filled with the highest joy in the battle.

**7.112.34**  Then, O great king, the delighted Pārtha answered Bhīmasena's roar on every side with the loud blare of musical instruments.

**7.112.35**  And when Vṛkodara had given the signal, filled with great gladness he advanced in the battle against Droṇa, the foremost of weapon-bearers.

**7.112.36**  Seeing thirty-one of your sons, great car-warriors all, slain, O great king, Duryodhana remembered those words of Vidura the steward.

**7.112.37**  "Now has come to pass that beneficial word of the steward,"—so reflecting, that king found no answer to make.

**7.112.38**  What your evil-minded son had spoken at the time of the dice-game, and the harsh words that Karṇa had spoken to Kṛṣṇā in the assembly—

**7.112.39**  in the presence of the sons of Pāṇḍu, and of yourself, O lord of peoples, and of all the Kauravas, and in the very presence of the preceptor—

**7.112.40**  "The Pāṇḍavas are utterly ruined, O Kṛṣṇā; they have gone to everlasting hell. Choose yourself another husband"—the fruit of that has now arrived.

**7.112.41**  When, having brought Draupadī into the assembly, they spoke harsh words to her, your sons enraged the Pāṇḍavas of terrible bows.

**7.112.42**  Loosing that fire of wrath which had abided in him thirteen years, Bhīmasena, O Kaurava, is bringing your sons to their end.

**7.112.43**  Lamenting much, the steward could find no peace with you, O best of the Bhāratas, you together with your sons; now reap the ripening of that fruit. Vikarṇa is slain, O lord of kings, and valiant Citrasena too.

**7.112.44**  The foremost among your sons, and other of your sons, great car-warriors—whomever Bhīma saw come within range of his eye, those sons of yours, O mighty-armed one, he slew in haste.

**7.112.45**  On your account I have beheld the host consumed as if by fire, by the arrows loosed in their thousands by the Pāṇḍava and by the Bull Karṇa.

**7.113.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Great was the misgovernance, O charioteer, mine above all herein; that has now come home, I think, O Saṃjaya, to me who grieve.

**7.113.2**  "What is gone is gone"—this was fixed in my mind; now what is to be done here, what shall I do, O Saṃjaya?

**7.113.3**  But how this destruction of heroes, born of my own misrule, came to pass—tell me that; I have grown steady, O Saṃjaya.

**7.113.4**  Saṃjaya said: Karṇa and Bhīma, O great king, putting forth their valour in the great battle, rained down showers of arrows like two rain-laden clouds.

**7.113.5**  Arrows marked with Bhīma's name, golden-feathered and whetted on stone, reaching Karṇa entered him as though cleaving his very life.

**7.113.6**  Even so was Bhīma covered in the fight, by hundreds and by thousands, with the shafts loosed from Karṇa, like venomous serpents.

**7.113.7**  From the arrows of those two falling on every side, O great king, there arose among your armies a tumult like that of the ocean.

**7.113.8**  By the arrows loosed from Bhīma's bow, O subduer of foes, your army was slaughtered in the midst of the host—dreadful shafts, the likeness of snakes of deadly poison.

**7.113.9**  Strewn with fallen elephants, O king, and with horses and men together, the earth appeared as if littered with trees uprooted by the wind.

**7.113.10**  Being slain in the battle by the arrows loosed from Bhīma's bow, your warriors fled, crying out, "What is this?"

**7.113.11**  Then that army of the Sindhus, the Sauvīras, and the Kauravas was scattered and driven off by the swift arrows of Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava.

**7.113.12**  Sore wounded with arrows for the most part, their horses, men, and mounts slain, they abandoned Karṇa and Bhīma and fled in every direction.

**7.113.13**  "Surely for Pārtha's sake the dwellers of heaven bewilder us, in that our host is being slain by the arrows that spring from Karṇa and Bhīma."

**7.113.14**  Speaking thus, your warriors, oppressed by fear, withdrew beyond arrow-range and stood there, eager only to watch the fight.

**7.113.15**  Then there flowed, in that great battle, a river of dreadful aspect, which especially heightened the terror of the timorous.

**7.113.16**  It rose from the streaming blood of elephants, horses, and men, and was thronged with lifeless men, elephants, and steeds.

**7.113.17**  With the trappings of elephants, horses, and cars, with their axle-poles and banners, and with chariots cast aside, their wheels, axles, and shafts broken—

**7.113.18**  with bows adorned with gold and of exceeding worth, with golden-feathered shafts, and with iron arrows by the thousand—

**7.113.19**  loosed by Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava like serpents set free, with masses of darts and lances, with swords and battle-axes—

**7.113.20**  and with maces, clubs, and spiked spears wrought with gold, with thunderbolt-darts of many shapes, with spears and bludgeons, and with gleaming hundred-slayers, the earth shone bright, O Bhārata.

**7.113.21**  With golden armlets and bracelets, with earrings and shining gems, with coats of mail and with hand-guards, with necklaces and ornaments of gold, O Bhārata—

**7.113.22**  with garments and parasols torn asunder, with yak-tail whisks and fans, with the cleft bodies of elephants, horses, and men, with weapons and the trappings of chariots—

**7.113.23**  with these manifold objects of every kind, fallen and flung about here and there, the earth shone like the firmament with its planets.

**7.113.24**  Beholding the unimaginable, wondrous, and more-than-human deeds of those two, amazement seized the Cāraṇas and the Siddhas.

**7.113.25**  As fire aided by the wind sweeps through dry brushwood, so was the course in battle of the son of Adhiratha, having Bhīma for his match; terrible was that course, casting down banners and cars and slaying horses, men, and elephants.

**7.113.26**  As a thicket of reeds is crushed by two elephants joined in combat, so was that great army brought low in the battle, O Bhārata; and supreme was the havoc wrought by Karṇa and Bhīma in the fight.

**7.114.1**  Saṃjaya said: Then Karṇa, O great king, having pierced Bhīma with three shafts, loosed showers of arrows, brilliant and manifold.

**7.114.2**  Though smitten by the son of the charioteer, O great king, the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena did not waver, like a mountain being riven.

**7.114.3**  Then Bhīmasena, O lord of kings, pierced Karṇa in the ear with a barbed, whetted, yellow-hued, feathered shaft in the fight.

**7.114.4**  He struck the great earring of refined gold from Karṇa's ear to the ground, O great king, like a blazing light falling from the sky.

**7.114.5**  Then with another broad-headed arrow the mighty Bhīma, as if smiling, struck the charioteer's son hard between the breasts.

**7.114.6**  Then again, in haste, Bhīma sped at him in the battle ten iron arrows of great swiftness, O Bhārata, like the rod of Yama.

**7.114.7**  Reaching the forehead of the charioteer's son, O sire, those arrows, driven by him, entered it as serpents enter an ant-hill.

**7.114.8**  With those arrows fixed in his forehead the charioteer's son shone forth, as he had of old when wearing a garland wrought of blue lotuses.

**7.114.9**  Then Karṇa, enraged in the fight, sore pressed by the strong bowman, mighty in speed, put forth his swiftness to slay Bhīmasena.

**7.114.10**  At him Karṇa, O king, impatient, strong, and wrathful, sped a hundred arrows feathered with vulture-plumes, O Bhārata.

**7.114.11**  Then the Pāṇḍava loosed fierce showers of arrows; heeding him not in the battle, he gave no thought to his prowess.

**7.114.12**  Then Karṇa, O great king, that scorcher of foes, in his wrath struck the wrathful-looking Pāṇḍava upon the breast with whetted shafts.

**7.114.13**  Like two storm-clouds they rained upon each other in the battle, terrifying one another with the cracking sounds of their bow-strings.

**7.114.14**  With manifold nets of arrows they covered each other in the fray, both wrathful in the battle, each seeking to repay deed with deed.

**7.114.15**  Then the mighty-armed Bhīma, having cut the bow of the high-souled Rādheya with a razor-tipped arrow, pierced Karṇa with a feathered shaft.

**7.114.16**  Casting aside that severed bow, the high-minded son of the charioteer took up another, swift-striking and able to bear a heavy strain.

**7.114.17**  And seeing the destruction of the host of the Kurus, the Sauvīras, and the Saindhavas, and the earth covered with fallen armour, banners, and weapons—

**7.114.18**  and beholding on every side the lifeless bodies of elephants, horses, and men, the form of the charioteer's son grew blazing with fury.

**7.114.19**  Twanging his great bow adorned with gold, Rādheya gazed upon Bhīma, O king, with a terrible eye.

**7.114.20**  Then the wrathful son of the charioteer, hurling his shafts, shone forth radiant like the autumn sun risen to the meridian.

**7.114.21**  Like the form of the sun blossoming with its rays, O king, was the dreadful form of the son of Adhiratha, ablaze with hundreds of arrows.

**7.114.22**  As he took up his swift shafts with both hands, set them to the string, drew them back, and loosed them, none in the battle could mark the interval.

**7.114.23**  As he discharged his shafts to the left and to the right, the weapon of Karṇa, O great king, dreadful as a wheel of fire, seemed drawn into a circle.

**7.114.24**  Golden-feathered and well-whetted, the arrows loosed from Karṇa's bow veiled, O great king, the quarters and the splendour of the sun.

**7.114.25**  Then in the sky was seen, in manifold array, a flight of gold-feathered arrows with smooth-bending joints, loosed from his bow.

**7.114.26**  Issuing from the bow of the son of Adhiratha, the shafts, ranged in lines, shone forth, O king, like cranes in the heavens.

**7.114.27**  Vulture-feathered, stone-whetted, adorned with gold, of great swiftness and blazing points—such arrows did the son of Adhiratha loose.

**7.114.28**  Hurled by the force of the bow and decked with gold, those arrows poured ceaselessly upon the chariot of Pārtha's son Bhīma.

**7.114.29**  Gem-wrought, they shone in the sky by the thousand—the arrows sped by Karṇa, like swarms of locusts.

**7.114.30**  Loosed from the bow of the son of Adhiratha, the falling shafts seemed, as they sped forth, to be a single long and towering arrow.

**7.114.31**  As a rain-cloud veils a mountain with its torrents, so did the wrathful Karṇa cover Bhīma with showers of arrows.

**7.114.32**  There, O Bhārata, your sons together with the Kurus beheld the strength, the valour, the prowess, and the resolve of Bhīma.

**7.114.33**  Heedless of that risen shower of arrows, swollen like the surging sea, the wrathful Bhīma rushed upon Karṇa.

**7.114.34**  The great gold-backed bow of Bhīma, O lord of peoples, drawn into a circle by his pull, seemed a second rainbow of Indra; from it the arrows came forth as if filling the firmament.

**7.114.35**  By the gold-feathered, smooth-jointed shafts of Bhīma there was wrought in the sky a garland that shone as if of gold.

**7.114.36**  Then the nets of arrows clinging in the sky, struck piece by piece by the feathered shafts of Bhīmasena, were scattered asunder.

**7.114.37**  By the floods of arrow-nets of both Karṇa and Bhīmasena, touching like sparks of fire and flying straight in the battle, the sky was wholly covered with flights of gold-feathered shafts.

**7.114.38**  Covering Bhīma with arrows of many kinds, the charioteer's son pressed upon him, making light of the prowess of that high-souled one.

**7.114.39**  As those two there loosed their nets of arrows, O sire, they seemed to become like winds, clashing one against the other.

**7.114.40**  At him Karṇa, in his wrath, sped sharp arrows burnished by the smith and wrought with gold, longing to slay him.

**7.114.41**  Those Bhīma cut down in mid-air with his shafts, each into three, and outdoing the charioteer's son he cried, "Stand and fight!"

**7.114.42**  Once more the mighty Pāṇḍava, brooking no insult and ablaze with wrath, let loose his fierce torrents of arrows, like a fire bent on consuming all.

**7.114.43**  But Karṇa, the charioteer's son, fearlessly received all those weapons of the warring son of Pāṇḍu, neutralizing them by the wizardry of his own missiles.

**7.114.44**  With his smooth-jointed shafts Karṇa Vaikartana cut apart Bhīma's quivers, his bowstring, and the reins and traces of his horses.

**7.114.45**  Then, having slain his horses, with three arrows he pierced his charioteer, who leapt down and fled swiftly to the chariot of Yuyudhāna.

**7.114.46**  As though smiling, the wrathful Rādheya, radiant as the fire of doom, severed Bhīma's banner and brought down his pennons.

**7.114.47**  Bereft of his bow, O great king, Bhīma seized the lance kept in his car, and whirling it in his fury, hurled it at Karṇa's chariot.

**7.114.48**  But the son of Adhiratha, straining hard, with ten arrows cut to pieces that gold-adorned lance as it came on, blazing like a great meteor.

**7.114.49**  Cleft into ten pieces by the shafts of Karṇa, it fell, O king — shafts loosed by that charioteer's son, fighter of wondrous skill, in the cause of his friend.

**7.114.50**  Then the son of Kuntī took up his shield and his gold-mounted sword, seeking now one of two ends — death or victory; but Karṇa, as if laughing, shattered them both in an instant.

**7.114.51**  Stripped of his shield, O great king, his chariot gone, swooning with rage, Bhīma whirled his sword and flung it in haste at Karṇa's car.

**7.114.52**  That keen-edged blade, having cut through the charioteer's son's bow and its string, fell to the earth like a serpent dropping from the sky.

**7.114.53**  Then, laughing, the son of Adhiratha, enraged, took up in the battle another bow — slayer of foes, firm-stringed, and swifter still.

**7.114.54**  Then mighty Bhīmasena, true in valor and roused to wrath, sprang up into the sky, troubling the heart of Karṇa.

**7.114.55**  Seeing this feat of him who sought victory in the fray, Rādheya, biding his moment, foiled Bhīmasena.

**7.114.56**  Not finding him — for Bhīma, his senses shaken, had crouched hidden upon a chariot floor — Karṇa came up to his banner and stood there upon the ground.

**7.114.57**  For this all the Kurus and the celestial bards honored Bhīma — that from his car he had sought to slay Karṇa, as Tārkṣya seizes a serpent.

**7.114.58**  His bow shorn away and his chariot lost, yet keeping to the duty of his order, Bhīma set his own car at his back and stood firm, still ready to fight.

**7.114.59**  Having broken his resolve, Rādheya then bore down upon the Pāṇḍava, furious, as he stood there in the battle, ready for combat.

**7.114.60**  The two mighty warriors met in that great arena, contending, roaring like two thunderclouds in the heavens at the close of the hot season.

**7.114.61**  Fierce was the encounter of those two wrathful lions among men, neither brooking the other in the fray, like that of a god and a demon.

**7.114.62**  His weapons spent and hard pressed by Karṇa, the son of Kuntī, seeing elephants slain by Arjuna lying fallen like mountains, and being weaponless, entered in among them to bar the path of Karṇa's chariot.

**7.114.63**  Reaching the herd of elephants and entering that rampart against chariots, the Pāṇḍava, desiring to keep his life, did not press his attack upon Rādheya.

**7.114.64**  Then, seeking a foothold, the son of Pṛthā, conqueror of hostile cities, heaved up an elephant slain by Dhanaṃjaya's shafts and stood his ground.

**7.114.65**  Karṇa with his arrows blasted that elephant of his to pieces; then the Pāṇḍava, roaring, flung the elephant's limbs at Karṇa.

**7.114.66**  Chariot-wheels, horses, draught-beasts — whatever he saw upon the ground, that the enraged Pāṇḍava caught up and hurled at Karṇa.

**7.114.67**  All this, as fast as it was flung, Karṇa cut apart with his sharp shafts; yet, weaponless though Bhīma was, Karṇa did not slay him, remembering the word he had given to Kuntī.

**7.114.68**  Rushing upon him, Karṇa touched him with the tip of his bow, and Rādheya, as if smiling, spoke thus to Bhīmasena:

**7.114.69**  "Again and again, you beardless dolt, you slave of your belly, you who have learned no weapon-craft — do not fight, you child, you coward in battle!"

**7.114.70**  "Where there is food of many kinds, things to chew and things to drink, O Pāṇḍava — there, foolish one, you belong; never anywhere in battle."

**7.114.71**  "Become an ascetic, Bhīma, and live on fruits, O most witless one; go to the forest, son of Kuntī — you are no master of warfare."

**7.114.72**  "You are fit for feeding on fruits and roots and for entertaining guests; I do not think you fit for the wielding of weapons, Vṛkodara."

**7.114.73**  "With flowers, roots, and fruits for your fare, amid vows and observances, you suit the forest, Bhīma — you are no master of warfare."

**7.114.74**  "What has war to do with the life of a sage? Go to the forest, Vṛkodara; you are not made for battle, my friend — take your delight in dwelling in the woods."

**7.114.75**  "Chivvying cooks and servants and slaves in the house, you are fit to thrash them in your rage for the sake of a meal, Vṛkodara."

**7.114.76**  And whatever galling things had passed in their boyhood, O lord of peoples, those old harsh deeds too he made him hear over and over.

**7.114.77**  Then again, as Bhīma cowered there, the Bull of men touched him with his bow, and laughing, addressed him once more:

**7.114.78**  "If you must fight, fall upon someone else; you should not fight with such as me. Those who battle men of my kind meet with this and worse."

**7.114.79**  "Or go to where the two Kṛṣṇas are — they will guard you in the fight; or go home, son of Kuntī. What have you, child, to do with war?"

**7.114.80**  Having thus stripped him of his chariot, Karṇa, O king, vaunted over him in the very presence of the Lion of the Vṛṣṇis and of the great-souled son of Pṛthā.

**7.114.81**  Then, O king, the hero whose banner bore the monkey, urged on by Keśava, sent stone-whetted arrows against the charioteer's son.

**7.114.82**  Then the gold-decked shafts loosed from the arm of Pṛthā's son, sprung from Gāṇḍīva, fell upon Karṇa as swans descend on the Krauñca mountain.

**7.114.83**  With arrows shot from Gāṇḍīva, taut like outstretched serpents, Dhanaṃjaya drove the charioteer's son back from Bhīmasena.

**7.114.84**  His bow shorn by Bhīma and himself struck by Dhanaṃjaya's shafts, Karṇa swiftly withdrew from Bhīma upon his great chariot.

**7.114.85**  And Bhīma too, that bull among men, mounting a horse of Sātyaki's, followed in the battle his brother, the Pāṇḍava Savyasācin.

**7.114.86**  Then, taking aim at Karṇa, Dhanaṃjaya in haste, his eyes red with wrath, sent forth an iron shaft as Death sends out the destroyer.

**7.114.87**  Like Garutmān in the sky stooping upon the foremost of serpents, that iron shaft, sped from Gāṇḍīva, flew swiftly down upon Karṇa.

**7.114.88**  That iron shaft Droṇa's son cut in mid-air with a feathered arrow, the great chariot-warrior seeking to deliver Karṇa from the peril of Dhanaṃjaya.

**7.114.89**  Then the wrathful Arjuna pierced Droṇa's son with sixty-four stone-honed arrows, O great king, crying, "Do not flee — stand fast!"

**7.114.90**  But Droṇa's son, sore beset by Dhanaṃjaya's shafts, swiftly plunged into the host thronged with rutting elephants and crowded with chariots.

**7.114.91**  Then with the roar of Gāṇḍīva the mighty son of Kuntī overwhelmed the twanging din of the gold-backed bows that sang upon the field.

**7.114.92**  Dhanaṃjaya, as Droṇa's son thus fled, pursued him from behind for no great distance, terrifying the host with his arrows.

**7.114.93**  Rending with his iron shafts the bodies of men, elephants, and horses, Arjuna scattered the host with arrows fledged in the plumes of heron and peacock.

**7.114.94**  That host, O best of the Bhāratas, with its horses, elephants, and men, the son of Pṛthā — offspring of the Chastiser of Pāka — straining hard, smote down utterly.

**7.115.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Day after day my blazing glory falls away, Saṃjaya; many of my warriors are slain. I deem this the turning of Time.

**7.115.2**  Dhanaṃjaya in his fury has entered my host — a host guarded by Droṇa and Karṇa, one that not even the gods could penetrate —

**7.115.3**  his prowess swelled by those two of mighty valor, joined with Kṛṣṇa and Bhīma and with the Bull of the Śinis.

**7.115.4**  From that hour grief burns me like a fire within my heart, for I see the lords of earth, the Saindhava among them, already in its grip.

**7.115.5**  Having done so grievous a wrong to the Diademed one, how can the king of the Sindhus, once come within his sight, escape with his life?

**7.115.6**  By reasoning I see, Saṃjaya, that the Saindhava is no more. Tell me, then, as I ask, how that battle came to pass.

**7.115.7**  And tell of him who, having shaken and churned that great army again and again, entered it alone in his wrath, as an elephant breaks into a lotus-pool.

**7.115.8**  Tell me truly of the battle of that Vṛṣṇi hero, of what he did for Dhanaṃjaya's sake — for in this you are skilled, Saṃjaya.

**7.115.9**  Saṃjaya said: Seeing Bhīma, that foremost of men, thus harried by Vaikartana and now moving away amid the heroes, O king, the hero of the Śinis followed after him in his chariot.

**7.115.10**  Roaring like the Wielder of the thunderbolt at the end of the heats, blazing like the sun at the close of the rains, he smote his foes with his firm bow, making your son's army tremble.

**7.115.11**  As that hero among men ranged the field, borne by horses bright as silver, all your chariot-warriors, O Bhārata, could not turn back that foremost of the Mādhavas.

**7.115.12**  But Alambusa, that best of kings, filled with indignation, fighting without retreat, bow in hand and clad in golden mail, rushed upon Sātyaki, the foremost of the Mādhavas, and stayed him.

**7.115.13**  Such an encounter arose between them, Bhārata, as had never been before; the warriors, both yours and the foes', all stood merely gazing at the two, splendid in battle.

**7.115.14**  Alambusa, that best of kings, with main force pierced him with ten shafts; but the Bull of the Śinis cut down those shafts with his own arrows even before they reached him.

**7.115.15**  Again, with three keen, well-feathered arrows like fire, drawn to the ear, he pierced him; rending his armor, they sank into Sātyaki's body.

**7.115.16**  Tearing his body with those blazing arrows, swift as fire and wind, with yet others Sātyaki forcibly struck down his four horses, bright as silver, with four shafts.

**7.115.17**  Thus struck by him, the swift grandson of Śini, in might like the Wielder of the discus, slew Alambusa's horses with four arrows of surpassing speed.

**7.115.18**  Then, with a broad-headed shaft like the fire of doom, he struck off the head of his charioteer, and severed from the trunk that radiant face, earringed and bright as the full moon.

**7.115.19**  Having slain in battle that son and grandson of a king, the crushing Bull of the Madhus then, O king, the hero turned back your troops and followed after Arjuna alone.

**7.115.20**  Seeing that best of the Vṛṣṇis come on, wheeling thus amid the foe and smiting the Kuru forces with his arrows, again and again, as the wind scatters masses of cloud —

**7.115.21**  his Sindhu-bred steeds, well broken, bright as cow's milk, jasmine, the moon, and snow, decked with nets of gold, those noble horses bore him wherever the lion among men desired.

**7.115.22**  Then your sons together, and other warriors of yours, rushed upon him in haste, O scion of Ajamīḍha, putting at their head, O Bhārata, your son Duḥśāsana, foremost of fighters.

**7.115.23**  Hemming in the son of Śini on every side in the battle, those who could withstand whole armies smote him; but that hero, the foremost of the Sātvatas, held them off with a net of arrows.

**7.115.24**  Swiftly driving them off with feathered shafts like fire, the slayer of foes, the grandson of Śini, raising his bow, struck down even the horses of Duḥśāsana, O scion of Ajamīḍha.

**7.116.1**  Saṃjaya said: As the mighty-armed one rose up against the chariot of Duḥśāsana, swift in the hour that called for swiftness and seeking Dhanaṃjaya's welfare —

**7.116.2**  the great archers of the Trigartas, with banners wrought of gold, surrounded the Ānarta hero who had plunged into the ocean of their host.

**7.116.3**  Then, hemming him in on all sides with their array of chariots, those wrathful, peerless bowmen overwhelmed him with showers of arrows.

**7.116.4**  Sātyaki, whose valour was unfailing, alone vanquished those princes who strove against him in the great battle—fifty foes laid low by his single hand.

**7.116.5**  He had reached the midst of the Bhārata host, loud with the clapping of palms, thronged with swords and spears and maces, like waters that offer no raft for crossing.

**7.116.6**  There in the fray we beheld the wondrous course of Śaineya: glimpsing him in the western quarter, by his swiftness we saw him next in the east.

**7.116.7**  North, south, east, and west he ranged, the hero moving as though he danced, as if he were a hundred chariots at once.

**7.116.8**  Beholding the feats of him who moved with the stride of a lion's prowess, the Trigartas turned back, anguished for their own kinsmen.

**7.116.9**  Then other warriors among the Śūrasenas checked him in the battle, restraining him with showers of arrows as goads restrain a maddened elephant.

**7.116.10**  Sātyaki, of inconceivable strength and valour, held those straining warriors off but a moment, and then did battle with the Kaliṅgas.

**7.116.11**  Having passed beyond that host of the Kaliṅgas, hard to traverse, the mighty-armed one drew near to Pārtha Dhanaṃjaya.

**7.116.12**  As a swimmer wearied in the water gains the shore at last, so Yuyudhāna, seeing that tiger among men, took heart again.

**7.116.13**  Beholding him approach, Keśava said to Arjuna: "Yonder comes Śaineya, O Pārtha, your follower in the field."

**7.116.14**  "This is your disciple and your friend, whose prowess never fails; counting all those warriors as so much straw, that bull among men has conquered them."

**7.116.15**  "Having wrought dread havoc among the Kaurava warriors, Sātyaki—dearer to you than your own breath, O Kirīṭin—now draws near."

**7.116.16**  "Having brought low Droṇa, the Bhoja, and Kṛtavarman with his arrows, Sātyaki comes toward Phalguna."

**7.116.17**  "Seeking the welfare of the Dharma-king, having slain warrior after chosen warrior—a hero and a master of arms—Sātyaki comes toward Phalguna."

**7.116.18**  "Having done a deed most hard to do in the midst of the host, the mighty one, longing to see you, comes toward the Pāṇḍava—Sātyaki draws near."

**7.116.19**  "Having fought with a single chariot against many great car-warriors, foremost the Preceptor among them, this Sātyaki, O Pārtha, comes onward."

**7.116.20**  "Relying on the strength of his own arms, having torn through the army, sent forth by the son of Dharma, this Sātyaki comes toward you, O Pārtha."

**7.116.21**  "He to whom no warrior among the Kauravas is in any wise an equal—he, O Kaunteya, comes onward: Sātyaki of unfailing valour."

**7.116.22**  "Loosed from the Kuru host like a lion from the midst of a herd of cattle, having slain whole armies, this Sātyaki comes toward you, O Pārtha."

**7.116.23**  "Having strewn the earth with the lotus-like faces of thousands of kings, O Pārtha, Sātyaki comes swiftly on."

**7.116.24**  "Having conquered Duryodhana together with his brothers in the battle, and slain Jalasaṃdha, Sātyaki comes swiftly on."

**7.116.25**  "Having made a river that runs in floods of blood, miry with gore, and cast down the Kauravas like so much grass, Sātyaki comes onward."

**7.116.26**  Then the son of Kuntī, far from glad, spoke these words to Keśava: "It pleases me not, O mighty-armed one, that Sātyaki comes toward me."

**7.116.27**  "For I do not know the tidings of the Dharma-king, O Keśava—whether, bereft of the Sātvata, he yet lives or no."

**7.116.28**  "By him, O mighty-armed one, that king ought to have been guarded; how then, O Kṛṣṇa, has this my follower forsaken him?"

**7.116.29**  "The king is left exposed to Droṇa, the Saindhava is not yet struck down, and this Bhūriśravas advances against Śaineya in the field."

**7.116.30**  "Now this is a burden heavier than the Saindhava laid upon me: I must learn how the king fares, and I must protect Sātyaki."

**7.116.31**  "And Jayadratha must be slain, and the sun is sinking low; and this mighty-armed one is now wearied and short of breath."

**7.116.32**  "Spent are his horses, O Mādhava, and his driver too; but Bhūriśravas is not weary, and he has comrades at his side, O Keśava."

**7.116.33**  "Might it now go well with him in this encounter? May Sātyaki of unfailing valour, that bull of Śini's line of mighty energy, not founder in a cow's hoofprint after crossing the very ocean!"

**7.116.34**  "May Sātyaki come through unharmed in his meeting with Bhūriśravas, that foremost of the Kauravas, a master of arms and a great soul."

**7.116.35**  "I count this a transgression on the part of the Dharma-king, O Keśava, who, casting aside his fear of the Preceptor, sends Sātyaki forth."

**7.116.36**  "Droṇa forever yearns to seize the Dharma-king, as a hawk on the wing yearns for its prey. Is the king, I wonder, yet safe?"

**7.117.1**  Saṃjaya said: Beholding that Sātvata, frenzied for battle, rushing on, Bhūriśravas, O king, in his wrath charged against him at once.

**7.117.2**  The mighty-armed Kaurava spoke to that bull of Śini's line: "By good fortune you have come this day within the range of my sight!"

**7.117.3**  "The desire long cherished I shall fulfil this day in combat; you shall not escape me alive unless you abandon the fight."

**7.117.4**  "Slaying you this day in battle—you who ever account yourself a hero, O Dāśārha—I shall gladden Suyodhana, king of the Kurus."

**7.117.5**  "This day, scorched by my shafts and fallen to the earth, you shall the two heroes Keśava and Arjuna behold together in the field."

**7.117.6**  "This day the king, the son of Dharma, by whom you were sent into this fray, hearing that you have been slain by me, shall at once be filled with shame."

**7.117.7**  "This day shall Pārtha Dhanaṃjaya know my prowess, when you lie struck down upon the earth, drenched in blood."

**7.117.8**  "This meeting with you, long desired, is come to me this day, as of old in the war of gods and demons the encounter of Śakra with Bali."

**7.117.9**  "This day I shall give you most dreadful battle, O Sātvata; then shall you know in truth my valour, my strength, and my manhood."

**7.117.10**  "This day, slain by me in battle, you shall fare to the city of Yama, as in the fray Rāvaṇa's son was slain by Lakṣmaṇa, the younger brother of Rāma."

**7.117.11**  "This day, O Mādhava, when you are slain, Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha and the Dharma-king, robbed of all heart, shall doubtless abandon the battle."

**7.117.12**  "This day, O Mādhava, having taken vengeance upon you with whetted shafts, I shall gladden the women of those whom you slew in the field."

**7.117.13**  "Come within the range of my sight, O Mādhava, you shall not escape, even as a little deer that has come within a lion's reach."

**7.117.14**  But Yuyudhāna, O king, answered him as though laughing: "O scion of Kuru, no terror dwells in me amid combat."

**7.117.15**  "He alone could slay me in battle who first could leave me weaponless; and he who would slay me in combat must strive through unending years to do it."

**7.117.16**  "What use this much idle talk? Set to the deed itself! Your thunder is as barren as that of an autumn cloud."

**7.117.17**  "Hearing this thundering of yours, O hero, laughter rises in me. Let the battle long desired in this world be ours this day, O Kaurava!"

**7.117.18**  "My mind hastens eagerly, sir, now that you long for battle. I shall not turn back this day, O basest of men, until I have slain you."

**7.117.19**  Then those two bulls among men, gashing one another with words, athirst to kill and wrought to utmost fury, fell upon each other in the fray.

**7.117.20**  Those two tigers among men, fierce and rivalrous, met in the battle like two enraged elephants frenzied with rut, contending for a she-elephant.

**7.117.21**  Bhūriśravas and Sātyaki, those tamers of foes, rained dreadful showers of arrows upon each other like two storm-clouds.

**7.117.22**  The son of Somadatta, O best of the Bhāratas, veiling Śaineya with swift-flying shafts and athirst to slay him, pierced him with whetted arrows.

**7.117.23**  Having pierced Sātyaki with ten shafts, the son of Somadatta then let fly yet more keen arrows, eager to slay that bull of Śini's line.

**7.117.24**  Those sharp arrows of his, O lord of peoples, Sātyaki devoured in mid-air by the magic of his weapons, O mighty one, before ever they reached him.

**7.117.25**  Each of those two heroes of noblest birth, who brought glory upon the Kuru and the Vṛṣṇi lines, rained showers of arrows upon the other.

**7.117.26**  As two tigers with their claws, as two great elephants with their tusks, so did they rend each other with chariot-spears and with arrows.

**7.117.27**  Piercing each other's limbs and pouring forth their blood, they held one another at bay, gamblers staking life itself in the play.

**7.117.28**  Thus those two of supreme deeds, who brought glory upon the Kuru and the Vṛṣṇi lines, fought one against the other like two leaders of elephant herds.

**7.117.29**  In no long time, with the world of Brahmā set before them, each striving to win the supreme abode, they smote upon one another.

**7.117.30**  Sātyaki and the son of Somadatta rained shafts upon each other as though in joy, while the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra looked on.

**7.117.31**  The hosts gazed there upon those two lords of warriors as they fought, like two herd-bull elephants battling for the sake of a she-elephant.

**7.117.32**  Having slain each other's horses and cut apart each other's bows, the two, bereft of their chariots, closed for sword-combat in that great battle.

**7.117.33**  Taking up their broad and gleaming shields of bull's hide, bright with figures, and drawing their swords from the scabbard, the two ranged about the field.

**7.117.34**  Moving along varied tracks and through their circling figures one by one, those crushers of foes in their wrath struck again and again at each other.

**7.117.35**  Swords in hand, in figured mail, adorned with golden necklets and armlets, those two who exulted in war, O king, dragged each other to and fro in the battle.

**7.117.36**  For a while, O lord of kings, having hauled each other about before the gaze of all the hosts, the two heroes drew breath again.

**7.117.37**  Having hewn apart with their swords the bright broad shields that warded off the shafts, those two tigers among men set themselves to wrestling with bare arms.

**7.117.38**  Broad-chested and long-armed, both skilled in the wrestler's art, they grappled with their arms as though with bars of iron.

**7.117.39**  Their blows of arm, their grips and counter-grips, sprung from skill and strength, were a delight to all the warriors there.

**7.117.40**  As those two best of men contended in the field, O king, there arose a fearful, mighty din, as of mountains of adamant.

**7.117.41**  Like two elephants with the points of their tusks, like two great bulls with their horns, those high-souled bulls of the Kuru and Sātvata lines did battle.

**7.117.42**  As the Sātvata fought on, his weapons now spent, Vāsudeva spoke then to Arjuna: "Behold him fighting without his chariot in the fray—the banner of all who bear the bow!"

**7.117.43**  "He entered the Bhārata host at your back, O Pāṇḍava, and was set upon by all the Bhāratas of mighty valour, O scion of Bharata."

**7.117.44**  "Worn out, that best of warriors has come upon Bhūriśravas, who advances athirst for battle. This is no even match, O Arjuna."

**7.117.45**  Then Bhūriśravas in his wrath, O king, lifting up Sātyaki, who was frenzied for the fight, dashed him down as a maddened elephant dashes down another in rut.

**7.117.46**  Even as those two foremost of warriors, Keśava and Arjuna, stationed wrathful upon their chariot, looked on at the battle, O king—

**7.117.47**  —then mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa spoke again to Arjuna: "See, that tiger of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas has fallen into the power of Somadatta's son!"

**7.117.48**  "Worn out and brought to the ground, after performing a deed most hard to do, is your own pupil, the brave Sātyaki. Protect him, Arjuna!"

**7.117.49**  "Let him not fall into the power of this lover of sacrifices, O best slayer of foes. For your own sake, O tiger among men, let it be done at once, O mighty one!"

**7.117.50**  Then Dhanaṃjaya, his mind exultant, said to Vāsudeva: "Look at that bull of the Kurus sporting with the foremost hero of the Vṛṣṇis—as a furious great elephant in the forest sports with the leader of a lion-pride."

**7.117.51**  A great cry of dismay went up from the armies, O bull of the Bhāratas, when the mighty-armed one, lifting Sātyaki up, struck him down to the ground.

**7.117.52**  Dragging the foremost of the Sātvatas like a lion hauling an elephant, the best of the Kurus, lavish in his sacrificial gifts, shone resplendent in the battle.

**7.117.53**  Then, drawing his sword from its sheath in the fray, Bhūriśravas seized Sātyaki by the hair and struck him on the chest with his foot.

**7.117.54**  Seeing the Sātvata thus being dragged about in the battle, O king, Vāsudeva spoke once more to Arjuna:

**7.117.55**  "Behold this tiger of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas fallen into the power of Somadatta's son—your own pupil, O mighty-armed one, second to none but you in archery!"

**7.117.56**  "Untrue is the show of valor, O Pārtha, when in this battle Bhūriśravas gets the better of Sātyaki of the Vṛṣṇis, whose own prowess is true."

**7.117.57**  Thus addressed by Vāsudeva, the mighty-armed son of Pāṇḍu honored Bhūriśravas in his heart for his conduct in the battle:

**7.117.58**  "Dragging the foremost of the Sātvatas about, as if in sport in the battle, this enhancer of the Kurus' glory delights me all the more."

**7.117.59**  "For he does not slay Sātyaki, the foremost of the Vṛṣṇi heroes; like a lion dragging a great elephant in the forest, so does he haul him about."

**7.117.60**  Thus having honored the Kaurava in his heart, O king, the mighty-armed Pārtha, Arjuna, replied to Vāsudeva:

**7.117.61**  "Since my gaze is fixed upon the lord of the Sindhus, I do not see him clearly, O Mādhava. Yet this hard deed I will do, for the Yādava's sake."

**7.117.62**  So saying, and carrying out the word of Vāsudeva, the son of Pāṇḍu with a feathered shaft severed the sword-wielding arm of that lover of sacrifices.

**7.118.1**  Saṃjaya said: That noble arm, still gripping the sword and bright with its fair armlet, fell to the ground, bringing the keenest grief to the world of the living.

**7.118.2**  That arm, raised to strike but cut off by the unseen Kirīṭin, fell swiftly to the earth like a five-headed serpent.

**7.118.3**  Seeing himself thus thwarted by Pārtha, the Kaurava released Sātyaki and in his wrath rebuked the son of Pāṇḍu:

**7.118.4**  "A cruel deed, alas, O son of Kuntī, you have done, in that you cut off my arm while I was looking elsewhere, my mind engaged with another."

**7.118.5**  "What will you say to King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma? 'Bhūriśravas was slain by me in battle while doing what?'"

**7.118.6**  "Was this the weapon taught you in person by great-souled Indra, O Pārtha, or by Rudra, or by Droṇa, or by Kṛpa?"

**7.118.7**  "Are you not indeed known throughout the world as one who knows his own duty, surpassing others? How then have you struck in battle a man not fighting against you?"

**7.118.8**  "Men of wisdom do not strike one who is heedless, one who is afraid, one whose chariot is gone, one who begs for mercy, or one caught in distress."

**7.118.9**  "This base conduct, practiced only by ignoble men—how have you, O Pārtha, performed so unworthy a deed?"

**7.118.10**  "For they say a noble deed is easy for a noble man, O Dhanaṃjaya; but an ignoble deed done by a noble man is the hardest thing on earth."

**7.118.11**  "In whatever company a man moves, O Pārtha, and in whatever circumstances he lives, he soon takes on its character—and this is seen now in you."

**7.118.12**  "How is it that you, born of a royal line, and a Kaurava above all, of fair conduct and faithful to your vows, have strayed from the duty of a warrior?"

**7.118.13**  "This utterly mean act, done by you for the Vṛṣṇi's sake, was surely the counsel of Vāsudeva—it does not befit you."

**7.118.14**  "For who that was not the friend of Kṛṣṇa would inflict such a calamity upon a man engaged in fighting with another?"

**7.118.15**  "The Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas are outcastes given to vile dealings, despised by their very nature—how, O Pārtha, have you made them your standard?"

**7.118.16**  Having said this, the mighty-armed and far-famed hero of the sacrificial-post banner abandoned Yuyudhāna and sat down upon the battlefield to fast unto death.

**7.118.17**  Spreading out arrows with his left hand, that man of holy marks, desiring to go to the world of Brahmā, then offered his life-breaths as an oblation into the breaths themselves.

**7.118.18**  Fixing his eyes upon the sun and his serene mind upon the waters, meditating on the great mystic doctrine and joined in yoga, he became a sage.

**7.118.19**  Then throughout all the host the men reproached Kṛṣṇa and Dhanaṃjaya, and they praised that bull among men.

**7.118.20**  Though thus reviled, the two Kṛṣṇas said nothing unkind in reply; and though thus praised, the bearer of the sacrificial-post banner felt no elation.

**7.118.21**  O king, Dhanaṃjaya, unable in his heart to bear those words of your sons and of Bhūriśravas as they spoke,

**7.118.22**  yet with a mind free of anger, as if reminding them, O Bhārata, the son of Pāṇḍu, Phalguna, spoke, almost with a tone of reproach:

**7.118.23**  "All the kings know this great vow of mine: that none of my own people may be slain by another, if he comes within the range of my arrows."

**7.118.24**  "O bearer of the sacrificial-post banner, reflect, and you ought not to censure me; for it is not right to blame another without first understanding the law."

**7.118.25**  "That in battle I cut off the arm of you who, weapon in hand, were bent on slaying the Vṛṣṇi hero—that is no conduct to be condemned."

**7.118.26**  "As for the slaying of Abhimanyu—a mere boy, his weapons laid down, his chariot lost, his armor gone—what righteous man, dear sir, would commend it?"

**7.118.27**  Thus addressed by Pārtha, Bhūriśravas touched the ground with his head, and with his left hand he flung aside his own severed right arm.

**7.118.28**  Having heard these words of Pārtha, the splendid bearer of the sacrificial-post banner, O great king, fell silent, his face bowed down.

**7.118.29**  Arjuna said: "The love I bear to the King of Righteousness, and to Bhīma, best of speakers, and to Nakula and Sahadeva—that same love I bear to you, O elder brother of Śala."

**7.118.30**  "With my leave, and that of great-souled Kṛṣṇa, go now to the worlds of those who have done holy deeds, even as Śibi, the son of Uśīnara, once did."

**7.118.31**  Saṃjaya said: Then the grandson of Śini, released by Somadatta's son, rose up and, taking up his sword, sought to cut off the head of that great-souled one.

**7.118.32**  Sātyaki sought to slay that sinless elder brother of Śala—the lavish giver of sacrificial gifts—who, while heedless, had already been struck down by the son of Pāṇḍu.

**7.118.33**  As all the troops cried out, Sātyaki, reviled by them and sick at heart, advanced upon him as he sat with his arm hewn off, like an elephant whose trunk has been severed.

**7.118.34**  Though restrained by Kṛṣṇa, by great-souled Pārtha, by Bhīma, by the two wheel-guards, by Aśvatthāman and by Kṛpa,

**7.118.35**  and by Karṇa, by Vṛṣasena and by the lord of the Sindhus as well, and amid the outcry of all the troops, he slew that man of disciplined vows.

**7.118.36**  As that Kaurava lord, his arm cut off by Pārtha, sat fasting unto death on the battlefield, Sātyaki struck off his head with his sword.

**7.118.37**  The troops did not applaud Sātyaki for that deed—that he had slain this glory of the Kurus who had already been struck down before by Arjuna.

**7.118.38**  There the Siddhas, the Cāraṇas, and men alike, beholding Bhūriśravas—the equal of the thousand-eyed Indra—slain in battle as he sat fasting,

**7.118.39**  the gods honored him, amazed at his deeds; and his own soldiers spoke many words taking his part.

**7.118.40**  "It is no fault of the Vṛṣṇi, for what was destined had to be so. Therefore you should bear him no grudge—wrath only brings grief to men."

**7.118.41**  "This hero was fated to be slain, and on that there should be no debate; for the Ordainer himself had appointed Sātyaki to be his death in battle."

**7.118.42**  Sātyaki said: "You who tell me, 'He must not be slain, he must not be slain,' with your talk of righteousness—most unrighteous men, you have wrapped yourselves in a mere cloak of righteousness!"

**7.118.43**  "When the boy, Subhadrā's son, stripped of his weapons, was slain by you in battle—where then had your righteousness gone?"

**7.118.44**  "This vow I once made, upon some taunt or other: that whoever should crush me in battle and, while I yet lived, strike me with his foot in fury—that enemy should be slain by me, even were he bound by the vows of a sage."

**7.118.45**  "You, who have eyes, deem me dead though I was struggling to strike back and still had my arm—such is the shallowness of your judgment! The retaliation I have wrought upon him was fitting, O bulls of the Kurus."

**7.118.46**  "That Pārtha, out of love for me and to keep his own vow, cut off this man's sword-bearing arm—by that very act I have been cheated of my due."

**7.118.47**  "What is to be must be, and fate, as it were, drives men to act. He has been slain in this fray—what unrighteous deed is there in that?"

**7.118.48**  "And moreover this verse was sung of old by Vālmīki upon the earth: 'Whatever brings harm to one's enemies, that very thing must be done.'"

**7.118.49**  Saṃjaya said: When this had been spoken, O great king, all the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas said nothing, but honored Bhūriśravas in their hearts.

**7.118.50**  For of him—purified by sacred chants at his great rites, glorious, the giver of countless thousands, now like a sage gone to the forest—of his slaying not one there approved.

**7.118.51**  The head of that bounteous, brave one, dark-blue-haired and dove-red of eye, lay severed like the head of a sacrificial horse set down to the north of the oblation-cart.

**7.118.52**  Purified by that splendor smitten down by the sword, he cast off his noble body in the great battle, and that bounteous one, worthy of the highest boons, rose upward, filling heaven and earth with his surpassing righteousness.

**7.119.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Unconquered by Droṇa, by Rādheya, by Vikarṇa and Kṛtavarman, that hero, having pledged himself to Yudhiṣṭhira, had crossed the ocean of the army.

**7.119.2**  How was it that he, unchecked in battle, came to be seized by the Kaurava Bhūriśravas and hurled by force to the ground?

**7.119.3**  Saṃjaya said: Hear, O king, the origin of the grandson of Śini in days of old, and that of Bhūriśravas as well, wherein lies your doubt, O lord of men.

**7.119.4**  From Atri was born Soma; of Soma, Budha is recorded; and Budha had one son, Purūravas, splendid as the great Indra.

**7.119.5**  Of Purūravas came Āyus; of Āyus, Nahuṣa is recorded; and of Nahuṣa, Yayāti, a royal sage held equal to the gods.

**7.119.6**  Of Yayāti by Devayānī, Yadu was born, the eldest son; and in the lineage of Yadu there arose one famed as Devamīḍha.

**7.119.7**  His son was the Yādava Śūra, honored throughout the three worlds; and of Śūra came his son, the foremost of men, the far-famed Vāsudeva.

**7.119.8**  Unsurpassed in archery, a brave man equal to Kārtavīrya in battle—and of like prowess, in that very line, was born King Śini.

**7.119.9**  Now at that very time, O king, at the self-choice ceremony of the daughter of great-souled Devaka, where all the warrior caste had assembled,

**7.119.10**  there indeed Śini, vanquishing all the kings, won the lady Devakī for Vāsudeva's sake and set her upon his chariot.

**7.119.11**  Seeing that Devakī standing on Śini's chariot, O king, the bull among men, the mighty Somadatta, could not endure it.

**7.119.12**  A combat arose between the two, O king, wondrous and astonishing, lasting half a day—a wrestling match of two mighty men, like that of Śakra and Prahrāda.

**7.119.13**  By Śini, Somadatta was overpowered and flung to the ground; and seizing him by the hair and raising his sword, Śini struck him with his foot.

**7.119.14**  In the midst of thousands of kings looking on from every side, out of pity he was released by him with the words, "Live!"

**7.119.15**  Reduced to that condition by him, Somadatta then, O honored one, gave himself up to indignation and set about propitiating Mahādeva.

**7.119.16**  Pleased with him, Mahādeva, the Lord, granter of boons among boons, offered him a choice; and that king chose his boon.

**7.119.17**  "I desire a son, O Blessed One, who shall slay the son of Śini, and in the midst of thousands of kings shall strike him down with his foot in battle."

**7.119.18**  Hearing those words of Somadatta, O king, the god said, "So be it," and there vanished.

**7.119.19**  By that granting of the boon he obtained Bhūriśravas of abundant sacrificial gifts; and in battle the son of Somadatta did indeed lay low the son of Śini.

**7.119.20**  This have I told you, O king, concerning that whereof you ask me; the Sātvatas cannot be conquered in battle, O bull among men.

**7.119.21**  Many among them are sure of their aim in combat and fight with wondrous skill; unbewildered, they are conquerors of gods, dānavas, and gandharvas; bent upon victory won by their own valor, they are not subject to any other's possession.

**7.119.22**  Nothing equal to the Vṛṣṇis is seen here, O lord—nothing that has been, that is, or that shall be, in strength, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.119.23**  They never slight a kinsman, and delight in the rule of their elders; neither gods, asuras, nor gandharvas, neither yakṣas, serpents, nor rākṣasas can vanquish the Vṛṣṇi heroes in war—still less men.

**7.119.24**  Toward the wealth of brahmins, of teachers, and of kinsmen they do no harm; and they are protectors of these, should any one of them fall into distress.

**7.119.25**  Wealthy yet not arrogant, devoted to brahmins, speakers of truth, they do not slight the powerful, and they raise up the wretched.

**7.119.26**  Ever devoted to the gods, self-controlled, generous, and free from boasting—therefore the wheel of the Vṛṣṇi heroes' dominion is never broken.

**7.119.27**  One might bear Mount Meru, or swim across the abode of sea-monsters, but he could not, having met the Vṛṣṇi heroes, come to their end, O king.

**7.119.28**  All this have I declared to you, wherein your doubt lay, O mighty one; O king of the Kurus, best of men, great indeed is your misconduct.

**7.120.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When that Kaurava Bhūriśravas had been slain in such a plight, tell me, Saṃjaya, how the battle raged on once more.

**7.120.2**  Saṃjaya said: When Bhūriśravas had passed on to the other world, O Bhārata, the mighty-armed Arjuna urged Vāsudeva onward.

**7.120.3**  "Drive the horses hard, Kṛṣṇa, to where King Jayadratha is; the maker of day hastens, O mighty-armed one, to its setting."

**7.120.4**  "For this great deed I have undertaken, O tiger among men; and this man is being guarded by the great chariot-warriors of the Kuru host."

**7.120.5**  "So drive the horses, Kṛṣṇa, that the sun shall not set, that my word may prove true, that I may slay Jayadratha."

**7.120.6**  Then the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, knower of horses, urged the silver-hued steeds onward toward the chariot of Jayadratha.

**7.120.7**  As he sped on, his shafts never failing, with arrows that flew as if leaping upward, the chief warriors of the host hastened to close round him, O great king.

**7.120.8**  Duryodhana and Karṇa and Vṛṣasena, the king of the Madras, Aśvatthāman and Kṛpa, and the lord of the Sindhus himself.

**7.120.9**  Drawing near, Bībhatsu beheld the lord of the Sindhus stationed at the front, and gazed upon him with eyes blazing with wrath, as if to burn him up.

**7.120.10**  Then King Duryodhana, seeing Arjuna advancing toward Jayadratha's chariot, swiftly said to the son of Rādhā:

**7.120.11**  "This, O Vaikartana, is the hour of battle; show forth your own strength, great soul. So act, Karṇa, that Jayadratha be not slain by Arjuna in the fight."

**7.120.12**  "Little of the day remains, O hero among men; strike down the foe now with floods of arrows. Once the day's end is reached, O foremost of men, our victory, Karṇa, shall surely be assured."

**7.120.13**  "If the lord of the Sindhus be but guarded until the setting of the sun, the son of Kuntī, his vow proved false, shall enter the fire."

**7.120.14**  "And on an earth bereft of Arjuna, O giver of honor, his brothers with their followers would not bear to live even for a moment."

**7.120.15**  "And with the sons of Pāṇḍu destroyed, we shall enjoy this earth, Karṇa, with its mountains, woods, and forests, its thorns plucked out."

**7.120.16**  "Smitten by fate and turned awry, O giver of honor, Pārtha, not knowing the doable from the undoable, made his vow in battle."

**7.120.17**  "Surely it was for his own destruction that the diademed son of Pāṇḍu made this vow, Karṇa, touching the slaying of Jayadratha."

**7.120.18**  "How, while you live, O unassailable son of Rādhā, shall Phalguna slay the Saindhava king before the sun has set?"

**7.120.19**  "Jayadratha, guarded at the battle's front by the king of the Madras and by the great-souled Kṛpa—how shall Dhanaṃjaya slay him?"

**7.120.20**  "And how, urged on by fate, shall Bībhatsu reach the lord of the Sindhus, who is guarded by Droṇa's son, by me, and by Duḥśāsana?"

**7.120.21**  "Many heroes are fighting, and the sun hangs low; I think, O giver of honor, that Pārtha shall not reach Jayadratha at all."

**7.120.22**  "Therefore, Karṇa, do you, together with me and with the other heroic great car-warriors, putting forth supreme effort, fight against Pārtha in the combat."

**7.120.23**  Thus addressed by your son, O honored one, the son of Rādhā spoke these words in answer to Duryodhana, the foremost of the Kurus:

**7.120.24**  "Sorely harassed in the fray, time and again, by the bowman Bhīmasena—that hero of unerring aim—with his nets of arrows,

**7.120.25**  "yet, resolved that I must stand, I stand even now in the battle, O giver of honor; though scorched by the shafts of war, no limb of mine so much as stirs."

**7.120.26**  "I shall fight, O king, in battle with all my utmost might, so that that chief of the Pāṇḍavas shall not slay the lord of the Sindhus."

**7.120.27**  "For while I fight and loose my whetted shafts, the hero Savyasācin Dhanaṃjaya shall not reach the lord of the Sindhus."

**7.120.28**  "Whatever ought to be done by one of power, who ever works for your good, that I shall do, O Kaurava; but victory rests with fate."

**7.120.29**  "Today I shall fight Arjuna, relying on my own manhood, for your sake, O tiger among men; but victory rests with fate."

**7.120.30**  "Today, O best of the Kurus, let all beings behold the dreadful, hair-raising battle of us two, of mine and Pārtha's."

**7.120.31**  While Karṇa and the Kaurava thus conversed in the field, Arjuna with his whetted shafts smote your host.

**7.120.32**  With keen-pointed arrows he severed in battle the arms of the unflinching heroes—arms like iron bars, like the trunks of elephants.

**7.120.33**  And the mighty-armed one clove with whetted shafts their heads, the trunks of elephants, the necks of horses, and the axles of chariots on every side.

**7.120.34**  With razor-edged shafts Bībhatsu cleft, each into two and into three, the blood-drenched horsemen who gripped their lances and pikes.

**7.120.35**  And the foremost of horses and elephants fell by thousands, with banners, parasols, bows, yak-tail fans, and heads.

**7.120.36**  Burning your host like a fire blazing up through dry brushwood, in but a little while Pārtha made the earth flooded over with blood.

**7.120.37**  Having made the greater part of your army's warriors slain, the mighty, unassailable hero of true valor bore down upon the lord of the Sindhus.

**7.120.38**  Bībhatsu, guarded by Bhīmasena and by the Sātvata, shone forth, O best of the Bhāratas, like a blazing fire.

**7.120.39**  Beholding Phalguna so stationed, your great bowmen, esteemed for their valor, bulls among men, could not endure it.

**7.120.40**  Duryodhana and Karṇa and Vṛṣasena, the king of the Madras, Aśvatthāman and Kṛpa, and the lord of the Sindhus himself—

**7.120.41**  these, enraged, for the Saindhava's sake hemmed in the diademed one, who danced along the chariot-paths to the twang of his bowstring and the slap of his palm-guard.

**7.120.42**  All skilled in war, fearless, they closed round Pārtha, the master of combat, as round Death with gaping jaws.

**7.120.43**  Keeping the lord of the Sindhus behind them, seeking to slay Arjuna and Acyuta, they longed for the sun's setting as the day-maker turned red.

**7.120.44**  With arms like the coils of serpents they drew their bows and loosed by hundreds at Phalguna shafts that gleamed like the rays of the sun.

**7.120.45**  But the diademed one, frenzied in battle, cleaving each of those loosed and flying shafts into two, three, and eight, pierced his foes in turn in the fray.

**7.120.46**  Then the son of Śāradvatī, whose banner bore the lion's tail, showing forth his own might, O king, withstood Arjuna.

**7.120.47**  Having pierced Pārtha with ten shafts and Vāsudeva with seven, he held his ground upon the chariot-paths, guarding the lord of the Sindhus.

**7.120.48**  Then all the foremost of the Kuru great car-warriors hemmed him in on every side with a vast array of chariots.

**7.120.49**  Twanging their bows and loosing their shafts, they guarded the lord of the Sindhus round about, by the command of your son.

**7.120.50**  There was seen the strength of the heroic Pārtha's arms, the inexhaustibility of his arrows, and the might of his bow Gāṇḍīva.

**7.120.51**  Warding off with his weapons the weapons of Droṇa's son and of the son of Śaradvat, he assailed every one of them, each with nine shafts.

**7.120.52**  Him Droṇa's son struck with twenty-five shafts, and Vṛṣasena with seven, Duryodhana with twenty, and Karṇa and Śalya each with three.

**7.120.53**  Roaring at him and piercing him again and again, and shaking their bows, they hemmed him in on every side.

**7.120.54**  Those great car-warriors, longing for the sun's setting, swiftly drew their ring of chariots close-locked on every side.

**7.120.55**  Bellowing at him and shaking their bows, they drenched him with dreadful shafts as the clouds drench a mountain with their waters.

**7.120.56**  There, O king, those heroes with arms like iron bars displayed their mighty celestial weapons upon the limbs of Dhanaṃjaya.

**7.120.57**  Having made the greater part of your army's warriors slain, the mighty, unassailable hero of true valor bore down upon the lord of the Sindhus.

**7.120.58**  Him Karṇa withstood in the combat, O king, with his swift arrows, before the very eyes of Bhīmasena and of the Sātvata, O Bhārata.

**7.120.59**  Him in turn the mighty-armed Pārtha pierced with ten shafts on the field of battle—the son of the charioteer—while all the host looked on.

**7.120.60**  And the Sātvata pierced Karṇa with three shafts, O honored one, and Bhīmasena with three, and Pārtha again with seven.

**7.120.61**  Karṇa, the great car-warrior, pierced them each in return with sixty shafts; and so, O king, there arose that battle of Karṇa against many.

**7.120.62**  There we beheld a marvel in the son of the charioteer, O honored one—that, wrathful and alone in the fray, he held three chariot-warriors at bay.

**7.120.63**  But the mighty-armed Phalguna struck Karṇa Vaikartana in the battle, with a full hundred shafts, upon all his vital parts.

**7.120.64**  His every limb bathed in blood, the valorous son of the charioteer, that hero, pierced Phalguna in return with fifty shafts; and seeing his deftness, Arjuna could not endure it in the fight.

**7.120.65**  Then Pārtha, severing his bow, pierced him between the breasts; the hero Dhanaṃjaya did so in haste, with nine shafts.

**7.120.66**  And to slay him in battle Dhanaṃjaya, swift in the hour that called for swiftness, hurled an arrow blazing like the sun.

**7.120.67**  But Droṇa's son, with a sharp crescent-headed shaft, cleft that arrow as it rushed upon him with speed, and so severed it fell to the earth.

**7.120.68**  Then the mighty son of the charioteer, Karṇa, the slayer of foes, took up another bow and, eager to repay blow with blow, covered Phalguna with arrows by the many thousands.

**7.120.69**  Those two great car-warriors, lions among men, bellowing like bulls, with their straight-flying shafts made the sky one mass of arrow-streams; veiled from sight by the floods of arrows, each struck at the other.

**7.120.70**  "I am Pārtha—stand and face me!" "I am Karṇa—stand, Phalguna!" Thus challenging each other, they pierced one another with the barbs of their words.

**7.120.71**  The two heroes fought in battle with skill, with swiftness, and with grace, and amid the gathering of all the warriors they were a sight worth beholding.

**7.120.72**  Praised in the fray by the throngs of Siddhas and Cāraṇas, O great king, they fought on, each seeking the other's death.

**7.120.73**  Then, O king, Duryodhana addressed your men: "Guard Rādheya with all your effort! The bull-like Karṇa has told me, 'I shall not turn back from the battle until I have slain Arjuna.'"

**7.120.74**  Meanwhile, O king, seeing Karṇa's prowess, Arjuna with arrows drawn to the ear sent Karṇa's four steeds to the realm of death with four excellent shafts.

**7.120.75**  With a broad-headed arrow he swept Karṇa's charioteer from the seat of the car, and covered him with shafts before the eyes of your son.

**7.120.76**  Overwhelmed in the fight, his horses slain and his driver slain, bewildered by the net of arrows, Karṇa could not tell what should be done.

**7.120.77**  Seeing him thus deprived of his car, O great king, Aśvatthāman took him up onto his own chariot, and once more did battle with Arjuna.

**7.120.78**  The king of the Madras pierced the son of Kuntī with thirty arrows, while Śāradvata struck Vāsudeva with twenty and smote Dhanaṃjaya with twelve bee-like shafts.

**7.120.79**  And the king of the Sindhus with four, and Vṛṣasena with seven, each in turn, O great king, pierced Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha.

**7.120.80**  In like manner Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī, pierced them in return—the son of Droṇa with sixty-four shafts and the king of the Madras with a hundred.

**7.120.81**  Having pierced the lord of the Sindhus with ten broad-headed arrows, Vṛṣasena with three shafts, and Śāradvata with twenty, Pārtha gave a great roar.

**7.120.82**  Wishing to thwart the vow of Savyasācin, your warriors together rushed swiftly upon Dhanaṃjaya.

**7.120.83**  Then Arjuna brought forth the weapon that cuts on every side, terrifying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; yet the Kurus advanced against the son of Pāṇḍu and, upon their costly chariots, poured down showers of arrows.

**7.120.84**  Then, O Bhārata, when that terrible, bewildering tumult arose, the diademed prince, far from being dazed, loosed his arrows undismayed.

**7.120.85**  Seeking to win back the kingdom, Savyasācin, remembering the sufferings he had borne for twelve years at the hands of the Kurus, that great soul, with countless arrows loosed from the Gāṇḍīva, covered every quarter of the sky.

**7.120.86**  The firmament seemed ablaze with falling meteors, and birds in multitudes alighted upon the corpses, as the diademed hero in his wrath slew his foes with his tawny-stringed bow, the Ājagava.

**7.120.87**  The diademed one, of great renown, conqueror of armies, with his mighty bow struck down with his shafts the foremost Kuru heroes—those mounted on the choicest horses and at the head of the great elephants.

**7.120.88**  And the kings, dreadful to behold, seizing heavy maces, iron bludgeons, swords and spears and great weapons, all at once rushed upon Pārtha in the fray.

**7.120.89**  But that hero, the mighty bowman, made those onrushing foes—with their chariots, horses, and elephants, and their bands of footmen—bereft of all their weapons and of their lives, swelling the realm of Yama.

**7.121.1**  Saṃjaya said: Pārtha, the splendid Dhanaṃjaya, ranged across the battlefield, displaying in all directions at once his wondrous weapons, a sight worth beholding.

**7.121.2**  As none can gaze upon the sun blazing in the sky at noon, so could no creature look full upon the Pāṇḍava.

**7.121.3**  The flights of arrows streaming from the Gāṇḍīva of that great soul we beheld in the battle like rows of wild geese across the sky.

**7.121.4**  Having warded off on every side the weapons of those heroes with his own weapons, he revealed his terrible self, fixed firmly upon his fierce work.

**7.121.5**  Bewildering those foremost car-warriors, as it were, with his iron shafts, Arjuna pressed past them all, O king, in his longing to slay Jayadratha.

**7.121.6**  Loosing his arrows in every direction, his dark-hued charioteer beside him, the splendid Dhanaṃjaya ranged swiftly across the field, a sight worth beholding.

**7.121.7**  The flights of arrows of that great-souled hero, as though wheeling through the air, were seen poised aloft by the hundreds and the thousands.

**7.121.8**  The mighty bowman drawing forth his shafts, the Pāṇḍava fitting them to the string, and the son of Kuntī loosing them—of these we could discern nothing then.

**7.121.9**  Having thrown into confusion all the quarters and all the car-warriors in the fray, O king, the son of Kuntī bore down upon Jayadratha and pierced him with sixty-four smooth-jointed arrows.

**7.121.10**  But the lord of the Sindhus, thus pierced by the arrows of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, did not endure it, raging like an elephant goaded by the hook.

**7.121.11**  He of the boar-banner swiftly loosed in battle at Savyasācin keen shafts—vulture-feathered, straight-flying, like venomous serpents, burnished by the smith.

**7.121.12**  With three iron shafts he pierced the Gāṇḍīva, Arjuna with six, the horses with eight, and the banner with a single feathered arrow.

**7.121.13**  Arjuna, scattering the sharp shafts sent by the Saindhava, at one stroke with two arrows severed from the body the head of the Saindhava's charioteer and his ornamented banner.

**7.121.14**  Its staff cut through, that great boar of the Sindhu king's banner, shattered and struck by the arrow, fell like a tongue of flame.

**7.121.15**  At that very moment, as the sun was swiftly setting, Janārdana in haste spoke to the Pāṇḍava:

**7.121.16**  "Dhanaṃjaya, cut off the head of the wicked Saindhava! The day-maker is about to descend behind the foremost of mountains. Hear, too, my word concerning the slaying of Jayadratha."

**7.121.17**  "Vṛddhakṣatra, the father of the Saindhava, is renowned throughout the world. After a long age he obtained the Saindhava as his son."

**7.121.18**  "And to that king, the foe-slaying Jayadratha, a disembodied voice, deep as the thunder of clouds, then spoke:"

**7.121.19**  "'This son of yours, O lord, shall be among mortals worthy of both your lineages in his virtues—in family, in conduct, in self-restraint, and the rest—foremost of Kṣatriyas in the world, ever honored by the brave.'"

**7.121.20**  "'Yet as this bowman fights his enemies in battle, an angered foe, unmarked upon the earth, shall cut off his head.'"

**7.121.21**  "Hearing this, O tamer of foes, the Sindhu king pondered long, and, tormented by love for his son, said this to all his kinsmen:"

**7.121.22**  "'Whoever, while my son fights in battle bearing his mighty burden, shall cast his head upon the earth—that man's head too shall burst into a hundred pieces; of this there is no doubt.'"

**7.121.23**  "Having spoken thus and set Jayadratha upon the throne, Vṛddhakṣatra went to the forest and gave himself to the practice of austerity."

**7.121.24**  "That radiant one, O you of the monkey-banner, is even now practicing terrible, hard-won austerity, just outside this field of Samantapañcaka."

**7.121.25**  "Therefore, O slayer of foes, when in this great battle you have cut off Jayadratha's head with a divine weapon of terrible and wondrous power—"

**7.121.26**  "—cast it, O younger brother of the Wind-god's son, still wearing its earrings, swiftly into the lap of Vṛddhakṣatra, O Bhārata, the head of the lord of the Sindhus."

**7.121.27**  "But if you let his head fall upon the ground, then your own head too shall burst into a hundred pieces; of this there is no doubt."

**7.121.28**  "And contrive it, O best of the Kurus, that this king, the lord of the earth, may not know of it—having recourse to the divine weapon."

**7.121.29**  "For there is nothing impossible or undoable for you in any of the three worlds entire, O delight of Vāsava."

**7.121.30**  Hearing these words, Arjuna, licking the corners of his mouth, took up an arrow whose touch was like Indra's thunderbolt, hallowed with divine spells—

**7.121.31**  —a shaft able to bear every burden, ever honored with perfumes and garlands; this Arjuna swiftly let fly, bent upon the slaying of the Saindhava.

**7.121.32**  That arrow, loosed from the Gāṇḍīva, swift as a hawk, bore off the head of the Saindhava as a hawk carries off a bird from the treetop.

**7.121.33**  And Dhanaṃjaya bore that head still higher with his arrows, to the dismay of his enemies and the joy of his friends.

**7.121.34**  Bearing it aloft on a cluster of arrows at that hour, the Pāṇḍava then carried that head beyond Samantapañcaka.

**7.121.35**  At that very moment, O revered one, the radiant king Vṛddhakṣatra, your kinsman by marriage, was performing his twilight worship.

**7.121.36**  As he sat at worship, Arjuna let fall into his lap the head of the Sindhu king, black-haired and still wearing its earrings.

**7.121.37**  That head with its fair earrings fell into the lap of King Vṛddhakṣatra unnoticed, O tamer of foes.

**7.121.38**  Then, as the wise Vṛddhakṣatra, his muttered prayers completed, rose up, that head suddenly slipped to the surface of the earth.

**7.121.39**  And then, when his son's head had fallen to the ground from that king's lap, his own head too, O tamer of foes, burst into a hundred pieces.

**7.121.40**  Then all beings were struck with the utmost wonder, and Vāsudeva praised Bībhatsu, that mighty car-warrior.

**7.121.41**  Then, beholding Jayadratha, the king of the Sindhus, slain, much water fell in grief from the eyes of your sons.

**7.121.42**  Bhīmasena too, as though signaling to the Pāṇḍava in the fray, filled heaven and earth with a great lion's roar.
