**7.121.43**  Hearing that mighty roar, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, judged that the Saindhava had been slain by the great-souled Phalguna.

**7.121.44**  Then, gladdening his own warriors with the clamor of instruments, he advanced into the battle against the son of Bharadvāja, eager to fight.

**7.121.45**  Then, O king, as the sun was setting, a hair-raising battle broke out between Droṇa and the Somakas.

**7.121.46**  Those great car-warriors, O king, seeking with all their might to slay the son of Bharadvāja now that the Saindhava was slain, fought on.

**7.121.47**  And the Pāṇḍavas, having won the victory and slain the Saindhava, then, frenzied with triumph, did battle with Droṇa on every side.

**7.121.48**  Arjuna too, O great king, having slain the king of the Sindhus, did battle in the fray with your warriors, those foremost of car-warriors.

**7.121.49**  Having fulfilled his earlier vow, the diademed hero scattered them on every side, as the king of the gods scatters the foes of the gods, and as the risen dispeller of darkness dispels the shadows.

**7.122.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When that hero, the Saindhava, had been slain by Savyasācin, tell me, Saṃjaya, what my men then did.

**7.122.2**  Saṃjaya said: Seeing the Saindhava slain in battle by Pārtha, O revered one, Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, was then overcome with wrath.

**7.122.3**  With a great shower of arrows he covered the Pāṇḍava, and Droṇa's son too, mounting his chariot, charged upon Pārtha, upon Phalguna.

**7.122.4**  Those two foremost of car-warriors, from their two chariots, both on either side, rained sharp arrows upon him, the best of car-warriors.

**7.122.5**  Thus assailed by those two mighty showers of arrows, that strong-armed one, the best of car-warriors, fell into the deepest distress.

**7.122.6**  Unwilling to slay in battle his teacher's kinsman and the son of his teacher, Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī, there displayed his mastery of the craft.

**7.122.7**  Warding off with his weapons the weapons of both Droṇa's son and the son of Śaradvat, he loosed at the two of them slow-flying arrows, having no wish to kill them.

**7.122.8**  Though the shafts, urged on toward victory, did not strike them too grievously, by their sheer multitude the two warriors were brought to the utmost anguish.

**7.122.9**  Then, O king, the son of Śaradvat, tormented by the arrows of Kuntī's son, sank down upon the floor of his chariot and fell into a swoon.

**7.122.10**  Perceiving his master reeling and stricken by arrows, and thinking him slain, the charioteer bore him away from the field.

**7.122.11**  When Kṛpa, son of Śaradvat, had collapsed in the battle, O great king, Aśvatthāman too withdrew from the Pāṇḍava to another part of the field.

**7.122.12**  Beholding the son of Śaradvat swooning, racked by arrows, the great archer Pārtha, there upon his chariot, lamented piteously.

**7.122.13**  Beholding this, the deeply wise Vidura had spoken to the king when wicked Suyodhana, destroyer of the lineage, was but newly born:

**7.122.14**  'Let this defiler of the line be sent rightly to the other world; for from him will arise a great terror for the chiefs of the Kurus.'

**7.122.15**  That word of the truth-speaker has now come to pass, for on his account I see Kṛpa today laid out upon a bed of arrows.

**7.122.16**  Fie upon the warrior's code, fie upon strength and manly valor! For who like me would do violence to a brāhmaṇa, his own teacher?

**7.122.17**  My teacher, son of a seer, the beloved friend of Droṇa — here he lies upon his chariot, oppressed by my arrows.

**7.122.18**  Though I wished it not, sorely afflicted by my shafts he sank upon his chariot; it is as though he wrings the very life from me.

**7.122.19**  For I, myself worn by arrows yet observant of the tenfold duty, have driven back with many shafts this man of splendor, lovely to behold.

**7.122.20**  His falling grieves me more even than the slaying of a son. See, Kṛṣṇa, how piteously he has sunk, undone, upon his own chariot.

**7.122.21**  Those bulls among men who, having received learning from their teachers, render to them here the objects of their desire — they attain to godhood.

**7.122.22**  But those basest of men who, having taken learning from their elders, then slay those very ones — such evil-doers go to hell.

**7.122.23**  Surely, then, this deed I have done today leads to hell — bringing low my teacher Kṛpa upon his chariot with a rain of arrows.

**7.122.24**  For when of old he was imparting the weapon to me, Kṛpa told me: 'In no wise, O Kaurava, is a blow ever to be struck against one's teacher.'

**7.122.25**  That word of my good and great-souled teacher I have not heeded — raining shafts upon that very man in battle.

**7.122.26**  Homage to that most worthy Gautama, who never flees the fight! Fie upon me, O Vārṣṇeya, who strike a blow against him!

**7.122.27**  While Savyasācin was thus lamenting over him, the son of Rādhā, beholding the lord of the Sindhus slain, rushed forward.

**7.122.28**  Seeing the son of Rādhā advancing, the great chariot-warrior Pārtha, smiling, spoke this word to the son of Devakī:

**7.122.29**  'There goes the son of Adhiratha toward Sātyaki's chariot; surely he cannot bear that Bhūriśravas was slain in the fray.'

**7.122.30**  'Wherever he goes, drive the horses thither, Janārdana, lest that bull Karṇa send Sātyaki down the road that Somadatta's son has trodden.'

**7.122.31**  Thus addressed by Savyasācin, the mighty-armed Keśava of great splendor replied with this word, fitting to the hour:

**7.122.32**  'Alone, O Pāṇḍava, this mighty-armed bull of the Sātvatas is a match enough for Karṇa — how much more so when joined by the two sons of Draupadī!'

**7.122.33**  'And the time is not yet fit, Pārtha, for your clash with Karṇa; for Indra's weapon stands by him, blazing like a great meteor, kept and honored, O slayer of foes, that he may loose it upon you.'

**7.122.34**  'Therefore let Karṇa go yonder against the Sātvata, come what may; I shall know, O Kaurava, the appointed hour of that evil-souled one.'

**7.122.35**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: That encounter of the Vārṣṇeya with the hero Karṇa, after Bhūriśravas was slain and the lord of the Sindhus brought down —

**7.122.36**  And Sātyaki, his car undone, what chariot did he mount? And who were the two Pāñcāla guards of his wheels? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.

**7.122.37**  Saṃjaya said: Come then, I shall describe to you all that befell in the great battle; listen calmly, and hear of your own misconduct.

**7.122.38**  For long before, O lord, this was in Kṛṣṇa's mind: that the hero Sātyaki was to be vanquished by Karṇa, whose banner bears the sacrificial post.

**7.122.39**  For Janārdana, O king, knows past and future; therefore, summoning his charioteer Dāruka, that mighty one gave command: 'Let my chariot be yoked betimes.'

**7.122.40**  For neither gods nor gandharvas, nor yakṣas, serpents, or rākṣasas, nor any men whatsoever, are there to vanquish the two Kṛṣṇas.

**7.122.41**  The gods, with the Grandsire at their head, and the siddhas, know this. Hear now of the matchless might of those two, and how that battle went.

**7.122.42**  Seeing Sātyaki bereft of his car and Karṇa with weapon upraised, Mādhava blew a mighty blast upon his ox-strong conch.

**7.122.43**  Dāruka, knowing the command and hearing the conch's note, brought up for him the chariot whose ensign of Garuḍa was raised on high.

**7.122.44**  With Keśava's leave, the grandson of Śini mounted that chariot driven by Dāruka, radiant as fire and the sun.

**7.122.45**  It was drawn by the steeds Sainya, Sugrīva, Meghapuṣpa, and Balāhaka — coursers that go where they will, towering, of great speed, adorned with trappings of gold.

**7.122.46**  Mounting that well-yoked chariot, like a celestial car, he rushed upon the son of Rādhā, sowing many arrows as he came.

**7.122.47**  Then too the two wheel-guards, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, leaving Dhanaṃjaya's chariot, advanced against the son of Rādhā.

**7.122.48**  The son of Rādhā too, O great king, loosing a downpour of arrows, in high fury charged the steadfast grandson of Śini in the fight.

**7.122.49**  No such battle, of gods or gandharvas, of asuras, serpents, or rākṣasas, was ever heard of, whether on earth or in heaven.

**7.122.50**  That host, with its chariots, horses, men, and elephants, stood still, O great king, its senses bewildered at beholding the feats of those two.

**7.122.51**  And all gazed upon that superhuman combat of those two foremost of men, O king, and upon the charioteering of Dāruka.

**7.122.52**  They marveled at the son of Kaśyapa as he stood at his post, with his goings forth and returnings, his wheelings and his turnings about.

**7.122.53**  And the gods, gandharvas, and dānavas in the vault of heaven were most intent to behold the battle of Karṇa and the grandson of Śini.

**7.122.54**  For their friends' sake the two strove on, rivals fierce and mettlesome in the fray — Karṇa, like an immortal, and Yuyudhāna, the son of Sātyaka.

**7.122.55**  Each upon the other, O great king, they rained their showers of arrows; and Karṇa battered the grandson of Śini with floods of shafts.

**7.122.56**  Unable to brook the slaying of the Kaurava and of Jalasaṃdha, Karṇa, filled with grief, hissed like a great serpent.

**7.122.57**  That tamer of foes, enraged, as if consuming the grandson of Śini with his very gaze, charged him again and again with vehemence in the fray.

**7.122.58**  But beholding him in his wrath, Sātyaki pierced him back with a mighty downpour of arrows, as one elephant withstands another.

**7.122.59**  Those two tigers among men, closing like swift and tireless tigers, hewed at each other in the battle, peerless in prowess.

**7.122.60**  Then the grandson of Śini, that tamer of foes, pierced Karṇa in every limb, again and again, with shafts all wrought of iron.

**7.122.61**  With a broad-headed arrow he swept his charioteer from the chariot-box, and with whetted shafts he slew his four white steeds.

**7.122.62**  Cleaving his banner a hundredfold with a hundred arrows, that bull among men left Karṇa without a car, before the very eyes of your son.

**7.122.63**  Then your bulls among men were dismayed, O king — Vṛṣasena, the son of Karṇa, and Śalya, the lord of the Madras,

**7.122.64**  and the son of Droṇa — they surrounded the grandson of Śini on every side; thereupon all became a tumult, and nothing could be discerned.

**7.122.65**  When the heroic son of the sūta had thus been left carless by Sātyaki, a cry of dismay arose, O king, throughout all the armies.

**7.122.66**  And Karṇa too, reeling, O king, tormented by the Sātvata's arrows, mounted Duryodhana's chariot, breathing hard.

**7.122.67**  Honoring the friendship he had borne your son from boyhood, and keeping the vow he had made when granted the kingdom,

**7.122.68**  even with Karṇa thus carless, the self-controlled Sātyaki did not slay your heroic sons, O king, with Duḥśāsana at their head.

**7.122.69**  Guarding too the vow Bhīmasena had once made of old, he made them carless and reeling, yet did not part them from their lives.

**7.122.70**  For the slaying of your sons had been pledged by Bhīmasena, and at the second dicing the slaying of Karṇa had been vowed by Pārtha.

**7.122.71**  Though they made every effort then to slay him, those foremost chariot-warriors with Karṇa at their head were unable to slay that Sātyaki.

**7.122.72**  The son of Droṇa, and Kṛtavarman, and likewise other great chariot-warriors — bulls among the kṣatriyas by the hundred — were vanquished with a single bow by one who sought the other world and the favor of the King of Righteousness.

**7.122.73**  Sātyaki, scourge of his foes, was equal in valor to the two Kṛṣṇas; in the world there is Kṛṣṇa, or Pārtha the bowman, or the grandson of Śini, that tiger among men — a fourth such is not to be found.

**7.122.74**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Mounting the unconquerable chariot of Vāsudeva, the youthful Sātyaki, the peer of Vāsudeva, left Karṇa without a car —

**7.122.75**  the car driven by Dāruka — proud of the strength of his own arms. Did Sātyaki then mount yet another chariot of his own?

**7.122.76**  This I wish to hear, for you are skilled in the telling; I deem him irresistible — tell me of it, Saṃjaya.

**7.122.77**  Saṃjaya said: Hear, O king, how the wise younger brother of Dāruka swiftly made ready for him another chariot, fashioned with every proper appointment —

**7.122.78**  bound with bands of iron and of gold, fitted with its pole, studded with a thousand stars, bearing a banner and pennon marked with a lion.

**7.122.79**  It was yoked with horses swift as the wind, caparisoned with golden trappings, white and bright as the moon, hardy, and heedless of every clamor.

**7.122.80**  With foremost steeds in armor of variegated gold, O lord of peoples — a chariot loud with the ringing of clustered bells, flashing with lances and javelins —

**7.122.81**  furnished with all the gear of war, abounding in many weapons — such a chariot, deep-voiced as a thundercloud, he made ready.

**7.122.82**  Mounting it, the grandson of Śini fell upon your host; and Dāruka, as he pleased, went off to the side of Keśava.

**7.122.83**  For Karṇa too, O great king, they brought up a chariot — drawn by goodly steeds, swifter still, white as the conch and as cow's milk, clad in armor of variegated gold,

**7.122.84**  furnished with girths of gold and with a banner, decked with well-wrought gear and pennon, a peerless car with a good driver, abounding in many weapons.

**7.122.85**  This they brought up, and mounting it Karṇa too charged upon his foes. All this have I told you, even as you asked of me.

**7.122.86**  Now learn further of the ruin born of your own misrule: one-and-thirty of your sons have been struck down by Bhīmasena,

**7.122.87**  with Durmukha, that ever-skillful and wondrous fighter, at their head; and heroes by the hundred have been slain by the Sātvata and by Arjuna.

**7.122.88**  Setting Bhīṣma and Bhagadatta at the forefront, good sir — thus, O king, has this destruction come to pass, all through your evil counsel.

**7.123.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the heroes on their side and on mine had thus fared, Saṃjaya, what then did Bhīma do? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.

**7.123.2**  Saṃjaya said: Bhīmasena, his chariot broken and stung by the barbed words of Karṇa, fell into the grip of fury and spoke this word to Phalguna.

**7.123.3**  Again and again he taunted me — 'Beardless oaf, fool, glutton, untrained in arms, do not fight, you child, you coward of the battlefield!' —

**7.123.4**  thus did Karṇa speak to me before your very eyes, Dhanaṃjaya. He who speaks so to me deserves death at my hands, and by him have I been so addressed, O Bhārata.

**7.123.5**  This vow, O mighty-armed one, I have taken together with you; as this is my charge, son of Kuntī, so is it yours — of this there is no doubt.

**7.123.6**  For his slaying, O best of men, remember this word of mine; so act, Dhanaṃjaya, that it be made true.

**7.123.7**  Hearing that word of Bhīma's, Arjuna of measureless valour drew a little closer in the battle and spoke to Karṇa.

**7.123.8**  Karṇa, O Karṇa, vain in your seeing, charioteer's son who praises only himself, mind set on unrighteousness — hear from me now what I shall tell you.

**7.123.9**  Twofold is the fortune of heroes in war: victory and defeat. And both are uncertain, Rādheya — even for Vāsava when he fights.

**7.123.10**  When you were near death at Yuyudhāna's hands, your chariot wrecked, you were spared and let go; and only by chance did you make Bhīmasena chariotless.

**7.123.11**  But this was unrighteous, Rādheya, that you spoke so to Bhīma — one who knows the law of war, who fights and does not flee, who fulfils to the utmost of his power a hero's work in the fray.

**7.123.12**  Before the eyes of all the armies, of Keśava and of me, you were made chariotless by Bhīmasena many a time in battle, yet the son of Pāṇḍu never spoke one harsh word to you.

**7.123.13**  But because you made Vṛkodara hear much that was cruel, and because Subhadrā's son was slain by you all in unfair fashion —

**7.123.14**  for that arrogance reap now its instant fruit. You cut his bowstring to your own undoing, O evil-minded one.

**7.123.15**  Therefore you, fool, are to be slain by me, together with your servants, your forces, and your steeds. Do all that you must do — a great terror has come upon you.

**7.123.16**  I shall slay your Vṛṣasena before your watching eyes in the fight; and whatever other kings shall come at me through delusion of mind, them too shall I slay, all of them — by truth I lay hand upon my weapon.

**7.123.17**  And when dull Duryodhana sees you — fool of unripe wit, overweening — struck down in battle, he shall grieve bitterly.

**7.123.18**  When Arjuna had vowed the slaying of Karṇa's son, a great and tumultuous clamour rose then among the chariot-warriors.

**7.123.19**  While that confused and dreadful battle was raging, the thousand-rayed sun, its beams grown faint, drew near the mountain of setting.

**7.123.20**  Then, O king, Hṛṣīkeśa embraced Bībhatsu, who stood at the battle's head, his vow fulfilled, and spoke thus to him.

**7.123.21**  By good fortune, Jiṣṇu, your great vow has been accomplished by you; and by good fortune the wicked Vṛddhakṣatra is slain together with his son.

**7.123.22**  Even an army of gods, Bhārata, on meeting Dhṛtarāṣṭra's host would sink in the battle, Jiṣṇu — of this there can be no doubt.

**7.123.23**  Though I ponder it, I see nowhere in the worlds, O tiger among men, any man but you who could do battle with this force.

**7.123.24**  Many guardians of the earth of great might, equal to you or greater, gathered for Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son's sake; yet, meeting you wrathful in battle, mailed though they were, they could not stand their ground.

**7.123.25**  Your prowess and your strength are like those of Rudra, Śakra, and Yama. No one could perform in battle such a feat as you alone have done this day, O scorcher of foes.

**7.123.26**  Even so, when the evil-souled Karṇa is slain with all his kin, I shall exalt you the more — conqueror of your enemies, slayer of your foes.

**7.123.27**  To him Arjuna replied: By your grace, Mādhava, this vow has been carried through by me — a vow hard to cross even for the gods.

**7.123.28**  No wonder is victory for those whose lord you are, Mādhava. By your grace Yudhiṣṭhira shall gain the whole earth.

**7.123.29**  Yours alone is the burden, Vārṣṇeya, yours alone the victory, O lord. We are yours to raise up and yours to command, slayer of Madhu.

**7.123.30**  Addressed thus, Kṛṣṇa, smiling, gently driving the horses on, showed to Pārtha that vast and cruel field of battle.

**7.123.31**  The blessed Kṛṣṇa said: Craving victory in war and far-famed glory, the heroes and the kings lie upon the earth, slain by your shafts.

**7.123.32**  Their weapons and ornaments scattered, their horses, chariots, and elephants undone, their armour cleft and shattered, they have come to utter ruin.

**7.123.33**  The living and the lifeless alike, endowed with surpassing radiance — these lords of men, though life has fled, seem still as though alive.

**7.123.34**  Behold the earth filled with their gold-feathered arrows, their many sharp weapons, their mounts and their armaments.

**7.123.35**  With cuirasses, with shields, with necklaces, with heads still bearing their earrings, with turbans, diadems, garlands, crest-jewels, and garments —

**7.123.36**  with necklets and armlets and bright gold ornaments, and with other gleaming jewels of every kind, the earth shines, O Bhārata.

**7.123.37**  With yak-tail whisks, with gay fans, with banners, with horses, chariots, and elephants, with coverlets of many sorts, and with the fly-whisks of the horses —

**7.123.38**  with richly patterned elephant-housings and with costly chariot-guards — behold the earth strewn over, as though robed in figured cloth.

**7.123.39**  Behold others fallen from their elephants — those caparisoned beasts — together with the elephants themselves, like lions tumbled from mountain peaks struck down by the thunderbolt.

**7.123.40**  Behold yet others sewn to the ground along with their horses, and the throngs of footmen and riders awash in floods of blood.

**7.123.41**  Saṃjaya said: Thus showing the field of battle to the Diademed One, Kṛṣṇa, joined by his own and filled with joy, sounded the conch Pāñcajanya.

**7.124.1**  Saṃjaya said: Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, leaping down from his chariot, O Bhārata, embraced the two Kṛṣṇas, overflowing with tears of joy.

**7.124.2**  Wiping his bright face, radiant as a white lotus, he spoke to Vāsudeva and to the Pāṇḍava Dhanaṃjaya.

**7.124.3**  By good fortune I behold you both, great chariot-warriors, your burden in battle crossed; and by good fortune the wicked lord of Sindhu, basest of men, is slain.

**7.124.4**  By good fortune, Kṛṣṇa, my great gladness has been brought to pass; and by good fortune the hosts of foes are plunged into an ocean of grief.

**7.124.5**  For those whose lord you are, the teacher of all the worlds, nothing in the three worlds is hard to achieve, O slayer of Madhu.

**7.124.6**  By your grace, Govinda, we shall vanquish our foes, even as of old, by your grace, the Chastiser of Pāka overcame the Dānavas.

**7.124.7**  Conquest of the earth, or even conquest of the three worlds, is assured, Vārṣṇeya, for those with whom you are pleased, Mādhava.

**7.124.8**  For them there is no sin, nor defeat in battle, whose lord is you, the lord of the lord of the thirty gods, with whom you are pleased, Mādhava.

**7.124.9**  By your grace, Hṛṣīkeśa, glorious Śakra, lord of the hosts of gods, won the conquest of the three worlds at the head of battle.

**7.124.10**  And by your grace, O lord of the thirty gods, the thirty themselves attained immortality, Kṛṣṇa, and enjoy imperishable worlds.

**7.124.11**  By a prowess sprung from your grace, O slayer of foes, Śakra attained lordship over the gods, having slain the Daityas by the thousands.

**7.124.12**  By your grace, Hṛṣīkeśa, the world of moving and unmoving things abides each in its own course, O hero, and engages in muttered prayer and oblation.

**7.124.13**  In the beginning all this was one ocean, wholly wrapped in darkness; by your grace the world attained to light, O best of men.

**7.124.14**  They who have taken refuge in Hṛṣīkeśa — creator of all the worlds, the supreme Self, the unfallen — are never at any time deluded.

**7.124.15**  They who are devoted to you, Hṛṣīkeśa — the god without beginning or end, the maker of the worlds, the imperishable — cross over all hardships.

**7.124.16**  To him who takes refuge in the supreme Person, the ancient One, that which is highest among all things primeval, the highest prosperity is ordained.

**7.124.17**  He who chanted forth the four Vedas, and he who is hymned within the Vedas — taking refuge in that great-souled one, a man attains a prosperity beyond all others.

**7.124.18**  He who is Dhanaṃjaya's friend and Dhanaṃjaya's good — taking refuge in that guardian of Dhanaṃjaya, a man thrives in happiness.

**7.124.19**  Thus addressed, those two great-souled ones, Keśava and the Pāṇḍava both, then spoke gladly to the king, the lord of the earth.

**7.124.20**  By the fire of your wrath the wicked King Jayadratha has been consumed; and the surging, vast host of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son in battle —

**7.124.21**  is being slain, is slain already, and shall perish utterly, O Bhārata; for these Kauravas are struck down by your anger, slayer of foes.

**7.124.22**  For having angered you, a hero who slays with a mere glance, ill-minded Suyodhana, together with his friends and kinsmen, shall yield up his life in the fray.

**7.124.23**  Struck down before by your wrath, Bhīṣma the grandsire of the Kurus, hard to conquer even by the gods, lies upon his bed of arrows.

**7.124.24**  Hard to win is victory in battle for those, O slayer of foes; truly they pass into the power of death with whom you are wrathful, Pāṇḍava.

**7.124.25**  Kingdom, life, beloved sons, and pleasures of every kind — soon do these perish for those with whom you are wrathful, O giver of honour.

**7.124.26**  I deem the Kauravas already destroyed, with their sons, their cattle, and their kin, now that you, ever devoted to the duty of kings, are wrathful, Yudhiṣṭhira.

**7.124.27**  Then mighty-armed Bhīma and the great chariot-warrior Sātyaki, having saluted their elder and superior, those two great bowmen stood gashed and torn by arrows, encircled by the Pāñcālas.

**7.124.28**  Beholding those two heroes glad before him, standing with hands folded in reverence, the son of Kuntī rejoiced over them both, Bhīma and Sātyaki.

**7.124.29**  By good fortune I behold you, heroes, delivered from the ocean of armies — from the unassailable Droṇa-crocodile, from the lair of the sea-monster Hārdikya; and by good fortune all the kings of the earth are vanquished in the fight.

**7.124.30**  By good fortune I behold you both victorious in the battle; and by good fortune Droṇa is overcome in the fray, and the mighty Hārdikya as well.

**7.124.31**  By good fortune I behold you, blameless ones, crossed safely over the ocean of armies — heroes glorious in battle, never fleeing the fight; and by good fortune I behold you both, who are dear to me as my own breath.

**7.124.32**  Having spoken thus, the Pāṇḍava king embraced Yuyudhāna and Vṛkodara, those tigers among men, and for very joy let fall his tears.

**7.124.33**  Then, O lord of peoples, the whole army of the Pāṇḍavas was filled with delight, and beholding their victory set its mind upon the battle still to come.

**7.125.1**  Saṃjaya said: When the lord of Sindhu was slain, O king, your son Suyodhana, his face wet with tears, wretched and bereft of hope of conquering his foes, thought that there was no warrior on earth equal to Arjuna.

**7.125.2**  Neither Droṇa, nor Rādheya, nor Aśvatthāman, nor Kṛpa was able to stand before him in his wrath — so he thought, good sir.

**7.125.3**  For Pārtha, having vanquished in battle all my great chariot-warriors, slew the lord of Sindhu in the fight, and none could turn him back.

**7.125.4**  In every way this great host of the Kauravas is already as good as slain; for it has no protector — not even Purandara himself in person.

**7.125.5**  He upon whom we leaned to raise our arms for battle — that Karṇa has been vanquished in the fight, and Jayadratha too is slain.

**7.125.6**  That Karṇa who hurled harsh words at the Pāṇḍavas in the midst of the assembly hall has been worsted in battle, and the lord of the Sindhus laid low as well.

**7.125.7**  That Karṇa, leaning on whose prowess I held the unfallen one who came seeking peace to be no more than a blade of grass — that very Karṇa has been beaten in the fight.

**7.125.8**  Thus crushed in spirit, O king, your son — he who has wronged the whole world — drew near to look upon Droṇa, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.125.9**  Then he recounted the whole of it: the great slaughter of the Kurus, the foes carrying off the victory, and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra going under.

**7.125.10**  Duryodhana said: Behold, O teacher, the havoc wrought among the consecrated kings — though we set in the forefront the hero Bhīṣma, my grandsire.

**7.125.11**  Having struck him down, this Śikhaṇḍin, greedy and swollen with pride, together with all the Pāñcālas presses upon the van of our army.

**7.125.12**  And another, unassailable — your own pupil, the ambidextrous archer — after destroying seven full armies, has slain King Jayadratha.

**7.125.13**  How shall I ever discharge my debt to friends who longed for my victory and served my cause, now that they have gone to the abode of Yama?

**7.125.14**  Those lords of the earth who sought to win the earth for my sake — they have forsaken dominion over the earth and now lie sleeping upon it.

**7.125.15**  I, a coward, having brought about such ruin of my friends — not by a thousand horse-sacrifices could I dare to redeem myself.

**7.125.16**  For me — the greedy, the sinful, the transgressor of righteousness — they strove and sought to conquer, and so have come to the dwelling of Vaivasvata.

**7.125.17**  How is it that the earth could not open a cleft to swallow me — fallen in conduct, betrayer of my own friends — there in the assembly of kings?

**7.125.18**  I could not save my grandsire, his limbs drenched in blood, lying in the midst of the kings — Bhīṣma struck down upon the field of battle.

**7.125.19**  When that unassailable conqueror of the world beyond meets me — ignoble man, betrayer of friends, doer of unrighteousness — what will he say to me?

**7.125.20**  Behold the mighty archer Jalasaṃdha, slain by Sātyaki — a hero who rose up for my sake and gave his life, a great chariot-warrior.

**7.125.21**  Seeing the Kāmboja struck down, and Alambusa too, and many other friends besides — what use to me now is the wish to live?

**7.125.22**  The heroes who, never turning their backs, exerted themselves and fell for my sake, striving with all their might to conquer my enemies —

**7.125.23**  to them, O scorcher of foes, I shall this day discharge my debt as best I can: I shall offer them the water of libation along the Yamunā.

**7.125.24**  Truly I vow it to you, O foremost of all who bear arms — I swear it by my sacrifices and pious works, by my valor, and by my sons —

**7.125.25**  having slain in battle all those Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍavas, I shall win peace — or else I shall go to share their world in the fight.

**7.125.26**  For now my allies, ill requited, no longer desire to aid me; they reckon the sons of Pāṇḍu worthier than us, O mighty-armed one.

**7.125.27**  Death itself has been ordained in battle by him whose vows are truth; yet you show indifference toward Dhanaṃjaya, because he is so apt a pupil.

**7.125.28**  And so all who wished to make me victorious have been struck down; in Karṇa alone do I now see one who still seeks my triumph.

**7.125.29**  The dull-witted man who, not truly knowing his friend, yet employs him in a friend's behalf — his purpose comes to nothing.

**7.125.30**  Such has been this enterprise of mine, contrived out of folly by those who only call themselves friends — by their crooked dealings, here and there, against a greedy and sinful man.

**7.125.31**  Slain is Jayadratha, and the valiant son of Somadatta, and the Abhīṣāhas, the Śūrasenas, the Śibis, and the Vasātis.

**7.125.32**  This very day I too shall go where those bulls among men have gone — slain for my sake in battle as they fought against the diademed one.

**7.125.33**  For I have no use for life bereft of those bulls among men. Let the teacher of the sons of Pāṇḍu grant me his leave to go.

**7.126.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the king of the Sindhus had been slain in battle by the ambidextrous archer, dear son, and Bhūriśravas likewise, what then was the temper of your minds?

**7.126.2**  And Droṇa, thus addressed by Duryodhana in the assembly of the Kurus — what did he say in reply to that? Tell me this, Saṃjaya.

**7.126.3**  Saṃjaya said: A great clamor of dismay arose among your troops, O Bhārata, when they beheld the lord of the Sindhus slain and Bhūriśravas as well.

**7.126.4**  They all scorned the whole of your son's counsel — that counsel by which warriors among the kṣatriyas had been slain by the hundred.

**7.126.5**  But Droṇa, hearing those words of your son, grew downcast in spirit; and after pondering a moment, sorely afflicted, he spoke.

**7.126.6**  O Duryodhana, why do you thus pierce me with the shafts of your words, when I have ever told you the ambidextrous archer is unconquerable in battle?

**7.126.7**  By this alone, O Kaurava, you might have understood Arjuna in war — that Śikhaṇḍin slew Bhīṣma while guarded by the diademed one.

**7.126.8**  When I saw one whom neither gods nor men could slay struck down in battle, even then I knew: this host of ours shall be no more.

**7.126.9**  When that hero is slain whom we held the bravest of men in all three worlds, what remnant do we still cling to?

**7.126.10**  Those dice which father Śakuni cast in the assembly of the Kurus — they were no dice but whetted arrows, tormentors of the foe.

**7.126.11**  Those very shafts, dear son, now slay us, driven on toward our undoing — the shafts of which Vidura warned you then, though you would not understand.

**7.126.12**  You would not heed those words of the great-souled, steadfast Vidura, though he cried them out for your welfare — auspicious counsel spoken for your good.

**7.126.13**  And now this dreadful thing is come to pass, this great slaughter — through your scorning of that counsel, Duryodhana, for your sake.

**7.126.14**  And in that you had Kṛṣṇā dragged before the assembly while we looked on — she undeserving of it, nobly born, a follower of every sacred duty —

**7.126.15**  of that unrighteousness, O son of Gāndhārī, you have now received the fruit; and were it not so, you would meet a sin still greater in the world beyond.

**7.126.16**  And in that you conquered the Pāṇḍavas at dice by foul play and drove them then into the forest, clad in the skins of black antelopes —

**7.126.17**  toward these men, who walk ever in righteousness as though they were my own sons — what man in the world, save me who am called a brāhmaṇa, would deal so treacherously?

**7.126.18**  This wrath of the Pāṇḍavas was brought down by you together with Śakuni, with Dhṛtarāṣṭra's assent, in the assembly of the Kurus.

**7.126.19**  Joined to it was Duḥśāsana, and Karṇa nourished it the more; and you, disregarding the steward's words, fed it again and again.

**7.126.20**  When all of you, overpowering Abhimanyu, hemmed him round while rallying about the king of the Sindhus — how then was that king slain in your very midst?

**7.126.21**  How, while you and Karṇa and Kṛpa and Śalya yet lived, and Aśvatthāman too, O Kaurava, did the lord of the Sindhus go to his death?

**7.126.22**  When all those kings of yours waited upon his fierce splendor to save the lord of the Sindhus — how was he slain in your very midst?

**7.126.23**  On me above all, O Duryodhana, and on you, that lord of earth set his hope of deliverance from Arjuna.

**7.126.24**  And now, since he found no rescue from Phalguna, I see no way at all to save my own life.

**7.126.25**  I see myself, as it were, sinking into the guilt that is Dhṛṣṭadyumna, so long as I have not slain the Pāñcālas together with that Śikhaṇḍin.

**7.126.26**  Why then do you pierce me with the shafts of your words while I burn with grief, O Bhārata, when you yourself were powerless to save the king of the Sindhus?

**7.126.27**  You did not see, in battle, the golden banner of Bhīṣma, the tireless-handed one whose word was truth — how then do you still hope for victory?

**7.126.28**  Where, in the midst of mighty chariot-warriors, the lord of the Sindhus was slain, and Bhūriśravas too — what remnant do you suppose is left there?

**7.126.29**  If the unassailable Kṛpa yet lives, O king — he who has not gone the road of the lord of the Sindhus — him I honor.

**7.126.30**  And in that I saw Bhīṣma slain before the very eyes of your younger brother Duḥśāsana, O Kaurava — Bhīṣma, who wrought deeds so hard to do, well-nigh unslayable in battle even by the gods with Vāsava at their head —

**7.126.31**  this I now think, O king: that the earth is no longer yours. For here, O Bhārata, the hosts of the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas, joined together, are charging upon me this day, honored sir.

**7.126.32**  Not until I have slain all the Pāñcālas will I loose my armor; in battle, O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, I shall do the deed that serves your good.

**7.126.33**  O king, say to my son Aśvatthāman in the fray: the Somakas must not be spared by one who would guard his own life.

**7.126.34**  And keep faith with the counsel your father gave you: stand firm in mercy, in self-restraint, in truth, and in uprightness.

**7.126.35**  Skilled in duty, gain, and pleasure, never letting duty or gain suffer harm, holding duty foremost — so should you perform your tasks, again and again.

**7.126.36**  The brāhmaṇas are to be gratified with eye and mind, and served according to one's power; nothing should be done to displease them, for they are like tongues of fire.

**7.126.37**  But now I plunge into the hostile ranks, O slayer of foes, for a great battle, O king — wounded as I am by the barb of your words.

**7.126.38**  And you, Duryodhana, hold the army together if you can; for even by night the Kurus and Sṛñjayas, roused to fury, will fight on.

**7.126.39**  So saying, Droṇa went forth against the Pāṇḍavas and Sṛñjayas, stealing away the splendor of the warriors as the sun steals the light of the stars.

**7.127.1**  Saṃjaya said: Then King Duryodhana, so goaded by Droṇa, fell into the grip of indignation and set his mind on battle alone.

**7.127.2**  And then your son Duryodhana said to Karṇa: Behold — the battle-array drawn up by the teacher, hard for the very gods to break, has been broken by the diademed son of Pāṇḍu with Kṛṣṇa for his ally.

**7.127.3**  While you exerted yourself, and the great-souled Droṇa too, and the foremost of warriors looked on, the lord of the Sindhus was struck down.

**7.127.4**  Behold, O son of Rādhā, the kings, the foremost upon earth in war, slain by Pārtha alone, as lesser beasts are slain by a lion.

**7.127.5**  Though I strove in the battle, O slayer of foes, my army has been brought to a scant remnant by the son of Śakra.

**7.127.6**  For how, if Droṇa had not willed it, could Phalguna in battle have broken that array so hard to break, however he might have striven in the fray?

**7.127.7**  For Phalguna is ever dear to the great-souled teacher; and so, O crusher of foes, he granted him passage without a fight.

**7.127.8**  Droṇa, scorcher of foes, having granted safety to the lord of the Sindhus in the fight, yet opened the gate for the diademed one — behold how poorly I am served.

**7.127.9**  Had I but given leave at the outset for the king of the Sindhus to go home, there would have been no slaughter of men in the battle.

**7.127.10**  Jayadratha, longing for life, was setting out toward home, having won safety from Droṇa in the fight — and I, ignoble, held him back.

**7.127.11**  This day my brothers, Citrasena and the rest, are spent in battle, having come up against Bhīmasena before our wicked-hearted eyes.

**7.127.12**  Karṇa said: Do not reproach the teacher; that brāhmaṇa fights with all his might. I deem the Pāṇḍavas unconquerable in the fray, even by Droṇa who knows every weapon.

**7.127.13**  For even so, passing him by, the white-horsed one broke through. The course of things is ordained by fate; I think there is nowhere any altering it.

**7.127.14**  Then, O Suyodhana, while we fought with the utmost of our power, the lord of the Sindhus was slain, O king; in this, destiny is reckoned the highest cause.

**7.127.15**  Though we strove our utmost together with you on the field of battle, destiny undid our manly valor and set us behind, for all our ceaseless striving with both cunning and prowess.

**7.127.16**  Whatever deed a man assailed by destiny may anywhere perform, that deed, once done, is undone again for him by destiny.

**7.127.17**  What is to be done by a man who is resolute and true, that he must do without misgiving; but success rests upon destiny.

**7.127.18**  By trickery the sons of Pṛthā were cheated, O Bhārata, and by poisoned draughts, and they were nearly burned in the house of lac, and they were vanquished at dice.

**7.127.19**  By recourse to statecraft they were sent away to the forest; yet whatever was thus contrived by effort was cast down by destiny.

**7.127.20**  Fight on, taking up your effort, and make death your only turning-back; as you strive and as they strive, destiny will go its own appointed way.

**7.127.21**  No deliberate good deed of theirs is anywhere to be seen, nor any wicked deed of yours, O hero, devoid of judgment, O upholder of the Kurus.

**7.127.22**  Destiny is the measure of every deed, good or otherwise; for destiny, whose work cannot be turned aside, keeps watch even over those who sleep.

**7.127.23**  Many were your armies and many likewise your warriors—not so those of the sons of Pāṇḍu; and yet the battle went thus.

**7.127.24**  By those few you many strikers have been brought to ruin; I think this is the work of destiny, by which manly valor has been brought to naught.

**7.127.25**  Saṃjaya said: While they were conversing thus at length on this and that, O lord of men, the battalions of the Pāṇḍavas appeared before them in the fray.

**7.127.26**  Then began the battle, chariots and elephants locked together, between your men and their foes, O king, through your own ill counsel.

**7.128.1**  Saṃjaya said: That host of yours, O lord of men, with its surging flood of elephants and horses, rushed upon the army of the Pāṇḍavas and gave it battle on every side.

**7.128.2**  The Pāñcālas and the Kurus, fighting one another, were as men consecrated for the great realm of Yama, for the world beyond.

**7.128.3**  Heroes closing with heroes pierced one another swiftly in the fight with arrows, lances, and spears, and led each other to the abode of Yama.

**7.128.4**  Between car-warriors and car-warriors a great and terrible battle, streaming with blood, broke out as they struck one another down.

**7.128.5**  And the elephants, O great king, closing upon one another, enraged and frenzied with rut, gored each other with their tusks.

**7.128.6**  Horsemen pierced horsemen with darts, spears, and battle-axes in the tumultuous fight, each seeking great renown.

**7.128.7**  And the foot-soldiers, O mighty-armed one, by the hundreds, weapons in hand, harried one another, O king, ever intent upon valor.

**7.128.8**  By the names of their lineages and their families, O venerable one, heard upon the field, we knew the Pāñcālas apart from the Kurus.

**7.128.9**  In the fray the warriors, ranging about without fear, sent one another to the world beyond with arrows, spears, and battle-axes.

**7.128.10**  By the arrows loosed in their thousands, O king, the ten quarters of the sky, even after the sun had set, no longer shone as before.

**7.128.11**  While the Pāṇḍava warriors were thus fighting on, Duryodhana, undaunted, O great king, plunged into that host.

**7.128.12**  Sorely stricken with grief at the slaying of the lord of the Sindhus, and resolving that he too must die, he entered the army of the foe.

**7.128.13**  Making the air resound with the rumble of his chariot and seeming to shake the earth, your son advanced against the host of the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.128.14**  That tumultuous clash between him and them, O Bhārata, became a great wreaking of destruction upon all the troops.

**7.128.15**  As the noonday sun blazing with its rays, so blazed your son in their midst with his waves of arrows.

**7.128.16**  The Pāṇḍavas could not even look upon that descendant of Bharata in the fight; their spirit roused only to flight, they had lost all heart for victory over the foe.

**7.128.17**  The Pāñcālas, slaughtered by the great-souled one, ran about in flight; and harried swiftly by the gold-feathered, keen-pointed arrows of your son the bowman, the Pāṇḍava soldiers fell.

**7.128.18**  Not such a feat in battle did your men perform as the king, your son, performed, O lord of peoples.

**7.128.19**  By your son that Pāṇḍava army was churned in the battle, like a lotus-pool with its blooming lilies trampled on every side by an elephant.

**7.128.20**  Like a lotus-pond robbed of its splendor when its waters fail and the wind and sun assail it, so became the Pāṇḍava army through the fiery might of your son.

**7.128.21**  Seeing the Pāṇḍava army stricken by your son, O Bhārata, the Pāñcālas, with Bhīmasena at their head, rushed upon him.

**7.128.22**  He pierced Bhīmasena with ten arrows, the two sons of Mādrī with three each, Virāṭa and Drupada with six, and Śikhaṇḍin with a hundred.

**7.128.23**  And Dhṛṣṭadyumna with seventy, the son of Dharma with seven, and the Kekayas and the Cedis with many whetted arrows.

**7.128.24**  Having pierced the Sātvata with five, the sons of Draupadī with three each, and Ghaṭotkaca in the battle, he roared like a lion.

**7.128.25**  And other warriors by the hundreds, with their elephants, horses, and chariots, he cut down in the fight with cruel arrows, like wrathful Death cutting down living beings.

**7.128.26**  As he was striking down those foes, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas cut his great gold-backed bow into three with two broad-headed shafts, O venerable one.

**7.128.27**  And he pierced him with ten well-aimed, sharpened arrows; but all of these, after piercing his vital parts, broke and fell to the ground.

**7.128.28**  Then the gladdened warriors gathered round Yudhiṣṭhira, as the gods gathered round Puraṃdara for the slaying of Vṛtra.

**7.128.29**  Then King Yudhiṣṭhira loosed at your son in the fray an arrow most hard to ward off, O venerable one; and grievously pierced by it, your son sank down upon his splendid chariot.

**7.128.30**  Then from the Pāñcāla troops there rose a great loud clamor on every side, O lord of kings, as they rejoiced, crying, 'The king is slain!'

**7.128.31**  And a fierce din of the twang of arrows was heard there, O venerable one; then Droṇa swiftly appeared upon that field.

**7.128.32**  And Duryodhana, heartened, taking up his stout bow, advanced upon King Yudhiṣṭhira the Pāṇḍava, crying, 'Stand, stand!'

**7.128.33**  The Pāñcālas, eager for the king, swiftly went out against him; but Droṇa received them, seeking to save the best of the Kurus, as the ray-shedding sun beats back clouds driven up by a fierce gale.

**7.128.34**  Then, O king, there was a great battle, swelling ever larger, between your men and their foes, all met together in their lust for combat.

**7.129.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the self-controlled preceptor, in his wrath, entered among the Pāṇḍavas, having justly rebuked my son Duryodhana for transgressing his counsel—

**7.129.2**  how did the Pāṇḍavas surround Droṇa, that mighty archer, the hero, as he ranged and stood firm in the battle he had entered?

**7.129.3**  Who guarded the right wheel of the great-souled preceptor, and who guarded the left, as he slew his foes in the fight?

**7.129.4**  Dancing along the chariot-paths, that foremost of all who bear arms, wrathful like a comet, how did he come to meet his death?

**7.129.5**  Saṃjaya said: In the late afternoon, having slain the lord of the Sindhus, the son of Pṛthā, joining the king, and Sātyaki, that great archer—the two rushed upon Droṇa himself.

**7.129.6**  Likewise Yudhiṣṭhira swiftly, and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava, each engaged with his own division, rushed upon Droṇa himself.

**7.129.7**  So too the wise Nakula and the unconquerable Sahadeva, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śatānīka, and Virāṭa with the Kekayas, the Matsyas and the Śālveya troops—all went against Droṇa in the fight.

**7.129.8**  And King Drupada too, guarded all about by the Pāñcālas, the father of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O king, advanced upon Droṇa himself.

**7.129.9**  The sons of Draupadī, those mighty archers, and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca, together with their troops, advanced upon Droṇa of great splendor.

**7.129.10**  And the Prabhadraka Pāñcālas, six thousand strikers strong, advanced upon Droṇa, with Śikhaṇḍin set at their head.

**7.129.11**  So too the other tigers among men, the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, banded together and turned upon Droṇa, that bull among the twice-born.

**7.129.12**  When those heroes had gone forth to battle, O bull of the Bhāratas, there came on a dreadful night, deepening the terror of the timid.

**7.129.13**  For the warriors it was a baleful, terrible night, O king, bound for the abode of Death, making an end of the lives of elephants, horses, and men.

**7.129.14**  In that dreadful night the jackals, howling on every side with flaming gobbets in their mouths, gave warning of a terrible peril.

**7.129.15**  And owls too appeared, foretelling vast terror, most dire of all in the host of the Kauravas.

**7.129.16**  Then among the armies, O lord of kings, there arose a great din, with the mighty sound of kettledrums and the boom of tabors,

**7.129.17**  and with the trumpeting of elephants and the neighing of horses and the clatter of falling hooves, a tumult arose on every side.

**7.129.18**  Then in the twilight there broke out a most dreadful battle, O great king, between Droṇa and the Sṛñjayas on every hand.

**7.129.19**  When the world was wrapped in darkness, nothing whatever could be discerned, with the dust raised up on every side by the host.

**7.129.20**  The blood of man and horse and elephant ran mingled together; we could no longer see the dust of the earth, shrouded as it was by the gore.

**7.129.21**  As of a thicket of bamboo burning by night upon a mountain, so arose a fearful crackling sound from the weapons that fell.

**7.129.22**  Neither one's own men nor the foe could be told apart, O king, in that enveloping darkness; at the onset of night the whole field became as if maddened.

**7.129.23**  The dust of the earth, O lord of kings, was laid by the blood; but with the golden mail and ornaments the darkness was lit up.

**7.129.24**  Then that Bhārata host, adorned with gems and gold, was like the star-strewn sky by night, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.129.25**  It rang with the cries of jackals and ravens, it was thronged with spears and banners, terrible with dreadful howls, resounding with roars and shouts.

**7.129.26**  Then there arose a great tumultuous uproar that made the hair stand on end, filling all the quarters, like the crash of mighty Indra's thunderbolt.

**7.129.27**  At midnight, O great king, that Bhārata army was seen lit up with armlets, earrings, golden necklaces, and weapons.

**7.129.28**  There the elephants and the chariots, decked with gold, appeared in the night like clouds shot through with lightning.

**7.129.29**  Swords, spears, maces, arrows, clubs, darts, and lances, as they fell in showers, were seen flashing like flames of fire.

**7.129.30**  With Duryodhana for its forewind, with chariots and elephants for its thunderheads, thundering with the blare of instruments, hung about with bows for lightning and with banners,

**7.129.31**  with Droṇa and the Pāṇḍavas for its rain-clouds, with swords, spears, and maces for its thunderbolts, with showers of arrows and missiles for its wind, fraught utterly with cold and heat—

**7.129.32**  that army—dreadful, astounding, fierce, life-severing, with no raft to cross it, most terrible—those who longed to fight entered in.

**7.129.33**  At that dreadful onset of night, resounding with a great uproar, that bred terror in the timid and swelled the joy of the brave—

**7.129.34**  As the dreadful night-battle raged on, terrible beyond measure, the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas, united and enraged, rushed upon Droṇa.

**7.129.35**  Whoever, O king, came to oppose that great-souled one face to face, all of these he turned away routed, and some of them he dispatched to the realm of Yama.

**7.130.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When that unassailable one of boundless might had plunged among the Sṛñjayas, impatient and roused to fury, what then was your resolve?

**7.130.2**  When that one of immeasurable spirit, having rebuked my son Duryodhana for transgressing the rules, had broken into the foe, how did Pārtha respond?

**7.130.3**  After the heroic ruler of the Saindhavas had been slain, and Bhūriśravas too, how did that one of great splendor, unconquered, advance against the Pāñcālas?

**7.130.4**  When that scorcher of foes, hard to assail, had broken in, what did Duryodhana think the fitting deed for the hour to be?

**7.130.5**  Which heroes followed that boon-granting warrior, best of the twice-born? Which heroes went behind that valiant one as he fought? Which fought before him as he struck down his enemies in battle?

**7.130.6**  I think, my lord, that all the Pāṇḍavas, tormented by the shafts of Bhāradvāja, were trembling like gaunt cattle in the winter cold.

**7.130.7**  Having broken into the Pāñcālas, that mighty archer, crusher of foes, that tiger among men—how then did he meet his dissolution?

**7.130.8**  When all the armies had clashed together, and in the night the great chariot-warriors had met and the varied hosts were thrown into turmoil, who among you then kept their wits about them?

**7.130.9**  You tell of my men—slain, beset, and overthrown, the chariot-warriors made chariotless in the fighting.

**7.130.10**  How then, Saṃjaya, did light come to these unflinching sons of Pṛthā there in the night, and how among the Kurus?

**7.130.11**  Saṃjaya said: As the night-battle raged on, O king, exceedingly terrible, the Pāṇḍavas with their soldiers rushed upon Droṇa in the dark.

**7.130.12**  Then Droṇa, with his swift-flying arrows, sent the Kekayas and the sons of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, every one of them, off to the realm of death.

**7.130.13**  Whatever great chariot-warriors stood before him, O king, all of these, descendant of Bharata, he sent to the world beyond.

**7.130.14**  Against that hero Bhāradvāja, the great chariot-warrior who was crushing all before him, the valorous Śibi, O king, advanced in wrath.

**7.130.15**  Beholding that great chariot-warrior of the Pāṇḍavas bearing down upon him, Droṇa pierced him with ten shafts all made of steel.

**7.130.16**  Śibi pierced him in return with thirty sharpened shafts, and smiling, with a broad-headed arrow, struck down his charioteer.

**7.130.17**  Then Droṇa, having slain the horses and the charioteer of that great-souled one, struck off his head, helmet and all, from his body.

**7.130.18**  Then the son of the Kaliṅga king, enraged at the earlier slaying of his father, charged upon Bhīmasena in battle with the army of the Kaliṅgas.

**7.130.19**  Having pierced Bhīma with five shafts, he wounded him again with seven, struck Viśoka with three, and his banner with a single feathered arrow.

**7.130.20**  But Vṛkodara, enraged, leaping from chariot to chariot, smote that enraged hero of the Kaliṅgas with his fist.

**7.130.21**  Struck in battle by the fist of the mighty Pāṇḍava, all his bones at once fell apart, each from the other.

**7.130.22**  Karṇa and that one's brothers, the great chariot-warriors, could not bear this; they struck Bhīmasena with iron shafts like venomous serpents.

**7.130.23**  Then Bhīma, abandoning the enemy's chariot, sprang to Dhruva's car, and crushed with his fist Dhruva, who was loosing shafts without pause; thus struck down by the mighty son of Pāṇḍu, he fell.

**7.130.24**  Having slain him, O great king, the mighty Bhīmasena reached the chariot of Jayarāta and roared again and again like a lion.

**7.130.25**  Seizing Jayarāta then, roaring, with the flat of his left hand he destroyed him as he stood there before the very eyes of Karṇa.

**7.130.26**  Karṇa then hurled a golden javelin at the Pāṇḍava, but the son of Pāṇḍu, laughing, caught that very weapon.

**7.130.27**  And the unassailable Vṛkodara flung it back at Karṇa in the fray, but Śakuni cut it down in mid-air with an oil-honed shaft.

**7.130.28**  Then your sons, O king, advanced upon Bhīma's chariot, covering Vṛkodara with a mighty rain of arrows.

**7.130.29**  Then Bhīma, as if laughing in the combat, dispatched Durmada's charioteer and horses to the realm of Yama with his shafts; whereupon Durmada leapt onto the car of Duṣkarṇa.

**7.130.30**  Those two brothers, scorchers of foes, mounted upon a single chariot, both charged at Bhīma in the midst of the battle's van, as two friends of the lord of waters might charge Tāraka, foremost of the Daityas.

**7.130.31**  Then Durmada and Duṣkarṇa, your two sons, mounting upon a single chariot, pierced Bhīma with their arrows.

**7.130.32**  Then, before the watching eyes of Karṇa, of Drauṇi, of Duryodhana, of Kṛpa, of Somadatta, and of Bāhlika, the Pāṇḍava—

**7.130.33**  —that tamer of foes drove the chariot of the heroes Durmada and Duṣkarṇa into the earth with a single stamp of his foot.

**7.130.34**  Then, enraged, he struck your two mighty, valiant sons Duṣkarṇa and Durmada with his fist and ground them down beneath his foot.

**7.130.35**  Then, as a cry of horror rose from the army, the kings, beholding Bhīma, said: "This is Rudra in the guise of Bhīma, hungering after the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."

**7.130.36**  Having said this, O descendant of Bharata, all the kings fled; senseless with fear, they drove their mounts, and no two of them ran together.

**7.130.37**  Then, when the host had been grievously shattered at the onset of night, the mighty Vṛkodara, honored by the bulls among kings, his eyes wide as opened lotuses, in his strength paid homage to King Yudhiṣṭhira.

**7.130.38**  Then the twins, Drupada, Virāṭa, the Kekayas, and Yudhiṣṭhira as well attained supreme delight, and they did high honor to Vṛkodara, as the gods honored Hara when Andhaka was slain.

**7.130.39**  Then your sons, peers of the son of Varuṇa, filled with fury, together with their great-souled preceptor, eager to fight, with chariots, foot-soldiers, and elephants, closely beset Vṛkodara on every side.

**7.130.40**  Then, as if enveloped in dense darkness, amid great terror, fear-inspiring and exceedingly grim at the onset of night, came the gladdening feast of jackals, wolves, and vultures—the wondrous battle of the great-souled foremost of kings.

**7.131.1**  Saṃjaya said: When his son, who had sat down to die by fasting, had been slain by Sātyaki, Somadatta, greatly enraged, spoke these words to Sātyaki:

**7.131.2**  "The duty of the warrior, ordained of old by the great-souled gods—abandoning that, O Sātvata, how is it you delight in the way of brigands?

**7.131.3**  How could a wise man, devoted to the warrior's law, strike in battle one who has turned away, who is helpless, who has laid down his arms and begs for mercy?

**7.131.4**  Two only among the Vṛṣṇis, they say, are renowned as great chariot-warriors—the mighty-armed Pradyumna and you, O Sātvata, in battle.

**7.131.5**  How could you commit so cruel and degrading a deed against one whose arm Pārtha had severed and who had sat down to die by fasting?

**7.131.6**  I swear, O Sātvata, by my two sons, by my sacrifices and good deeds, that before this night is over—if I fail to slay you who fancy yourself a hero—

**7.131.7**  —unguarded by the victorious Pārtha, together with your sons and younger brothers, O disgrace of the Vṛṣṇis, then may I fall into a dreadful hell."

**7.131.8**  Having spoken thus, the mighty Somadatta, in great wrath, blew his conch with a piercing blast and roared a lion's roar.

**7.131.9**  Then the lotus-petal-eyed, lion-toothed, mighty Sātvata, greatly enraged, said this to Somadatta:

**7.131.10**  "Slain is the hero Bhūriśravas, your son, the great chariot-warrior, and Śala too, O king, worn down by grief for his brother's ruin.

**7.131.11**  You too I shall slay this day, together with your sons, your cattle, and your kin. Stand fast now in battle, on your guard—you are a Kaurava above all others.

**7.131.12**  In King Yudhiṣṭhira, charity, self-restraint, purity, non-violence, modesty, firmness, and forbearance—all these dwell forever and never depart.

**7.131.13**  By the splendor of him whose banner bears the drum, you have already been slain of old; with Karṇa and the son of Subala, you shall meet your destruction in battle."

**7.131.14**  "I swear by the feet of Kṛṣṇa and by all my sacred works—if, roused to fury in battle, I do not slay you, you wretch, together with your son. But if you flee and quit the field, then you shall go free."

**7.131.15**  Having thus addressed each other, their eyes red with wrath, those two best of men set to work to hurl their shafts together.

**7.131.16**  Then Duryodhana, with a thousand elephants and ten thousand chariots, took his stand, surrounding Somadatta.

**7.131.17**  And Śakuni, greatly enraged, foremost of all bearers of weapons, your mighty-armed young brother-in-law, hard as the thunderbolt, surrounded by sons and grandsons and brothers of Indra's prowess—

**7.131.18**  —with fully a hundred thousand horse, that wise one guarded the mighty archer Somadatta on every side.

**7.131.19**  Guarded by the mighty, he covered Sātyaki with his shafts; and seeing him overwhelmed by the smooth-jointed arrows, Dhṛṣṭadyumna in wrath advanced, taking with him a great host.

**7.131.20**  Like the roar of oceans lashed by a furious gale, O king, was the din of those floods of warriors striking down one another.

**7.131.21**  Somadatta pierced the Sātvata with nine shafts, and Sātyaki struck that bull of the Kurus with ten.

**7.131.22**  Deeply wounded in battle by that strong, firm-bowed warrior, he sank down upon the floor of his chariot and swooned, his senses gone.

**7.131.23**  Seeing him fallen senseless, his charioteer, moving with all speed, bore the hero Somadatta, that great chariot-warrior, away from the field.

**7.131.24**  Beholding the Sātvata senseless and tormented by Yuyudhāna's shafts, Drauṇi in wrath charged upon him at the battle's head.

**7.131.25**  Seeing him bearing down upon Śaineya's chariot, the son of Bhīmasena, greatly enraged, held off the foe.

**7.131.26**  Terrible, wrought of black iron, vast, draped with bear-skin, yoked to mounts that resembled elephants but were neither horses nor elephants—

**7.131.27**  —set upon eight creaking wheels with gaping axles, gleaming with a banner that bore a vulture-king with uplifted beak—

**7.131.28**  —mounting that great chariot with its blood-wet banner, adorned with garlands of entrails and fitted with eight wheels—

**7.131.29**  —surrounded by a whole army of Rākṣasas of dreadful form, bearing spears and maces, wielding crags and trees in their hands—

**7.131.30**  —beholding him with his great bow uplifted, the kings were dismayed, as though at the close of an age they saw Death himself, staff in hand.

**7.131.31**  Tormented by fear, your son's army was thrown into turmoil, like the Gaṅgā with her waves running high, her eddies churned up by the wind.

**7.131.32**  Terrified by the lion's roar that Ghaṭotkaca raised, the elephants let flow their urine, and the men were sorely shaken.

**7.131.33**  Then a great rain of stones fell there on every side over the earth, hurled by the Rākṣasas whose strength swells at the hour of twilight.

**7.131.34**  And iron discs, bhuśuṇḍis, javelins and lances, spears, śataghnīs, and battle-axes too fell thick and unbroken.

**7.131.35**  Seeing that fierce and exceedingly savage battle, the lords of men, your sons, and Karṇa, shaken, fled in all directions.

**7.131.36**  There alone the proud Drauṇi, glorying in the might of his weapons, was not shaken, and with his shafts he scattered the illusion wrought by Ghaṭotkaca.

**7.131.37**  When his illusion was destroyed, the wrathful Ghaṭotkaca let fly dreadful shafts, and they fell upon Aśvatthāman.

**7.131.38**  Like serpents frenzied with rage rushing into an anthill, those swift, gold-feathered, stone-whetted shafts, smeared with blood, pierced the son of Śāradvatī and plunged into the earth.

**7.131.39**  But Aśvatthāman, enraged, nimble of hand and full of majesty, pierced the furious Ghaṭotkaca with ten arrows.

**7.131.40**  Ghaṭotkaca, struck deep in his vital parts by Droṇa's son and sorely pained, seized a discus fitted with a hundred thousand spokes.

**7.131.41**  Its rim keen as a razor, gleaming like the rising sun and adorned with gems and diamonds, the son of Bhīmasena hurled it at Aśvatthāman, eager to slay him.

**7.131.42**  Speeding on with mighty force, it was deflected by Droṇa's son with his arrows; like the resolve of a luckless man, it fell to the ground in vain.

**7.131.43**  Then Ghaṭotkaca, seeing the discus struck down, swiftly covered Droṇa's son with arrows, as Svarbhānu covers the sun.

**7.131.44**  The glorious son of Ghaṭotkaca, like a heap of broken collyrium, blocked the advancing son of Droṇa as a king of mountains withstands the storm-wind.

**7.131.45**  Assailed by the arrows of Bhīmasena's grandson, Añjanaparvan, he shone like Mount Meru tormented by the torrents of a cloud.

**7.131.46**  But Aśvatthāman, unshaken, with the valor of Rudra, Upendra, and Indra, severed the banner of Añjanaparvan with a single arrow.

**7.131.47**  With two he felled the charioteer, with three the triple shaft of the car; with one he cut his bow, and with four he slew his four horses.

**7.131.48**  As the carless warrior raised in his hand a sword studded with golden drops, with a keen-pointed shaft he clove it in two.

**7.131.49**  A mace banded with gold, O king, was swiftly whirled aloft and flung by Haiḍimba's son; but it too, struck by the arrows of Droṇa's son, fell.

**7.131.50**  Then, springing into the sky and roaring like a cloud of doom, Añjanaparvan rained down a shower of trees from the vault of heaven.

**7.131.51**  Then Droṇa's son pierced the illusion-wielding son of Ghaṭotkaca in the sky with his shafts, as the sun pierces a cloud with its rays.

**7.131.52**  Descending, he again took his stand upon his gold-wrought car, the glorious Añjanaparvan, lofty as a mountain.

**7.131.53**  Droṇa's son slew that Añjanaparvan, the grandson of Bhīma, clad in iron mail, as Maheśvara slew Andhaka.

**7.131.54**  Then, seeing his mighty son slain by Aśvatthāman, he came near to Droṇa's son, his armlets trembling with rage.

**7.131.55**  Unflinching, he spoke these words to the hero, the son of Śāradvatī's daughter, who was consuming the Pāṇḍava host like a raging fire a forest:

**7.131.56**  "Stay, stay! You shall not depart alive from me, O son of Droṇa. This day I shall slay you as the fire-god's son slew Krauñca."

**7.131.57**  Aśvatthāman said: "Go, child, and fight with the others, you whose valor is that of the immortals; for it is not fitting, O son of Haiḍimbā, that a father be assailed by a son."

**7.131.58**  "Truly I bear no wrath toward you, O son of Haiḍimbā; yet a creature filled with rage may slay even his own self."

**7.131.59**  Saṃjaya said: Hearing this, his eyes coppery with anger and stricken with grief for his son, the son of Bhīmasena, sorely vexed, addressed Aśvatthāman:

**7.131.60**  "Am I a coward, O son of Droṇa, like a common man in battle? Indeed I am sprung from Bhīma, in the vast lineage of the Kurus."

**7.131.61**  "I am a son of the Pāṇḍavas, who never turn back in battle; I am overlord of the rākṣasas, equal in strength to the ten-necked one."

**7.131.62**  "Stay, stay! You shall not depart alive from me, O son of Droṇa. This day I shall drive out your lust for battle on the field of war."

**7.131.63**  Having spoken thus, his eyes coppery with rage, the rākṣasa of mighty strength rushed in fury upon Droṇa's son, as a lion upon a lordly elephant.

**7.131.64**  Ghaṭotkaca rained upon Droṇa's son, the bull among chariot-warriors, arrows as large as chariot-axles, as a raincloud pours down its torrents.

**7.131.65**  Droṇa's son shattered that shower of arrows with his own arrows before it reached him; then in mid-air there arose, as it were, another battle of shafts.

**7.131.66**  Then with the sparks struck out by the clashing of weapons, the sky at the threshold of night gleamed as though painted bright with fireflies.

**7.131.67**  Seeing his illusion destroyed by the battle-proud son of Droṇa, Ghaṭotkaca then, vanishing once more, conjured up another illusion.

**7.131.68**  He became a towering mountain, its peaks dense with trees, vast, streaming with cascades of spears, javelins, swords, and clubs.

**7.131.69**  Seeing that mountain, dark as a heap of collyrium, and the many masses of weapons falling from it, Droṇa's son was not shaken.

**7.131.70**  Then Droṇa's son, smiling as it were, sent forth the thunderbolt weapon; struck by that weapon, the king of mountains swiftly vanished.

**7.131.71**  Then, becoming a dark raincloud arched with the rainbow in the sky, most fierce, he covered Droṇa's son in battle with showers of stones.

**7.131.72**  Then the son of Droṇa, foremost of those who know weapons, fitting the wind-weapon to his bow, scattered the dark cloud that had risen up.

**7.131.73**  Droṇa's son, that best of men, covering all the quarters on every side with his hosts of arrows, slew a hundred thousand chariots.

**7.131.74**  He saw Ghaṭotkaca coming again on his car, his bow drawn wide, undaunted, surrounded by many rākṣasas —

**7.131.75**  like lions and tigers, with the prowess of rutting elephants, mounted on elephants, on chariots, and on the backs of horses,

**7.131.76**  their mouths, heads, and necks gaping wide — together with the followers of Haiḍimbā, with Paulastya demons and dark-natured fiends of fierce valor.

**7.131.77**  with heroes bearing weapons of every kind, decked in armor of every kind, mighty in strength, terrible of cry, their eyes rolling in fury.

**7.131.78**  Then, beholding your son disheartened at the rākṣasas, frenzied for battle, drawn up for the fight, Droṇa's son said:

**7.131.79**  "Stand firm, Duryodhana, this day, and let no agitation be felt by you, together with these heroic brothers and these kings of Indra's valor."

**7.131.80**  "I shall slay your foes; there is no defeat for you. Truly I promise you this — reassure your army."

**7.131.81**  Duryodhana said: "I think it no wonder that this mind of yours is so great, and that your devotion to us is supreme, O joy of Gautama's line."

**7.131.82**  Saṃjaya said: Having thus addressed Aśvatthāman, he then spoke to Subala's son, encircled by a hundred thousand chariots that graced the battlefield:

**7.131.83**  "With sixty thousand elephants go forth against Dhanaṃjaya — Karṇa and Vṛṣasena and Kṛpa and Nīla as well,"

**7.131.84**  "the Northerners and Kṛtavarman, Purumitra, Śrutārpaṇa, Duḥśāsana and Nikumbha, Kuṇḍabhedin, Urukrama,"

**7.131.85**  "Puraṃjaya, Dṛḍharatha, Patākin, Hemapaṅkaja, Śalya, Aruṇi, and Indrasena, Saṃjaya, Vijaya, Jaya,"

**7.131.86**  "Kamalākṣa, Pūru, Krāthin, Jayavarman, Sudarśana — these shall follow you, with sixty thousand foot-soldiers."

**7.131.87**  "Slay Bhīma and both the twins and the King of Righteousness, O uncle, as the lord of the gods slew the asuras; my hope of victory rests in you."

**7.131.88**  "Slay the sons of Kuntī, O uncle, torn by the arrows of Droṇa's son and grievously wounded in body, as the fire-god's son slew the asuras."

**7.131.89**  Thus addressed by your son, Subala's son went forth swiftly, eager to please your sons, O king, and longing to burn up the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.131.90**  Then in the night the battle between Droṇa's son and the rākṣasa grew most tumultuous on the field, like that between Śakra and Prahrāda.

**7.131.91**  Then Ghaṭotkaca, enraged, struck the son of Gautamī in the chest with ten firm arrows, like venom and fire.

**7.131.92**  Struck hard by those arrows loosed by Bhīma's son, he reeled as he stood in the midst of his car, like a tree shaken by the wind.

**7.131.93**  And again, with an añjalika shaft, Ghaṭotkaca swiftly cut the bright bow that rested in the hand of Droṇa's son.

**7.131.94**  Then Droṇa's son, taking up another great bow that could bear the strain, rained down sharp shafts as a raincloud pours its torrents.

**7.131.95**  Then the son of Śāradvatī's daughter, O Bhārata, sent forth foe-destroying, gold-feathered, sky-ranging shafts against the sky-rangers.

**7.131.96**  That troop of broad-chested rākṣasas, tormented by his arrows, appeared like a frenzied herd of elephants thrown into disarray by lions.

**7.131.97**  Scattering the rākṣasas with their horses, drivers, and cars, the mighty one consumed them as the blessed Fire consumes all beings at the world's end.

**7.131.98**  Having burned with his arrows a whole akṣauhiṇī of the night-roving demons, he shone resplendent, as of old the god Maheśvara shone in heaven when he burned Tripura.

**7.131.99**  Like the fierce Fire that has burned up all beings at the end of an age, Droṇa's son, best of the victorious, shone forth, having burned your foes.

**7.131.100**  Among those thousands of kings on the Pāṇḍava side, O Bhārata, none could so much as look upon Droṇa's son in battle, save the hero Ghaṭotkaca, the mighty lord of the rākṣasas.

**7.131.101**  He once more, O best of the Bhāratas, his eyes red-cornered with wrath, clapping palm against palm and biting his lip, said in fury to his charioteer, "Bear me toward the son of Droṇa."

**7.131.102**  On that car of dreadful form, bannered with victory-pennons, the slayer of foes went forth once more to single combat with the son of Droṇa.

**7.131.103**  Then the rākṣasa in his fury hurled at the son of Droṇa a thunderbolt of dreadful might, eight-wheeled and fashioned by Rudra.

**7.131.104**  Droṇa's son, leaping down and laying his bow upon the car, caught it, and flung it back; whereupon the rākṣasa sprang from his own chariot.

**7.131.105**  Reducing the car with its horses, driver, and banner to ashes, that thunderbolt of great splendor and dreadful fierceness clove the earth and entered it.

**7.131.106**  Beholding that deed of Droṇa's son — how, leaping down, he had caught the dreadful weapon fashioned by Śaṃkara — all beings did him honor.

**7.131.107**  Then, O king, the son of Bhīmasena, going to the car of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, loosed sharp arrows once again into the broad chest of Droṇa's son.

**7.131.108**  Dhṛṣṭadyumna too, undaunted, loosed gold-feathered shafts like serpents' venom into the breast of Droṇa's son.

**7.131.109**  Then Droṇa's son loosed iron shafts by the thousand against those two; and they in turn struck down his arrows with shafts bright as tongues of flame.

**7.131.110**  Most fierce grew the battle between those two lions among men and Droṇa's son, O bull of the Bhāratas, gladdening the hearts of the warriors.

**7.131.111**  Then with a thousand chariots, three hundred elephants, and six thousand horses, Bhīma came to that place.

**7.131.112**  Then the righteous son of Droṇa, untiring in his deeds, gave battle to Bhīma's son the rākṣasa and to Dhṛṣṭadyumna with his followers.

**7.131.113**  There Droṇa's son displayed a most wondrous valor, such as could not be matched by any other among all beings, O Bhārata.

**7.131.114**  In the mere span between two blinks of an eye, with his sharp arrows he laid low a whole akṣauhiṇī of rākṣasas, with their horses, drivers, cars, and elephants.

**7.131.115**  Before the very eyes of Bhīmasena, of Haiḍimbā's son, of Pārṣata, of the twins, of the son of Dharma, of Vijaya, and of Acyuta.

**7.131.116**  Smitten deep by straight-flying iron shafts, the elephants fell to the earth like twin-peaked mountains.

**7.131.117**  With elephants' trunks cut off and writhing here and there, the earth, strewn with them, gleamed as though with crawling serpents.

**7.131.118**  With royal parasols on golden staves flung down, the earth shone like the sky strewn with planets, the moon and sun risen together at the dissolution of an age.

**7.131.119**  Its frogs were the upreared standards, its broad turtles the kettledrums; it was thronged with rows of swans that were the parasols, and garlanded with foam that was the yak-tail whisks.

**7.131.120**  Its great crocodiles were herons and vultures, and it teemed with fish that were the manifold weapons; chariots flung up were its high banks, and its lovely trees were the bright pennons.

**7.131.121**  Most terrible it was, with arrows for its small fish and lances and spears for its fierce water-snakes; marrow and flesh were its deep mire, and headless trunks the boats adrift upon it.

**7.131.122**  Dappled with hair for its waterweed, it brought faintness upon the timid; it had its rise in the wasting of the bodies of great elephants, of horses, and of warriors.

**7.131.123**  Droṇa's son set flowing this river, whose mighty current was a flood of blood, whose roar was the anguished cry of warriors, and which surged with waves of gore.

**7.131.124**  It coursed onward into the most fearful great ocean that is Yama's abode; and having slain the rākṣasas with his arrows, Droṇa's son fell to tormenting the son of Hiḍimbā.

**7.131.125**  Then once more, in towering wrath, the mighty son of Droṇa pierced the sons of Pṛthā together with Vṛkodara and the grandson of Pṛṣata, smiting them with showers of iron shafts.

**7.131.126**  The lordly warrior slew Drupada's son named Suratha, and then in battle Śrutaṃjaya, the younger brother of Suratha.

**7.131.127**  Balānīka, Jayānīka, and Jayāśva he struck down; and Śrutāhvaya too, O king of kings, the son of Droṇa dispatched to Yama's realm.

**7.131.128**  And with three other keen, well-feathered shafts he led the mighty Śatruṃjaya, garlanded in gold, into the world of Indra.

**7.131.129**  He slew Pṛṣadhra and the proud Candradeva, and the sons of Kuntibhoja in that battle he killed, ten of them with ten shafts.

**7.131.130**  Then Aśvatthāman, in mighty wrath, fitting a dreadful straight-flying shaft, drew the bow to his ear and loosed that surpassing arrow, terrible as the rod of Yama, swiftly aimed at Ghaṭotkaca.

**7.131.131**  That great arrow, cleaving the heart of the rākṣasa, swiftly entered the earth, feathers and all, O lord of the world.

**7.131.132**  Knowing him slain and fallen, the great chariot-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O king of kings, bore him away upon another chariot from the presence of Droṇa's son.

**7.131.133**  And so, O king, having routed in battle the army of Yudhiṣṭhira until its chariots turned their backs, the heroic son of Droṇa roared aloud, honored by all beings and by your sons, O Bhārata.

**7.131.134**  Then with the night-rangers slain and fallen on every side, their bodies riven and hacked by hundreds of arrows, the earth was made impassable and most terrible, as though heaped with mountain peaks of the dead.

**7.131.135**  The hosts of siddhas, gandharvas, and piśācas, the nāgas, the suparṇas, the ancestors, and the birds, the throngs of rākṣasas and the multitudes of spirits, the apsarases and the gods—all honored that son of Droṇa.

**7.132.1**  Saṃjaya said: Seeing the sons of Drupada and the sons of Kuntibhoja, and rākṣasas by the thousand, slain by the son of Droṇa—

**7.132.2**  Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the grandson of Pṛṣata, and Yuyudhāna, girding themselves, set their minds firmly upon battle.

**7.132.3**  Somadatta, enraged once more at the sight of Sātyaki in the fray, covered him on every side with a mighty rain of arrows.

**7.132.4**  Then there arose a battle exceedingly dreadful and terror-breeding, between your men and the foe, all of them hungering for victory.

**7.132.5**  For the sake of the Sātvata, Bhīma pierced the Kaurava with ten shafts; and Somadatta in turn struck that hero with a hundred.

**7.132.6**  But the Sātvata, mightily enraged, pierced him—aged, yet rich in every virtue like Yayāti the son of Nahuṣa, and overwhelmed with grief for his sons—

**7.132.7**  —he pierced him with ten keen shafts that fell like thunderbolts, and striking him with a spear besides, pierced him again with seven.
