**7.132.8**  Then, for the sake of Sātyaki, Bhīmasena hurled at the head of Somadatta a fresh and sturdy iron-bound mace, terrible to behold.

**7.132.9**  And Sātyaki in his wrath loosed at Somadatta's breast a surpassing shaft, fair-feathered and whetted, blazing like fire in the fight.

**7.132.10**  At one and the same moment the dread mace and the arrow fell upon the body of Somadatta, and that great chariot-warrior dropped down.

**7.132.11**  When his son was struck senseless, Bāhlika rushed forward, pouring down floods of arrows like a cloud raining at the appointed season.

**7.132.12**  Then Bhīma, for the sake of the Sātvata, sorely pressing the great-souled Bāhlika with nine shafts, pierced him at the forefront of the battle.

**7.132.13**  But the son of Pratīpa, enraged, that mighty-armed one, drove a spear into Bhīma's breast as Purandara hurls the thunderbolt.

**7.132.14**  Struck by it, Bhīma trembled and swooned; but regaining his senses, the strong one hurled his mace at him.

**7.132.15**  Sped by the Pāṇḍava, it carried off Bāhlika's head; and slain, he fell to the earth like a great mountain shattered by the thunderbolt.

**7.132.16**  When that hero Bāhlika, that bull among men, was slain, ten of your sons, the equals of the son of Daśaratha, assailed Bhīma.

**7.132.17**  Slaying those sons of yours with ten iron shafts, Bhīma then overwhelmed Vṛṣasena, the beloved son of Karṇa.

**7.132.18**  Then Vṛṣaratha, a renowned brother of Karṇa, struck Bhīma with iron shafts; and him too the mighty one slew.

**7.132.19**  Then the hero Bhīma, having slain with his iron shafts seven chariot-warriors among your brothers-in-law, O Bhārata, crushed Śatacandra.

**7.132.20**  Unable to brook the slaying of the great chariot-warrior Śatacandra, the heroic brothers of Śakuni—Gajākṣa, Śarabha, and Vibhu—rushed upon Bhīmasena and smote him with keen shafts.

**7.132.21**  Galled by their iron shafts, like a bull beneath the rushing rain, the exceedingly strong Bhīma slew those five chariot-warriors with five arrows; and seeing those heroes slain, the foremost of kings wavered.

**7.132.22**  Then Yudhiṣṭhira in his wrath shattered your host, before the very eyes of the pitcher-born Droṇa and of your sons, O sinless one.

**7.132.23**  The Ambaṣṭhas, the Mālavas, the valiant Trigartas, and the Śibis as well—these troops Yudhiṣṭhira sent off in battle to the world of Death.

**7.132.24**  Cutting down the Abhīṣāhas, the Śūrasenas, the Bāhlīkas, and the Vasātis, the king made the earth a mire of blood.

**7.132.25**  The valiant troops of the Yaudheyas, the Āraṭṭas, the Rājanyas, and the Madrakas—these Yudhiṣṭhira sent off in battle with his arrows to the world of Death.

**7.132.26**  "Strike! Seize him! Take him! Pierce him! Cut him down!"—such was the tumultuous clamor that rose about the chariot of Yudhiṣṭhira.

**7.132.27**  Seeing Yudhiṣṭhira routing the troops, Droṇa, urged on by your son, overwhelmed him with arrows.

**7.132.28**  Droṇa, in supreme wrath, pierced the king with the missile of Vāyu; but the other foiled that celestial weapon with a weapon of his own.

**7.132.29**  That weapon foiled, the son of Bharadvāja, in supreme wrath and bent on slaying the son of Pāṇḍu, hurled at Yudhiṣṭhira the missiles of Varuṇa, of Yama, of Agni, of Tvaṣṭṛ, and of Savitṛ.

**7.132.30**  Those weapons, hurled and being hurled, the mighty-armed son of Dharma, unshaken before the pitcher-born one, struck down with weapons of his own.

**7.132.31**  But wishing to make good his vow, the pitcher-born one, intent upon your sons' welfare and bent on slaying the son of Dharma, brought forth the Aindra weapon and that of Prajāpati, O Bhārata.

**7.132.32**  The lord of the Kurus, moving with the gait of elephant and lion, broad of chest, large and red of eye, undiminished in splendor, brought forth another weapon, the missile of great Indra, and therewith destroyed those two weapons of his.

**7.132.33**  His weapons being thwarted, Droṇa, filled with wrath and longing to slay Yudhiṣṭhira, raised up the Brāhma weapon.

**7.132.34**  Then I could perceive nothing at all, for a dreadful darkness shrouded everything, and all beings were seized with utmost terror, O lord of the earth.

**7.132.35**  Seeing the weapon of Brahmā raised aloft, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Kuntī warded off that weapon with the weapon of Brahmā itself, O king of kings.

**7.132.36**  Then the chief warriors praised those two bulls among men, Droṇa and the son of Pṛthā, great archers both, skilled in every mode of warfare.

**7.132.37**  Then, leaving aside the son of Kuntī, Droṇa, his eyes red with rage, scattered Drupada's host with the missile of Vāyu, O Bhārata.

**7.132.38**  Smitten by Droṇa, the Pāñcālas fled in terror, before the very eyes of Bhīmasena and the great-souled son of Pṛthā.

**7.132.39**  Then the Diademed one and Bhīma swiftly turned back, hemming in your army with two great lines of chariots.

**7.132.40**  Bībhatsu on the right flank, and Vṛkodara on the left, rained down upon the son of Bharadvāja with two mighty floods of arrows.

**7.132.41**  Then the Sṛñjayas and the mighty Pāñcālas followed those two, O great king, and the Matsyas together with the Sātvatas.

**7.132.42**  Then that Bhārata army, being slaughtered by the Diademed one, could not be held back—though Droṇa himself and your son strove to restrain them, the warriors could not then be checked, O great king.

**7.133.1**  Saṃjaya said: Seeing that mighty host of the Pāṇḍavas surging up, and deeming it irresistible, Duryodhana spoke to Karṇa.

**7.133.2**  "The hour has come, O lover of your friends, the hour of friends; save in battle all our warriors, O mighty Karṇa,

**7.133.3**  —beset on every side by the Pāñcālas, the Matsyas, the Kaikeyas, and the great chariot-warriors among the Pāṇḍavas, all enraged and hissing like serpents.

**7.133.4**  These Pāṇḍavas roar in their exultation, flushed with the look of victory, and many a host of Pāñcāla chariots besides, each rival to Indra."

**7.133.5**  Karṇa said: "Even if Purandara himself should come hither to rescue the son of Pṛthā, swiftly vanquishing him too, I shall thereafter slay the Pāṇḍava.

**7.133.6**  Truly I promise you—take heart, O Bhārata—I shall slay the sons of Pāṇḍu and the Pāñcālas gathered against us.

**7.133.7**  I promise you victory, as the son of Agni promised it to Vāsava; for I live, O king, only that your good may be wrought by me.

**7.133.8**  Of all the sons of Pṛthā, Phalguna is the strongest; against him I shall loose the unfailing spear fashioned by Śakra.

**7.133.9**  When that great archer is slain, his brothers, O giver of honor, will fall under your sway, or else go once more to the forest."

**7.133.10**  "While I live, O Kaurava, nowhere give way to despair; I shall conquer in battle all the Pāṇḍavas together,

**7.133.11**  —and the Pāñcālas, the Kekayas, and the Vṛṣṇis assembled too; shattering them to fragments with floods of arrows, I shall give you the earth."

**7.133.12**  Saṃjaya said: To Karṇa, speaking thus, the mighty-armed Kṛpa, son of Śaradvat, replied, smiling as it were, in these words to the charioteer's son:

**7.133.13**  "Fine, fine, Karṇa! With you for protector, the bull of the Kurus has indeed found a protector—O Rādheya, if only it could be accomplished by words!

**7.133.14**  Many a time, Karṇa, you boast in the presence of the Kaurava; yet no prowess of yours is anywhere to be seen, nor any strength.

**7.133.15**  Your encounters with the sons of Pāṇḍu have been seen many times in battle, and everywhere you have been vanquished by the Pāṇḍavas, O son of a charioteer.

**7.133.16**  When the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was being carried off by the gandharvas, Karṇa, the armies fought on, but you alone took to flight.

**7.133.17**  And in the city of Virāṭa too, all the Kauravas gathered together were vanquished in battle by the son of Pṛthā—you as well, Karṇa, together with your brothers.

**7.133.18**  Unequal as you are even to Phalguna alone on the field of battle, how do you presume to conquer all the Pāṇḍavas together with Kṛṣṇa?

**7.133.19**  Fight without speaking, Karṇa; you boast overmuch, son of a charioteer. To show valor rather than proclaim it—that is the vow of the good.

**7.133.20**  Having thundered like an autumn cloud that holds no water, you are seen, Karṇa, to come to nothing, O son of a charioteer—and this the king does not perceive.

**7.133.21**  You thunder, Rādheya, only so long as you do not behold the son of Pṛthā; once you have seen him before you, that thundering of yours will be hard to come by."

**7.133.22**  You roar because you have not yet met the arrows of Phalguna; once you are pierced by Pārtha's shafts, your roaring will be hard to come by.

**7.133.23**  Kṣatriyas are valiant with their arms, the twice-born are valiant with their words; Phalguna is valiant with his bow, but Karṇa is valiant only in his daydreams.

**7.133.24**  Thus harshly upbraided by Śāradvata, Karṇa, the foremost of those who strike, then spoke these words to Kṛpa.

**7.133.25**  Heroes ever roar, like the storm clouds in the rains; and swiftly they yield their fruit, as seed sown in its season.

**7.133.26**  I see no fault in this — that heroes, at the head of battle, should boast in one way or another while they bear up the burden of the fight.

**7.133.27**  Whatever burden a man resolves in his mind to carry, fate surely comes to his aid in that undertaking.

**7.133.28**  If I, having resolve for my companion, bear up the burden in my mind and roar, O brahmin, what of yours is lost thereby?

**7.133.29**  Heroes do not roar in vain, like rain clouds laden with water; the wise roar only after knowing their own strength.

**7.133.30**  And so today, braced for battle, I am eager to conquer by my swiftness both Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava united; that is why I roar, O Gautama.

**7.133.31**  Behold, O brahmin, with your followers, the fruit of this roaring of mine: having slain the sons of Pāṇḍu in battle, together with Kṛṣṇa and the Sātvatas, I shall give to Duryodhana an earth cleansed of its thorns.

**7.133.32**  Kṛpa said: I cannot accept this babbling of your daydreams, O son of a sūta, when you would hurl yourself against the two Kṛṣṇas and the Pāṇḍava, the King of Righteousness.

**7.133.33**  There victory is certain, Karṇa, where stand those two masters of war; even when arrayed for battle, the two Kṛṣṇas and the Pāṇḍava are unconquerable by gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, men, serpents, and rākṣasas.

**7.133.34**  Devoted to the brahmins, truthful in speech, self-controlled, a worshipper of teachers and gods, ever delighting in dharma, and above all skilled in arms, steadfast and grateful — such is Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma.

**7.133.35**  And his brothers are mighty, practised in every weapon, devoted to the service of their elders, wise, ever true to dharma, and renowned.

**7.133.36**  Their kinsmen too are valiant as Indra, loyal, and skilled in striking — Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin, the son of Durmukha, and Janamejaya;

**7.133.37**  Candrasena, Bhadrasena, Kīrtidharman, Dhruva, Dhara, Vasucandra, Dāmacandra, Siṃhacandra, and Suvedhana;

**7.133.38**  and likewise the sons of Drupada, and Drupada himself, knower of the great weapons, for whose cause the king of the Matsyas with his followers stands ready;

**7.133.39**  Śatānīka, Sudarśana, Śrutānīka, Śrutadhvaja, Balānīka, Jayānīka, Jayāśva, and Rathavāhana;

**7.133.40**  Candrodaya and Kāmaratha, the noble brothers of Virāṭa, the twins, the sons of Draupadī, and the rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca — for those in whose cause these fight, there is no destruction.

**7.133.41**  Truly, if they wished, Bhīma and Phalguna could by the power of their weapons make an utter end of the whole world — with its gods, asuras, and men, its hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas, its spirits, serpents, and elephants.

**7.133.42**  And Yudhiṣṭhira could burn up the earth with his terrible glance; while Śauri of immeasurable strength stands armed for their cause — how then, Karṇa, do you presume to conquer those foes in battle?

**7.133.43**  This is ever a great folly of yours, O son of a sūta — that you should presume to fight in battle against Śauri.

**7.133.44**  Saṃjaya said: Thus addressed, O bull of the Bhāratas, the son of Rādhā laughed aloud, and then Karṇa spoke to the teacher, Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat.

**7.133.45**  True are the words you have spoken, O brahmin, concerning the Pāṇḍavas; these and many other virtues do indeed dwell in the sons of Pāṇḍu.

**7.133.46**  The Pārthas are unconquerable in battle even by the gods led by Vāsava, with the daityas, yakṣas, gandharvas, piśācas, serpents, and rākṣasas; yet still I shall conquer the Pārthas with the dart given me by Vāsava.

**7.133.47**  This unfailing dart was given to me by Śakra, O brahmin; with it I shall strike down Savyasācin in the fray.

**7.133.48**  And once that Pāṇḍava is slain, Kṛṣṇa and his own brothers, bereft of Arjuna, will in no wise be able to enjoy the earth.

**7.133.49**  And when all of them have perished, this earth with her oceans will, without effort, fall under the sway of the son of Kuru, O Gautama.

**7.133.50**  By sound policy all aims are accomplished here — of that there is no doubt; knowing this purpose, I roar accordingly, O Gautama.

**7.133.51**  But you are old, and a brahmin, and unable in battle, and besides you bear affection for the Pārthas; out of folly you despise me.

**7.133.52**  If you speak to me again in this unwelcome way, O brahmin, then, raising my sword, I will cut out your tongue, you fool.

**7.133.53**  And as for your wishing to extol the Pāṇḍavas in this battle, O brahmin, frightening all the Kaurava armies, you fool — hear too my words on this, as I rightly speak them, O twice-born.

**7.133.54**  Duryodhana and Droṇa, Śakuni, Durmukha, Jaya, Duḥśāsana, Vṛṣasena, the king of the Madras, and you yourself, Somadatta and Bhūri, and likewise Aśvatthāman and Viviṃśati —

**7.133.55**  where all these masters of war stand arrayed for battle, what foe, even one equal in might to Śakra, could conquer them in the fray?

**7.133.56**  For these heroes, skilled in arms, mighty, longing for heaven, knowers of dharma and adept in war, could slay even the gods in battle.

**7.133.57**  These will stand in the battle, seeking the slaughter of the Pāṇḍavas, arrayed and longing for the victory of the son of Kuru.

**7.133.58**  I hold that victory rests with fate, even for the most mighty — for there lies Bhīṣma of the great arms, covered with a hundred arrows.

**7.133.59**  Vikarṇa and Citrasena, Bāhlika and Jayadratha, Bhūriśravas and Jaya, Jalasaṃdha and Sudakṣiṇa,

**7.133.60**  and Śala, foremost among chariot-warriors, and the valiant Bhagadatta — these and other kings, hard to conquer even by the gods,

**7.133.61**  these heroes, mightier still, have been slain in battle by the Pāṇḍavas. What else but the working of fate do you suppose it, O basest of men?

**7.133.62**  And those foes of Duryodhana whom you ceaselessly praise, O brahmin — of them too the heroes have been slain by hundreds and by thousands.

**7.133.63**  The whole armies of the Kurus are wasting away together with the Pāṇḍavas; in this I see no special might of the Pāṇḍavas at all.

**7.133.64**  Those whom you ever deem so mighty, O basest of brahmins — I will strive with all my strength to fight against them in battle. For the welfare of Duryodhana I shall fight; but victory rests with fate.

**7.134.1**  Saṃjaya said: Seeing his maternal uncle thus harshly reviled by the son of the sūta, Aśvatthāman, raising his sword, rushed swiftly upon him in a fury.

**7.134.2**  Aśvatthāman said: Look here, Karṇa, you of wretched mind! Stand fast now, basest of men — this day I shall lift your head from your body, you utter fool.

**7.134.3**  Saṃjaya said: As he sprang up in his fury, O great king, King Duryodhana himself restrained him, and so did Kṛpa, foremost of men.

**7.134.4**  Karṇa said: This brahmin is a hero, a boaster in battle, and dull of wit, the basest of his kind — let him come up against my prowess; release him, O best of the Kurus.

**7.134.5**  Aśvatthāman said: This of yours we forgive, O son of a sūta, you utter fool; but this overweening arrogance of yours Phalguna will destroy.

**7.134.6**  Duryodhana said: Aśvatthāman, be appeased; you ought to forgive, O bestower of honour. No anger at all should be shown toward the son of the sūta.

**7.134.7**  Upon you, upon Karṇa, Kṛpa, Droṇa, the king of the Madras, and the son of Subala rests our great task; be appeased, O best of brahmins.

**7.134.8**  For lo, all these Pāṇḍavas, eager to fight against the son of Rādhā, are advancing toward us, O brahmin, challenging us on every side.

**7.134.9**  Saṃjaya said: And Karṇa too, foremost of chariot-warriors, the valiant one, raising his bow and surrounded by the chief Kauravas as Śakra by the hosts of gods, took his stand, blazing with splendour and relying on the strength of his own arms.

**7.134.10**  Then began the battle of the enraged Karṇa with the Pāṇḍavas, O great king, resounding with the roars of lions.

**7.134.11**  Then those Pāṇḍavas, O king, and the renowned Pāñcālas, seeing Karṇa of the mighty arms, raised a loud cry.

**7.134.12**  "Here is Karṇa! Where now is Karṇa? Stand, Karṇa, in this great battle! Fight against us, you wicked-souled, basest of men!"

**7.134.13**  And others, seeing the son of Rādhā, their eyes red with rage, said: "Let this arrogant, dull-witted son of the sūta be slain!"

**7.134.14**  "There is no use for all you tigers among kings in his living; this wicked man is the unending, ceaseless foe of the Pārthas."

**7.134.15**  "For he is the very root of our calamities, planted firm in Duryodhana's counsel — slay him!" So crying, the kṣatriyas rushed upon him together.

**7.134.16**  With a great shower of arrows the mighty chariot-warriors, urged on by the Pāṇḍava, covered him over, seeking the death of the son of the sūta.

**7.134.17**  But seeing all those great chariot-warriors thus rushing on, the son of the sūta neither faltered nor gave way to fear.

**7.134.18**  Beholding that surging ocean of an army, vast as a city, he who was unvanquished in battles sought to bring cheer to your sons.

**7.134.19**  The strong one, swift in action and of great might, held back that army on every side with a flood of arrows, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.134.20**  Then the kings checked him with a rain of arrows, shaking their bows by hundreds and by thousands; they did battle with the son of Rādhā as the hosts of daityas with Śakra.

**7.134.21**  But that rain of arrows loosed by the kings Karṇa scattered on every side with a mighty rain of arrows of his own, O lord.

**7.134.22**  That battle of theirs, each seeking to repay blow with counter-blow, became like the battle of Śakra with the dānavas in the war of gods and asuras.

**7.134.23**  There we beheld the marvellous swiftness of the son of the sūta — that even striving in battle, his foes could not reach him in the fight.

**7.134.24**  Warding off those floods of arrows from the kings, the great chariot-warrior, son of Rādhā, sent forth keen shafts marked with his own name into their yokes and chariot-poles, their parasols and banners and horses.

**7.134.25**  Then those kings, thrown into confusion and sorely pressed by Karṇa, wandered hither and thither, like cattle tormented by the cold.

**7.134.26**  Here and there we looked upon throngs of horses, elephants, and chariot-warriors being slaughtered, struck down by Karṇa.

**7.134.27**  With heads fallen, O king, and with arms strewn on every side, the whole earth was carpeted with those of heroes who never turned back.

**7.134.28**  With the slain and the dying and those groaning on every side, the battlefield grew terrible, like the city of Vaivasvata.

**7.134.29**  Then King Duryodhana, beholding the prowess of Karṇa, approached Aśvatthāman and spoke these words.

**7.134.30**  "Yonder Karṇa, arrayed for battle, fights against all the kings; behold this army fleeing, sore pressed by the arrows of Karṇa, like the demonic host shattered by Kārttikeya."

**7.134.31**  "Seeing this army vanquished in battle by the wise Karṇa, here comes Bībhatsu, longing to slay the son of the sūta."

**7.134.32**  "So let such measures be devised that, before our very eyes, the Pāṇḍava may not slay the great chariot-warrior, the son of the sūta, in this battle."

**7.134.33**  Then Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, Śalya, and the great chariot-warrior the son of Hṛdika went forth against Pārtha, seeking to protect the son of the sūta.

**7.134.34**  Seeing the son of Kuntī advancing like Vṛtra against the army of the gods, Karṇa then went forth to meet him, glorious as Śakra.

**7.134.35**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Seeing the enraged Phalguna, like Yama the all-ending at the world's close, what response, O sūta, did Karṇa Vaikartana make?

**7.134.36**  For that great chariot-warrior ever vied with Pārtha, and hoped to conquer Bībhatsu in dreadful battle.

**7.134.37**  What response, then, O sūta, did Karṇa Vaikartana make to that unending enemy, now suddenly come upon him?

**7.134.38**  Saṃjaya said: Seeing the Pāṇḍava advancing, Karṇa, wholly unshaken, went forth to meet Dhanaṃjaya as one elephant goes forth against another.

**7.134.39**  As Vaikartana rushed upon him with speed, the radiant Pāṇḍava, scorcher of foes, held him off with straight-flying shafts.

**7.134.40**  Karṇa, O sire, covered him with a net of arrows, and in his fury pierced him with three straight-flying shafts.

**7.134.41**  The mighty Pārtha would not endure that nimbleness of his; against him he loosed arrows whetted on stone, bright-tipped and straight-flying.

**7.134.42**  Thirty of them the scorcher of foes sent against the Sūta's son, and the valiant one, enraged, pierced him with a single shaft.

**7.134.43**  With an iron shaft, as if smiling, the strong one struck him on the tip of his left arm, and by the force of that wound the bow fell from Karṇa's hand.

**7.134.44**  Taking up that bow again in half the blink of an eye, the mighty one, deft of hand, covered Phalguna with floods of arrows.

**7.134.45**  But that rain of arrows loosed by the Sūta's son, O Bhārata, Dhanaṃjaya, as if smiling, scattered with a downpour of shafts of his own.

**7.134.46**  Closing upon each other, O king, those two great archers, each striving to repay the other's stroke, veiled each other with showers of arrows.

**7.134.47**  Wondrous was that battle of Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava upon the field, like the fight of two wild elephants enraged over a she-elephant in heat.

**7.134.48**  Then Pārtha, the great archer, beholding Karṇa's prowess, with all speed cut through his bow at the grip.

**7.134.49**  With broad-headed shafts he sent the four horses to the abode of Yama, and the scorcher of foes struck the charioteer's head from his body.

**7.134.50**  Then him, his bow severed, his horses slain, his charioteer slain, Pārtha, the joy of Pāṇḍu's line, pierced with four arrows.

**7.134.51**  Swiftly leaping down from the car whose horses were slain, that bull among men, sore pressed by arrows, swiftly mounted Kṛpa's chariot.

**7.134.52**  Seeing Rādheya defeated, O bull of the Bhāratas, your men, driven by Dhanaṃjaya's arrows, fled in all ten directions.

**7.134.53**  Beholding them in flight, King Duryodhana, O sovereign, turned them back and spoke these words.

**7.134.54**  Enough of flight, you heroes! Stand fast, you bulls among Kṣatriyas! Lo, I myself go into the battle to slay Pārtha; I shall slay the Pārthas together with the Pāñcālas and the Somakas.

**7.134.55**  This day, as I fight against the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, the Pārthas shall behold my valor, like that of Time at the dissolution of an age.

**7.134.56**  This day the warriors shall behold in the battle the nets of my arrows loosed by the thousand, like advancing swarms of locusts.

**7.134.57**  This day the soldiers shall behold in the fight the arrowy rain poured forth by me, the bowman, like a thundercloud's at the close of the hot season.

**7.134.58**  This day in battle I shall conquer Pārtha with smooth-jointed shafts. Stand fast in the fight, you heroes; cast away your fear of Phalguna.

**7.134.59**  For having met my might, Phalguna shall not prevail over it, even as the sea, abode of sea-monsters, prevails not against the shore it meets.

**7.134.60**  Having spoken thus, the king, hard to assail, his eyes red with wrath, advanced toward Phalguna, encircled by a great host.

**7.134.61**  Seeing that mighty-armed one set forth, Śāradvata then approached Aśvatthāman and spoke these words.

**7.134.62**  This mighty-armed king, full of indignation, swooning with wrath, has taken up the way of the moth toward the flame and seeks to fight Phalguna.

**7.134.63**  Before this tiger among men, having closed with Pārtha, yields up his life beneath our very eyes, restrain the Kaurava.

**7.134.64**  Before the heroic Kaurava king comes within range of Phalguna's arrows, restrain him at once.

**7.134.65**  Before the king is reduced to ashes by Pārtha's dreadful arrows, like serpents loosed from their slough, let him be turned back from the battle.

**7.134.66**  It seems unfitting to me, O giver of honor, that while we stand here the king should go alone, unaided, to fight Pārtha.

**7.134.67**  Hard to keep, I deem, is the life of the Kaurava, fighting against the diademed Pārtha, as is an elephant's against a tiger.

**7.134.68**  Thus addressed by his uncle, Drauṇi, foremost of weapon-bearers, spoke in haste these words to Duryodhana.

**7.134.69**  While I live, O son of Gāndhārī, you ought not to go into battle, slighting me, O Kaurava, who am ever a seeker of your good.

**7.134.70**  You need feel no alarm for Pārtha's victory; I shall hold Pārtha off. Stay back, Suyodhana.

**7.134.71**  Duryodhana said: The teacher guards the sons of Pāṇḍu as though they were his own children, and you too, O best of the twice-born, ever show indifference toward them.

**7.134.72**  Whether your prowess in battle is feeble through my own ill fortune, or for the sake of pleasing the Dharma-king, or of Draupadī—that I do not know.

**7.134.73**  Fie upon me, the greedy one, for whose sake all these kinsmen, deserving of joy and unconquered, are come to the utmost grief!

**7.134.74**  For what foremost of weapon-bearers, equal in battle to Maheśvara, being able, would not destroy his foes—unless he were the son of Gautamī?

**7.134.75**  Aśvatthāman, be gracious; destroy these enemies of mine. Within range of your weapons not even the gods are able to stand, O sinless one.

**7.134.76**  Slay the Pāñcālas and the Somakas with their followers, O Drauṇi; the rest we shall slay, guarded by you alone.

**7.134.77**  For these Somakas, O Brahman, and the glorious Pāñcālas, in their fury range through my armies like a forest fire.

**7.134.78**  Hold them back, O mighty-armed, and the Kekayas too, O best of men, before, guarded by the diademed one, they leave nothing of us remaining.

**7.134.79**  Whether at the first or at the last, this deed is yours, O sire; you were born, O mighty-armed, for the slaughter of the Pāñcālas.

**7.134.80**  You shall make the whole world free of Pāñcālas, O imperishable one; thus have the perfected ones spoken, and so shall it surely come to pass.

**7.134.81**  Within range of your weapons the gods themselves with Vāsava are unable to stand—how much less the Pārthas with the Pāñcālas? This word of mine is the truth.

**7.135.1**  Saṃjaya said: Thus addressed by Duryodhana, Drauṇi, fierce in battle, replied: "It is as you say, O mighty-armed Kaurava."

**7.135.2**  Dear indeed are the Pāṇḍavas ever to me and to my father, and dear likewise are we two to them; yet not in war, O chief of the Kurus. With all our strength, my friend, we fight, casting away our lives without fear.

**7.135.3**  I, and Karṇa, and Śalya, and Kṛpa, and Hārdikya too—in the twinkling of an eye we could destroy the Pāṇḍava host, O best of kings.

**7.135.4**  And they too could destroy the Kaurava host in half the twinkling of an eye, O chief of the Kurus, mighty-armed one, were we not present in the battle.

**7.135.5**  We fight the Pāṇḍavas with all our power, and they would fight us; yet when energy meets energy, O Bhārata, it comes to a standstill.

**7.135.6**  The army of the Pāṇḍavas cannot be conquered by mere onset while the sons of Pāṇḍu live—this truth I tell you.

**7.135.7**  Fighting for their own cause, the able sons of Pāṇḍu—why should they not slay your armies, O Bhārata?

**7.135.8**  For you, O king, are most greedy, and skilled in deceit, O Kaurava, suspicious of everyone and proud; therefore you mistrust us also.

**7.135.9**  But I, putting forth my utmost effort for your sake, having cast away my life, here go into the battle for you, O joy of the Kurus.

**7.135.10**  I shall fight with the foes and conquer the very best of them; I shall fight with the Pāñcālas, with the Somakas and the Kekayas, and with the sons of Pāṇḍu in battle, to please you, O subduer of foes.

**7.135.11**  This day, scorched by my arrows, the Pāñcālas and the Somakas shall scatter in every direction, like cattle harried by a lion.

**7.135.12**  This day, beholding my prowess, King Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma, together with the Somakas, shall deem the whole world to be made of Aśvatthāman.

**7.135.13**  Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma, shall come to despair, beholding the Pāñcālas slain in battle together with the Somakas.

**7.135.14**  Whoever shall fight against me in battle, them I shall slay, O Bhārata; for those heroes, once come within the reach of my arms, would not escape.

**7.135.15**  Having thus spoken to your son Duryodhana, the mighty-armed one turned to the fight, putting all the bowmen to flight—that best of living beings, eager to do your sons a kindness.

**7.135.16**  Then the son of Gautamī addressed the Pāñcālas with the Kekayas: "Strike all of you here upon my body, you great chariot-warriors; stand firm and fight, displaying your deftness with weapons."

**7.135.17**  Thus addressed, they all let fall a rain of weapons upon Drauṇi, O great king, as rain-clouds pour down water.

**7.135.18**  Striking down those arrows, Drauṇi crushed ten warriors before the very faces of the sons of Pāṇḍu and of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O lord.

**7.135.19**  Being slain in the battle, the Pāñcālas and the Sṛñjayas forsook Drauṇi on the field and fled in all ten directions.

**7.135.20**  Seeing those heroic Pāñcālas with the Somakas in flight, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O great king, rushed upon Drauṇi in the fight.

**7.135.21**  Then, surrounded by a hundred chariots of heroes who never turned back, gleaming with gold and roaring like rain-laden clouds—

**7.135.22**  the son of the Pāñcāla king, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the great chariot-warrior, beholding his warriors struck down, spoke these words to Drauṇi.

**7.135.23**  "O evil-minded son of the teacher, what is it to you that others are slain? Close with me, if you are a hero in battle. I shall slay you—stand now before me!"

**7.135.24**  Then the valorous Dhṛṣṭadyumna struck that son of the teacher with sharp shafts that pierce the vital parts, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.135.25**  Those swift arrows, ranged in rows, gold-feathered and bright-tipped, rending the whole body, entered into Drauṇi, like unbridled bees seeking honey upon a flowering tree.

**7.135.26**  Sorely pierced and greatly enraged, like a serpent trodden underfoot, the proud Drauṇi, unshaken, arrow in hand, spoke.

**7.135.27**  "Dhṛṣṭadyumna, stand firm and wait a moment, while with whetted arrows I send you to the abode of Yama."

**7.135.28**  Having spoken thus to the son of Pṛṣata, Drauṇi, slayer of hostile heroes, deft of hand, covered him on every side with floods of arrows.

**7.135.29**  Being thus veiled in battle by Drauṇi, the son of the Pāñcāla king, fierce in war, then assailed Drauṇi with taunting words.

**7.135.30**  "You know not my vow, nor yet my birth from a Brahman: when I have slain Droṇa, then you too are to be slain by me, O most evil-minded one. Therefore I slay you not today, while Droṇa yet lives, in the battle."

**7.135.31**  "But upon this night now come, before it dawns, O most evil-minded one, having slain your father this day, then you too in battle I shall lead to the realm of the dead—thus is it fixed in my mind."

**7.135.32**  "What hatred you bear toward the Pārthas, what devotion toward the Kauravas—show it, standing firm; you shall not escape me with your life."

**7.135.33**  "For that twice-born man who, forsaking his Brahmanhood, takes delight in the duties of a Kṣatriya, deserves to be slain by all the world—as do you, O basest of men."

**7.135.34**  Thus addressed with harsh speech by the son of Pṛṣata, that best of the twice-born gathered fierce wrath and cried, "Stand, stand!"

**7.135.35**  As if consuming him with his eyes, he gazed upon the son of Pṛṣata, and, hissing like a serpent, covered him with arrows.

**7.135.36**  Being thus veiled in battle by Drauṇi, O best of kings, that best of chariot-warriors stood encompassed by all the Pāñcāla armies.

**7.135.37**  The mighty-armed one did not waver, resting upon his own steadfastness, and he loosed manifold arrows upon Aśvatthāman.

**7.135.38**  Once more the two turned back to the battle in which life itself was the wager, those two unforgiving great archers warding off each other with floods of arrows, pouring forth showers of shafts on every side.

**7.135.39**  Beholding the dreadful and terrifying combat of the son of Droṇa and the son of Pṛṣata, the bands of Siddhas and Cāraṇas honored it with praise.

**7.135.40**  Filling the sky and the quarters with their floods of arrows, the two fought unseen, having wrought a great darkness with their shafts.

**7.135.41**  As though dancing in the fray, their bows drawn into perfect circles, each strove to slay the other, each longing to vanquish the other.

**7.135.42**  The two mighty-armed warriors fought with skill, with swiftness, and with mastery, honored in the battle by thousands of the foremost fighters.

**7.135.43**  Seeing the two locked in combat in the fray like two wild elephants in the forest, a tumultuous joy arose in both armies.

**7.135.44**  There were roars like the lion's roar, and they blew their conches, O honored one, and instruments were sounded by the hundreds and the thousands.

**7.135.45**  In that tumultuous battle, which swelled the terror of the timid, the combat for a moment then stood evenly matched.

**7.135.46**  Then, O great king, the son of Droṇa, having struck down the banner, the bow, the parasol, both the flank-guarding charioteers, the driver, and the four horses of the high-souled son of Pṛṣata, charged upon him in the fray.

**7.135.47**  And all those Pāñcālas the immeasurable-souled one routed by the hundreds and the thousands with his straight-jointed arrows.

**7.135.48**  Then the army of the Pāṇḍavas trembled, O bull of the Bhāratas, beholding the mighty feat of Droṇa's son, like that of Vāsava in battle.

**7.135.49**  Slaying a hundred of the Pāñcālas with a hundred shafts, the great chariot-warrior, and with three sharp arrows slaying three great chariot-warriors,

**7.135.50**  the son of Droṇa, before the very eyes of Drupada's son and of Phalguna, destroyed the greater part of the Pāñcālas who stood their ground.

**7.135.51**  Those Pāñcālas, being slaughtered in the battle together with the Sṛñjayas, fled, abandoning the son of Droṇa, their chariots and banners scattered.

**7.135.52**  Having conquered his foes in the battle, the son of Droṇa, that great chariot-warrior, roared a mighty roar, like a thundercloud at the close of the hot season.

**7.135.53**  Having slain many heroes, Aśvatthāman shone forth like the fire that reduces all beings to ashes at the end of an age.

**7.135.54**  Honored in the battle by the Kauravas, having vanquished hosts of foes by the thousands, the valiant son of Droṇa shone forth like the lord of the gods after slaying the hosts of his enemies.

**7.136.1**  Saṃjaya said: Then Yudhiṣṭhira and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava, O great king, surrounded the son of Droṇa on every side.

**7.136.2**  Then King Duryodhana, guarded by the son of Bharadvāja, advanced upon the Pāṇḍavas in battle, and thereupon a combat ensued, dreadful in aspect, O great king, swelling the terror of the timid.

**7.136.3**  The Ambaṣṭhas, the Mālavas, the Vaṅgas, the Śibis, and the Traigartas as well — those bands the wrathful Yudhiṣṭhira dispatched to the realm of Death.

**7.136.4**  Cutting down the Abhīṣāhas, the Śūrasenas, and the Kṣatriyas frenzied for war, Bhīma made the earth a mire of blood.

**7.136.5**  The Yaudheyas, the Āraṭṭas, the princes, and the bands of Madrakas in the battle the Diademed One dispatched to the realm of Death with his sharp arrows.

**7.136.6**  Sorely afflicted by straight-flying iron shafts driven deep, the elephants fell to the earth like two-peaked mountains.

**7.136.7**  With the severed trunks of elephants writhing here and there, the earth, strewn with them, glowed as though covered with gliding serpents.

**7.136.8**  With the cast-down royal parasols, bright with gold, the earth shone like the sky strewn with the sun, the moon, and the other heavenly bodies at the dissolution of an age.

**7.136.9**  "Slay! Strike without fear! Pierce! Cut them down!" — such was the tumultuous cry around the chariot of him whose horses were red.

**7.136.10**  But Droṇa, exceedingly enraged, with the Wind-weapon in the battle scattered them, as the irresistible wind scatters the clouds.

**7.136.11**  Those Pāñcālas, being slain by Droṇa, fled in terror, even before the eyes of Bhīmasena and of the high-souled Pārtha.

**7.136.12**  Then the Diademed One and Bhīma suddenly turned back, encircling thy host with a great array of chariots.

**7.136.13**  Bībhatsu on the right flank and Vṛkodara on the north, the two rained upon the son of Bharadvāja with their two great floods of arrows.

**7.136.14**  Then the Sṛñjayas and the Pāñcāla great chariot-warriors followed those two, O great king, and the Matsyas together with the Somakas.

**7.136.15**  Likewise the noble car-warriors and strikers of thy son advanced with a great host toward the chariot of Droṇa.

**7.136.16**  Then that Bhārata army, being slaughtered by the Diademed One, and overcome by darkness and by sleep, was again torn asunder.

**7.136.17**  Though held back by Droṇa and by thy son himself, the warriors could not then be restrained, O great king.

**7.136.18**  That great army, rent by the arrows of the son of Pāṇḍu, fled in all directions as the world was wrapped in darkness.

**7.136.19**  Abandoning their mounts by the hundreds, some of the kings there fled, O great king, seized with terror on every side.

**7.137.1**  Saṃjaya said: Beholding Somadatta brandishing his mighty bow, Sātyaki said to his charioteer, "Bear me toward Somadatta.

**7.137.2**  For without slaying in the fray my foe, the Bāhlika, basest of the Kauravas, I will not turn back from the battle, O charioteer — this word of mine is true."

**7.137.3**  Then the driver urged on those swift Saindhava steeds, conch-colored, outstripping every sound in the battle.

**7.137.4**  With the speed of thought and of the wind, they bore Yuyudhāna, O king, as of old the tawny steeds bore Indra when he set out to slay the Daityas.

**7.137.5**  Seeing the impetuous Sātvata rushing upon him in the fray, the mighty-armed Somadatta, undismayed, advanced to meet him.

**7.137.6**  Loosing showers of arrows like a rain-laden storm-cloud, he covered the grandson of Śini, as a cloud covers the sun.

**7.137.7**  And undismayed in the battle, Sātyaki covered that bull of the Kurus on every side with floods of arrows, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.137.8**  Somadatta pierced that Mādhava in the breast with sixty shafts, and Sātyaki too, O king, struck him with sharp arrows.

**7.137.9**  Those two bulls among men, gashed by each other's arrows, shone like two kiṃśuka trees in fair flower at the flowering season.

**7.137.10**  Their every limb drenched with blood, those bringers of glory to the Kurus and the Vṛṣṇis gazed upon each other as though scorching one another with their eyes.

**7.137.11**  Ranging along the circling paths of their chariots, those two crushers of foes were of dreadful aspect, like two rain-laden clouds.

**7.137.12**  Their bodies pierced through by arrows, bristling on all sides, wounded by shafts, they appeared, O lord of kings, like two porcupines.

**7.137.13**  Studded with gold-feathered arrows, the two shone forth, O king, like two forest trees covered with fireflies in the rains.

**7.137.14**  Their every limb set ablaze, as it were, by arrows, those two great chariot-warriors appeared in the fray, wrathful, like two elephants amid firebrands.

**7.137.15**  Then in the battle, O great king, Somadatta the great chariot-warrior, with a crescent-headed arrow, cut asunder the mighty bow of the Mādhava.

**7.137.16**  Then he assailed him with twenty-five arrows, and, making haste at the hour for haste, with ten more shafts.

**7.137.17**  Then, taking up another, swifter bow, Sātyaki quickly pierced Somadatta with five arrows.

**7.137.18**  Then with another broad-headed shaft Sātyaki cut down the golden banner of the Bāhlika in the fray, O king, as though smiling.

**7.137.19**  But Somadatta, undismayed, seeing his standard struck down, covered the grandson of Śini with twenty-five arrows.

**7.137.20**  The Sātvata too, enraged in the battle, with a sharp razor-edged arrow cut asunder the bow of the bowman Somadatta in the fray.

**7.137.21**  Then he covered him in many places with a hundred straight-jointed, gold-feathered arrows, O king, like an elephant with a broken tusk.

**7.137.22**  Then, taking up another bow, the mighty Somadatta, that great chariot-warrior, covered Sātyaki with a shower of arrows.

**7.137.23**  But the wrathful Sātyaki pierced Somadatta in the fray, and Somadatta in turn afflicted Sātyaki with a net of arrows.

**7.137.24**  For the Sātvata's sake Bhīma struck the son of Bāhlika with ten arrows, and Somadatta too, undismayed, smote the grandson of Śini with shafts.

**7.137.25**  Then for the Sātvata's sake the son of Bhīmasena hurled a new, stout, and dreadful iron club at the breast of Somadatta.

**7.137.26**  That iron club of terrible aspect, rushing on with speed, the Kaurava cut in two in the fray, as though smiling.

**7.137.27**  That great iron club, cleft in two, fell down like the great peak of a mountain riven by the thunderbolt.

**7.137.28**  Then Sātyaki, O king, in the combat cut asunder Somadatta's bow with a broad-headed shaft, and his leather glove with five arrows.

**7.137.29**  And with four arrows he swiftly dispatched the four excellent steeds to the presence of the king of the dead, O Bhārata.

**7.137.30**  And with a straight-jointed broad-headed shaft that tiger among chariot-warriors, the bull of Śini's line, smiling, severed the charioteer's head from his body.

**7.137.31**  Then the Sātvata loosed a most terrible arrow, blazing like fire, gold-feathered and whetted on stone, O king.

**7.137.32**  That excellent shaft, loosed by the mighty grandson of Śini, dreadful, fell swiftly upon his breast, O lord, O Bhārata.

**7.137.33**  Sorely pierced by the mighty Sātvata, that great chariot-warrior, the mighty-armed Somadatta, fell down and died.

**7.137.34**  Seeing Somadatta slain there, the great chariot-warriors rushed upon Yuyudhāna with a great shower of arrows.

**7.137.35**  Seeing Yuyudhāna being overwhelmed with arrows, Yudhiṣṭhira, with a great host, charged upon Droṇa's array.

**7.137.36**  Then the wrathful Yudhiṣṭhira routed with his arrows the mighty force of thy men, before the very eyes of the son of Bharadvāja.

**7.137.37**  But Droṇa, seeing Yudhiṣṭhira putting his troops to flight, rushed upon him with speed, his eyes reddened with wrath.

**7.137.38**  Then with seven well-sharpened arrows he pierced the Pārtha; and, sorely pierced himself, the mighty-armed one, licking the corners of his mouth, cut down Yudhiṣṭhira's banner and his bow as well.

**7.137.39**  His bow severed, that best of kings, making haste at the hour for haste, quickly took up another stout bow in the fray.

**7.137.40**  Then the king pierced Droṇa, together with his horses, driver, banner, and chariot, with a thousand arrows; and that seemed a marvel.

**7.137.41**  Then for a moment, shaken and afflicted by the stroke of those arrows, Droṇa sank down upon the floor of his chariot, O best of the Bhāratas.

**7.137.42**  Then, regaining his senses in a moment, that best of the twice-born, seized with great wrath, loosed the Wind-weapon.

**7.137.43**  Then the valiant Pārtha, undismayed, drawing his bow, checked that weapon with a weapon of his own in the fray, O Bhārata.

**7.137.44**  Then Vāsudeva spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī: "Mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, hear what I am about to tell you."

**7.137.45**  "Withdraw from battle against Droṇa, O best of the Bhāratas, for Droṇa forever hungers to take you captive in the fray."

**7.137.46**  "I do not think this combat with him is fit for you; he who was born for his destruction shall slay him tomorrow."

**7.137.47**  "Avoid the preceptor and go to where King Suyodhana is, and where Bhīma, that tiger among chariot-warriors, fights against the Kauravas."

**7.137.48**  Hearing the words of Vāsudeva, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Righteousness, reflected for a moment upon that terrible battle.

**7.137.49**  Then that slayer of foes swiftly set out for where Bhīma stood his ground, striking down your warriors like Death with jaws agape.

**7.137.50**  With the mighty thunder of his chariot he made the face of the earth resound, filling the ten directions with his roar like a rain-cloud at the close of the hot season.

**7.137.51**  The son of Pāṇḍu guarded the rear of Bhīma as he slew his enemies, while Droṇa too scattered the Pāṇḍavas and Pāñcālas at the onset of night.

**7.138.1**  Saṃjaya said: As that battle, dreadful of form and fraught with terror, raged on, the world being veiled in darkness and in dust, O lord of the earth, the warriors stationed in the fray could not see one another.

**7.138.2**  By guesswork and by signals that great combat was waged, a churning of men, elephants, and horses, supremely making the hair stand on end.

**7.138.3**  The heroes Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa, and Bhīma, the son of Pṛṣata, and Sātyaki threw each other's armies into turmoil, O best of kings.

**7.138.4**  The armies, slaughtered on every side by those great chariot-warriors, fled in all directions, hemmed in by darkness and by dust.

**7.138.5**  Those warriors, scattering in every direction with terror-stricken hearts, were cut down, O great king, even as they ran in the fray.

**7.138.6**  Thousands of great chariot-warriors slew one another in the fight, bewildered in the blind darkness, by the counsel of your son.

**7.138.7**  Then all the armies and the leaders of the host, O Bhārata, fell into confusion there in the battle, the field being shrouded in darkness.

**7.138.8**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: As they were churned about by the Pāṇḍavas, their vigor struck down, sunk in blind darkness, what then was the resolve of your people?

**7.138.9**  How, Saṃjaya, did light come again among them, or among my armies, when the world was so enveloped in darkness?

**7.138.10**  Saṃjaya said: Then all the armies that survived the slaughter, appointing their commanders, formed up their battle-array once more.

**7.138.11**  Droṇa stood in front, Śalya at the rear, while Droṇa's son and the son of Subala held the flanks; and the king himself, O king, moved forward in the night guarding all his forces.

**7.138.12**  And Duryodhana, O prince, spoke gently to all the bands of foot-soldiers: "Lay aside your finest weapons, all of you, and take blazing lamps in your hands."

**7.138.13**  Urged on by that best of princes, they gladly took up the lamps; and the banner-bearing host, marshalled anew, shone with the light of fire in the night.

**7.138.14**  With costly and celestial ornaments, and with weapons flashing as they clashed together, the lamps arrayed in an instant straightway lit up the whole banner-bearing host.

**7.138.15**  All the armies, attended on every hand by foot-soldiers bearing fire and oil, appeared, illumined in the night, like rain-clouds in the sky lit up by lightning.

**7.138.16**  When the host was thus illumined, Droṇa, blazing like fire and scorching all around, shone forth, O lord of kings, clad in golden mail, like the garlanded sun at its zenith.

**7.138.17**  Upon the ornaments of pure gold, the bright necklaces, the quivers, and the burnished weapons, the reflected radiance of the fire then played there.

**7.138.18**  The slung maces and gleaming iron clubs, and the spears whirling upon the chariots, O scion of Ajamīḍha, blazing, again and again kindled reflected gleams with their rays.

**7.138.19**  The parasols and the trains of yak-tail fans, and the great blazing torches likewise, O king, and the golden garlands swaying upon the struggling warriors shone resplendent there.

**7.138.20**  Radiant with the gleam of weapons, and with the glow of the lamps, and lit up by the brightness of the ornaments, that host, O king, became exceedingly resplendent.

**7.138.21**  The burnished weapons, drenched with blood, brandished by the heroes and tearing into bodies, gave forth a flashing radiance there, like lightning in the sky at the end of the hot season.

**7.138.22**  The faces of the men, shaken by the force of blows, striking and rushing in with speed, shone forth then like great lotuses stirred by the wind.

**7.138.23**  As in a great forest ablaze with wildfire even the splendor of the sun would be lost, so blazed your banner-bearing host, O Bhārata, fearsome of form amid that great terror.

**7.138.24**  Beholding our host thus brightly ablaze, the sons of Pṛthā in like haste urged on the bands of foot-soldiers throughout all their armies, and they too made lamps.

**7.138.25**  Seven lamps were set on each elephant, and ten lamps on each chariot, two upon every horse's back, and others at the flanks, others upon the standards, and others at the rear.

**7.138.26**  And in all the armies others stood at the flanks, behind, in front, and all around; and others in the midst, with blazing fire in their hands, ranged through both the hosts.

**7.138.27**  Throughout all the armies the bands of foot-soldiers, mingled with the throngs of elephants, chariots, and horses, and others in the midst with blazing fire in their hands, lit up the host of the son of Pāṇḍu.

**7.138.28**  By that blazing host the other mighty host blazed in turn, as fire is kindled to a glow by the radiant, light-giving orb of the day-making sun.

**7.138.29**  The radiance of the two hosts, overspreading earth and sky, swelled across all the quarters; and by that brilliance their army and yours became exceedingly bright.

**7.138.30**  By that brilliance mounting to heaven the hosts of the gods were roused, O king, and the throngs of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas, and all the Apsarases gathered there.

**7.138.31**  Thronged with gods and Gandharvas, with hosts of Yakṣas, lords of Asuras, and Apsarases, and with slain heroes ascending to heaven, that battlefield became like unto the celestial realm.

**7.138.32**  Ablaze with lamps amid the press of chariots, horses, and elephants, its steeds driven in rout by furious warriors, that mighty host with its arrayed chariots, horses, and elephants became like the battle-array of gods and Asuras.

**7.138.33**  With its fierce winds of massed spears, its clouds of great chariots, its thunder of cars and steeds, its downpour of weapon-floods and its streams of blood for rain, that battle of men and kings raged on through the night.

**7.138.34**  In that field the great-souled chief of the twice-born, likened to a mighty fire, scorching the Pāṇḍavas, was as the sun risen to its zenith with its rays at the close of the rains, O lord of men.

**7.139.1**  Saṃjaya said: When the world was thus illumined, yet shrouded in dust and darkness, the heroes came together, each seeking the destruction of the other.

**7.139.2**  Meeting in battle, O king, bearing weapons, lances, and swords, they glared at one another, each having wronged the other.

**7.139.3**  With thousands of lamps blazing on every side, the earth then shone, O Bhārata, like the sky bright with its planets.

**7.139.4**  With hundreds of blazing torches the battlefield shone resplendent, as the earth would seem to burn at the dissolution of the worlds.

**7.139.5**  All the quarters were lit up by those lamps on every side; they shone like trees beset with fireflies in the early dusk of the rains.

**7.139.6**  Then the heroes engaged hero against hero, each apart; elephants closed with elephants, and steeds met with steeds.

**7.139.7**  Chariots met with the foremost of chariots, filled with eager joy, in that dread onset of night, by the command of your son.

**7.139.8**  Then Arjuna, O great king, scattered the host of the Kauravas, applying himself with speed and destroying all the princes.

**7.139.9**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When that furious and unbearable one, the unassailable, had broken into my son's army, what then was the resolve of your people?

**7.139.10**  What did the armies think when that scorcher of foes broke in, and what fitting deed did Duryodhana judge the hour to require?

**7.139.11**  Who went forth against that hero, that tamer of foes, in the fight? Who guarded the right wheel of Droṇa's car, and who the left?

**7.139.12**  What heroes stood at the back of that hero as he fought, and who advanced before him as he slew his enemies in battle?

**7.139.13**  When that mighty bowman, unconquered, broke into the Pāñcālas, that tiger among men, valiant, seeming to dance along the chariot-paths—

**7.139.14**  and Droṇa burned with his shafts the ranks of Pāñcāla chariots, like wrathful fire whose banner is smoke—how then did he come to his death?

**7.139.15**  You tell of the foes as unflustered and unvanquished, yet you report mine as slain, despondent, and scattered, my chariot-warriors stripped of their cars in the battles.

**7.139.16**  Saṃjaya said: Perceiving the intent of Droṇa, who wished to fight on through that night, Duryodhana, O great king, addressed his obedient brothers.

**7.139.17**  Vikarṇa and Citrasena, and the mighty-armed Kaurava, the unassailable long-armed one, and those who followed at their heels—

**7.139.18**  "Strive valiantly, all of you, and guard Droṇa from behind; let the son of Hṛdika guard the right wheel and Śalya likewise the left."

**7.139.19**  And those valiant great chariot-warriors of the Trigartas who had survived the slaughter—all of them your son urged forward to the van.

**7.139.20**  "The preceptor is well girt for battle, and the Pāṇḍavas strive hard; guard him, then, well prepared, as he slays his enemies in the fray."

**7.139.21**  "For Droṇa is mighty in battle, quick of hand and full of valor; he could vanquish even the thirty gods in fight—how much more the sons of Pṛthā with the Somakas."

**7.139.22**  "Therefore do you all, united and striving hard, O great chariot-warriors, guard Droṇa from the Pāñcāla prince Dhṛṣṭadyumna, that great car-warrior."

**7.139.23**  "Among the armies of the Pāṇḍavas I see no warrior, O kings, who could conquer Droṇa in battle, save Dhṛṣṭadyumna alone."

**7.139.24**  "Therefore I deem it best to guard the son of Bharadvāja with all our might; protected, he will slay the Somakas and the Sṛñjayas together with their kings."

**7.139.25**  "And when all the Sṛñjayas are slain at the head of the host, Droṇa's son will destroy Dhṛṣṭadyumna in battle, beyond all doubt."

**7.139.26**  "So too will Karṇa, that great chariot-warrior, conquer Arjuna in battle; and I myself, clad in mail, shall vanquish Bhīmasena in the fight."

**7.139.27**  "Plainly, then, victory shall be mine for ages to come; therefore guard Droṇa in the battle, O great chariot-warriors."

**7.139.28**  Having spoken thus, O best of the Bhāratas, your son Duryodhana then drew up the army in that terrible darkness.

**7.139.29**  Then that dread battle was waged by night, O bull of the Bhāratas, between the two armies, each longing for victory.

**7.139.30**  Arjuna pressed hard upon the Kaurava host, and the Kauravas upon Arjuna; with showers of varied weapons they tormented one another.

**7.139.31**  Droṇa's son covered the king of the Pāñcālas, and the son of Bharadvāja the Sṛñjayas, in the fray, with their straight-jointed arrows.

**7.139.32**  Of the armies of the Pāṇḍavas and Pāñcālas, and of the Kauravas, O venerable one, there arose a dreadful din as they struck one another down.

**7.139.33**  Never by us, nor by those before us, was such a thing seen before as that battle which raged that night, fraught with the greatest terror.

**7.140.1**  Saṃjaya said: As that fierce night-battle, the destroyer of all beings, raged on, O lord of peoples, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,

**7.140.2**  spoke to the Pāṇḍavas and to the Pāñcālas with the Somakas: "Charge forward, go against Droṇa himself with intent to slay."

**7.140.3**  At the word of your king, O king, the Pāñcālas and the Somakas alike bore down upon Droṇa, uttering fearful roars.

**7.140.4**  We, roaring back at them and burning with wrath, went forth against them in the fray to the utmost of our power, our zeal, and our strength.

**7.140.5**  And Kṛtavarman, the son of Hṛdika, rushed upon Yudhiṣṭhira, who sought to slay Droṇa, as one rutting elephant charges another.

**7.140.6**  As the grandson of Śini was scattering showers of arrows on every side, O king, the Kaurava Bhūri rushed upon him at the forefront of the battle.

**7.140.7**  And as Sahadeva, that great chariot-warrior, came on, eager to reach Droṇa, Karṇa the son of Vikartana, O king, held back that son of Pāṇḍu.

**7.140.8**  And as Bhīmasena advanced like Death with jaws gaping wide, Duryodhana himself went forth in the fight to meet him, as one goes to meet hostile Death.

**7.140.9**  And as Nakula, the foremost of warriors, skilled in every mode of combat, advanced, Śakuni the son of Subala, O king, swiftly held him in check.

**7.140.10**  And as Śikhaṇḍin, the best of chariot-warriors, came on in his car, Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat, O king, withstood him in the battle.

**7.140.11**  And as Prativindhya advanced with horses hued like peacocks, Duḥśāsana, O great king, straining himself, held back that straining foe.

**7.140.12**  And as the son of Bhīmasena advanced, expert in a hundred illusions, Aśvatthāman, upholding his father's honour, drove him back.

**7.140.13**  And Vṛṣasena held back in battle Drupada, that great chariot-warrior, together with his troops and his foot-soldiers, as he sought to reach Droṇa.

**7.140.14**  And as Virāṭa came on swiftly, bent upon Droṇa's death, the king of the Madras, greatly enraged, held him in check, O descendant of Bharata.

**7.140.15**  And as Śatānīka, the son of Nakula, advanced impetuously in the fray, desiring Droṇa's slaughter, Citrasena swiftly checked him with his shafts.

**7.140.16**  And as Arjuna, the foremost of warriors, that mighty chariot-fighter, came rushing on, Alambusa, O great king, the lord of the Rākṣasas, held him back.

**7.140.17**  And as Droṇa, that mighty bowman, was slaying his foes in the battle, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the Pāñcāla, with a joyful mien, withstood him.

**7.140.18**  And the other great chariot-warriors of the sons of Pāṇḍu who came on, your own car-warriors, O king, withstood with all their might.

**7.140.19**  Riders of elephants, swiftly closing with their elephants in that great battle, were seen to fight by the hundreds and the thousands.

**7.140.20**  At midnight, O king, the horses, charging at one another, were seen rushing on with speed like winged mountains.

**7.140.21**  Horsemen, with lances, javelins, and spears in hand, closed with horsemen, O great king, each roaring out his own war-cry.

**7.140.22**  And many men there met one another in throngs, with maces and clubs and weapons of every kind.

**7.140.23**  And Kṛtavarman the son of Hṛdika, full of wrath, held back Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, as the shore holds back the surging sea.

**7.140.24**  But Yudhiṣṭhira, having pierced the son of Hṛdika with five swift arrows, struck him again with twenty, and cried, 'Stand! Stand!'

**7.140.25**  But Kṛtavarman, greatly enraged, O sire, cut off with a broad-headed shaft the bow of the son of Dharma, and pierced him with seven.

**7.140.26**  Then taking up another bow, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Dharma planted ten arrows in the arms and breast of the son of Hṛdika.

**7.140.27**  And the Mādhava, thus pierced in battle by the son of Dharma, O sire, trembled with rage and afflicted him with seven shafts.

**7.140.28**  The son of Pṛthā, cutting off his bow and severing his leather glove, sped at him five whetted arrows, sharpened on stone, O king.

**7.140.29**  Those fierce shafts, piercing his gold-wrought, costly armour, entered the earth like serpents entering an anthill.

**7.140.30**  In the mere twinkling of the eyes, taking up another bow, he pierced the son of Pāṇḍu with sixty arrows and his charioteer with nine.

**7.140.31**  Then the son of Pāṇḍu, of immeasurable soul, laying his great bow upon his car, hurled at him a dart like a serpent, O best of the Bhāratas.

**7.140.32**  That great dart, adorned with gold, flung by the son of Pāṇḍu, piercing his right arm, entered the surface of the earth.

**7.140.33**  At that very moment, the son of Pṛthā, taking up his bow again, covered the son of Hṛdika with arrows of smooth joints.

**7.140.34**  Then in the battle that hero, the foremost car-warrior of the Vṛṣṇis, in half the twinkling of an eye made Yudhiṣṭhira bereft of horses, charioteer, and car.

**7.140.35**  Then the eldest son of Pāṇḍu took up sword and shield; but the Mādhava shattered them with his whetted shafts in the fight.

**7.140.36**  Then taking up a gold-shafted, irresistible lance, Yudhiṣṭhira swiftly sped it in the battle at the son of Hṛdika.

**7.140.37**  As it came hurtling, loosed from the arm of the king of righteousness, the deft-handed son of Hṛdika cut it in two, as if with a smile.

**7.140.38**  Then in the fight he covered the son of Dharma with a hundred arrows, and in his wrath rent his armour with his sharp shafts.

**7.140.39**  That armour of the high-souled one, cut through by the shafts of the son of Hṛdika, fell apart in the battle, O king, like a net of stars falling from the sky.

**7.140.40**  With his bow cut off, deprived of his car, his armour shattered, tormented by arrows, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Dharma swiftly withdrew from the battle.

**7.140.41**  And Kṛtavarman, of great strength, having vanquished Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Dharma, once more guarded the wheel of Droṇa's car.

**7.141.1**  Saṃjaya said: But Bhūri in the battle, O king, drove back the grandson of Śini, that best of car-warriors, as he rushed on, even as one turns an elephant from the watering-place.

**7.141.2**  Then Sātyaki, enraged, swiftly pierced him in the heart with five whetted shafts, and his blood gushed forth.

**7.141.3**  In the same way the Kaurava, in the fight, pierced the grandson of Śini, that warrior intoxicated with battle, with ten sharp arrows between the shoulders.

**7.141.4**  The two of them, O great king, gashed each other sorely with arrows, their eyes red with rage, twanging their bows in their fury.

**7.141.5**  There arose between those two, O great king, a most dreadful rain of weapons, as in their wrath they loosed their shafts, resembling Yama the destroyer.

**7.141.6**  Covering each other with arrows, O king, they stood firm in the battle, and for a while their combat seemed evenly matched.

**7.141.7**  Then the grandson of Śini, enraged, O great king, as if smiling, cut off in the battle the bow of the high-souled Kaurava.

**7.141.8**  Then, as he was bereft of his bow, he swiftly pierced him in the heart with nine whetted shafts, and cried, 'Stand! Stand!'

**7.141.9**  Deeply pierced by his powerful foe, that scorcher of foes took up another bow and pierced the Sātvata in return.

**7.141.10**  Having pierced the Sātvata with three arrows, O lord of peoples, he cut off his bow with a very sharp broad-headed shaft, as if laughing.

**7.141.11**  His bow severed, O great king, Sātyaki, swooning with rage, hurled at his broad breast a dart of great velocity.

**7.141.12**  His body cleft by that dart, he fell from his excellent car, like the ruddy-bodied planet Mars, with its blazing rays, falling by chance from the sky.

**7.141.13**  Seeing that hero slain, Aśvatthāman, the great car-warrior, rushed with speed against the grandson of Śini in the battle, and rained upon him a flood of arrows, as a cloud rains upon Meru.

**7.141.14**  As he furiously bore down upon the car of the grandson of Śini, Ghaṭotkaca, the great car-warrior, O king, loosing a roar, spoke.

**7.141.15**  'Stand, stand! Thou shalt not escape me alive, O son of Droṇa. This day I shall slay thee as the lord Skanda slew the buffalo; this day, on the field of battle, I shall drive out thy appetite for war.'

**7.141.16**  Having spoken thus, the Rākṣasa, that slayer of hostile heroes, his eyes coppery with rage, rushed in wrath upon the son of Droṇa, as a lion upon a lordly elephant.

**7.141.17**  Ghaṭotkaca rained upon the son of Droṇa, that bull among car-warriors, arrows as large as chariot-axles, as a cloud rains down its torrents.

**7.141.18**  But that downpour of arrows, as it came, the son of Droṇa, smiling, swiftly shattered in the battle with shafts like venomous serpents.

**7.141.19**  Then with hundreds of sharp, swift arrows that pierce the vitals, O subduer of foes, he covered Ghaṭotkaca, the lord of the Rākṣasas.

**7.141.20**  Studded all over with his arrows, that Rākṣasa, at the head of the battle, shone, O great king, like a porcupine bristling with its quills.

**7.141.21**  Then the valiant son of Bhīmasena, filled with rage, cut into the son of Droṇa with fierce arrows that sounded like the thunderbolt.

**7.141.22**  With razor-edged shafts and crescent-headed arrows, with iron shafts and bearded darts, with boar-eared and reed-like points, and with sharp barbed missiles.

**7.141.23**  That matchless rain of weapons, sounding like the thunderbolt, as it fell upon him, the son of Droṇa, undismayed of sense, in his wrath—

**7.141.24**  —that hard-to-bear downpour he, of mighty energy, dispelled with dreadful arrows charged with celestial weapons, as the wind scatters great clouds.

**7.141.25**  Then in the sky there arose, as it were, another battle of arrows, dreadful of aspect, O great king, that heightened the joy of the warriors.

**7.141.26**  Then with the sparks struck up by the clash of weapons on every side, the sky at the onset of night shone as if covered with fireflies.

**7.141.27**  The son of Droṇa, veiling all the quarters round about with his hosts of arrows, to please your sons, overwhelmed the Rākṣasa.

**7.141.28**  Then in the dead of deep night there raged the combat between the son of Droṇa and the Rākṣasa, like that between Śakra and Prahrāda.

**7.141.29**  Then Ghaṭotkaca, greatly enraged, struck the son of Droṇa on the breast in the fight with ten arrows resembling the fire of doom.

**7.141.30**  Pierced by those long shafts of the mighty Rākṣasa, the son of Droṇa reeled in the battle like a tree shaken by the wind, and, falling into a swoon, he clung to the staff of his banner.

**7.141.31**  Then all your army cried out in dismay, O ruler of men, and all your men deemed him slain, O lord of peoples.

**7.141.32**  Seeing Aśvatthāman reduced to such a plight in the battle, the Pāñcālas and the Sṛñjayas set up a leonine roar.

**7.141.33**  Then regaining his senses, Aśvatthāman of great strength, that grinder of foes, gripping his bow firmly with his left hand—

**7.141.34**  —with the bow drawn full to the ear, loosed a surpassing arrow, dreadful as the rod of Yama, aimed swiftly at Ghaṭotkaca.

**7.141.35**  That excellent shaft, cleaving the heart of that Rākṣasa, fierce and fair-feathered, entered the earth, O lord of the world.

**7.141.36**  Deeply pierced, O great king, that lord of the Rākṣasas, mighty though he was, sank down upon the floor of his car, struck by the son of Droṇa, proud of his battle.

**7.141.37**  Seeing the son of Hiḍimbā swooning, his charioteer, in alarm, swiftly bore him away from the field, out of the presence of the son of Droṇa.

**7.141.38**  Having thus pierced Ghaṭotkaca, the lord of the Rākṣasas, in the battle, the son of Droṇa, of great might, sent forth a tremendous roar.

**7.141.39**  Honoured by your sons and by all the warriors, O descendant of Bharata, he blazed forth in his body like the sun at noon.

**7.141.40**  And as Bhīmasena fought his way toward the car of the son of Bharadvāja, king Duryodhana himself pierced him in return with sharp arrows.

**7.141.41**  Bhīmasena pierced him with nine arrows, O sire, and Duryodhana too pierced him in return with twenty shafts.

**7.141.42**  The two of them, veiled with arrows, were seen on the field of battle like the moon and the sun in the sky shrouded by a mass of clouds.

**7.141.43**  Then king Duryodhana pierced Bhīma with five feathered shafts, O best of the Bhāratas, and cried, 'Stand! Stand!'

**7.141.44**  Bhīma, cutting off his bow and his banner with nine arrows, pierced that best of the Kauravas with ninety shafts of smooth joints.

**7.141.45**  Then Duryodhana, enraged, my lord, loosed his arrows at Bhīmasena, O king, in the sight of all the bowmen.

**7.141.46**  Striking down those shafts that had sped from Duryodhana's bow, Bhīma pierced the Kaurava with twenty-five small arrows.

**7.141.47**  But Duryodhana, in great wrath, my lord, cut Bhīmasena's bow with a razor-tipped arrow and struck him back with ten.

**7.141.48**  Then taking up another bow, the mighty Bhīmasena swiftly pierced the king with seven sharpened shafts.

**7.141.49**  That bow too he swiftly cut, light-handed as he was, and so the second, the third, the fourth, and the fifth.

**7.141.50**  Each bow that Bhīma took up, O great king, your son cut asunder, flushed with the look of victory and swollen with arrogance, O great king.

**7.141.51**  Then, his bows being cut again and again, in the battle he hurled a fair lance wrought wholly of steel.

**7.141.52**  Before that lance could reach him, the Kaurava cut it into three pieces, while all the world looked on, and high-souled Bhīma as well.

**7.141.53**  Then Bhīma, O great king, whirled his heavy and brightly gleaming mace and flung it with force against Duryodhana's chariot.

**7.141.54**  Then that heavy mace, in an instant, crushed the horses of your son in the fight, and his charioteer too, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.141.55**  But your son, O lord of kings, leaping at once from his gold-adorned chariot, sprang into the car of high-souled Nandaka.

**7.141.56**  Then Bhīma, deeming your son, that great car-warrior, slain, let forth a mighty lion's roar, as though to terrify the Kauravas.

**7.141.57**  Your soldiers too believed the king was slain, and on every side they all cried out, 'Alas! Alas!'

**7.141.58**  Hearing that outcry of all the terrified warriors, and hearing the roar of high-souled Bhīmasena, O king—

**7.141.59**  then King Yudhiṣṭhira, believing Suyodhana slain, advanced with speed to where Pārtha, the Wolf-bellied, stood.

**7.141.60**  The Pāñcālas, the Kekayas, the Matsyas, and the Sṛñjayas, O lord of peoples, with their whole strength rushed upon Droṇa, eager to fight.

**7.141.61**  There befell a great battle between Droṇa and his foes, of men sunk in dreadful darkness, slaying one another.

**7.142.1**  Saṃjaya said: As Sahadeva came on, seeking to reach Droṇa, O lord of peoples, Karṇa, son of Vikartana, held him back in the fight, O Bhārata.

**7.142.2**  But Sahadeva, having pierced Rādheya with nine swift arrows, struck him again with ten sharpened, smooth-jointed shafts.

**7.142.3**  Karṇa pierced him back with a hundred smooth-jointed arrows and swiftly cut his strung bow, light-handed as he was.

**7.142.4**  Then taking up another bow, the valiant son of Mādrī pierced Karṇa with twenty shafts, and that seemed a marvel.

**7.142.5**  Karṇa, slaying his horses with smooth-jointed arrows, swiftly dispatched his charioteer to the abode of Yama with a broad-headed shaft.

**7.142.6**  Sahadeva, his chariot lost, took up sword and shield; these too Karṇa shattered with his arrows, as though laughing.

**7.142.7**  Then he hurled in the battle a heavy, most dreadful great mace, bright with gold, against the chariot of the son of Vikartana.

**7.142.8**  As it came hurtling on, sped by Sahadeva, Karṇa checked it with his arrows and brought it down to the ground.

**7.142.9**  Seeing the mace struck down, Sahadeva in haste flung a lance at Karṇa; that too he cut to pieces with his shafts.

**7.142.10**  Then in agitation, swiftly leaping down from his fine chariot, Sahadeva, O great king, seeing Karṇa standing firm, seized a chariot-wheel and hurled it at the son of Adhiratha.

**7.142.11**  As it came rushing on, like the upraised wheel of Time, the son of the sūta cut it apart with many thousands of arrows.

**7.142.12**  That wheel being made vain by the great-souled one, and being held off by his shafts, Sahadeva withdrew from the fight.

**7.142.13**  Rushing after him for a moment, O bull of the Bhāratas, Rādheya, laughing, spoke these words to Sahadeva, O lord of peoples:

**7.142.14**  'Do not fight in battle, O hero, with car-warriors who surpass you; contend with your equals, O son of Mādrī—do not doubt my word.'

**7.142.15**  Then, prodding him with the tip of his bow, he spoke again: 'There Arjuna, intent in battle, fights against the Kurus; go thither, O son of Mādrī, or home, if you think it best.'

**7.142.16**  Having spoken thus, Karṇa, the foremost of car-warriors, drove on with his chariot toward the armies of the Pāñcālas and Pāṇḍavas, as though laughing.

**7.142.17**  Though the son of Mādrī was within reach of death, the slayer of foes did not slay him in the battle, remembering Kuntī's word, O king—that great car-warrior, true to his vow.

**7.142.18**  Then Sahadeva, O king, downcast and stricken with arrows, and scorched by the dart of Karṇa's words, grew weary of his life.

**7.142.19**  Yet that great car-warrior in haste mounted the chariot of the high-souled Pāñcāla prince Janamejaya in the battle.

**7.142.20**  As Virāṭa came swiftly on with his army, bent on Droṇa, the king of the Madras covered that bowman with a flood of arrows.

**7.142.21**  Between those two firm bowmen there arose in battle a combat such as was of old, O king, between Jambha and Vāsava.

**7.142.22**  The king of the Madras, O great king, swiftly struck Virāṭa, lord of armies, with a hundred sharp, smooth-jointed shafts.

**7.142.23**  The king pierced him back with nine sharpened arrows, then again with seventy-three, and yet again with a hundred.

**7.142.24**  The lord of the Madras, slaying his four chariot-horses, struck down from the chariot-box both his charioteer and his banner in the fight.

**7.142.25**  Swiftly leaping down from the chariot whose horses were slain, the great car-warrior stood twanging his bow and loosing sharp arrows.

**7.142.26**  Then Śatānīka, seeing his brother's horses slain, charged up swiftly with his chariot while all the world looked on.

**7.142.27**  As Śatānīka came on in that great battle, the king of the Madras, having pierced him with many shafts, sent him to the abode of Yama.

**7.142.28**  That hero being slain, Virāṭa, best of car-warriors, swiftly mounted that very same banner-garlanded chariot.

**7.142.29**  Then, his eyes wide with wrath, his valor doubled, he swiftly covered the chariot of the Madra king with his feathered shafts.

**7.142.30**  Then the lord of the Madras, enraged, struck Virāṭa, lord of armies, hard upon the breast with a hundred smooth-jointed arrows.

**7.142.31**  Sore wounded, O great king, Virāṭa sank down upon the chariot-box, and a fierce swoon came over him, O bull of the Bhāratas; his charioteer bore him away from the battle, mangled by the arrows.

**7.142.32**  Then that great host fled away in the night, O Bhārata, slaughtered by the hundreds of arrows of Śalya, the splendor of battle.

**7.142.33**  Seeing that army routed, Vāsudeva and Dhanaṃjaya went, O lord of kings, to where Śalya stood his ground.

**7.142.34**  But against those two advanced, O king, the lord of the Rākṣasas, Alambusa, mounted upon a peerless chariot fitted with eight wheels—

**7.142.35**  yoked with goblins of dreadful aspect, horse-faced, its banner wet with blood, decked with red garlands, dreadful, all of black iron, vast, and covered with bear-skin—

**7.142.36**  resplendent with a banner bearing a terrible, bright-winged, wide-eyed, screeching king of vultures with uplifted beak.

**7.142.37**  That Rākṣasa shone, O king, like a heap of broken collyrium, and barred the advancing Arjuna as a king of mountains bars the storm-wind, raining showers of arrows, O king, by the hundred upon Arjuna's head.

**7.142.38**  Most fierce was the battle in that field between the man and the Rākṣasa, gladdening the hearts of all who beheld it, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.142.39**  Arjuna smote him with a full hundred feathered shafts and with nine sharp arrows cut down his uplifted banner.

**7.142.40**  With three arrows he struck the charioteer, with three the triple chariot-pole, with one he cut the bow, with four the four horses; and with a single shaft he cleft in two the sword that the carless one had raised.

**7.142.41**  Then, O bull of the Bhāratas, Pārtha tormented the lord of the Rākṣasas with four sharpened arrows; and he, thus pierced, fled away in fear.

**7.142.42**  Having vanquished him, Arjuna swiftly drew near to Droṇa, scattering showers of arrows, O king, among men, elephants, and horses.

**7.142.43**  Slaughtered, O great king, by the illustrious Pāṇḍava, the soldiers fell to the earth like trees felled by the wind.

**7.142.44**  As they were being cut down by the high-souled Phalguna, the whole army of your sons fled away, O lord of peoples.

**7.143.1**  Saṃjaya said: As Śatānīka swiftly consumed your host with arrows, your son Citrasena held him back, O Bhārata.

**7.143.2**  Nakula's son sorely afflicted Citrasena with an iron shaft, and he in turn pierced him back with ten sharpened arrows.

**7.143.3**  Citrasena, O great king, struck Śatānīka again in the battle, full upon the breast, with nine sharpened arrows.

**7.143.4**  Nakula's son with his smooth-jointed shafts struck the armor from his body, and that seemed a marvel.

**7.143.5**  Stripped of his armor, your son shone forth brilliantly, O king, like a serpent that has cast its slough in season, O lord of kings.

**7.143.6**  Then Nakula's son with his sharpened arrows cut down his banner and his bow as well, O great king, while he strove in the fight.

**7.143.7**  His bow severed and his armor gone in the battle, that great car-warrior, O great king, took up another bow that rends the foe.
