**7.143.8**  Then swiftly Citrasena, the great car-warrior of the Bharatas, enraged, pierced Nakula's son with nine arrows in the battle.

**7.143.9**  Then Śatānīka, that best of men, in great wrath, my lord, slew the four horses and the charioteer of Citrasena.

**7.143.10**  Leaping down from that chariot, the mighty great car-warrior Citrasena tormented Nakula's son with twenty-five arrows.

**7.143.11**  As he wrought that deed, the son of Nakula in the battle cut, with a crescent-headed arrow, his jewel-adorned bow.

**7.143.12**  His bow severed, his chariot lost, his horses and charioteer slain, he swiftly mounted the chariot of the high-souled son of Hṛdika.

**7.143.13**  But as Drupada, that great car-warrior, came on with his army, seeking Droṇa, Vṛṣasena swiftly advanced against him, scattering hundreds of arrows.

**7.143.14**  But Yajñasena in the battle pierced Karṇa's son, that great car-warrior, with sixty arrows in the arms and the chest, O sinless one.

**7.143.15**  But Vṛṣasena, greatly enraged, struck Yajñasena, who stood upon his chariot, full upon the breast with many sharp shafts.

**7.143.16**  Both of them, their bodies driven through with arrows, bristling with shafts in the battle, shone forth, O great king, like two porcupines with their quills.

**7.143.17**  With gold-feathered, straight-tipped arrows their coats of mail cut through, drenched in streams of blood, they shone forth in that great battle.

**7.143.18**  Bright as refined gold, splendid, wondrous as two wishing-trees, and like two kiṃśuka trees in full bloom, they blazed upon the field of battle.

**7.143.19**  Then Vṛṣasena, O king, having pierced Drupada with nine arrows, struck him with seventy, and again with three other shafts.

**7.143.20**  Then, loosing thousands of arrows, the son of Karṇa shone forth, O great king, like a raincloud pouring down its torrents.

**7.143.21**  Then Drupada's host, its armor cleft asunder by his shafts, broke and fled in the battle, O king, in that dreadful hour of midnight.

**7.143.22**  With the burning lamps cast away and blazing on every side, the earth gleamed, O king, like a cloudless sky studded with planets.

**7.143.23**  And with the fallen armlets the earth gleamed, O great king, as a raincloud gleams with lightning in the season of the rains.

**7.143.24**  Then the Somakas, terrified by the son of Karṇa, fled in all directions, as the Dānavas, struck with fear of Indra, fled in the Tāraka war.

**7.143.25**  Tormented by him in battle and taking to flight, the Somakas shone forth, O great king, lit up by the lamps.

**7.143.26**  Having vanquished them in battle, the son of Karṇa blazed forth like the sun, the hot-rayed one, reaching its noonday height, O Bhārata.

**7.143.27**  Among those thousands of kings, both your own and the foe's, Vṛṣasena alone stood blazing in his might.

**7.143.28**  Having conquered in battle the brave great chariot-warriors of the Somakas, he hastened swiftly to where King Yudhiṣṭhira stood.

**7.143.29**  Then your son Duḥśāsana, that great chariot-warrior, advanced to meet the enraged Prativindhya, who was consuming the foe in battle.

**7.143.30**  The encounter of those two, O king, was a wondrous sight, like that of Mercury and Venus in a cloudless sky.

**7.143.31**  As Prativindhya was performing a deed hard to do in the battle, Duḥśāsana pierced him in the forehead with three arrows.

**7.143.32**  Sorely wounded by your mighty son, the archer, the great-armed one shone forth like a mountain with its peak.

**7.143.33**  But Prativindhya, that great chariot-warrior, having pierced Duḥśāsana in battle with nine shafts, struck him again with seven.

**7.143.34**  There, O Bhārata, your son performed a deed hard to do, for he struck down Prativindhya's horses with his fierce arrows.

**7.143.35**  With a broad-headed shaft he brought down his charioteer and his banner, and shattered the chariot of that archer into a hundred pieces, O king.

**7.143.36**  And the pennons, the quivers, the reins, and the traces, O lord, he cut to bits in his wrath with his smooth-jointed arrows.

**7.143.37**  But that righteous one, robbed of his chariot, stood firm, bow in hand, and fought your son, showering forth many hundreds of arrows.

**7.143.38**  With a razor-edged shaft he cut his bow, like one skilled of hand, and then, his bow severed, tormented him with ten broad-headed arrows.

**7.143.39**  Seeing him there bereft of his chariot, his brothers, those great chariot-warriors, came on with speed, together with a great army.

**7.143.40**  Then he leaped onto the shining car of Sutasoma and, taking up a bow, O great king, pierced your son.

**7.143.41**  Then all your warriors, surrounding your son, advanced into the fray, encompassed by a great army.

**7.143.42**  Then a battle broke out between your men and theirs, O Bhārata, in that dreadful hour of midnight, swelling the kingdom of Yama.

**7.144.1**  Saṃjaya said: As Nakula, furious in the fight, was slaying your host, the son of Subala rushed at him in wrath and cried, "Stand, stand!"

**7.144.2**  Those two heroes, fixed in enmity and each longing for the other's death, struck at one another with arrows loosed from bows drawn to their full length.

**7.144.3**  Even as the son of Subala swiftly let fly his showers of arrows, so too did Nakula, O king, displaying his training in the fight.

**7.144.4**  Both those heroes in the battle, bristling then with arrows, shone forth, O great king, like the silk-cotton tree with its thorns.

**7.144.5**  Eyeing each other askance, O king, with eyes wide open and reddened with rage, they seemed to consume one another.

**7.144.6**  But your brother-in-law, full of wrath, as if laughing, pierced the son of Mādrī in the heart with a single sharp barbed shaft.

**7.144.7**  Sorely wounded by your brother-in-law the archer, Nakula sank down upon the floor of his chariot, and a swoon came over him.

**7.144.8**  Seeing his bitter, arrogant foe brought to such a pass, Śakuni roared, O king, like a raincloud at the end of the hot season.

**7.144.9**  Then, regaining his senses, Nakula, the joy of Pāṇḍu, rushed once more at the son of Subala like Death with gaping jaws.

**7.144.10**  In his wrath he pierced Śakuni with sixty shafts, O bull of the Bhāratas, and again with a full hundred iron arrows between the breasts.

**7.144.11**  Then he cut his arrow-laden bow at the grip, and swiftly cutting down his banner, he cast it from the chariot to the ground.

**7.144.12**  Sorely wounded, O great king, he sank down upon the floor of his chariot; and seeing your brother-in-law fallen senseless, O blameless one, his charioteer swiftly bore him away by chariot from the front of the host.

**7.144.13**  Then the Pārthas and their followers raised a shout; and Nakula, the scorcher of foes, having vanquished his enemies in battle, said wrathfully to his charioteer, "Bear me toward Droṇa's host."

**7.144.14**  Hearing that word of the wise son of Mādrī, the charioteer drove on in the battle, O king, to where Droṇa was fighting.

**7.144.15**  But as Śikhaṇḍin sought to reach Droṇa in the battle, O lord of peoples, Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat, intent and very swift, advanced to meet him.

**7.144.16**  As the descendant of Gautama, that tamer of foes, came on swiftly toward Droṇa, Śikhaṇḍin, as if laughing, pierced him with nine broad-headed arrows.

**7.144.17**  The preceptor, O great king, having pierced him with five swift shafts, struck him again with twenty, that doer of good to your sons.

**7.144.18**  A great battle there was between those two, terrible in form, O lord of peoples, as in the war of gods and Asuras between Śambara and the king of the gods.

**7.144.19**  Those two great chariot-warriors made the sky veiled with a web of arrows; the night, by nature terrible in aspect, became more terrible still.

**7.144.20**  And the night, O best of the Bhāratas, was for the war-loving warriors like the Night of Doom, terrible in aspect and fraught with fear.

**7.144.21**  But Śikhaṇḍin, O great king, cut Gautama's great bow, strung and with arrow fitted, with a crescent-headed shaft.

**7.144.22**  At this Kṛpa, in wrath, O king, hurled a dreadful spear, gold-shafted, sharp of point, polished by the smith.

**7.144.23**  That oncoming spear Śikhaṇḍin cut with many arrows, and it fell blazing to the earth, lighting it up with its great splendor.

**7.144.24**  Then taking up another bow, the descendant of Gautama, that best of chariot-warriors, covered Śikhaṇḍin with sharp arrows, O great king.

**7.144.25**  Overwhelmed in battle by the illustrious descendant of Gautama, Śikhaṇḍin, that best of chariot-warriors, sank down upon the floor of his car.

**7.144.26**  And seeing him sinking down in the fight, Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat smote him with many arrows, as if eager to slay him, O Bhārata.

**7.144.27**  Seeing that son of Yajñasena, the great chariot-warrior, turned away in the battle, the Pāñcālas and the Somakas surrounded him on every side.

**7.144.28**  And likewise your sons, with a great army, surrounded that best of the twice-born; and so the battle was joined again.

**7.144.29**  And of the chariots rushing against one another in the battle, O king, there arose a tumultuous din like that of roaring clouds.

**7.144.30**  Of the rushing horsemen and the elephants too, O lord of peoples, set against one another, O king, the field of battle showed a cruel sight.

**7.144.31**  At the tramp of the running foot-soldiers the earth trembled, O great king, like a woman shuddering with fear.

**7.144.32**  Chariots, falling upon chariots and rushing on with greater speed, seized them in numbers, O king, as crows seize locusts.

**7.144.33**  And likewise the great elephants in full rut, holding their ground in that very spot, seized the rutting elephants, O Bhārata.

**7.144.34**  Horseman closing with horseman, and foot-soldier with foot-soldier, joining battle in their fury, did not pass one another by.

**7.144.35**  Of the running, the fleeing, and those who turned back again, there arose there among the hosts a most tumultuous din in the night.

**7.144.36**  And the blazing lamps upon the chariots, elephants, and horses appeared, O great king, like great meteors fallen from the sky.

**7.144.37**  That night, O best of the Bhāratas, lit up by the lamps, became like day, O king, at the head of the battle.

**7.144.38**  As the darkness pervaded by the sun perishes in the world, so the terrible darkness vanished, adorned by the blazing lamps.

**7.144.39**  The radiance of the weapons, the armor, and the jewels of those great-souled ones was all swallowed up, outshone by those lamps.

**7.144.40**  In that uproarious battle raging at the onset of night, a father slew his son in the fight, O most excellent of the Bhāratas.

**7.144.41**  And a son in his bewilderment slew his father, a friend his friend, a kinsman his kinsman, and an uncle his sister's son.

**7.144.42**  Friends slew friends and foes slew foes, each striking the other; the battle in the night was without restraint, terrible and fraught with fear.

**7.145.1**  Saṃjaya said: As that most tumultuous and fearful battle raged on, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O great king, advanced straight against Droṇa.

**7.145.2**  Stroking his excellent bow and drawing its string again and again, he advanced upon Droṇa's chariot, adorned with gold.

**7.145.3**  As Dhṛṣṭadyumna then came on, eager to make an end of Droṇa, the Pāñcālas, together with the Pāṇḍavas, surrounded him, O great king.

**7.145.4**  Seeing Droṇa, that best of preceptors, thus encompassed, your sons, intent on every side, guarded Droṇa in the fray.

**7.145.5**  Then those two oceans of host met at the onset of night, like two dreadful seas lashed by the wind, their creatures churned into turmoil.

**7.145.6**  Then the prince of the Pāñcālas, O great king, swiftly pierced Droṇa in the heart with five arrows, and uttered a lion's roar.

**7.145.7**  Droṇa, having pierced him with twenty-five shafts in the battle, O Bhārata, cut with another broad-headed arrow his bright-shining bow.

**7.145.8**  But Dhṛṣṭadyumna, sorely pierced by Droṇa, O bull of the Bhāratas, swiftly cast aside that bow, biting his lip.

**7.145.9**  Then, in his wrath, O great king, the mighty Dhṛṣṭadyumna took up another excellent bow, eager to make an end of Droṇa.

**7.145.10**  And drawing his wondrous bow to his ear, that slayer of hostile heroes then loosed a terrible shaft to make an end of Droṇa.

**7.145.11**  That terrible arrow, loosed by the mighty one in the great battle, lit up that host like the risen sun.

**7.145.12**  Seeing that terrible arrow, the gods, Gandharvas, and men spoke these words, O king: "May it be well with Droṇa in the battle."

**7.145.13**  But that shaft, before it reached the preceptor's chariot, Karṇa cut into twelve pieces, O king, like one skilled of hand.

**7.145.14**  Cut into many pieces by the charioteer's son, O king, O venerable one, that arrow, severed by Karṇa's shafts, swiftly fell.

**7.145.15**  Having cut that arrow in the battle with his smooth-jointed shafts, Karṇa pierced Dhṛṣṭadyumna in the fight with ten arrows.

**7.145.16**  Droṇa's son struck him with five arrows, and Droṇa himself with seven; Śalya with nine shafts, and Duḥśāsana likewise with three.

**7.145.17**  Duryodhana with twenty, and Śakuni too with five — all those great chariot-warriors swiftly pierced the prince of the Pāñcālas.

**7.145.18**  Wounded by those seven heroes who fought in battle to shield Droṇa, he, O king, without dismay struck back at each one with three arrows apiece, and pierced Droṇa, Droṇa's son, Karṇa, and your own son.

**7.145.19**  Pierced by that bowman, those best of charioteers each in turn swiftly wounded Dhṛṣṭadyumna again in the fray, each with five shafts.

**7.145.20**  But Drumasena, enraged, O king, pierced him with a feathered shaft and swiftly with three other arrows, crying, 'Stand! Stand!'

**7.145.21**  But he pierced him in return with three keen, straight-flying arrows, gold-feathered and whetted on stone, deadly bringers of death in battle.

**7.145.22**  Then with another broad-headed shaft the valiant one struck from its body the head of Drumasena, bright with golden earrings.

**7.145.23**  That head fell to the earth in the battle, its lips bitten fast together, like a ripe palm-fruit shaken loose by a mighty wind.

**7.145.24**  And having pierced those heroes again with well-sharpened arrows, the hero with broad-headed shafts cut apart the bow of Rādheya, that artful fighter.

**7.145.25**  But Karṇa could not endure that severing of his bow — fierce beyond measure, like a lion whose tail has been cut off.

**7.145.26**  Taking up another bow, his eyes red with rage and breathing hard, he rained floods of arrows upon that mighty Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

**7.145.27**  Seeing Karṇa thus enraged, those six bull-like chariot-warriors swiftly surrounded the son of the Pāñcāla king, eager to slay him.

**7.145.28**  Beset before those six foremost warriors of your side, Dhṛṣṭadyumna seemed to us to have come into the very mouth of death.

**7.145.29**  At that very moment the Dāśārha Sātyaki, scattering his arrows, came to the aid of the valiant Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

**7.145.30**  As that great archer Sātyaki, fierce in battle, drew near, Rādheya pierced him in return with ten straight-flying arrows.

**7.145.31**  Sātyaki, O great king, pierced him in turn with ten arrows before the eyes of all the heroes, crying, 'You shall not escape! Stand!'

**7.145.32**  Then between the mighty Sātyaki and the great-souled Karṇa there came a dreadful encounter, like that between Bali and Vāsava.

**7.145.33**  That bull among kṣatriyas, terrifying the warriors with the slap of his palm against the bowstring, Sātyaki struck back at the lotus-eyed Karṇa.

**7.145.34**  The mighty son of the charioteer, as if making the earth tremble with the twang of his bow, fought back against Sātyaki, O great king.

**7.145.35**  With cleaving shafts, with eared and iron arrows, with calf-tooth heads and razor-edged points, with hundreds of arrows besides, Karṇa pierced the grandson of Śini.

**7.145.36**  And likewise Yuyudhāna too, foremost chariot-warrior of the Vṛṣṇis, rained arrows upon Karṇa; and that combat was evenly matched.

**7.145.37**  And your warriors, O great king, together with Karṇa's mailed son, swiftly pierced Sātyaki on every side with sharpened arrows.

**7.145.38**  Warding off the weapons of those men and of Karṇa with his own weapons, O lord, the enraged Sātyaki struck Vṛṣasena in the breast.

**7.145.39**  Pierced through by that arrow, O lord of peoples, the valiant Vṛṣasena, swooning, let fall his bow and sank down upon his chariot.

**7.145.40**  Then Karṇa, that great chariot-warrior, believing Vṛṣasena slain and burning with grief for his son, pressed hard upon Sātyaki in return.

**7.145.41**  Though hard pressed by Karṇa, the great chariot-warrior Yuyudhāna pierced Karṇa with many arrows, hastening again and again.

**7.145.42**  Having pierced Karṇa with ten arrows and Vṛṣasena with seven, the Sātvata cut apart the bows of them both together with the guards upon their hands.

**7.145.43**  Then those two, stringing other bows that struck terror into foes, pierced Yuyudhāna on every side with sharpened arrows.

**7.145.44**  While that battle raged on, with its slaughter of the noblest heroes, the great twang of the Gāṇḍīva was heard above all, O king.

**7.145.45**  Hearing the rumble of the chariot and the twang of the Gāṇḍīva, the son of the charioteer, O king, spoke these words to Duryodhana.

**7.145.46**  This mighty roar of the Gāṇḍīva comes from him who has slain all the Śibis, the foremost of men, and the great-bowed Pauravas.

**7.145.47**  The din of his chariot is heard like the roar of Vāsava himself; plainly the Pāṇḍava is performing a deed worthy of his name.

**7.145.48**  This Bhārata host, O king, is being torn asunder in many directions; the scattered ranks can hold their ground nowhere at all.

**7.145.49**  Like a mass of clouds scattered by the wind it is torn apart, having met Savyasācin, like a broken ship upon the sea.

**7.145.50**  From the foremost warriors fleeing, pierced by the hundreds with arrows loosed from the Gāṇḍīva, a great cry is heard, O king — at midnight, O tiger among kings, like thunder in the sky.

**7.145.51**  Hear the cries of dismay, the abundant lion-roars, and the sounds of many kinds rising up about the chariot of Arjuna.

**7.145.52**  Here in our midst stands Sātyaki, the basest of the Sātvatas; if he be brought within our reach as a target here, we shall conquer all our foes.

**7.145.53**  And here the son of the Pāñcāla king is locked with Droṇa, surrounded on every side, O king, by the noblest of warriors.

**7.145.54**  If we should slay Sātyaki and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata, then beyond doubt, O great king, our victory would be assured.

**7.145.55**  As we did with the son of Subhadrā, let us surround these two heroes, these great chariot-warriors, and strive, O great king, to slay the Vṛṣṇi and the son of Pṛṣata.

**7.145.56**  Savyasācin advances against Droṇa's army in front, O Bhārata, knowing that Sātyaki is locked in combat with many bulls among the Kurus.

**7.145.57**  Let many of our foremost, best of chariot-warriors go there, before Pārtha learns that Sātyaki is beset by many.

**7.145.58**  Hasten, O heroes, eagerly in the loosing of your arrows, so that this Mādhava may swiftly pass to the world beyond.

**7.145.59**  Having learned Karṇa's counsel, your son spoke to the son of Subala, as Indra in battle, O king, once spoke to the glorious Viṣṇu.

**7.145.60**  'Surrounded by ten thousand elephants that never turn back, and ringed by ten thousand chariots, go against Dhanaṃjaya.'

**7.145.61**  'Duḥśāsana, Durviṣaha, Subāhu, and Duṣpradharṣaṇa — these shall follow you, encircled by many footmen.'

**7.145.62**  'Slay the two Kṛṣṇas, O mighty-armed uncle, and the Dharma-king too, and Nakula and Sahadeva and Bhīmasena, O Bhārata.'

**7.145.63**  'As the gods place their hope of victory in the lord of the gods, so does my hope rest upon you. Slay, O uncle, the sons of Kuntī, as the son of Agni slew the Asuras.'

**7.145.64**  Thus addressed by your son, the son of Subala marched against the Pārthas with a great army and with your sons as well, O lord.

**7.145.65**  To please your sons, longing to consume the joy-bringing sons of Pāṇḍu, then arose the battle between your men and the foe.

**7.145.66**  When the son of Subala had marched against the host of the Pāṇḍavas, O king, the son of the charioteer, joined with a great force, advanced against the Sātvata.

**7.145.67**  He charged swiftly into the fight, scattering many hundreds of arrows; and likewise all the Pāṇḍavas closed protectively around Sātyaki.

**7.145.68**  Then a great battle was fought by night, O Bhārata, between Droṇa on the one side and the heroic Dhṛṣṭadyumna with the great-souled Pāñcālas on the other.

**7.146.1**  Saṃjaya said: Then they all rushed forward in haste, frenzied in battle, unable to bear it and filled with fury, toward the chariot of Yuyudhāna.

**7.146.2**  With their well-equipped chariots adorned with gold and silver, O king, and with horsemen and elephants, they surrounded the Sātvata.

**7.146.3**  Then, hemming him in on every side as in a stockade, those great chariot-warriors raised their lion-roars, threatening Sātyaki.

**7.146.4**  Those mighty heroes, hastening and seeking the death of the Mādhava, rained sharp arrows upon Sātyaki of true valor.

**7.146.5**  Seeing them swiftly descending upon him, the grandson of Śini, slayer of hostile heroes, that mighty-armed one received them, loosing many arrows in return.

**7.146.6**  There the hero Sātyaki, great archer fierce in battle, cut off heads with terrible arrows whose joints were bent low.

**7.146.7**  The trunks of elephants, the necks of horses, and arms still grasping their weapons — these the Mādhava brought down with razor-headed shafts among your men.

**7.146.8**  With fallen yak-tail whisks and white parasols, O Bhārata, the earth became filled, like the sky with stars, O lord.

**7.146.9**  As they battled with Yuyudhāna in the fray, O Bhārata, there arose a tumultuous din, like the wailing of departed spirits.

**7.146.10**  By that mighty sound the earth was filled, and the night became fierce of aspect and terrifying.

**7.146.11**  Seeing the army torn apart and struck down by Yuyudhāna's arrows, and hearing the vast hair-raising clamor at midnight,

**7.146.12**  your son, that best of chariot-warriors, O king, said again and again to his charioteer, 'Drive the horses to where this sound arises.'

**7.146.13**  Thus urged on, the charioteer then drove those excellent horses toward the chariot of Yuyudhāna.

**7.146.14**  Then Duryodhana, enraged, firm of bow, untiring, swift of hand, and skilled in varied modes of warfare, rushed upon Yuyudhāna.

**7.146.15**  Then with arrows loosed from a fully drawn bow, feeders on flesh and blood, the Mādhava pierced Duryodhana in return with twelve shafts.

**7.146.16**  Duryodhana, thus already wounded before by those arrows, pierced the grandson of Śini in return with ten shafts, unable to bear it.

**7.146.17**  Then there arose a confused and terrible battle, O bull of the Bhāratas, between all the Pāñcālas and the Bhāratas.

**7.146.18**  The grandson of Śini, enraged in the fight, pierced your son, that great chariot-warrior, in the breast with eighty arrows, O Bhārata.

**7.146.19**  Then in the battle he sent his horses with arrows to the abode of Yama, and swiftly with a feathered shaft brought down his charioteer from the car.

**7.146.20**  Standing upon his car whose horses were slain, your son, O lord of peoples, loosed sharpened arrows toward the chariot of the grandson of Śini.

**7.146.21**  Those fifty arrows sent forth by your son, O king, the grandson of Śini, deft of hand, cut to pieces in the battle.

**7.146.22**  Then with another broad-headed shaft the impetuous one, in the fight, cut your son's great bow at the grip, O honored sir.

**7.146.23**  Bereft of his chariot and of his bow, that lord and master of all the world swiftly mounted the gleaming car of Kṛtavarman.

**7.146.24**  When Duryodhana had turned away, the grandson of Śini put your army to flight with his arrows in the dead of night, O lord of peoples.

**7.146.25**  And Śakuni, O king, surrounding Arjuna on every side with many thousands of chariots, with elephants by the thousand, and with thousands of horses, raised a tumult all around.

**7.146.26**  Scattering great celestial weapons against Arjuna, those kṣatriyas, driven on by fate, did battle with Arjuna.

**7.146.27**  Those thousands of chariots, elephants, and horses Arjuna held back, exerting himself and working a vast destruction.

**7.146.28**  Then in the battle the valiant Śakuni, son of Subala, pierced Arjuna with sharpened arrows, smiling as he did so.

**7.146.29**  And again with a hundred shafts he beset that mighty car-warrior; but Arjuna, O Bhārata, pierced him in turn with twenty in the fight.

**7.146.30**  Then he struck the other great archers, three shafts to each; and having checked them with showers of arrows in the fight, O king, Dhanaṃjaya slew your warriors as the wielder of the thunderbolt slays the Asuras.

**7.146.31**  Strewn with severed arms, O great king, and with bodies by the thousand, the earth there shone as though it were covered over with flowers.

**7.146.32**  Having pierced Śakuni once more with five smooth-jointed shafts, he smote Ulūka with three, and with three more of solid iron.

**7.146.33**  Ulūka, thus pierced, struck Vāsudeva in return, and roared a mighty roar that filled the surface of the earth.

**7.146.34**  But Arjuna, advancing swiftly, cut asunder the bow of Śakuni and sent his four steeds toward the abode of Yama.

**7.146.35**  Then leaping down from his car, O bull of the Bhāratas, the son of Subala swiftly mounted the chariot of Ulūka, O lord of peoples.

**7.146.36**  Mounted upon a single car, those two mighty car-warriors, father and son, drenched Pārtha with arrows as two upreared clouds drench a mountain.

**7.146.37**  But the Pāṇḍava, having pierced them both, O great king, with sharpened arrows, and routing your host, scattered them by the hundred with his shafts.

**7.146.38**  As clouds are scattered on every side by the wind, so were your forces scattered, O king, O lord of peoples.

**7.146.39**  That army, O best of the Bhāratas, thus being slaughtered in the night, fled in every direction, looking about in its terror, tormented by fear.

**7.146.40**  Some abandoned their steeds in the battle, while others, urging them on, ran bewildered hither and thither in that dreadful darkness.

**7.146.41**  Having vanquished your warriors in the battle, O bull of the Bhāratas, Vāsudeva and Dhanaṃjaya, full of joy, blew their conches.

**7.146.42**  Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O great king, having pierced Droṇa with three arrows, swiftly cut the bowstring of his bow with a sharpened shaft.

**7.146.43**  Laying that bow aside in its rest, Droṇa, the crusher of warriors, the valiant one, took up another bow, swift and of greater strength.

**7.146.44**  Then Droṇa, having pierced Dhṛṣṭadyumna with seven swift arrows, struck his charioteer with five shafts, O king, in the fray.

**7.146.45**  Checking him swiftly with arrows, the mighty car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna scattered the Kaurava army by the hundred and by the thousand.

**7.146.46**  While that army of your son was being slaughtered, O honored one, a fearful river arose, rolling with waves of streaming blood.

**7.146.47**  Between the two armies it flowed, bearing along men, horses, and elephants, like the Vaitaraṇī, O king, that runs toward the city of Yama's realm.

**7.146.48**  Having routed that host, the glorious Dhṛṣṭadyumna shone forth in his splendor, as Śakra among the hosts of the gods.

**7.146.49**  Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin, the twins, and Yuyudhāna, and the Pāṇḍava Vṛkodara blew their great conches.

**7.146.50**  Having vanquished thousands of your car-warriors, the mighty Pāṇḍava car-warriors, radiant with victory, raised lion-like roars.

**7.146.51**  Frenzied with their triumph, they did so before the very eyes of your son, of Karṇa, of the valiant Droṇa, and of Droṇa's son, O lord of peoples.

**7.147.1**  Saṃjaya said: Seeing his own army routed and slaughtered by those great-souled ones, your son, O lord of peoples, was overcome with a mighty wrath.

**7.147.2**  Suddenly approaching Karṇa and Droṇa, the foremost of victors, and yielding to his indignation, that knower of speech spoke these words.

**7.147.3**  By you two, enraged, was this battle set afoot, when you had seen the lord of the Sindhus slain in combat by Savyasācin.

**7.147.4**  Yet now, though able to gain the victory there, you look on as though unable, while my host is being slaughtered by the strength of the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.147.5**  If I am to be forsaken by you, then you should not have said to me, O bestowers of honor: 'We two shall conquer the sons of Pāṇḍu in battle.'

**7.147.6**  It was upon hearing that word, assented to by you both, that I waged with the Pāṇḍavas this enmity that destroys warriors.

**7.147.7**  If I am not to be abandoned by you, O bulls among men, then fight, O mighty heroes, with prowess worthy of you.

**7.147.8**  Goaded by your son with the lash of words, those two heroes set about the fight like two serpents that have been struck.

**7.147.9**  Then those two foremost of car-warriors, the best bowmen in all the world, rushed in battle upon the Pārthas led by the grandson of Śini.

**7.147.10**  And likewise the Pārthas, gathered together and surrounded by their own host, advanced against those two heroes, roaring again and again.

**7.147.11**  Then Droṇa, the great archer, foremost of all bearers of arms, enraged, swiftly pierced the bull of the Śinis with ten shafts.

**7.147.12**  And Karṇa with ten arrows, and your son with seven, and Vṛṣasena with ten, and the son of Subala with seven — these, O Kaurava, beset the grandson of Śini in the tumult.

**7.147.13**  And seeing Droṇa in the battle smiting the Pāṇḍava host, the Somakas swiftly pierced him on every side with showers of arrows.

**7.147.14**  Then Droṇa bore away the lives of the warriors, O lord of peoples, as the sun with its rays bears away the darkness, O king, O Bhārata.

**7.147.15**  From the Pāñcālas being slaughtered by Droṇa, O lord of peoples, there was heard a tumultuous clamor as they cried out to one another.

**7.147.16**  Some abandoning their sons, some their fathers, some their brothers and maternal uncles, some their nephews and comrades, and likewise their kinsmen and friends, they fled in haste, longing to keep their lives.

**7.147.17**  Others, deluded by their bewilderment, went straight against him; and other warriors of the Pāṇḍavas went thus to the world beyond.

**7.147.18**  That Pāṇḍava army, thus being slaughtered, fled in the night, O king, casting aside their torches by the thousand.

**7.147.19**  This took place before the very eyes of Bhīmasena, of Vijaya, of Acyuta, of the twins, of the son of Dharma, and of the son of Pṛṣata as they looked on.

**7.147.20**  With the world wrapped in darkness, nothing could be discerned; but by the light of the Kauravas the routed foes were seen.

**7.147.21**  As that host fled, the two mighty car-warriors Droṇa and Karṇa smote them from behind, O king, pouring out many shafts.

**7.147.22**  When the Pāñcālas were broken and shattered on every side, Janārdana, with downcast heart, addressed Phalguna in reply.

**7.147.23**  These two great archers, Droṇa and Karṇa, joined together, are sorely smiting the son of Pṛṣata, Sātyaki, and the Pāñcālas with their shafts.

**7.147.24**  By the arrow-shower of these two our mighty car-warriors are broken; and though I strive to hold them, O son of Kuntī, the army does not stand firm.

**7.147.25**  Let us two, with all our forces well marshaled and with weapons upraised, make our utmost effort to beat back Droṇa and the son of the charioteer.

**7.147.26**  For these two are mighty, valiant, skilled in arms, and radiant with victory; if neglected, in their wrath they would destroy our army this very night. Yonder comes the terrible Bhīma, having rallied his host once more.

**7.147.27**  Seeing Vṛkodara thus coming on, Janārdana there, O king, spoke once more, as though gladdening the Pāṇḍava.

**7.147.28**  Yonder Bhīma, glorious in battle, encircled by the Somakas and the Pāṇḍavas, in his fury rushes with speed upon the mighty Droṇa and Karṇa.

**7.147.29**  Joined with him and with the mighty Pāñcāla car-warriors, do battle, O delight of Pāṇḍu, to bring heart to all the armies.

**7.147.30**  Then those two tigers among men, Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava together, having reached Droṇa and Karṇa, took their stand at the head of the battle.

**7.147.31**  Then that great army of Yudhiṣṭhira turned back once more; and thereupon Droṇa and Karṇa crushed the foe in the fight.

**7.147.32**  That tumultuous, mighty clash arose in the night, O king, like the meeting of two oceans swollen by the rising of the moon.

**7.147.33**  Then, casting the lamps from their hands, your army fought against the Pāṇḍavas like madmen at the dying of the day.

**7.147.34**  With all enveloped by dust and by darkness, exceedingly dreadful, those who sought victory fought only by name and lineage.

**7.147.35**  For the names proclaimed by the kings as they smote were heard, O great king, in that battle as at a self-choice ceremony.

**7.147.36**  All at once there was silence; then again a mighty din arose of those enraged and fighting, of the victors and the vanquished alike.

**7.147.37**  Wherever lamps were seen, O best of the Kurus, there those heroes fell upon them like moths.

**7.147.38**  As they thus fought, the deep night advanced, O lord of kings, upon the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas on every side.

**7.148.1**  Saṃjaya said: Then Karṇa, slayer of hostile heroes, beholding the son of Pṛṣata in the battle, struck him on the breast with ten arrows that pierce the vital parts.

**7.148.2**  Dhṛṣṭadyumna too, O honored one, pierced him swiftly in return with five shafts, and joyously cried, 'Stand, stand!'

**7.148.3**  Those two great car-warriors, having covered each other with arrows in the fray, again pierced one another with shafts loosed at full stretch.

**7.148.4**  Then in the fight Karṇa pierced with his shafts the charioteer and the four steeds of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the chief of the Pāñcālas.

**7.148.5**  And he cut asunder his excellent bow with sharpened arrows, and with a broad-headed shaft felled his charioteer from the body of the car.

**7.148.6**  But Dhṛṣṭadyumna, his car destroyed, his steeds slain and his charioteer slain, seizing a fearful iron club, crushed the horses of Karṇa.

**7.148.7**  And pierced by him with many arrows like venomous serpents, he then made his way on foot to the host of Yudhiṣṭhira, and mounted the car of Sahadeva, O honored one.

**7.148.8**  To the car of Karṇa, too, the charioteer yoked other steeds, conch-colored, of great swiftness, born of the Sindhu country, and well-trained to draw.

**7.148.9**  And Rādheya, having found his mark, strove hard and pressed the mighty car-warriors of the Pāñcālas with his arrows as a cloud presses the mountains.

**7.148.10**  That great host of the Pāñcālas, sorely pressed by Karṇa, fled away in utter terror, like a doe tormented by a lion.

**7.148.11**  Men fallen swiftly from horses and from elephants to the ground, and from chariots, were seen here and there.

**7.148.12**  With razor-edged shafts in that great battle Karṇa cut off the arms of one warrior as he fled, and his head as well, with its earrings.

**7.148.13**  And he cut off the thighs of another seated upon an elephant, O lord of peoples, and of one mounted on the back of a horse, and of one standing on the ground, O honored one.

**7.148.14**  Many a mighty car-warrior fleeing did not even perceive that his own limbs and his mounts had been severed in the fight.

**7.148.15**  Those Pāñcālas, slaughtered in the battle together with the Sṛñjayas, fancied the son of the charioteer present even at the mere stirring of a blade of grass.

**7.148.16**  Bereft of their senses, they took even their own fleeing warrior in the battle to be Karṇa himself, and so in their terror they fled.

**7.148.17**  Those broken divisions as they fled, O Bhārata, Karṇa swiftly pursued from behind, scattering his arrows.

**7.148.18**  Gazing at one another, utterly bewildered and senseless, they were unable to hold their ground, harried as they were by that great-souled one.

**7.148.19**  Struck down by Karṇa's deadliest arrows, O king, and by Droṇa, the Pāñcālas fled in every direction, glancing all around them as they ran.

**7.148.20**  Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, seeing his own army routed, resolved upon retreat, and spoke these words to Phalguna.

**7.148.21**  Behold Karṇa, the mighty archer, standing firm with bow in hand in the terrible hour of midnight, blazing like the sun.

**7.148.22**  Ceaselessly is heard, O Pārtha, the cry of your kinsmen pierced by Karṇa's shafts, wailing like men who have no protector.

**7.148.23**  Seeing him nock and loose his swift arrows, victorious in his valor, I am certain he will surely destroy us.

**7.148.24**  Whatever next deed you judge fit for this hour, one that will bring about the slaying of Karṇa—do it, O Dhanaṃjaya.

**7.148.25**  Thus addressed, the mighty-armed Pārtha then spoke to Kṛṣṇa—for the king, the son of Kuntī, was filled with fear at the overwhelming valor of Rādheya.

**7.148.26**  Matters being thus, let you decide quickly, again and again, what befits the hour against Karṇa's host—for the army is fleeing.

**7.148.27**  Of those broken and driven by Droṇa's arrows, O slayer of Madhu, and terrified by Karṇa, there is no holding their ground.

**7.148.28**  And I see Karṇa ranging without fear, showering the noble car-warriors as they flee with his sharp-pointed shafts.

**7.148.29**  I cannot bear to endure his exploits at the battle's front before my eyes, O tiger of the Vṛṣṇis, as a serpent cannot endure the touch of a foot.

**7.148.30**  So let you drive swiftly to where Karṇa, the great car-warrior, stands: either I shall slay him, or he shall slay me, O slayer of Madhu.

**7.148.31**  Vāsudeva said: I see Karṇa, O son of Kuntī, ranging in battle like the king of the gods—that tiger among men, of more than human valor.

**7.148.32**  There is no other in this battle who can stand against him, O Dhanaṃjaya, save you, tiger among men, or the rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca.

**7.148.33**  Yet I do not deem this the fitting hour, O sinless and mighty-armed one, for your encounter with the sūta's son in combat.

**7.148.34**  For the dart of Vāsava abides with him, blazing like a great meteor, and it bears a dreadful form meant, O mighty-armed one, for you.

**7.148.35**  Let mighty Ghaṭotkaca instead go forth against Rādheya, for he was begotten by the strong Bhīma, and his prowess is that of a god.

**7.148.36**  In him reside celestial weapons, and those of the rākṣasas and asuras; ever devoted to you and seeking your good is Ghaṭotkaca. He will conquer Karṇa in battle—of this I have no doubt.

**7.148.37**  Saṃjaya said: Having so spoken to Pārtha, the mighty-armed, lotus-eyed one summoned that rākṣasa, and at once it appeared before them.

**7.148.38**  Armored, arrow-bearing, sword in hand and bow withal, O lord of peoples, he saluted Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava Dhanaṃjaya, and gladly said to him: Here I am—command me.

**7.148.39**  Then to that son of Hiḍimbā, cloud-hued, with blazing face and blazing earrings, the Dāśārha spoke, smiling the while.

**7.148.40**  Ghaṭotkaca, mark well what I shall tell you, my son: the hour of valor has come for you, and for no other man.

**7.148.41**  Be you, for your kinsmen who are sinking, like a raft; manifold are your weapons, and yours too is the magic of the rākṣasas.

**7.148.42**  Behold, son of Hiḍimbā, the host of the Pāṇḍavas driven by Karṇa at the battle's front like cattle driven by a herdsman.

**7.148.43**  This Karṇa, the mighty archer, wise and firm in valor, slays the bulls among kṣatriyas within the Pāṇḍava ranks.

**7.148.44**  Though they pour down great showers of arrows, the firm-bowed warriors cannot hold their ground, oppressed by the flame of his shafts.

**7.148.45**  Tormented at midnight by the sūta's son with his rain of arrows, these Pāñcālas flee like deer from the terror of a lion.

**7.148.46**  Of this sūta's son, swollen so with might in combat, there is no other check save you, O you of fearsome valor.

**7.148.47**  So do you, mighty-armed one, perform here a deed worthy of yourself, of your maternal uncles and your fathers, of your splendor and the strength of your weapons.

**7.148.48**  For this very end, son of Hiḍimbā, do men desire sons—that one might deliver them from sorrow. Deliver, then, your kinsmen.

**7.148.49**  For terrible is the strength of your weapons, and unmatchable your magic spells, ever as you fight in battle, O delight of Bhīma.

**7.148.50**  For the Pāṇḍavas, shattered by Karṇa's keen shafts and sinking amid the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, be the farther shore, O scorcher of foes.

**7.148.51**  For by night the rākṣasas grow yet more boundless in valor—strong, well-nigh invincible, heroic, and ranging in their might.

**7.148.52**  Slay Karṇa, the mighty archer, at midnight in battle by your magic; the Pārthas, with Dhṛṣṭadyumna at their head, will slay Droṇa.

**7.148.53**  Hearing the words of Keśava, Bībhatsu too, O scion of Kuru, addressed the rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca, tamer of foes.

**7.148.54**  Ghaṭotkaca, you yourself, and long-armed Sātyaki, and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava—these in my judgment are foremost among all our hosts.

**7.148.55**  Let you, then, go forth to fight a single-chariot duel with Karṇa this night; Sātyaki, the great car-warrior, shall be the guardian of your rear.

**7.148.56**  Slay the hero Karṇa in battle, aided by the Sātvata, as Indra of old slew Tāraka with Skanda at his side.

**7.148.57**  Ghaṭotkaca said: I am a match for Karṇa, O best of men, and a match for Droṇa too, and for the other high-souled kṣatriyas skilled in arms.

**7.148.58**  This very night I shall give the sūta's son such a battle as men will tell of for as long as the earth endures.

**7.148.59**  And here I shall spare neither the brave, nor the frightened, nor those who join their palms in surrender; all alike I shall slay, holding to the rākṣasa's code.

**7.148.60**  Saṃjaya said: Having so spoken, the mighty-armed son of Hiḍimbā, slayer of hostile heroes, advanced upon Karṇa in the tumult, striking terror into your army.

**7.148.61**  As he rushed on in fury, like a serpent of blazing maw, the supreme archer, the sūta's son, met him with arrows and received his onset.

**7.148.62**  Then there arose between those two, Karṇa and the rākṣasa, a roaring battle in the night, O tiger among kings, like that between Śakra and Prahrāda.

**7.149.1**  Saṃjaya said: Seeing Ghaṭotkaca, O king, advance with hot haste toward the chariot of the sūta's son, eager to slay Karṇa in the fray—

**7.149.2**  your son spoke these words to Duḥśāsana: This rākṣasa, beholding Karṇa's prowess, comes swiftly on in battle.

**7.149.3**  He rushes upon Karṇa—ward off that great car-warrior. Go, surrounded by a mighty force, to where the strong one stands.

**7.149.4**  Karṇa Vaikartana means to do battle with the rākṣasa; guard Karṇa in the fight, ever watchful and ringed about with troops, O giver of honor.

**7.149.5**  Meanwhile, O king, the mighty son of Jaṭāsura, foremost of those who strike, came to Duryodhana and spoke.

**7.149.6**  Duryodhana, your foes the Pāṇḍavas, renowned and maddened in war, I wish to slay with their followers, if you but command me.

**7.149.7**  Jaṭāsura, my father, foremost of rākṣasas, was of old struck down by the base Pārthas, who worked a rite to slay rākṣasas. I wish to avenge him; with your leave, lord, let me go.

**7.149.8**  Then the king, well pleased, said to him again and again: With Droṇa, Karṇa, and the rest at my side, I am equal to the slaying of foes; but go you, at my command, and conquer Ghaṭotkaca in battle.

**7.149.9**  Saying "So be it," the huge-bodied son of Jaṭāsura challenged Ghaṭotkaca and covered the son of Bhīmasena with weapons of every kind.

**7.149.10**  Alaṃbala and Karṇa and the unassailable host of the Kurus the son of Hiḍimbā churned single-handed, as a great gale churns the rain-clouds.

**7.149.11**  Then Alaṃbala, swiftly marking the chariot wrought of illusion, assailed Ghaṭotkaca with showers of arrows of every fashion.

**7.149.12**  And having pierced the son of Bhīmasena with many shafts, Alaṃbala scattered the host of the Pāṇḍavas with his floods of arrows.

**7.149.13**  Driven before him, O sir, the armies of the Pāṇḍavas were scattered abroad at midnight like clouds dispersed by the wind.

**7.149.14**  Likewise the host of the Kurus, driven by Ghaṭotkaca's arrows, fled at midnight, O king, casting away their torches by the thousand.

**7.149.15**  Then Alaṃbala in wrath struck the son of Bhīmasena in that great affray with keen arrows, as one goads a great elephant with hooks.

**7.149.16**  His car, his driver, and all his weapons Ghaṭotkaca cut to fragments fine as sesame, and roared most terribly.

**7.149.17**  Then he rained his floods of arrows upon Karṇa, upon the other Kurus by the thousand, and upon Alaṃbala, as a cloud pours upon the unmoving Meru.

**7.149.18**  Then the army of the Kurus, harried by the rākṣasa, was thrown into turmoil, and the fourfold host crushed one another, rank upon rank.

**7.149.19**  The son of Jaṭāsura, O great king, his chariot lost and his driver slain, in fury smote Ghaṭotkaca hard in the battle with his fist.

**7.149.20**  Struck by that fist, Ghaṭotkaca reeled, as a mountain with its woods and thickets and clustered trees trembles in an earthquake.

**7.149.21**  Then with his arm like an iron bludgeon, the bane of hosts of foes, the son of Bhīmasena smote the son of Jaṭāsura fiercely with his fist.

**7.149.22**  Having crushed him, the son of Hiḍimbā in wrath seized him swiftly and with arms like Indra's banner-staffs dashed him down upon the earth.

**7.149.23**  Alaṃbala in turn flung the rākṣasa off, then lifted Ghaṭotkaca high and in rage dashed him too down upon the earth.

**7.149.24**  Then there arose between those two roaring giants, Ghaṭotkaca and Alaṃbala, a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end.

**7.149.25**  Each surpassing the other, those two masters of illusion fought with their spells, mighty in valor, like Indra and the son of Virocana.

**7.149.26**  Becoming now fire and ocean, now Garuḍa and Takṣaka, now cloud and great wind, now thunderbolt and great mountain, now elephant and tiger, now Svarbhānu and the sun—

**7.149.27**  thus conjuring a hundred illusions, each longing to slay the other, Alaṃbala and Ghaṭotkaca fought on in marvelous fashion.

**7.149.28**  With iron bars and maces, with darts and mallets and lances, with clubs and mountain-peaks, they smote each other.

**7.149.29**  Now with horses, now with elephants, now on foot, now from chariots, those two foremost rākṣasas, great masters of magic, did battle in the fray.

**7.149.30**  Then Ghaṭotkaca, O king, longing to slay Alaṃbala and exceedingly wrathful, sprang up and swooped down upon him like a hawk.

**7.149.31**  And seizing that huge-bodied lord of rākṣasas, Alaṃbala, he raised him aloft and dashed him to the ground, as Viṣṇu in battle slew Maya.

**7.149.32**  Then Ghaṭotkaca, taking up a sword of wondrous aspect, severed from the trunk the dreadful, hideous-looking head.

**7.149.33**  Grasping that blood-smeared head by the hair, the rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca went swiftly toward Duryodhana's chariot.

**7.149.34**  Drawing near, the mighty-armed rākṣasa, smiling, cast onto his chariot the head with its disfigured face and hair, and uttered a fearful cry like a thunder-cloud in the rains.

**7.149.35**  And then, O king, he spoke these words to Duryodhana: Here is your ally slain; his valor you have seen. Soon you shall see this same end fall upon Karṇa—and upon yourself as well.

**7.149.36**  Having so spoken, he then advanced toward Karṇa, O lord of men, pouring forth hundreds of sharp arrows and loosing them upon Karṇa's head.

**7.149.37**  Then there arose, O great king, a battle of dreadful form and terrifying aspect—astounding to behold—in the clash between the man and the rākṣasa.

**7.150.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When Karṇa, the son of Vikartana, and the rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca closed with each other at the dead of night—how did that battle unfold?

**7.150.2**  What manner of fight did that terrible rākṣasa wage? What was his chariot like, and his illusions, and all his weapons?

**7.150.3**  What size were his horses, his chariot-banner, and his bow? What was his armor like, and his throat-guard? Being asked, tell me all this, Saṃjaya, for you are skilled in such telling.

**7.150.4**  Saṃjaya said: Red-eyed he was, huge of body, copper-faced, with a sunken belly, his hair bristling upward, his beard tawny, his ears like spikes, his jaws enormous.

**7.150.5**  His mouth was split open to the ears, his fangs sharp, his look terrible, his tongue and lips long and coppery, his brows drooping, his nose thick.

**7.150.6**  Dark of limb, red of neck, mountainous in stature, fearsome—of vast body, mighty arms, a huge head, and great strength.

**7.150.7**  His hair was dishevelled, his touch rough, his calves swollen and knotted, his haunches thick, his navel sunk, his bulk loose-fleshed and immense.

**7.150.8**  He bore ornaments upon his hands, that master of great illusion, and armlets too, wearing upon his breast a golden gorget like a mountain girdled with a garland of fire.

**7.150.9**  Upon his head shone a diadem, wrought of gold and gleaming, adorned with figures of many forms, bright as an arched gateway.

**7.150.10**  He wore earrings bright as the rising sun, a fair golden garland, and a broad cuirass of bronze of great splendor.

**7.150.11**  His great chariot rang with the sound of a hundred bells, flew red banners and pennons, was sheathed in bearskin, and measured a full nalva across.

**7.150.12**  He stood mounted upon it, garlanded with banners, furnished with every choice weapon, fitted with eight wheels, deep-voiced as a thundercloud.

**7.150.13**  There the horses that drew it were like elephants, red-eyed and terrible, of color and speed at will, mighty and yoked to the car.

**7.150.14**  His charioteer was a rākṣasa, Virūpākṣa, with blazing face and earrings, who gathered up the horses in battle with reins bright as the sun's rays; and joined with him he stood, as the sun stands with Aruṇa.

**7.150.15**  Like a great mountain wreathed in a vast cloud, a towering banner reaching to the sky was raised upon his car—a flesh-eating vulture, crimson-headed, most fearful to behold.

**7.150.16**  Drawing back a stout-stringed bow that roared like Indra's thunderbolt—a clear span of a cubit thick and twelve cubits in length—

**7.150.17**  and covering all the quarters with arrows the size of chariot-axles, he bore down upon Karṇa in that night that carries off heroes.

**7.150.18**  As he drew his bow, planted firm and standing upon his car, the twang of his bowstring was heard like the crashing of the thunderbolt.

**7.150.19**  Terrified by him, O Bhārata, all your armies trembled like the great waves of the sea.

**7.150.20**  Beholding that misshapen, terrible one rushing upon him, the son of Rādhā, as though smiling, swiftly came forth to meet him.

**7.150.21**  Then Karṇa advanced against him, loosing shafts against him as he loosed his own from close at hand—like elephant against elephant, like bull-leader of the herd against bull.

**7.150.22**  Tumultuous, O lord of peoples, was that encounter of the two, of Karṇa and the rākṣasa, O king, like the clash of Indra and Śambara.

**7.150.23**  Seizing their bows of dreadful sound and mighty force, the two covered each other over, hewing at one another with great arrows.

**7.150.24**  Then with smooth-jointed shafts loosed from bows drawn to the full, each held off the other, piercing through the bronze armor on both.

**7.150.25**  Like tigers with their claws, like great elephants with their tusks, the two tore at each other with chariot-lances and with arrows.

**7.150.26**  Cleaving each other's limbs and fitting their shafts to the string, scorched by the volleys of arrows, neither could so much as look upon the other.

**7.150.27**  Their every limb wounded, bathed in floods of blood, the two shone like ochre mountains streaming with water.

**7.150.28**  Their bodies pierced by arrow-points, rending one another, those two of great splendor, though they strove, could not make each other waver.

**7.150.29**  That night-battle that was joined went on long and seemed evenly matched, O king, as Karṇa and the rākṣasa gambled with their very lives in the fray.

**7.150.30**  As Karṇa fitted his sharp arrows and shot them ceaselessly, both your own men and the foe were struck with dread by the roar of his bow; yet, O king, Karṇa could not gain the upper hand over Ghaṭotkaca.

**7.150.31**  Then that best of weapon-knowers brought forth a celestial weapon; and seeing the celestial weapon loosed by Karṇa, the rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca, son of a Pāṇḍava, brought forth a mighty illusion.

**7.150.32**  He appeared encircled by a vast host of rākṣasas of dreadful form, bearing spears and mallets, and crags and trees in their hands.

**7.150.33**  Beholding him with his great bow upraised, those kings were shaken, as though Death the ender of beings were coming on, wielding the terrible rod of Time.

**7.150.34**  Affrighted by the lion-roar that Ghaṭotkaca sent forth, the elephants let flow their urine, and the men were sorely shaken.

**7.150.35**  Then a most fierce and mighty rain of stones fell on every side, loosed at midnight by the overwhelming forces of the rākṣasas.

**7.150.36**  Iron discs, fire-tubes, lances and javelins, spears, śataghnīs and pikes fell thick and unbroken.

**7.150.37**  Beholding that grim and most savage fight, the kings, and your sons, and the warriors, shaken with terror, fled in all directions.

**7.150.38**  There Karṇa alone, proud and exulting in the might of his weapons, did not waver, but scattered with his shafts the illusion that Ghaṭotkaca had wrought.

**7.150.39**  And when his illusion was undone, Ghaṭotkaca in his fury loosed dreadful arrows, and they entered the son of the sūta.

**7.150.40**  Then those arrows, drenched in blood, having pierced Karṇa in that great battle, entered the earth like serpents enraged.

**7.150.41**  But the son of the sūta, in great wrath, swift of hand and full of valor, overpassing Ghaṭotkaca's onset, pierced him with ten arrows.

**7.150.42**  Ghaṭotkaca, struck through in his vital parts by the sūta's son and sorely pained, took up a celestial discus of a thousand spokes.

**7.150.43**  Razor-edged, bright as the rising sun, adorned with gems and jewels—the son of Bhīma, in his wrath, hurled it at the son of Adhiratha, eager to slay him.

**7.150.44**  Cast with great speed but flung aside by Karṇa's shafts, it fell vainly to the ground like the resolve of an ill-fated man.

**7.150.45**  But Ghaṭotkaca, enraged at seeing his discus brought down, covered Karṇa over with arrows as Svarbhānu covers the sun.

**7.150.46**  But the son of the sūta, unflinching, of prowess like Rudra, Upendra, and Indra, swiftly covered Ghaṭotkaca's chariot with his feathered shafts.

**7.150.47**  Then a mace ringed with gold, whirled and hurled by the enraged Ghaṭotkaca—that too, struck down by Karṇa's arrows, fell to earth.

**7.150.48**  Then, leaping up into the sky, roaring like a cloud of doom, the huge-bodied one rained down a rain of trees from the vault of heaven.

**7.150.49**  Then Karṇa pierced the illusion-wielding son of Bhīmasena in the sky with his shafts, as the sun pierces a cloud with its rays.

**7.150.50**  Having slain all his horses and shattered his chariot into a hundred pieces, Karṇa rained down arrows upon him like Parjanya pouring rain.

**7.150.51**  There was not on his body a two-fingers' space left unpierced, and in a moment he seemed like a porcupine bristling with quills.

**7.150.52**  Neither his horses, nor his chariot, nor his banner, nor Ghaṭotkaca himself could they see in the battle, so covered over was he by floods of arrows.

**7.150.53**  But he, beating down Karṇa's celestial weapon with a weapon of his own, that master of illusion fought the son of the sūta with a battle of illusions.

**7.150.54**  He fought Karṇa then with illusion and with swiftness of hand, unseen, darting through the meshes of arrows in the sky.

**7.150.55**  The son of Bhīma, that master of mighty illusion, O best of Kurus, wrought a great illusion, bewildering the foe, O Bhārata.

**7.150.56**  That one of ill-omened face, fashioning hideous mouths, devoured by his illusion the celestial weapons of the sūta's son.

**7.150.57**  And again the huge-bodied one, cut into a hundred pieces in the fight, seemed to fall lifeless and spent from the sky; and deeming him slain, the bulls of the Kurus raised a shout.

**7.150.58**  But then, in all the quarters, he was seen again with fresh bodies, that huge-bodied one with a hundred heads and a hundred bellies.

**7.150.59**  The mighty-armed one appeared like the mountain Maināka; and again that rākṣasa, becoming no larger than a thumb, rose up sideways and upward like a swelling wave of the sea.

**7.150.60**  And cleaving the earth, he plunged again into the waters; and then he was seen there rising up once more from another place.

**7.150.61**  Then descending, he stood again upon a gold-wrought chariot, mailed for battle, having veiled earth and sky and the quarters with his illusion.

**7.150.62**  Drawing near to Karṇa's chariot, his face aquiver with its swinging earrings, unshaken he spoke this word to the son of the sūta, O lord of peoples:

**7.150.63**  "Stand now! You shall not depart alive from me, son of the sūta. This day on the field of battle I shall cure you of your appetite for war."

**7.150.64**  So saying, that rākṣasa of cruel prowess, his eyes coppery with rage, sprang up into the air and laughed aloud, and smote Karṇa as a lion smites a lordly elephant.

**7.150.65**  Ghaṭotkaca rained upon Karṇa, that bull among chariot-warriors, arrows the size of chariot-axles, as a cloud rains its torrents; but Karṇa beat down that rain of arrows while it was yet far off.

**7.150.66**  And seeing his illusion undone by Karṇa, O bull of the Bhāratas, Ghaṭotkaca, vanishing, sent forth yet another illusion.

**7.150.67**  He became a mountain, lofty, its peaks dense with trees, vast, streaming forth a flood of spears, lances, swords, and maces.

**7.150.68**  Beholding that mountain dark as a heap of collyrium, pouring down dread weapons in its cataracts, Karṇa was not shaken.

**7.150.69**  Then Karṇa, as though smiling, sent forth a celestial weapon; and by that weapon the lord of mountains was scattered and vanished away.

**7.150.70**  Then, becoming a dark cloud in the sky, hung with Indra's bow, most fierce, he poured a rain of stones upon the son of the sūta.

**7.150.71**  Then, fitting the weapon of Vāyu, that best of weapon-knowers, Karṇa the son of Vikartana, the bull among men, scattered that cloud of doom.

**7.150.72**  Then Karṇa, covering all the quarters utterly with his hosts of arrows, destroyed, O great king, the weapon that Ghaṭotkaca had loosed.

**7.150.73**  Then, laughing in the fight, the mighty son of Bhīma brought forth a great illusion against Karṇa, that great chariot-warrior.

**7.150.74**  Seeing Ghaṭotkaca, that foremost of chariot-warriors, coming on again undismayed upon his car, surrounded by many rākṣasas—

**7.150.75**  rākṣasas like lions and tigers, with the prowess of rutting elephants, some on elephant-back, some on chariots, and some upon the backs of horses—

**7.150.76**  surrounded by cruel and dreadful ones bearing manifold weapons and adorned with manifold armor—Ghaṭotkaca compassed about like Vāsava by the Maruts—beholding him, Karṇa the great archer gave battle to the rākṣasa.

**7.150.77**  Then Ghaṭotkaca, piercing Karṇa with five swift shafts, raised a fearful roar, striking terror into all the kings.

**7.150.78**  And again, with an añjalika arrow, Ghaṭotkaca swiftly severed the great bow, together with its store of shafts, that was held in Karṇa's hand.

**7.150.79**  Then taking up another bow, stout, able to bear the strain, and great, Karṇa drew it back by force, raised high like the bow of Indra.

**7.150.80**  Then, great king, Karṇa loosed his arrows—gold-feathered, foe-slaying—against the sky-roving rākṣasas.

**7.150.81**  That host of broad-chested demons, tormented by his shafts, was thrown into confusion like a wild herd of elephants harried by a lion.

**7.150.82**  Scattering the rākṣasas with his arrows, together with their horses, charioteers, and elephants, the mighty lord consumed them as the blessed fire devours all beings at the ending of an age.

**7.150.83**  Having slain the host of rākṣasas, the son of the charioteer shone forth like the god Maheśvara of old in heaven, when he had burned the three cities to ash.

**7.150.84**  Among those thousands of kings on the Pāṇḍava side, good sir, not one, O lord of the earth, was able even to look upon him.

**7.150.85**  None save Ghaṭotkaca, O king—that mighty lord of the rākṣasas, endowed with terrible valor and strength, and now enraged like the son of Vivasvat himself.

**7.150.86**  From the eyes of that enraged one fire was born, O king, as flaming drops of oil fall blazing from two great meteors.

**7.150.87**  Smiting palm against palm and biting his lip, he mounted once more a chariot newly fashioned by his magic.

**7.150.88**  It was yoked with mounts like elephants—asses with the faces of fiends—and in his wrath he said to his driver: "Bear me against the son of the charioteer."

**7.150.89**  And so, O lord of peoples, that foremost of chariot-warriors went forth again in his fearsome car to a duel with the son of the charioteer.

**7.150.90**  Once more in his fury the rākṣasa hurled at the son of the charioteer a most terrible eight-wheeled thunderbolt, fashioned by Rudra.

**7.150.91**  Leaping up, Karṇa caught it, laying his bow aside in the chariot, and flung it back at him; whereupon the rākṣasa sprang down from his car.

**7.150.92**  That weapon of great brilliance reduced the chariot, with its horses, driver, and banner, to ashes, then cleft the earth and entered it; and the gods marveled at the sight.

**7.150.93**  All beings straightway honored Karṇa, in that he had leaped up and seized the great god-fashioned thunderbolt.

**7.150.94**  Having done this in battle, Karṇa mounted his chariot again, and then the son of the charioteer, scorcher of foes, let fly his iron shafts.

**7.150.95**  What Karṇa then accomplished in that battle, dreadful to behold, no other among all beings could have done, O bestower of honor.

**7.150.96**  Struck by his iron shafts as a mountain by streams of rain, the rākṣasa—like a city of the gandharvas—vanished once again.

**7.150.97**  Thus that great wielder of illusion, slayer of foes, by his magic and his swiftness foiled those celestial weapons.

**7.150.98**  Though his weapons were thus baffled by that rākṣasa's sorcery, Karṇa, undismayed, fought back against the demon.

**7.150.99**  Then, enraged, O great king, the mighty son of Bhīmasena multiplied himself into many forms, striking terror into the lords of men.

**7.150.100**  Then from every quarter there came rushing lions, tigers, and hyenas, fire-tongued serpents, and birds with beaks of iron.

**7.150.101**  Strewn upon by the keen arrows loosed from Karṇa's bow, that one—seeming like a city, a mountain, a forest—vanished there once more.

**7.150.102**  And rākṣasas and piśācas, fiends and ravening wolves, eager to devour Karṇa, rushed upon him from every side, and then sought to terrify him with savage cries.

**7.150.103**  With many dreadful weapons upraised and dripping with blood they came; yet Karṇa pierced each one of them with several swift shafts.

**7.150.104**  Having beaten back that rākṣasa illusion with a celestial weapon, he struck down his foe's horses with smooth-jointed arrows.

**7.150.105**  Shattered, their bodies mangled and their backs cleft by his shafts, they sank to the earth before the very eyes of that rākṣasa.

**7.150.106**  His illusion broken, the son of Hiḍimbā then said to Karṇa, son of Vikartana, "This one has ordained your death," and vanished away.

**7.151.1**  Saṃjaya said: While the combat between Karṇa and the rākṣasa was thus raging, Alāyudha, a valiant lord of the rākṣasas, advanced to the fray.

**7.151.2**  Attended by a great army, ringed about by thousands of misshapen rākṣasas—warriors who wore all manner of forms—he came to Suyodhana, brooding upon an old enmity.

**7.151.3**  For his valiant kinsman Baka, devourer of brahmins, had been slain, and Kirmīra of great might, and likewise his friend Hiḍimba.

**7.151.4**  Recalling that old enmity, long harbored, and learning of this battle by night, he longed to slay Bhīma in the fight.

**7.151.5**  Like a rutting elephant, like an angry serpent, athirst for battle, he spoke these words to Duryodhana:

**7.151.6**  "You know, great king, how by Bhīma the rākṣasas Hiḍimba, Baka, and Kirmīra—my kinsmen—were slain.

**7.151.7**  And of old he laid violent hands upon the maiden Hiḍimbā—what need to say more?—setting at naught both other rākṣasas and ourselves.

**7.151.8**  To slay him with his band, O king, together with his horses, chariots, and elephants—and Hiḍimbā's son too, with his counselors—I have come hither myself.

**7.151.9**  This day I shall slay all the sons of Kuntī, with Vāsudeva at their head, and devour them, together with all my followers. Hold back all your forces; we shall fight the Pāṇḍavas."

**7.151.10**  Hearing these words of his, Duryodhana was glad, and, surrounded by his brothers, he honored him and replied:

**7.151.11**  "With you and your band at our head we shall fight our foes; for my soldiers, bent on ending the feud, will not hold back."

**7.151.12**  "So be it," said that bull among rākṣasas to the king, and swiftly he advanced upon Bhīma, attended by his man-eaters.

**7.151.13**  With blazing form, in a chariot bright as the sun, even such, O lord of kings, as the one in which Ghaṭotkaca rode.

**7.151.14**  His great car too was of matchless thunder, adorned with many arched gateways, its frame sheathed in bear-hides, vast as a measure of land.

**7.151.15**  His steeds too were swift, huge-bodied as elephants, harsh-voiced—a hundred yoked, mighty of frame, feeders on flesh and blood.

**7.151.16**  The din of his chariot too was like the roar of a great thundercloud; his bow too was vast, strong-stringed, and mightier still.

**7.151.17**  His arrows too were like axle-shafts, gold-feathered, whetted on stone; and that mighty-armed hero was every bit the equal of Ghaṭotkaca.

**7.151.18**  His banner too, guarded by jackal and crow, blazed like fire or the sun; in form, too, more splendid even than Ghaṭotkaca's, its face wildly aglow.

**7.151.19**  With glittering armlets, garlanded with a blazing diadem, girt with a wreath and turban and a fastened sword, bearing mace and sling, club and plough, and bow—huge in stature as an elephant.

**7.151.20**  In that chariot bright as fire, driving the Pāṇḍava host in rout, he shone as he wheeled through the battle, like a lightning-garlanded cloud in the sky.

**7.151.21**  And all those foremost lords of men, mighty, armored and shield-bearing, filled with joy, fought there on every side, O king—the heroic warriors of the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.152.1**  Saṃjaya said: Beholding that doer of dreadful deeds arrived for the battle, all the Kurus alike gave way to joy.

**7.152.2**  And so too your sons, with Duryodhana at their head, were like men without a raft who, finding one, would cross the sea.

**7.152.3**  Reckoning themselves as it were born anew, the princes then welcomed Alāyudha, lord of the rākṣasas, and did him honor.

**7.152.4**  While that more-than-mortal combat, fearsome to behold, raged on through the night between Karṇa and the rākṣasa, dreadful in its sight,

**7.152.5**  the Pāñcālas with their kings looked on, smiling; and your men too, O king, swayed this way and that.

**7.152.6**  Droṇa, Droṇa's son, Kṛpa, and the rest cried out, "This cannot be!"—dismayed at beholding that feat of Hiḍimbā's son upon the field of battle.

**7.152.7**  All grew agitated, given over to wailing and stunned out of their senses; your host, great king, despaired of Karṇa's life.

**7.152.8**  But Duryodhana, seeing Karṇa fallen into utmost distress, summoned Alāyudha, lord of the rākṣasas, and spoke to him thus:

**7.152.9**  "This Karṇa, son of Vikartana, is locked with Hiḍimbā's son, and is performing a mighty feat, such as befits him in the fray.

**7.152.10**  Behold these valiant princes slain by the son of Bhīmasena, struck down by his many weapons like trees by a tusker.

**7.152.11**  This share in the battle, here amid the kings, I have set apart for you. With your own consent, O hero, fall upon him in your might and destroy him.

**7.152.12**  That wicked Ghaṭotkaca, tormentor of foes, leaning upon the power of illusion, has long been wearing down Karṇa, son of Vikartana."

**7.152.13**  Thus addressed by the king, that rākṣasa of fierce prowess, mighty of arm, said "So be it," and rushed upon Ghaṭotkaca.

**7.152.14**  Then the son of Bhīmasena too, O lord, left off from Karṇa and crushed with his shafts the foe that came against him.

**7.152.15**  Between those two enraged lords of the rākṣasas there arose a battle, as between two rutting elephants in the forest contending for a cow.

**7.152.16**  Freed of the rākṣasa, Karṇa too, foremost of chariot-warriors, charged upon Bhīmasena in his chariot bright as the sun.

**7.152.17**  Heedless of him as he came on, Bhīma saw Ghaṭotkaca beset in the battle by Alāyudha, as a bull might be by a lion.

**7.152.18**  In his chariot shaped like the sun, Bhīma, foremost of strikers, scattering floods of arrows, advanced against Alāyudha's car.

**7.152.19**  Seeing him approach, Alāyudha then, O lord, left off from Ghaṭotkaca and challenged Bhīmasena.

**7.152.20**  Bhīma, the bringer of doom to rākṣasas, O lord, rushing suddenly upon him, overwhelmed that lord of the rākṣasas and his band with showers of arrows.

**7.152.21**  And so too Alāyudha, O king, that subduer of foes, rained again and again upon the son of Kuntī shafts whetted on stone and flying straight.

**7.152.22**  And all those rākṣasas, terrible, bearing weapons of every kind, rushed upon Bhīmasena, seeking victory for your sons.

**7.152.23**  Battered by those powerful foes, the mighty Bhīmasena pierced them each, with five sharp arrows apiece.

**7.152.24**  Slain by Bhīma, those rākṣasas, born of the ass's womb, raised a tumult of howls and fled in all ten directions.

**7.152.25**  Seeing them put to terror by Bhīma, the mighty rākṣasa rushed upon him with speed and overwhelmed him with arrows.

**7.152.26**  Bhīmasena wore him down in the battle with sharp-pointed shafts; but Alāyudha cut off some of those arrows loosed by Bhīma in the fray, and some he caught in his haste.

**7.152.27**  Beholding that lord of the rākṣasas, Bhīma of dreadful prowess then hurled with force his mace, like the fall of the thunderbolt.

**7.152.28**  As that mace came hurtling on, wreathed in flame, the rākṣasa struck it with his own mace; and Bhīma's mace turned back upon him.

**7.152.29**  The son of Kuntī overwhelmed the lord of the rākṣasas with showers of arrows; but those too the rākṣasa rendered vain with his keen shafts.

**7.152.30**  And all those rākṣasa soldiers of fearsome form, at the command of the lord of the rākṣasas, fell to slaughtering chariots and elephants.

**7.152.31**  The Pāñcālas and Sṛñjayas, the horses and the great elephants, found no respite there, sorely afflicted by the rākṣasas.

**7.152.32**  Seeing that most terrible turn of the great battle, the best of men spoke these words to Dhanaṃjaya:

**7.152.33**  "Look, O mighty-armed one, Bhīma has fallen under the power of the lord of the rākṣasas. Go to his aid, O Pāṇḍava, and do not hesitate."

**7.152.34**  "Let Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, together with the sons of Draupadī, those great chariot-warriors, advance upon Karṇa."

**7.152.35**  "Let Nakula and Sahadeva, and the valiant Yuyudhāna, slay the other rākṣasas at your command, O Pāṇḍava."

**7.152.36**  "And you yourself, O mighty-armed tiger among men, hold back this host that has Droṇa at its head, for a great peril has come upon us."

**7.152.37**  When Kṛṣṇa had spoken thus, the great chariot-warriors, as directed, advanced in battle against Vaikartana Karṇa and against the other rākṣasas.

**7.152.38**  Then with arrows like venomous serpents, loosed from a bow drawn to its full, the mighty lord of the rākṣasas severed the bow of Bhīma.

**7.152.39**  And with sharp shafts that mighty one slew his horses and his charioteer in battle, O Bhārata, before the very eyes of Bhīmasena.

**7.152.40**  His horses slain and his charioteer slain, he leapt down from the body of the chariot and, roaring aloud, hurled at him his heavy and terrible mace.

**7.152.41**  Then, as that great mace came hurtling on with a fearsome roar, the dread rākṣasa struck it down with his own mace, and let forth a shout.

**7.152.42**  Beholding that terrible, terror-striking feat of the lord of the rākṣasas, Bhīmasena, his spirit elated, swiftly took up his mace.

**7.152.43**  A tumultuous combat broke out between the man and the rākṣasa, the crash of their falling maces making the earth tremble violently.

**7.152.44**  Their maces flung away, the two closed once more upon each other and smote one another with fists that crashed like thunderbolts.

**7.152.45**  Seizing whatever lay at hand—chariot-wheels, yokes, axles, chariot-frames, and gear—the two furious warriors struck each other down.

**7.152.46**  Streaming blood, grappling with one another, they dragged each other back and forth again and again, like two great rutting elephants.

**7.152.47**  Hṛṣīkeśa, devoted to the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas, beheld this; and to protect Bhīmasena he urged on the son of Hiḍimbā.

**7.153.1**  Saṃjaya said: Seeing Bhīma hard pressed in battle, seized close at hand by the rākṣasa, Vāsudeva then spoke these words to Ghaṭotkaca:

**7.153.2**  "Look, O mighty-armed one of great splendor, how Bhīma is held fast at close quarters by the rākṣasa, in the sight of all the armies and of you yourself."

**7.153.3**  "Leave off Karṇa, and quickly slay Alāyudha, lord of the rākṣasas, O mighty-armed one; Karṇa you shall slay afterward."

**7.153.4**  Hearing the words of the Vṛṣṇi hero, the valiant Ghaṭotkaca left off Karṇa and fought with the lord of the rākṣasas, the brother of Baka; and a most tumultuous combat arose between those two rākṣasas in the night.

**7.153.5**  Now the warriors of Alāyudha, rākṣasas terrible to behold, brave and gripping their bows, were rushing on with speed.

**7.153.6**  Weapons in hand and greatly enraged, Yuyudhāna the great chariot-warrior, with Nakula and Sahadeva, cut them down with sharp arrows.

**7.153.7**  And in that battle, O king, the diademed Bībhatsu scattered all those bulls among the kṣatriyas, loosing his arrows on every side.

**7.153.8**  And Karṇa in that battle, O king, drove off the princes—Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin and the rest, the great chariot-warriors of the Pāñcālas.

**7.153.9**  Seeing them being slaughtered, Bhīma of terrible prowess advanced swiftly upon Karṇa, scattering his shafts in the battle.

**7.153.10**  Then, having slain the rākṣasas, Nakula and Sahadeva and Sātyaki the great chariot-warrior came to where the son of the sūta stood; they engaged Karṇa in battle, while the Pāñcālas engaged Droṇa.

**7.153.11**  But Alāyudha, in great fury, struck Ghaṭotkaca, that crusher of foes, upon the head with a huge iron club.

**7.153.12**  By that blow the mighty son of Bhīmasena was a little dazed, yet, valorous as he was, he steadied himself.

**7.153.13**  Then in that combat he hurled at him a mace adorned with gold, bright as blazing fire and decked with a hundred bells.

**7.153.14**  Loosed with force by that doer of terrible deeds, the loud-clanging mace ground his horses, his charioteer, and his chariot to powder.

**7.153.15**  His horses, wheels, and axle broken, his banner and chariot-pole shattered, he sprang up swiftly from the chariot, taking to rākṣasa sorcery.

**7.153.16**  Resorting to that illusion, he rained down a great flood of blood, and the sky grew thick with murky clouds, lit by flashes of lightning.

**7.153.17**  Then came the fall of thunderbolts with lightning and crashing thunder, and a mighty crackling din arose there in that great battle.

**7.153.18**  Seeing the illusion wrought by one rākṣasa, the other rākṣasa, the son of Hiḍimbā, sprang upward and undid that illusion by an illusion of his own.

**7.153.19**  When the master of illusion saw his illusion destroyed, by illusion he loosed a most violent rain of stones upon Ghaṭotkaca.

**7.153.20**  That terrible rain of stones the valiant one scattered to all quarters with a downpour of arrows, and the deed seemed a marvel.

**7.153.21**  Then the two rained down upon each other with weapons of every kind—with iron clubs, spears, maces, pestles, and mallets,

**7.153.22**  with trident-staves and swords, with lances, javelins, and pikes, with iron shafts, sharp broad-headed arrows, ordinary arrows, discuses, and battle-axes,

**7.153.23**  with iron balls, with slings, with ox-headed clubs and mortars, and with all manner of great-branched trees torn up by the roots.

**7.153.24**  With śamī, pīlu, and karīra trees, and with śamyāka too, O Bhārata, with iṅgudas and jujubes, and with kovidāras in full flower,

**7.153.25**  with palāśas and arimedas, with great plakṣas, banyans, and pippal trees, they smote one another in that combat.

**7.153.26**  And with mountain-peaks of every sort, studded with manifold minerals, they fought; and the din of these was great, as of thunderbolts splitting asunder.

**7.153.27**  Terrible was that combat between the son of Bhīma and Alāyudha, O king, like the strife of old between those lords of the monkeys, Vālin and Sugrīva.

**7.153.28**  Having fought with terrible weapons of every kind and with arrows, the two seized their sharp swords and smote at one another.

**7.153.29**  Rushing each upon the other, those two of vast bodies and mighty strength grasped one another by the hair and gripped each other with their arms.

**7.153.30**  Their limbs torn, those two of vast frame streamed with sweat and blood, O ruler of men, like two mountains drenched with rain.

**7.153.31**  Then, falling upon him with speed, the son of Hiḍimbā whirled the rākṣasa about, hurled him down with all his might, and struck off his great head.
