**7.153.32**  And bearing off that head adorned with its two earrings, the mighty one then let forth a most tumultuous roar.

**7.153.33**  Seeing slain that vast-bodied crusher of foes, the kinsman of Baka, the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas raised their lion-roars.

**7.153.34**  Then, when that rākṣasa had been laid low, the Pāṇḍavas sounded thousands of kettledrums and tens of thousands of conches.

**7.153.35**  Most rich in victory did that night become for them, and it shone resplendent all around, garlanded with lamps.

**7.153.36**  And the mighty son of Bhīmasena flung the lifeless head of Alāyudha down before Duryodhana.

**7.153.37**  Then King Duryodhana, seeing Alāyudha slain, became utterly stricken with dismay, together with his army, O Bhārata.

**7.153.38**  For that one, coming of his own accord and remembering an old and grievous enmity, had promised him: "I will slay Bhīmasena in battle."

**7.153.39**  The king had believed that Bhīma would surely be slain by him, and had reckoned upon long life for himself and for his brothers.

**7.153.40**  But seeing him struck down by the son of Bhīmasena, he reckoned the vow of Bhīmasena as good as fulfilled.

**7.154.1**  Saṃjaya said: Having slain the rākṣasa Alāyudha, Ghaṭotkaca, his spirit elated, standing before the host, let forth roars of every kind.

**7.154.2**  Hearing that tumultuous cry of his, which made the elephants tremble, a most dreadful fear came upon your men, O great king.

**7.154.3**  Seeing the mighty son of Bhīmasena entangled with Alāyudha, the mighty-armed Karṇa rushed upon the Pāñcālas.

**7.154.4**  With ten arrows each—firm shafts with bent joints, loosed from a fully drawn bow—he pierced Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin.

**7.154.5**  Then with excellent iron shafts he set trembling Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, and the noble chariot-warrior Sātyaki, with his arrows.

**7.154.6**  As all of them plied their bows there, to left and right, their bows appeared as so many circles, O ruler of men.

**7.154.7**  The twang of their bowstrings and the rattle of their chariot-rims grew tumultuous in the night, like the roar of clouds at the close of the hot season.

**7.154.8**  With the twang of bowstrings and the rattle of rims for its thunder, with bows for its lightning and circled bow-arcs for its banner-peaks, raining a turbid downpour of arrow-floods—such a battle-cloud did he become, O king.

**7.154.9**  Unshakable as a mountain, with might equal to a mountain's, Vaikartana the crusher of enemy hosts shattered in battle that uprushing great downpour, O lord of men.

**7.154.10**  Then with peerless, sharp arrows like falling thunderbolts, their shafts bright with gold, the great-souled Vaikartana, intent upon the welfare of your sons, drove off his foes in the battle.

**7.154.11**  Some had their banners hewn and broken, some had their bodies torn and pierced by his shafts, some were stripped of charioteer, and some of horses—so swiftly were they made by Vaikartana.

**7.154.12**  Finding no refuge in the battle, they fell back upon the host of Yudhiṣṭhira; and beholding them broken and turned to flight, Ghaṭotkaca was seized with exceeding wrath.

**7.154.13**  Mounting that splendid chariot bright with gold and gems, he roared aloud like a lion, and drawing near to Vaikartana Karṇa, he pierced him with shafts like thunderbolts.

**7.154.14**  With barbed darts, iron shafts, and arrows; with tubular and staff-like arrows, and calf-toothed ones; with boar-eared and horn-tipped shafts, and with showers of razor-arrows, the two made the sky resound.

**7.154.15**  The mid-air, veiled in showers of arrows flying crosswise through the battle, shone with the blazing radiance of golden-feathered shafts, as though with garlands of many-colored flowers.

**7.154.16**  Evenly matched and of incomparable might, the two struck at one another with their finest weapons; and in that battle no one could mark any difference between those two foremost of heroes.

**7.154.17**  Most wondrous and most splendid in form was that battle between the son of the Sun and the son of Bhīma, turbulent and terrible with the fall of weapons, blazing as if in the sky between Rāhu and the radiant Sun.

**7.154.18**  When Ghaṭotkaca could gain no advantage over Karṇa, O king, then that foremost of those skilled in weapons brought forth a fearsome missile.

**7.154.19**  With that weapon the rākṣasa, the son of Hiḍimbā, first slew Karṇa's horses and his charioteer, and then swiftly vanished from sight.

**7.154.20**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When that rākṣasa, that fighter by guile, had thus vanished, tell me, Saṃjaya, what my men then did.

**7.154.21**  Saṃjaya said: Knowing that the rākṣasa had vanished, all the Kurus cried out together: "How shall this rākṣasa, this fighter by guile, unseen, not slay Karṇa in the battle?"

**7.154.22**  Then Karṇa, fighting with deft and dazzling skill in weapons, covered every quarter with nets of arrows; yet no creature there was struck, in the mid-air made dark with his shafts.

**7.154.23**  Neither drawing out an arrow, nor fitting it to the string, nor touching his quivers with his fingertips could the son of the sūta be seen, so swift was he—yet he covered the whole sky with arrows.

**7.154.24**  Then we beheld an illusion wrought in the mid-air by the rākṣasa—horrible, frightful, and dread—glowing red as a blood-hued cloud, blazing fierce like a tongue of fire.

**7.154.25**  Then out of it lightnings broke forth, and blazing meteors too, O lord of the Kurus; and another sound arose, most terrible, as of thousands of kettledrums thundering.

**7.154.26**  Then there rained down arrows with golden shafts, and spears, lances, clubs, and every kind of weapon, battle-axes and swords washed bright with oil, and flame-tipped pikes and javelins.

**7.154.27**  Iron-bound bludgeons gleaming with spikes, gaily-wrought maces and keen-edged spears, heavy clubs bound about with bands of gold, and śataghnīs appeared on every side.

**7.154.28**  Great boulders fell here and there by the thousand, charged with lightning and with thunderbolts, and discus-wheels rimmed with many hundred blades appeared, blazing with the splendour of fire.

**7.154.29**  That vast and blazing downpour as it fell—of spears and stones and battle-axes, of lances, swords, thunderbolts, lightnings, and mallets—Karṇa could not beat back with his floods of arrows.

**7.154.30**  Of horses falling, struck down by arrows, of elephants falling, smitten by thunderbolts, and of great chariot-warriors crushed by stones, a mighty din arose as they came toppling down.

**7.154.31**  Battered on every side by Ghaṭotkaca with that fearful rain of weapons of every kind, the host of Duryodhana was seen reeling in distress, whirling about and spinning round.

**7.154.32**  Crying out in horror, surging back upon itself, dissolving away in utter dismay—yet those foremost of men, out of their noble temper, did not then turn their faces from the fight.

**7.154.33**  Beholding that most dreadful, terrible, demon-conjured downpour of mighty weapons as it fell, and seeing the floods of their troops struck down, a great fear entered your sons.

**7.154.34**  And jackals with tongues blazing like fire, howling by the hundred with dreadful cries, and the troops of demons roaring—seeing these, the warriors of the kings were filled with anguish.

**7.154.35**  Those demons, with flaming tongues and mouths and sharp fangs, hideous, their bodies huge as mountains, ranging the sky with spears clutched fast in their hands, poured down their volleys as storm-clouds pour the rain.

**7.154.36**  Struck by them with arrows, spears, and pikes, with terrible maces and with blazing bludgeons, with thunderbolts, with tridents, with strokes of lightning, with discuses, and crushed by śataghnīs, the warriors fell.

**7.154.37**  Slings, bhuśuṇḍis, stone-balls, śataghnīs, and posts bound about with bands of black iron showered down upon your son's army, and so dread a confusion broke forth.

**7.154.38**  Their entrails spilled out, their heads shattered, their limbs broken, the warriors lay there strewn; horses were torn open and elephants smashed, and chariots ground to powder by the stones.

**7.154.39**  Thus loosing that great rain of weapons, those night-prowlers, dread of form upon the earth, conjured into being there by Ghaṭotkaca's sorcery, spared neither the suppliant nor the frightened.

**7.154.40**  In that grim slaughter of the Kuru heroes, loosed by Time itself, in the ruin of the warriors, the Kauravas, broken, fled away all at once, every one of them, crying aloud.

**7.154.41**  "Flee, O Kurus! There is no help in this! The gods with Indra slay us for the Pāṇḍavas' sake!"—and as those Bhāratas thus sank down, there was no island of refuge for any of them there.

**7.154.42**  While that tumultuous uproar went on, and the host of the Kurus, broken, melted away, the ordering of the ranks grown invisible, neither Kurus nor others could be told apart.

**7.154.43**  In that dreadful, boundless rout, all the quarters, as we gazed, appeared empty; and Karṇa alone, O king, I saw there, breasting that downpour of weapons with his chest.

**7.154.44**  Then he veiled the sky with his arrows, battling against the demon's celestial sorcery; modest, performing a noble deed scarce to be done, the son of the charioteer was not bewildered in the fray.

**7.154.45**  Then in their fear all looked up toward Karṇa, O king—the men of Sindhu and the Bāhlīkas alike—honouring his steadiness in the battle, even as they watched the demon prevailing.

**7.154.46**  A śataghnī fitted with wheels, hurled by the demon, slew all four horses together at once; sinking to their knees, they came down upon the earth, lifeless, their teeth and eyes and tongues all gone.

**7.154.47**  Then, dismounting from the car whose horses were slain, his mind composed though the Kurus fled and his celestial weapon was being undone by sorcery, he was not bewildered, but pondered what the hour required.

**7.154.48**  Then all the Kurus cried out, beholding Karṇa and that dread sorcery: "With the spear, O Karṇa, slay the demon now, this instant! These Kurus, these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, are perishing!

**7.154.49**  What will Bhīma and Pārtha do to us then? Slay this demon who scorches us at midnight! He who delivers us from this battle of dread aspect—he it is who could make us face the Pārthas in the fight.

**7.154.50**  Therefore slay this demon of dreadful form with the spear that was given you by Vāsava! Let not all the Kauravas, peers of Indra, with their warriors, O Karṇa, be lost at the onset of night!"

**7.154.51**  Hard pressed by the demon there at midnight, and seeing, O king, his army perishing, and hearing the loud lament of the Kauravas, Karṇa set his mind upon loosing the spear.

**7.154.52**  Wrathful as a lion and beyond all bearing, he would brook no thwarting of him in that battle; and so he took up that supreme, victory-giving, irresistible spear, resolved to slay the demon.

**7.154.53**  That spear, O king, which had been laid by for years on end, kept honoured for the slaying of Phalguna in battle—the supreme spear that Śakra gave to the son of the charioteer in exchange for his earrings—

**7.154.54**  That spear, licking the air and blazing bright, bound with snares like the very Night of the Ender, like the sister of Death, like a flaming meteor—Vaikartana hurled it at the demon.

**7.154.55**  Seeing that supreme, body-shattering weapon blazing in the charioteer's son's hand, the demon fled away in terror, O king, having made himself the size of a Vindhya foothill.

**7.154.56**  Beholding the spear poised in the crook of Karṇa's arm, the spirits of the air cried out, O lord of men; tumultuous winds blew, O king, and lightning with a crash of thunder struck the earth.

**7.154.57**  Blazing, it burned that sorcery to ashes, and cleaving deep through the demon's heart, it soared aloft, shining in the night, passing in among the spaces of the stars.

**7.154.58**  Having fought with manifold and wondrous volleys of weapons—celestial, human, and demonic—the hero, roaring his many dreadful roars, was made to yield up his dear life by the spear of Śakra.

**7.154.59**  And this further marvel, of wondrous form, he wrought as a deed for the destruction of his foes: in that hour, his vitals pierced through by the spear, he shone, O king, like a mountain wreathed in cloud.

**7.154.60**  Then from the sky there fell, his life gone out, that lord of demons, his body cleft, upon the earth—head downward, his limbs grown rigid, his tongue lolling out—Ghaṭotkaca, having taken on a vast form.

**7.154.61**  That son of Bhīmasena, dread in his deeds, having made his shape fearful and huge, fell down; and even slain, he thus crushed a whole quarter of your army, striking terror into the Kauravas.

**7.154.62**  Then, mingled with their lion-roars, the kettledrums and conches, tabors and war-drums sounded; and seeing the sorcery burned away and the demon slain, the Kauravas, rejoicing, shouted aloud.

**7.154.63**  Then Karṇa, honoured by the Kurus as Śakra was by the Maruts at the slaying of Vṛtra, mounted the chariot beside your son who stood upon it, and rejoicing entered his own army.

**7.155.1**  Saṃjaya said: Seeing the son of Hiḍimbā slain and strewn upon the ground like a fallen mountain, the Pāṇḍavas were all downcast in spirit, their eyes blurred with tears.

**7.155.2**  But Vāsudeva, overwhelmed with a mighty joy, roared a roar like a lion, as though to dismay the foe, O Bhārata; and having let forth that great roar, he embraced Phalguna.

**7.155.3**  Having sounded that great cry and drawn in the reins, he danced, wrapped about with joy, like a tree shaken by the wind.

**7.155.4**  Then, whirling about and clapping Pārtha again and again upon the arms, Acyuta, standing in the body of the chariot, shouted aloud once more in his delight.

**7.155.5**  Knowing that the mighty Vāsudeva was glad at heart, Arjuna spoke, O king, like one whose own heart was not much gladdened.

**7.155.6**  "This great rejoicing of yours today is out of place, O Madhusūdana, when a fresh occasion for grief has come upon us through the slaying of Hiḍimbā's son.

**7.155.7**  Our armies have turned their faces from the field, seeing Ghaṭotkaca slain, and we ourselves are sore distressed at the fall of Hiḍimbā's son.

**7.155.8**  Surely the cause of this cannot be a slight one, O Janārdana; therefore, being asked, tell me now the truth of it, O best of the truthful.

**7.155.9**  If this be no secret of yours, you should declare it, O subduer of foes; tell me now, O Madhusūdana, the cause of this break in your composure."

**7.155.10**  "Like a churning of the ocean, like a shifting of Meru, so do I count this light-hearted conduct of yours, O Janārdana."

**7.155.11**  Vāsudeva said: Hear from me, O Dhanaṃjaya, the cause of this great joy that has come upon me—a thing that on the instant brings the highest gladness to the heart.

**7.155.12**  Now that this spear has been spent upon Ghaṭotkaca, O greatly resplendent one, know Karṇa, O Dhanaṃjaya, to be as good as slain in battle this very moment.

**7.155.13**  Were the spear yet in Karṇa's hand, what man in the world is there who could stand before him in battle, as before Kārttikeya himself?

**7.155.14**  By good fortune his armour was taken from him, by good fortune his earrings were carried off, and by good fortune his unfailing spear has been spent upon Ghaṭotkaca.

**7.155.15**  For had he still his armour and his earrings as well, the mighty Karṇa, alone, could have conquered the three worlds, gods and all.

**7.155.16**  Neither Vāsava, nor Kubera, nor Varuṇa the lord of waters, nor Yama would dare to close with Karṇa in battle.

**7.155.17**  Though you drew the Gāṇḍīva and I bore the discus Sudarśana, we two could not have conquered in battle that bull among men so armed.

**7.155.18**  But for your good, by Śakra, through a stratagem, this conqueror of hostile cities was robbed of his earrings and stripped of his armour.

**7.155.19**  Because he cut away that armour and those two bright earrings of his and gave them to Śakra, Karṇa is therefore remembered as Vaikartana, 'the Cutter.'

**7.155.20**  Like an angry venomous serpent stilled by the power of a spell, so does Karṇa appear to me today, like a fire whose flame is quenched.

**7.155.21**  From the very day, O mighty-armed one, that the spear was given to Karṇa by the great-souled Vāsava—the spear that has now been spent upon Ghaṭotkaca—

**7.155.22**  —obtaining it in exchange for his earrings and his celestial armour, the bull Karṇa, once he had it, deemed you slain in battle for good and all.

**7.155.23**  Yet even so, this man can be slain by no one else but you, O tiger among men; I swear it by my truth, O sinless one.

**7.155.24**  Devoted to the brahmins, truthful in speech, given to austerity, steadfast in his vows, and compassionate even toward his foes—therefore is Karṇa remembered as Vṛṣa, the bull of virtue.

**7.155.25**  Greedy for battle, mighty-armed, his bow ever bent and ready, like a lion in the forest crushing the lords of rutting elephant-herds, he leaves the tiger-warriors of the chariots stripped of their pride in the forefront of the fight.

**7.155.26**  Like the sun gone to mid-heaven, he cannot be looked upon, O tiger among men, by the great-souled foremost of your warriors—his thousand rays the web of his arrows, like the day-maker in autumn.

**7.155.27**  As a rain-cloud at the end of the hot season, he pours down his streams of arrows; Karṇa, a thundercloud of celestial weapons, is like Parjanya laden with rain—yet today he is brought down to mere mortal estate, parted from the gift of Śakra.

**7.155.28**  There is but one way for his slaying: in a moment of opening, you yourself unheedless while he is heedless, when he has come to grief and his chariot-wheel has sunk in the earth—then you must strike him down first, taking thought and choosing your moment.

**7.155.29**  Jarāsaṃdha, and the king of the Cedis, that great soul, and the mighty Ekalavya the Niṣāda—all of these, one by one, were slain by me alone, by this device or that, for your good.

**7.155.30**  And other lords of demons too were slain—chief among them Hiḍimba, Kirmīra, and Baka—and Alāyudha, the crusher of hostile hosts, and the swift Ghaṭotkaca, dreadful in his deeds.

**7.156.1**  Arjuna said: How, and by what devices, O Janārdana, were Jarāsaṃdha and the other lords of the earth made to be slain for our good?

**7.156.2**  Vāsudeva said: Jarāsaṃdha, and the king of the Cedis, and the mighty son of the Niṣāda—had they not been slain before, they would now be a source of terror.

**7.156.3**  Suyodhana would surely have sought out those foremost of chariot-warriors, and they, forever hostile to us, would have taken the side of the Kauravas.

**7.156.4**  For those great-souled heroes, masters of weapons and steadfast in fight, would have guarded the whole host of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons like immortals.

**7.156.5**  The son of the charioteer, and Jarāsaṃdha, and the king of the Cedis, and the son of the Niṣāda—leaning upon Suyodhana, they would have scorched this earth.

**7.156.6**  Hear from me, O Dhanaṃjaya, the devices by which they were slain; for without such stratagems they were unconquerable in battle even by the gods.

**7.156.7**  Each one of them, alone and singly, O Pārtha, could have given battle to the whole host of the gods, guarded though it be by the World-Guardians.

**7.156.8**  For Jarāsaṃdha, enraged and provoked by the son of Rohiṇī, hurled, to slay us, a mace with a blood-red mouth.

**7.156.9**  Cleaving as it were a parting through the sky, with the radiance of fire, it was seen falling like the thunderbolt loosed by Śakra.

**7.156.10**  Seeing that mace come hurtling down, the son of Rohiṇī, to beat it back, let fly the weapon called Sthūṇākarṇa.

**7.156.11**  Checked by the force of that weapon, the mace fell down upon the earth, rending the goddess Earth and seeming to make the very mountains tremble.

**7.156.12**  There a dreadful demoness, swift in her might, Jarā by name, had joined together at his birth that subduer of foes, Jarāsaṃdha.

**7.156.13**  Born of two mothers, his body in two halves, each apart from the other, he was joined together by her—and because she joined him, he is remembered as Jarāsaṃdha.

**7.156.14**  And that rākṣasī, brought down to the earth, O Pārtha, was slain together with her sons and kinsmen by that mace and by the weapon Sthūṇākarṇa.

**7.156.15**  Deprived thus of his mace, Jarāsaṃdha in the great battle was slain by Bhīmasena before your very eyes, O Dhanaṃjaya.

**7.156.16**  For had the mighty Jarāsaṃdha held the mace in his hand, the gods themselves with Indra would not have been able to slay him in battle, O best of men.

**7.156.17**  It was for your sake that the Niṣāda's son, of true valor, was parted from his thumb—when, by a stratagem, he had made Droṇa his teacher.

**7.156.18**  That son of the Niṣāda, of firm valor, his finger-guard bound on, shooting alone, a forest-dweller, shone like a second Rāma.

**7.156.19**  For with his thumb intact, Ekalavya could never have been vanquished in battle, O Pārtha, by gods or dānavas, by rākṣasas or serpents.

**7.156.20**  How then could a mere mortal even dare to look upon him—firm of grip, accomplished, ever shooting his shafts by day and by night?

**7.156.21**  For your sake he was slain by me at the forefront of battle; and the valiant king of the Cedis was struck down before your very eyes.

**7.156.22**  He too could not be conquered in battle by all the gods and asuras together; and it was for his slaying, and that of the other foes of the gods, that I was born.

**7.156.23**  As your ally, O tiger among men, out of desire for the welfare of the worlds—Hiḍimba, Baka, and Kirmīra, equal in life-force to Rāvaṇa, destroyers of the Brahmins' sacrifices, were brought low by Bhīmasena.

**7.156.24**  So too the sorcerer Alāyudha was slain by Hiḍimbā's son; and Hiḍimbā's son in turn, by a stratagem, was killed by Karṇa with the spear.

**7.156.25**  For had Karṇa not slain him with the spear in the great battle, that Ghaṭotkaca, Bhīmasena's son, would have had to be slain by me.

**7.156.26**  He was not slain by me before, out of my wish to do what was dear to you; for this rākṣasa was a hater of Brahmins and a hater of sacrifices.

**7.156.27**  A destroyer of dharma, evil of soul—therefore he was struck down; and the spear given by Indra was, by a stratagem, made to fail, O sinless one.

**7.156.28**  For those who would destroy dharma are to be slain by me, O Pāṇḍava; this is my imperishable vow, made for the establishment of dharma.

**7.156.29**  Sacred knowledge, truth, self-restraint, purity, dharma, modesty, prosperity, fortitude, forbearance—wherever these are, there I ever delight: by truth I swear it to you.

**7.156.30**  You must not grieve on account of Karṇa, the son of the Sun; I will teach you the means by which you shall overcome him.

**7.156.31**  And Vṛkodara shall slay Suyodhana in battle; the means of his slaying too I will declare to you, O Pāṇḍava.

**7.156.32**  But this tumultuous din swells against the enemy's host, and your own troops are scattering in flight to the ten directions.

**7.156.33**  For the Kauravas, having found their mark, are shattering your army; and Droṇa, best of strikers, is burning down your forces.

**7.157.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the spear of the Sūta's son was wasted upon the slaying of a single hero, why, passing over all the rest, did he not hurl it at Pārtha?

**7.157.2**  For with him slain, all the Pāṇḍavas and Sṛñjayas would have been slain; why, by the slaying of that one hero, did he not seize victory in the war?

**7.157.3**  "Once challenged, I will not turn back"—such was Phalguna's great vow; therefore the Sūta's son had only to challenge him himself.

**7.157.4**  Then, having drawn Phalguna into a chariot-duel, why did the bull-like Karṇa not slay him with Indra's gift? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.

**7.157.5**  Surely my son is bereft of wisdom and without true allies; his designs thwarted by his foes—how then could he ever conquer his enemies?

**7.157.6**  For that supreme spear of his, the very mainstay of his victory—that spear was made by Vāsudeva to be spent upon Ghaṭotkaca.

**7.157.7**  As a bilva fruit in the hand of a crippled man is snatched away by one stronger, so that unfailing spear was made to fail upon Ghaṭotkaca.

**7.157.8**  As when a boar and a dog fight and, both being destroyed, the dog-eater gains the spoil—so too, O learned one, I deem it was Vāsudeva who gained from the combat of Karṇa and Hiḍimbā's son.

**7.157.9**  For if Ghaṭotkaca should slay Karṇa, that would be the greater gain for the Pāṇḍavas; and if the son of the Sun should slay him, even so the purpose would be achieved through the loss of the spear.

**7.157.10**  Thus the wise Vāsudeva, lion among men, having weighed this in his wisdom, set Ghaṭotkaca to fight the Sūta's son in battle, doing what was dear and beneficial to the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.157.11**  Saṃjaya said: Knowing this intent in Karṇa, O king, the slayer of Madhu then set the lord of the rākṣasas to the chariot-duel.

**7.157.12**  The deeply wise Janārdana set mighty Ghaṭotkaca to draw forth the unfailing spear, O king—amid your evil counsels.

**7.157.13**  Then indeed our purpose would have been accomplished, O scion of Kuru, had Kṛṣṇa not been guarding that Pārtha from Karṇa, the great chariot-warrior.

**7.157.14**  With his horses, his banner, and his chariot, O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pārtha would have fallen to the earth in battle—but for Janārdana, the lord and master of all yogas.

**7.157.15**  Guarded by those many devices, O king, Pārtha, protected by Kṛṣṇa, conquers his foes face to face.

**7.157.16**  But it was above all from the unfailing spear that Kṛṣṇa guarded the Pāṇḍava; for that spear, once hurled, would have struck down Kuntī's son as a thunderbolt fells a tree.

**7.157.17**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: A maker of strife, ill in counsel, and yet deeming himself wise is my son—he for whom this means of slaying, the path to victory, has been let slip.

**7.157.18**  And how was this let slip by you too, O son of Gavalgaṇa—that you, O deeply wise one, did not make this matter understood?

**7.157.19**  Saṃjaya said: Night after night, this very counsel was urged, ever and again, by Duryodhana, by Śakuni, by me, and by Duḥśāsana:

**7.157.20**  "Tomorrow, Karṇa, leave aside all the troops and slay Dhanaṃjaya; then shall we make the Pāṇḍus and Pāñcālas serve us like menials."

**7.157.21**  "Or else, with Pārtha slain, the Vārṣṇeya would set up some other among the Pāṇḍus in the fight; therefore let Kṛṣṇa be struck down."

**7.157.22**  "For Kṛṣṇa is the root of the Pāṇḍus, and Pārtha is the trunk risen up; the other sons of Pṛthā are as the branches, and the Pāñcālas may be called the leaves."

**7.157.23**  "The Pāṇḍavas have Kṛṣṇa for their refuge, Kṛṣṇa for their strength, Kṛṣṇa for their lord; Kṛṣṇa is their supreme recourse, as the moon among the lights of heaven."

**7.157.24**  "Therefore, son of the Sūta, leaving aside the leaves, the branches, and the trunk, cut down Kṛṣṇa, the root of the Pāṇḍus, everywhere and always."

**7.157.25**  "For if Karṇa should slay the Dāśārha, the joy of the Yādavas, then the whole earth, O king, would fall under your sway—of that there is no doubt."

**7.157.26**  "For if that great soul, the joy of the Yadu line and of the Pāṇḍavas, were slain and lay upon the earth, then surely, O lord of men, the whole world, with its mountains, seas, and forests, would pass under your sway."

**7.157.27**  But this resolve, though so taken, faltered in the hour of battle, while the immeasurable Hṛṣīkeśa, lord of the thirty gods, kept watch.

**7.157.28**  For Keśava ever guards Arjuna, the son of Kuntī; he did not wish to set him in the battle face to face with the Sūta's son.

**7.157.29**  And the unfallen one set other noble chariot-warriors against him, thinking, "How may I make that unfailing spear to fail?"—O lord.

**7.157.30**  Then mighty-armed Sātyaki, of true valor, that tiger among chariot-warriors, asked Kṛṣṇa concerning Karṇa, the great chariot-warrior:

**7.157.31**  "There was this confidence placed in Karṇa, O you of measureless valor, by reason of the spear; why then was it not loosed by the Sūta's son upon Phalguna?"

**7.157.32**  Vāsudeva said: Duḥśāsana, Karṇa, and Śakuni, together with the king of the Sindhus, ever took counsel, with Duryodhana at their head:

**7.157.33**  "Karṇa, Karṇa, mighty archer, of measureless prowess in battle—this spear of yours must be loosed upon none other, O best of the victorious—

**7.157.34**  "—save upon the great chariot-warrior Pārtha, Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī; for he is the most glorious among them, as Vāsava among the gods."

**7.157.35**  "With him slain, all the Pāṇḍavas along with the Sṛñjayas will be as souls departed, like gods bereft of their sacred fires."

**7.157.36**  And "So be it" was Karṇa's pledge, O bull of the Śini line; yet ever in Karṇa's heart was the slaying of the wielder of Gāṇḍīva.

**7.157.37**  But it was I myself who bewildered the son of Rādhā, O best of warriors, so that he did not loose the spear upon the Pāṇḍava of the white steeds.

**7.157.38**  For, knowing that spear to be the death of Phalguna who longs to fight, I have had no sleep nor any gladness of mind, O best of warriors.

**7.157.39**  But now, having seen that spear made to fail upon Ghaṭotkaca, O bull of the Śini line, I behold Dhanaṃjaya this day delivered from the very jaws of death.

**7.157.40**  Not my father, nor my mother, nor you, nor my brothers, nor even my own life is so to be guarded as Bībhatsu in battle.

**7.157.41**  Were there anything beyond the sovereignty of the three worlds, however hard to win, I would not desire it, O Sātvata, if it lacked Pārtha, Dhanaṃjaya.

**7.157.42**  Therefore a very great joy has come to me this day, O Yuyudhāna, beholding Pārtha, Dhanaṃjaya, as one returned from the dead.

**7.157.43**  And for this reason was the rākṣasa sent by me against Karṇa in the battle; for no other was able to press Karṇa hard in the combat by night.

**7.157.44**  Saṃjaya said: Thus did the son of Devakī speak then to Sātyaki—he who was devoted to Dhanaṃjaya's welfare and ever delighted in what was dear to him.

**7.158.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Great was the misjudgment of Karṇa, Duryodhana, and the rest, of Śakuni the son of Subala—and yours above all, my son.

**7.158.2**  For you knew that spear, slayer of one alone, ever in battle unstoppable and unbearable even to the gods with Vāsava;

**7.158.3**  why then was it not loosed by Karṇa when battle was first joined, neither upon the son of Devakī nor upon Phalguna, O Saṃjaya?

**7.158.4**  Saṃjaya said: When all of us had withdrawn from the fighting, O lord of peoples, this counsel arose in the night, O best of the Kuru line:

**7.158.5**  "At the very break of day, when tomorrow comes, this spear must be loosed upon Keśava or upon Arjuna, Karṇa, Karṇa"—thus, again and again.

**7.158.6**  But then, when daybreak came, O king, by the will of the gods that resolve was lost again to Karṇa and to the other warriors.

**7.158.7**  I deem fate supreme indeed, in that Karṇa, with the spear set in his very hand, did not slay in battle either Pārtha or Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī.

**7.158.8**  That spear, resting in his hand, raised aloft like the Night of Doom—because his judgment was struck down by fate, Karṇa did not loose it.

**7.158.9**  Bewildered by the gods' own magic, he loosed not Vāsava's spear, O lord, for the slaying of Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, nor of Pārtha, the peer of Śakra.

**7.158.10**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: By fate alone were you undone, and by your own judgment, and by Keśava's; for Vāsava's spear was spent in slaying Ghaṭotkaca, who was but as a blade of grass.

**7.158.11**  And Karṇa, and my sons, and all the other kings as well, by this ill-conceived design have gone to the abode of Vaivasvata.

**7.158.12**  But tell me yet again how the battle of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas went forward then, when Hiḍimbā's son had been slain.

**7.158.13**  And those striking warriors who charged upon Droṇa in ordered ranks—the Sṛñjayas together with the Pāñcālas—how too did they wage the fight?

**7.158.14**  Droṇa, made fierce by the slaying of Somadatta's son and of the Sindhu king, casting away his very life in his fury, plunging into the host—

**7.158.15**  —like a tiger stretching itself, like Death with jaws agape: how did the Pāṇḍus and Sṛñjayas advance against Droṇa as he loosed his shafts?

**7.158.16**  And those who guarded the teacher, with Duryodhana at their head — Aśvatthāman, Karṇa, and Kṛpa — what, my son, did they too do in the battle?

**7.158.17**  When Savyasācin and Vṛkodara sought to slay the son of Bharadvāja, how did my men close with them in the fight? Tell me, Saṃjaya.

**7.158.18**  By the slaying of the king of the Sindhus and by the slaying of Ghaṭotkaca, these men were made furious and greatly enraged — how did they wage the battle in the night?

**7.158.19**  Saṃjaya said: When the rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca had been slain by Karṇa in the night, O king, and your men, eager for battle, were roaring in their delight,

**7.158.20**  as they charged on with fury and the army was being cut down, deep in the night the king fell into the utmost wretchedness.

**7.158.21**  And the mighty-armed scorcher of foes said to Bhīmasena: "Hold back, O mighty-armed one, the host of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son; at the death of Haiḍimba's son a great stupor has come over me."

**7.158.22**  Having so charged Bhīma, the king sat down upon his own chariot, his face filled with tears and sighing again and again; beholding Karṇa's prowess, he sank into a dreadful despondency.

**7.158.23**  Seeing him so stricken, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words: "Grieve not, son of Kuntī; such faltering does not befit you, O best of the Bhāratas, as it would a common man."

**7.158.24**  "Rise, O king, fight, bear the heavy yoke, O lord; should faltering overtake you, victory itself would fall into doubt."

**7.158.25**  Hearing Kṛṣṇa's words, the Dharma King Yudhiṣṭhira wiped his eyes with both hands and spoke to Kṛṣṇa:

**7.158.26**  "Known to you, O mighty-armed one, is the highest course of all duties; the guilt of slaying a brahmin belongs to him who does not recognize a kindness done to him."

**7.158.27**  "For when we dwelt in the forest, the great-souled son of Hiḍimbā, though still but a boy, rendered us his aid, O Janārdana."

**7.158.28**  "When he learned that the white-steeded Pāṇḍava had gone in quest of weapons, that mighty archer, O Kṛṣṇa, attended upon me in the Kāmyaka forest, and dwelt with us all the while Dhanaṃjaya was absent."

**7.158.29**  "On the journey to Gandhamādana we were carried across the hard passes by him, and the weary Pāñcālī was borne upon the back of that great-souled one."

**7.158.30**  "And from the very outset of the battles, whatever this one performed — a hard task accomplished for my sake by that great-souled one, O lord —"

**7.158.31**  "and the love I bear by nature for Sahadeva, O Janārdana — even that love, doubled, I bore for Ghaṭotkaca, lord of the rākṣasas."

**7.158.32**  "Devoted to me was that mighty-armed one, and I was dear to him, and he was dear to me — and through him, O Vārṣṇeya, I am sunk in despair, tormented by grief."

**7.158.33**  "Look, O Vārṣṇeya, at the armies being driven in rout by the Kauravas; look at Droṇa and Karṇa, those great chariot-warriors, locked in the fight."

**7.158.34**  "At dead of night behold the Pāṇḍava army crushed by these two, as a great thicket of reeds is trampled by two rutting elephants."

**7.158.35**  "Heedless of the strength of Bhīmasena's arms, O Mādhava, and of the varied weaponry of Pārtha, the Kauravas press on in their might."

**7.158.36**  "Here are Droṇa and Karṇa, and king Suyodhana too, having slain the rākṣasa in battle, roaring in their joy upon the field."

**7.158.37**  "How, while we yet live, and you too, O Janārdana, has Haiḍimba met his death, fallen upon by the son of the sūta?"

**7.158.38**  "Setting us all at naught, before the very eyes of Savyasācin, the mighty rākṣasa, Bhīmasena's son, has been slain, O Kṛṣṇa."

**7.158.39**  "When Abhimanyu was slain by the evil-souled sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the great chariot-warrior Savyasācin was not there in that battle, O Kṛṣṇa."

**7.158.40**  "And we were all held off by the evil-souled lord of the Sindhus; Droṇa, together with his son, was the instrument in that deed."

**7.158.41**  "The means of the slaying was taught to Karṇa by the teacher himself, who cut in two with his sword the sword of the struggling boy."

**7.158.42**  "As he stood in his distress, Kṛtavarman, like one without pity, suddenly slew his horses and both his rear-guard charioteers; thus did the other mighty archers bring down the son of Subhadrā in the fight."

**7.158.43**  "And for but a slight cause, O Kṛṣṇa, the lord of the Sindhus was slain by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, O best of the Yādavas — and even that is not greatly to my liking."

**7.158.44**  "If the slaying of an enemy were proper and to be done by the Pāṇḍavas, then it was Droṇa and Karṇa who should first have been slain in battle — such is my judgment."

**7.158.45**  "For these two are the root of our sorrows, O bull among men; relying upon these two in battle, Suyodhana is filled with confidence."

**7.158.46**  "Where Droṇa ought to have been slain, and the sūta's son with his followers, there the mighty-armed one slew instead the far-dwelling lord of the Sindhus."

**7.158.47**  "Yet without fail the subduing of the sūta's son must be wrought by me; therefore I shall go myself, O hero, in my desire to slay Karṇa, while the mighty-armed Bhīmasena is engaged with Droṇa's host."

**7.158.48**  Having spoken thus, Yudhiṣṭhira hastened swiftly forth, twanging his great bow and blowing a fearsome blast upon his conch.

**7.158.49**  Then, surrounded by a thousand chariots, three hundred elephants, five thousand horse, and three thousand Prabhadrakas, Śikhaṇḍin followed swiftly behind the king.

**7.158.50**  Then, clad in mail, the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas, with Yudhiṣṭhira at their head, beat their kettledrums and blew their conches.

**7.158.51**  Then the mighty-armed Vāsudeva said to Dhanaṃjaya: "Here goes Yudhiṣṭhira in haste, possessed by wrath and bent on slaying the sūta's son; to neglect him would not be fitting."

**7.158.52**  Having spoken thus, Hṛṣīkeśa swiftly urged on the horses, and Janārdana followed after the king, who had gone far ahead.

**7.158.53**  Seeing him rushing on in his desire to slay the sūta's son, his resolve broken by grief and as if burning with fire, Vyāsa came up and spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma:

**7.158.54**  "By good fortune Phalguna lives, though he met Karṇa in battle; for that one, longing to slay Savyasācin, kept his lance in reserve."

**7.158.55**  "And by good fortune, O bull of the Bhāratas, the victorious one did not come to single combat with him; for these two rivals would have loosed against each other their celestial weapons in every kind."

**7.158.56**  "And as his weapons were struck down and the son of the sūta was hard pressed, he would surely have hurled in battle the lance of Vāsava, O Yudhiṣṭhira."

**7.158.57**  "Then a dreadful calamity would have befallen you, O best of the Bhāratas; by good fortune it was the rākṣasa who was slain in the fight by the sūta's son, O bestower of honour."

**7.158.58**  "Making the lance of Vāsava the occasion, he was carried off by Time; for your sake, my son, was the rākṣasa slain in battle."

**7.158.59**  "Be not wrathful, O best of the Bhāratas, nor set your mind upon grief; this is the end of all living beings here, O Yudhiṣṭhira."

**7.158.60**  "Together with all your brothers and the great-souled kings, do battle against the Kauravas, O king, O Bhārata; and on the fifth day the earth shall be yours."

**7.158.61**  "And ever, O tiger among men, dwell upon righteousness alone — upon mercy, austerity, charity, forbearance, and truth, O Pāṇḍava."

**7.158.62**  "Cherish these with the highest delight; where dharma is, there is victory." Having so spoken to the Pāṇḍava, Vyāsa vanished then and there.

**7.159.1**  Saṃjaya said: When Ghaṭotkaca had been slain by the sūta's son that night, the son of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira, fell under the sway of grief and indignation.

**7.159.2**  Seeing your mighty host held back by Bhīma, he said this to Dhṛṣṭadyumna: "Hold off the pitcher-born one."

**7.159.3**  "For you were born from the fire for the destruction of Droṇa, armed with arrows, mailed, sword-bearing, bow-wielding, a scorcher of foes; charge joyfully into battle, and let there be no fear in you at all."

**7.159.4**  "Let Janamejaya and Śikhaṇḍin and Daurmukhi, rich in glory, charge in their joy upon the pitcher-born one from every side."

**7.159.5**  "Let Nakula and Sahadeva, the sons of Draupadī, the Prabhadrakas, and Drupada and Virāṭa, attended by their sons and brothers,"

**7.159.6**  "and Sātyaki and the Kekayas, and the Pāṇḍava Dhanaṃjaya — let them charge with fury in their desire to slay the son of Bharadvāja."

**7.159.7**  "And likewise let all the chariot-warriors, every elephant and horse there is, and the foot-soldiers, bring the great chariot-warrior Droṇa to bay in battle."

**7.159.8**  Thus commanded by the great-souled Pāṇḍava, they all charged with fury upon the pitcher-born one, eager for battle.

**7.159.9**  As the Pāṇḍavas came on suddenly with all their effort, Droṇa, the best of weapon-bearers, received them in battle.

**7.159.10**  Then king Duryodhana, with all his effort, greatly enraged, charged upon the Pāṇḍavas, wishing to preserve Droṇa's life.

**7.159.11**  Then there broke out a battle of warriors and mounts grown weary, of Pāṇḍavas and Kurus roaring at one another.

**7.159.12**  Blinded by sleep, O great king, and worn out in the fray, those great chariot-warriors could not summon up any exertion in the battle.

**7.159.13**  And that night of three watches, dreadful of aspect and terrifying, became like a night of a thousand watches, life-destroying, above all to those being slain and to the wounded.

**7.159.14**  Ah, what a night it grew to be, above all for those blinded by sleep! For all the warriors, yours and the foe's alike, were without spirit and downcast in heart, their weapons spent, their arrows gone.

**7.159.15**  Yet, enduring as they were and possessed of shame above all else, looking to their own duty, they did not forsake their own battle-line.

**7.159.16**  Some men, casting away their weapons, lay blinded by sleep — some upon elephants, some upon chariots, and some upon horses, O Bhārata.

**7.159.17**  Blinded by sleep, the chieftains were aware of no exertion at all; those warriors sent one another in battle to the abode of Yama.

**7.159.18**  Others, sunk as in a dream and bereft of sense, took men for foes and in the battle struck down their own selves, their own people, and the enemy alike.

**7.159.19**  Uttering all manner of cries, blinded by sleep in that great battle, they stood saying "We must fight," though their eyes were fast clinging with slumber.

**7.159.20**  Some heroes, crushing one another in the fray and blinded by sleep, struck one another down in the battle, O king, in that fearsome darkness.

**7.159.21**  Many men, sorely stupefied by sleep, did not even perceive in the battle that their own selves were being struck down by the foe.

**7.159.22**  Perceiving such a plight among them, Bībhatsu, that bull among men, spoke aloud these words, making the quarters resound:

**7.159.23**  "You are all weary and blinded by sleep, mounts and all, and the army is enveloped in darkness and in thick clouds of dust."

**7.159.24**  "If you, O soldiers, think it good, then desist, and close your eyes here upon this very battlefield for a little while."

**7.159.25**  "Then, sleep gone and rested, when the moon has risen again, you Kurus and Pāṇḍavas shall once more dispatch one another to heaven."

**7.159.26**  Hearing that word of the righteous one, the armies, knowing every duty, found it good, and spoke thus to one another:

**7.159.27**  They cried out, "Karṇa, O Karṇa!" and, "O Duryodhana!" — "Desist! the host of the Pāṇḍavas has indeed left off the fight," O king.

**7.159.28**  And as Phalguna cried out thus on every side, the army of the Pāṇḍavas and yours too left off the battle, O Bhārata.

**7.159.29**  That word of the great-souled one the gods and the sages, and all the noble-hearted armies, applauded with delight.

**7.159.30**  Honouring that gentle word, all the wearied armies slept for a little while, O king, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.159.31**  And your banner-host, O Bhārata, having gained its rest and won its ease, paid honour to the hero Arjuna.

**7.159.32**  "In you abide the Vedas and the weapons; in you both wisdom and valour; in you dwells dharma, O mighty-armed one, and compassion for all beings, O sinless one."

**7.159.33**  "And the well-being we, restored, wish for you, O Pārtha — may it be yours; and swiftly may you attain, O hero, the dear desires of your heart."

**7.159.34**  Thus praising that tiger among men, the great car-warriors, overcome by sleep, fell silent, O lord of the people.

**7.159.35**  Some slept upon the backs of horses, others within the boxes of their chariots, others seated on the shoulders of elephants, and still others upon the bare ground.

**7.159.36**  With their weapons, with their maces, with their swords and battle-axes, with their lances and armor, the men slept each apart from the other.

**7.159.37**  Those elephants, blind with sleep, with their trunks coiling like serpents' bodies and dusted with the earth's powder, cooled the ground with the breath of their nostrils.

**7.159.38**  The elephants, breathing upon the surface of the earth, shone there like sundered mountains breathed upon by great serpents.

**7.159.39**  The horses, with their golden harnesses, made the level ground uneven, gashing the earth with the points of their hooves; and there, O king of kings, with their yokes hung with garlands, they slept, still harnessed everywhere to their teams.

**7.159.40**  That host, thus broken by sleep, slept speechless, like a wondrous picture laid out upon a canvas by skilled hands.

**7.159.41**  Those young warriors, wearing earrings, their limbs gashed by one another's arrows, slept clinging to the temple-globes of the elephants, as though pressed against the breasts of their beloved women.

**7.159.42**  Then the eastern quarter of Indra was adorned by the moon, the lord of the water-lilies, pale as the cheek of a lovely woman, the delight of the eyes.

**7.159.43**  Then, after a little while, the blessed lord marked with the hare showed his reddish glow in the east, the radiant one swallowing up the brilliance of the stars.

**7.159.44**  And following that reddish dawn, the moon, little by little, let fall a great net of rays bright as gold.

**7.159.45**  Driving away the darkness with their splendor, those rays of the moon slowly spread over all the quarters, over the sky, and over the earth as well.

**7.159.46**  Then in a moment the world became as though made of light, and the darkness, dim and unillumined, swiftly fled away.

**7.159.47**  When the world was lit up again and the moon, lord of the night, had become as bright as day, then, O king, the creatures that roam by night roamed about—or roamed no more.

**7.159.48**  That army, being awakened by the rays of the moon, O king, came awake like a great grove of lotuses upon the water.

**7.159.49**  As the ocean, stirred up at the rising of the moon, would surge in agitation, so did that sea of armies surge, stirred up at the moon's rising.

**7.159.50**  Then once more the battle broke out, O lord of the people, for the destruction of the world among men who longed for the world beyond.

**7.160.1**  Saṃjaya said: Then Duryodhana, approaching Droṇa, spoke these words, given over to wrath, kindling both joy and ardor.

**7.160.2**  Enemies who in battle were resting, worn out with toil, dejected in spirit, and who had found their opening—these are above all not to be borne with.

**7.160.3**  Yet this we endured, out of a wish to please you; and now these Pāṇḍavas, well rested, have grown the stronger.

**7.160.4**  In every way we are fallen short, in vigor and in strength, while they, protected by you, wax greater again and again.

**7.160.5**  All the celestial weapons, the Brahmā-weapon and the rest—all of these abide above all in you alone.

**7.160.6**  Neither the Pāṇḍavas, nor we, nor any other bowmen in the world are a match for you when you fight—this truth I tell you.

**7.160.7**  O best of the twice-born, knowing every weapon, you could slay these worlds with their gods, asuras, and gandharvas by your celestial arms—of this there is no doubt.

**7.160.8**  Yet you bear with these men, who are above all afraid of you—whether you do so out of regard for their pupilship, or for my own ill fortune.

**7.160.9**  Thus stung and provoked by your son, O king, Droṇa, filled with anger, spoke these words to Duryodhana.

**7.160.10**  Old though I am, I strive with utmost power in battle, Duryodhana; and beyond this, greedy for victory, I must even stoop to a base deed—all these folk who know not weapons must be slain by me who knows them.

**7.160.11**  Whatever you judge, be it good or be it evil, that indeed I shall do, O Kaurava, at your word, and not otherwise.

**7.160.12**  Having slain all the Pāñcālas and shown my valor in battle, I shall lay aside my armor, O king—by my truth I lay my hand upon my weapon and swear it.

**7.160.13**  And as for your thinking that Arjuna the son of Kuntī is weary in battle—hear, O mighty-armed Kaurava, in truth, of his prowess.

**7.160.14**  Neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor the yakṣas, nor the rākṣasas dare to withstand in battle Savyasācin when he is enraged.

**7.160.15**  By him at Khāṇḍava the blessed lord of the gods himself was withstood, and though he poured down rain, he was checked by that great-souled one with his arrows.

**7.160.16**  Yakṣas, nāgas, and daityas, and others puffed up with their strength, were slain by that lord among men—this too is known to you.

**7.160.17**  In the cattle-expedition the gandharvas, Citrasena and the rest, were vanquished, and you yourselves, being carried off by them, were set free by that firm-bowed one.

**7.160.18**  The Nivātakavacas, too, the foes of the gods, who could not be slain in battle by the celestials, were conquered by that hero.

**7.160.19**  Thousands of dānavas dwelling in Hiraṇyapura that tiger among men subdued—how then can he be withstood by mortal men?

**7.160.20**  And it is before your very eyes that this whole host of yours has been wasted by the son of Pāṇḍu, while we strove on, O lord of the people.

**7.160.21**  As Droṇa thus extolled Arjuna, your son, enraged, O king, spoke to him once more these words.

**7.160.22**  I, Duḥśāsana, Karṇa, and Śakuni my maternal uncle shall slay Arjuna in battle this day, after dividing the Bhārata host in two.

**7.160.23**  Hearing that speech of his, the son of Bharadvāja, as though laughing, fell in with the king and said, "May it be well with you."

**7.160.24**  For who—what warrior—could destroy the wielder of Gāṇḍīva, blazing as if with splendor, the inexhaustible one, that bull among warriors?

**7.160.25**  Him neither the lord of wealth, nor Indra, nor Yama, nor the lord of the waters, nor asuras, serpents, and rākṣasas could destroy, weapons and all.

**7.160.26**  Only fools speak such things as those you utter, O Bhārata; for having met Arjuna in battle, who could return home unscathed?

**7.160.27**  But you, suspicious of everyone, harsh, fixed upon evil, would have those devoted to your welfare speak now this thing and now that.

**7.160.28**  Go yourself, then, against the son of Kuntī—delay not, for your own sake; you too hope to fight, for you are nobly born and a warrior.

**7.160.29**  Why will you have all these kings, who are guiltless, slain? You are the root of this enmity—therefore go yourself against Arjuna.

**7.160.30**  Here is your wise maternal uncle, the son of Gāndhāra, devoted to the warrior's duty—that gambler of crooked dice—let him march against Arjuna in battle.

**7.160.31**  This man, skilled at dice, crooked, a gamester, a cheat, a deceiver, a player versed in trickery, shall conquer the Pāṇḍavas in battle!

**7.160.32**  Endlessly have you and Karṇa boasted in your glee, again and again, vainly and out of folly, in the very hearing of Dhṛtarāṣṭra:

**7.160.33**  "I, dear son, and Karṇa, and my brother Duḥśāsana—we three together shall slay the sons of Pāṇḍu in battle."

**7.160.34**  Such boasting of yours has been heard in assembly after assembly—now make good that vow, and prove yourself a man of his word along with them.

**7.160.35**  Here stands before you the Pāṇḍava, your foe, not to be withstood—look to the warrior's duty; more praiseworthy for you is death than such a victory.

**7.160.36**  Gifts you have given, pleasures enjoyed, scriptures studied, and the lordship you longed for attained; your task is fulfilled and you are free of debt—fear not, fight the Pāṇḍava.

**7.160.37**  Having spoken thus, Droṇa turned in battle toward where the foes were, and then, the army being divided in two, the fight began once more.

**7.161.1**  Saṃjaya said: When but a third part of the night remained, the battle raged on between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, both filled with eager joy, O lord of the people.

**7.161.2**  Then Aruṇa, the forerunner of the sun, stealing away the splendor of the moon, brought on the dawn, making the heavens as if coppery red.

**7.161.3**  Then, the army being divided in two, Droṇa, with Duryodhana at his head, charged against the Somakas, the Pāṇḍavas, and the Pāñcālas.

**7.161.4**  Seeing the Kurus split in two, Mādhava said to Arjuna: "These foes, these Kurus, let me bring round to your left, O Savyasācin."

**7.161.5**  Granting Mādhava leave with the word "Do so," Dhanaṃjaya wheeled round, keeping the two great archers Droṇa and Karṇa to his left.

**7.161.6**  But the conqueror of hostile cities, learning Kṛṣṇa's intent and seeing Bhīmasena posted at the forefront of the fray, drew near to him.

**7.161.7**  Bhīma said: Arjuna, Arjuna, Bībhatsu, hear my words truly: the hour has come for which a warrior-woman bears a son.

**7.161.8**  If, now that this hour has come, you do not seize the better course, then, your worth set at naught, you will be playing the part of a coward in disguise of mercy.

**7.161.9**  By your valor pay off your debt to truth, to fortune, to duty, and to fame; break through the line, O best of fighters—make an end of these, O Savyasācin.

**7.161.10**  Saṃjaya said: That Savyasācin, urged on by Bhīma and by Keśava, passed beyond Karṇa and Droṇa and beset the foe on every side.

**7.161.11**  As he came on at the forefront of the fray, consuming those bulls among warriors, the bulls among warriors strove with all their might against him, yet could not check him, growing as he was like a kindled fire.

**7.161.12**  Then Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni the son of Subala rained down floods of arrows upon Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī.

**7.161.13**  Setting at naught the weapons of all of them, that foremost of those who know the highest weapons, O king of kings, overwhelmed them with showers of arrows.

**7.161.14**  Warding off weapons with weapons, the light-handed Dhanaṃjaya pierced each of them with ten sharpened arrows apiece.

**7.161.15**  A storm of dust was raised up, and likewise a storm of arrows, and a fearful darkness, and a mighty din arose at that time.

**7.161.16**  Neither sky nor earth nor the quarters could be discerned, things having come to such a pass; bewildered by the dust raised by the army, all became as if blind.

**7.161.17**  Neither they nor we, O king, could make out one another; only by guesswork did the kings keep up the fight.

**7.161.18**  Car-warriors bereft of their chariots, O king, closing with one another, grappled by the hair, by the armor, and by the arms.

**7.161.19**  Car-warriors whose horses and charioteers were slain, motionless and stricken with fear, appeared there then as though scarcely alive.

**7.161.20**  The horses, clinging to slain elephants that lay like mountains, appeared lifeless, and so too did their riders along with them.

**7.161.21**  Then, withdrawing from the combat to the northern quarter, Droṇa stood in the battle like a smokeless fire.

**7.161.22**  But seeing him drawn off apart from the forefront of the fray, the armies of the Pāṇḍavas trembled, O lord of the people.

**7.161.23**  Beholding Droṇa, resplendent and graced with glory, blazing as if with splendor, the foes shook, wavered, and grew faint, O sire.

**7.161.24**  As he challenged the enemy host like an elephant in must, they did not reckon they could conquer him, even as the dānavas could not hope to conquer Vāsava.

**7.161.25**  Some were robbed of all spirit, some of the high-minded were filled with wrath, some became amazed, and some were seized with indignation.

**7.161.26**  Some of the kings ground their finger-tips against their hands, while others, swooning with anger, bit their lips with their teeth.

**7.161.27**  Some flung their weapons at him, others crushed his arms in their grip, and yet others, men of mighty vigor who had renounced all care for their lives, hurled themselves upon Droṇa.

**7.161.28**  The Pāñcālas above all, sorely afflicted by Droṇa's shafts and racked with anguish, closed with him in battle, O lord of kings.

**7.161.29**  Then Virāṭa and Drupada advanced against Droṇa in the fight as he ranged through the conflict, well-nigh unconquerable in war.

**7.161.30**  Then the three grandsons of Drupada, O lord of peoples, and the mighty bowmen of the Cedis bore down upon Droṇa in battle.

**7.161.31**  With three whetted arrows Droṇa took the lives of those three grandsons of Drupada, and slain they fell to the earth.

**7.161.32**  Then Droṇa conquered in the fight the Cedis, the Kekayas, and the Sṛñjayas, and the great chariot-warrior, son of Bharadvāja, vanquished all the Matsyas as well.

**7.161.33**  Then Drupada in his wrath poured down a rain of arrows upon Droṇa, O great king, and Virāṭa did likewise in the encounter.

**7.161.34**  Then Droṇa, crusher of foes, with two well-burnished broad-headed shafts dispatched both Drupada and Virāṭa to the abode of Vaivasvata.

**7.161.35**  When Virāṭa and Drupada were slain, and the Kekayas likewise, and the Cedis and Matsyas and Pāñcālas as well, and when the three heroes who were Drupada's grandsons had been killed—

**7.161.36**  beholding that deed of Droṇa, the high-minded Dhṛṣṭadyumna, filled with wrath and grief, swore an oath in the midst of the chariot-warriors:

**7.161.37**  "Let that man fall from the merit of his sacrifices and pious works, from his Kṣatriya estate and his Brahmin standing, who today lets Droṇa go free, or who turns his back upon Droṇa."

**7.161.38**  Having thus pledged himself in the midst of all the bowmen, the Pāñcāla prince, slayer of enemy heroes, advanced upon Droṇa together with his host; the Pāñcālas struck at Droṇa from one side and the Pāṇḍavas from the other.

**7.161.39**  And Duryodhana and Karṇa, and Śakuni the son of Subala, and his foremost brothers—these guarded Droṇa in the battle.

**7.161.40**  Droṇa being thus guarded in the fray by those great-souled warriors, the Pāñcālas, strive as they might, could not so much as look upon him.

**7.161.41**  Thereupon Bhīmasena grew angry with Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O venerable one, and that bull among men cut him with harsh words:

**7.161.42**  "Born in the line of Drupada, most learned in all weapons—what Kṣatriya worthy of the name would stand and merely gaze upon his foe before him?

**7.161.43**  Having suffered the slaying of his father and his sons, what man would let the matter slip—above all after swearing an oath in the assembly of kings?

**7.161.44**  Like the fire of Vaiśvānara kindled bright by its own splendor, this Droṇa, with bow and arrows for his fuel, consumes the Kṣatriya host with his blazing might.

**7.161.45**  Before he leaves the army of the Pāṇḍavas without a remnant—stand and watch my deed: I go straight against Droṇa myself."

**7.161.46**  Having spoken thus, Vṛkodara in his wrath plunged into Droṇa's division, scattering your army with firm shafts loosed from a bow drawn to the full.

**7.161.47**  Dhṛṣṭadyumna the Pāñcāla too, breaking into the great host, came upon Droṇa in the fight; and then a great tumult arose.

**7.161.48**  Never before had we seen or heard of such a battle as this, O king: at sunrise a great confusion arose.

**7.161.49**  Throngs of chariots were seen locked together, O venerable one, and the bodies of the slain lay scattered all about.

**7.161.50**  Some, making their way elsewhere, were set upon by others on the road; some who had turned away were struck from behind, and others were struck upon the flank.

**7.161.51**  So that close-grappled fighting grew exceedingly terrible; and presently the sun reached the twilight hour.

**7.162.1**  Saṃjaya said: Even so, O great king, those warriors in their armor, at the forefront of battle, did homage to the thousand-rayed sun as it came to the hour of twilight.

**7.162.2**  But when the thousand-rayed one rose again, gleaming like molten gold, and the worlds were lit with its light, the battle was renewed.

**7.162.3**  Those single combats which had been joined there before the dawn, O Bhārata, were taken up afresh when the sun had risen.

**7.162.4**  Horses met chariots, elephants met horses, foot-soldiers met the great tuskers, horse closed with horse and foot-soldier with foot-soldier; and the warriors, locked together and torn apart, fell upon one another in the battle.

**7.162.5**  Spent with their night-long labors, and now scorched by the sun's heat, their limbs beset by hunger and thirst, many of them swooned away.

**7.162.6**  Of the conches, kettledrums, and tabors, of the trumpeting elephants, and of the bows stretched wide and twanging—

**7.162.7**  a din arose, O king, that touched the very heavens, O bull of the Bhāratas—the noise of fleeing foot-soldiers and of weapons hurled down,

**7.162.8**  of horses neighing and chariots wheeling about, of men crying out and roaring—and a great tumult arose.

**7.162.9**  Swelling ever greater, the tumultuous roar mounted to the sky in a mighty voice; and the anguished cries of those mangled by manifold weapons, writhing where they lay,

**7.162.10**  were heard loud upon the earth; and great was the misery then—of foot-soldiers, horses, chariots, and elephants falling and fallen.

**7.162.11**  As all those hosts became entangled together in countless ways, one's own struck down one's own, foes struck one's own, one's own struck foes, and foes struck foes.

**7.162.12**  Swords loosed by the arms of heroes flashed among the warriors and the elephants like washermen's paddles at the washing of garments.

**7.162.13**  Of the blades raised high and beaten together by the arms of heroes there came that very sound, as of garments being pounded at the wash.

**7.162.14**  With half-swords and broadswords, with lances and battle-axes, a great close-quarters fight was joined, hand to hand and exceedingly terrible.

**7.162.15**  Rising from the bodies of elephants and horses, bearing along the corpses of men, well filled with weapons for its fish, its mire made of flesh and blood,

**7.162.16**  loud with the cries of the stricken, foaming with banners and garments—such a river the heroes set flowing, that bore men onward to the other world.

**7.162.17**  Tormented by arrows and spears, worn out, their wits dulled and bewildered by the night, the elephants and horses stood there, bracing every limb; and the heroes, their faces parched, with their heads adorned by lovely earrings—

**7.162.18**  and with the other implements of war glittering here and there, with the dead and the half-dead, and thronged by packs of carrion-eaters, the whole battlefield was so strewn that there was no path left for a chariot anywhere upon it.

**7.162.19**  As the wheels sank deep, the horses—mustering their spirit—somehow dragged the chariots on, weary, trembling, tormented by arrows, those steeds endowed with good breeding, mettle, and strength, the equals of elephants.

**7.162.20**  All that host, O Bhārata, was then reeling, frenzied, fearful, and distressed—save only those two, Droṇa and Arjuna.

**7.162.21**  They two were the refuge, they two the recourse of the afflicted; yet others, approaching those two, went only to the abode of Vaivasvata.

**7.162.22**  The whole great army of the Kauravas was thrown into confusion, and so too the host of the Pāñcālas locked with it; nothing whatever could be made out.

**7.162.23**  As that great destruction of the royal houses arose upon the earth—like the playground of Death, swelling the terror of the timid—

**7.162.24**  there neither Karṇa nor Droṇa, neither Arjuna nor Yudhiṣṭhira, neither Bhīmasena nor the twins, neither the Pāñcāla prince nor Sātyaki,

**7.162.25**  nor Duḥśāsana, nor Droṇa's son, nor Duryodhana and the son of Subala, nor Kṛpa, nor the king of the Madras, nor even Kṛtavarman—

**7.162.26**  nor any others, nor even our own selves, nor the earth, nor the quarters of the sky—none of these could we see, O king, all locked in the press of the host and veiled in dust.

**7.162.27**  When the whirling, dreadful tumult arose and a cloud of dust mounted up, men deemed that a second night had come upon them.

**7.162.28**  The Kauravas were not to be known, nor the Pāñcālas, nor the Pāṇḍavas; neither the quarters, nor the sky, nor the earth, nor level ground from broken could be told apart.

**7.162.29**  Whomever came within the touch of their hands, whether foe or even one of their own, the men, eager for victory, struck down in that battle.

**7.162.30**  But because the dust had been thrown up, and through the sprinkling of blood, and through the swiftness of the wind, the dust of the earth was laid.

**7.162.31**  There the elephants, horses, warriors, chariot-fighters, and foot-soldiers, drenched in blood, shone like groves of pārijāta in flower.

**7.162.32**  Then Duryodhana, Karṇa, Droṇa, and Duḥśāsana—four chariot-warriors—closed in combat with four of the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.162.33**  Duryodhana with his brother engaged the twins, Rādheya engaged Vṛkodara, and Arjuna engaged the son of Bharadvāja.

**7.162.34**  That dread and mighty marvel all beheld on every side—the superhuman clash of those fierce bulls among chariot-warriors.

**7.162.35**  With their varied chariot-courses, all crowded with wondrous cars, the chariot-fighters watched the marvelous battle of those warriors who fought in marvelous ways.

**7.162.36**  Straining and valorous, each longing to overcome the other, they showered down their rains of arrows like thunderclouds at the close of the hot season.

**7.162.37**  Mounted upon their chariots bright as the sun, those bulls among men shone like autumn clouds drawn up together.

**7.162.38**  Those rival mighty bowmen, putting forth their utmost effort, the bearers of the bow, went at one another like rutting bull-elephants.

**7.162.39**  Surely the body knows no breaking when its appointed hour has not yet come—for there not all those great chariot-warriors perished together at once.

**7.162.40**  With severed arms and legs, with heads adorned by lovely earrings, with bows, arrows, javelins, swords, axes, and spears,

**7.162.41**  with nālīka shafts, razor-edged and iron arrows, with claw-spikes, lances, and pikes, and with other excellent burnished weapons of manifold forms,

**7.162.42**  with bright body-armor of many shapes, with wondrous chariots shattered, and with slain elephants and horses,

**7.162.43**  with empty chariots vast as towns, their warriors slain and their banners cut down, and with riderless, terrified horses dragging them this way and that,

**7.162.44**  with steeds running swift as the wind again and again, decked out yet their heroes slain, with fans and coats of mail and banners fallen down,

**7.162.45**  with parasols, ornaments, garments, and sweetly fragrant garlands, with necklaces, diadems, crowns, turbans, and clusters of little bells,

**7.162.46**  with breast-jewels, golden ornaments, and crest-gems, the battlefield there was strewn as the sky is strewn with the host of stars.

**7.162.47**  Then there came an encounter between Duryodhana and Nakula—the one wrathful and indignant, the other indignant and wrathful.

**7.162.48**  Then the son of Mādrī wheeled rightward about your son, joyfully scattering arrows by the hundred; and a great roar went up at that.

**7.162.49**  Circled rightward in the battle by his exceedingly indignant cousin, he too in his indignation wheeled rightward about him in turn.

**7.162.50**  But as your son sought to wheel rightward in return, the brilliant Nakula, skilled in wondrous maneuvers, held him back.

**7.162.51**  Checking him on every side and pressing him with a net of arrows, Nakula made him turn away; and the soldiers applauded that feat.

**7.162.52**  "Stand, stand!" cried Nakula to your son, calling to mind all the sorrows brought about by your ill counsel.

**7.163.1**  Saṃjaya said: Then Duḥśāsana in his wrath rushed upon Sahadeva, all but making the earth tremble with the fierce speed of his chariot.

**7.163.2**  As he bore swiftly down, the son of Mādrī, that scourge of foes, with a broad-headed shaft severed the head of his charioteer, helmet and all.

**7.163.3**  Neither Duḥśāsana nor any soldier marked that the charioteer's head had been struck off by Sahadeva, so swiftly was it done.

**7.163.4**  But when the horses, no longer held in check, ran on at their own pleasure, then Duḥśāsana realized that his charioteer had lost his senses.

**7.163.5**  Skilled himself in handling horses, he reined them in upon the field and, foremost of chariot-warriors, fought on with a craft at once dazzling, swift, and sure.

**7.163.6**  Both his own men and his foes in that battle honored this feat of his—that with charioteer slain he ranged across the field as one without fear.

**7.163.7**  But Sahadeva covered those horses with his sharp arrows, and tormented by the shafts they at once bolted this way and that.

**7.163.8**  Since the reins entangled him, he let go his bow; and when he plied his bow in action, he again let go the reins.

**7.163.9**  In those openings the son of Mādrī covered him with arrows; but Karṇa, seeking to save your son, swooped into the breach.

**7.163.10**  Then Vṛkodara struck Karṇa with three well-aimed broad-headed shafts, drawn back to the ear, upon both arms and on the chest, and roared aloud.

**7.163.11**  Karṇa turned upon him like a serpent that has been trodden on, and then there arose a tumultuous battle between Bhīma and the son of Rādhā.

**7.163.12**  Like two enraged bulls, both with eyes rolling, the two in fury fell upon each other with tremendous speed.

**7.163.13**  As those two passionate warriors closed and locked together, and the fall of their arrows could no longer divide them, the fight turned to a duel of maces.

**7.163.14**  With his mace Bhīmasena at once shattered the pole of Karṇa's chariot, O king, and that seemed a marvel.

**7.163.15**  Then the valiant son of Rādhā took up a mace and hurled it at Bhīma's chariot; but Bhīma with his own mace broke that mace asunder.

**7.163.16**  Then Bhīma again flung a heavy mace at the charioteer; but Karṇa struck it back with ten well-feathered, well-aimed shafts, and then with others, so that it returned once more toward Bhīma.

**7.163.17**  By the recoiling fall of that mace Bhīma's tall banner came down, and his charioteer, struck by it, swooned away.

**7.163.18**  Maddened with wrath, he loosed eight arrows at Karṇa—at his banner, his bow, and his quiver, O Bhārata.

**7.163.19**  Then again the son of Rādhā with chariot-shafts swiftly slew his antelope-colored horses, and both his flank-guarding drivers as well.

**7.163.20**  His chariot disabled, Bhīma the foe-subduer leapt onto Nakula's car, as a lion springs to a mountain peak.

**7.163.21**  Meanwhile Droṇa and Arjuna, those great chariot-warriors, teacher and pupil, both masters of striking in battle, fought on wondrously, O lord of kings.

**7.163.22**  With swift nocking of arrows and with the wheeling combat of their two cars, they bewildered both the eyes and the minds of men.

**7.163.23**  Our warriors and the foes alike all paused, beholding that never-before-seen combat of teacher and pupil.

**7.163.24**  As they drove their cars in wondrous, ever-shifting courses through the midst of the army, each hero sought to keep the other on his right; and the warriors gazed upon their prowess, filled with amazement.

**7.163.25**  Mighty was the battle that arose between those two, Droṇa and the son of Pāṇḍu, O great king, like that of two hawks in the sky contending for a piece of flesh.

**7.163.26**  Whatever Droṇa attempted in his desire to defeat the son of Kuntī, all of it the Pāṇḍava at once countered, laughing the while.

**7.163.27**  When Droṇa found he could not gain the upper hand over the Pāṇḍava, then, skilled in the ways of celestial weapons, he brought forth his missiles.

**7.163.28**  The weapons of Indra, of Paśupati, of Tvaṣṭṛ, of Vāyu, and of Varuṇa—each as it sped from Droṇa's bow, Dhanaṃjaya struck down.

**7.163.29**  When the Pāṇḍava duly quelled his weapons with weapons, Droṇa then overwhelmed Pārtha with the highest celestial missiles.

**7.163.30**  Whatever weapon he loosed at Pārtha in his will to conquer, Arjuna fashioned the very means to undo that weapon.

**7.163.31**  As Arjuna duly quelled even his celestial weapons, Droṇa honored Arjuna within his very heart.

**7.163.32**  And he reckoned himself, O Bhārata, exalted upon the earth above all who know the use of arms, by reason of such a pupil.

**7.163.33**  Held in check by Pārtha thus before the great-souled host, yet striving on, with a smile and with affection he warded Arjuna off in turn.

**7.163.34**  Then in the firmament the gods and gandharvas by the thousand, the sages and the hosts of siddhas, took their stand, eager to behold.

**7.163.35**  Thronged with apsarases and crowded with yakṣas and rākṣasas, the splendid sky grew dense as though massed with clouds.

**7.163.36**  There unseen voices passed back and forth again and again, joined in praise of Droṇa and of the great-souled Pārtha, as the weapons were loosed, setting the ten directions ablaze.

**7.163.37**  "This is no human combat, nor of the asuras, nor of the rākṣasas, nor of the gods, nor of the gandharvas; surely this is supreme and Brahmic. Wondrous and marvelous is this—never have we seen its like, nor heard of it."

**7.163.38**  "The teacher surpasses the Pāṇḍava, and the Pāṇḍava surpasses Droṇa; no difference between the two can be discerned by any weapon."

**7.163.39**  "Were Rudra to divide himself in two and fight himself against himself, there a comparison might be drawn—but nowhere else is it to be found."

**7.163.40**  "In the teacher knowledge dwells alone; in the Pāṇḍava, knowledge and discipline both. In the teacher valor dwells alone; in the Pāṇḍava, strength and valor both."

**7.163.41**  "These two great bowmen cannot be flung down in battle by their foes; and should they so will it, the two could slay the whole world together with its gods."

**7.163.42**  Thus spoke, O great king, beholding those two bulls among men, the invisible beings and the visible ones, in throng upon throng.

**7.163.43**  Then the great-minded Droṇa brought forth the Brāhma weapon, scorching in the battle both Pārtha and the unseen beings.

**7.163.44**  Then the earth trembled with its mountains, forests, and trees; a turbulent wind blew, and the oceans too were stirred to their depths.

**7.163.45**  Then great terror seized the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, and indeed all beings, when that weapon was raised by the great-souled one.

**7.163.46**  Then Pārtha too, unshaken, quelled that weapon with the Brahmā weapon itself, O lord of kings, and so brought all to calm.

**7.163.47**  When neither of the two could be brought to the end of the other, then by a confused melee that combat was thrown into disorder.

**7.163.48**  Thereafter nothing whatever could be made out, O lord of the people, once the tumultuous fray of Droṇa and the Pāṇḍava was joined upon the field.

**7.163.49**  With the sky overspread by nets of arrows as by masses of cloud, not a single creature that moves through the air could fly there then.

**7.164.1**  Saṃjaya said: While that slaughter of men, horses, and elephants was thus going on, Duḥśāsana, O great king, did battle with Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

**7.164.2**  He, mounted on his golden car and sore wounded by Duḥśāsana's arrows, in his wrath covered the horses of your son with his shafts.

**7.164.3**  In an instant that chariot of his, with its banner and its charioteer, was no longer to be seen, O great king, so thickly was it studded with the arrows of Pārṣata.

**7.164.4**  But Duḥśāsana, O lord of kings, harried by the nets of arrows, could not stand before the great-souled prince of the Pāñcālas.

**7.164.5**  And Pārṣata, having turned Duḥśāsana away with his arrows, scattering thousands of shafts, advanced upon Droṇa himself in the battle.

**7.164.6**  The son of Hṛdika, Kṛtavarman, moved into the breach, and three brothers as well, and they hemmed him in on every side.

**7.164.7**  The twins, those bulls among men, followed close behind to guard him as he bore down on Droṇa, blazing like fire.

**7.164.8**  All those seven great chariot-warriors joined battle, wrathful and resolute, having set death itself before them.

**7.164.9**  Pure of soul and pure of conduct, O king, with heaven held before them, they waged a noble fight, each longing to conquer the other.

**7.164.10**  Of stainless birth and stainless deeds, those wise lords of men fought a righteous fight, with eyes fixed upon the highest goal.

**7.164.11**  There was nothing unrighteous in that combat, no fighting without proper weapons; no barbed arrow was there, no hollow reed-shaft, no poisoned dart, nor any double-headed one.

**7.164.12**  No needle-pointed shaft was there, no brown one, none tipped with the bone of ox or elephant; no arrow was barbed, none foul, and none that flew crooked.

**7.164.13**  Straight and pure alone were all the weapons they bore, as they sought through fair fighting the higher worlds and renown besides.

**7.164.14**  Then there was a tumultuous combat, free of every fault, between four of your warriors and those three of the Pāṇḍava side.

**7.164.15**  But Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O king, leaving those bulls among your chariot-warriors—seeing them held off by the twins—and swift with his weapons, advanced upon Droṇa.

**7.164.16**  Held back by those two lions among men, the four heroes closed together with them, like winds dashing between two mountains.
