**7.164.17**  The twins, those foremost of chariot-warriors, each engaged two cars; and meanwhile Dhṛṣṭadyumna bore down upon Droṇa.

**7.164.18**  Seeing the Pāñcāla, battle-frenzied, advancing upon Droṇa, and those others locked in combat with the twins, Duryodhana rushed into the gap.

**7.164.19**  Duryodhana, O great king, scattering arrows that drink blood; but Sātyaki, swifter still, turned again to meet him.

**7.164.20**  Drawing near to each other, those two—the Kuru and the Mādhava, tigers among men—came together fearless and laughing.

**7.164.21**  Recalling with fondness all that had passed between them in their boyhood, they gazed upon one another and laughed again and again.

**7.164.22**  Then King Duryodhana spoke in answer to Sātyaki, his ever-dear friend, reproaching his own conduct:

**7.164.23**  "A curse upon anger, O friend, a curse upon greed, a curse upon delusion, a curse upon wrath! A curse upon the way of the warrior, and a curse upon brute strength of the breast!"

**7.164.24**  "—that you should take aim at me, and I at you, O bull of the Śini race! For you are dearer to me than my own life, and I have ever been so to you."

**7.164.25**  "I remember all those things that passed between us in our boyhood; but now upon the field of battle all of it is undone. What else but through anger and greed do I fight you this day, O Sātvata?"

**7.164.26**  To him who spoke thus, O king, Sātyaki, master of the highest weapons, made answer with a laugh, raising aloft his sharp shafts:

**7.164.27**  "This is no assembly hall, O prince, nor the teacher's dwelling, where once, O king, we sported together when we met."

**7.164.28**  Duryodhana said: "Whither has that play of our boyhood gone, O bull of the Śini race, and whence again has this battle come? For time is hard to overpass."

**7.164.29**  "What need have we of wealth, or of the craving for wealth, that here we all do battle, gathered together out of greed for riches?"

**7.164.30**  Saṃjaya said: To the king who spoke thus the Mādhava replied: "Such has ever been the way of the warrior, that here he slays even his elders."

**7.164.31**  "If I am dear to you, O king, then slay me, and do not delay; through you may I go to the worlds won by good deeds, O bull of the Bhāratas."

**7.164.32**  "What power and strength are yours, show them quickly upon me; I do not wish to behold this—the great calamity that befalls one's friends."

**7.164.33**  Having spoken plainly thus and made his reply, Sātyaki advanced swiftly, unperturbed and heedless of all, O lord of the people.

**7.164.34**  Beholding him as he came on, your son met him, and your son covered Śaineya with arrows, O king.

**7.164.35**  Then a terrible battle broke out between those two lions, the Kuru and the Mādhava, each enraged against the other, like a duel between an elephant and a lion.

**7.164.36**  Then Duryodhana struck the Sātvata, that warrior frenzied for battle, in return with ten sharp arrows loosed from a fully drawn bow.

**7.164.37**  Sātyaki struck him back likewise with ten arrows, and again in that fight with fifty, with thirty, and with ten more.

**7.164.38**  As Duryodhana was fitting his shafts, Sātyaki swiftly cut apart his bow with its arrow already nocked, and rained his own shafts down upon him.

**7.164.39**  Pierced deep and shaken, O great king, Duryodhana, tormented by the arrows of the Dāśārha, withdrew to another chariot.

**7.164.40**  But once he had recovered, your son again advanced upon Sātyaki, loosing networks of arrows against the chariot of Yuyudhāna.

**7.164.41**  And so Sātyaki too loosed his arrows in a steady stream against Duryodhana's chariot, O king, and a tumult of close fighting arose.

**7.164.42**  There, from the arrows hurled and falling on every side, a great roar arose, like fire raging through a vast thicket.

**7.164.43**  Seeing the Mādhava, that foremost of chariot-warriors, gaining the upper hand, Karṇa swiftly rushed in, eager to save your son.

**7.164.44**  But the mighty Bhīmasena would not endure this; he rushed swiftly upon Karṇa, loosing many shafts.

**7.164.45**  Karṇa, as if laughing, beat back his sharp arrows, cut apart his bow and shafts, and struck down his charioteer with his own arrows.

**7.164.46**  But Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava, enraged, took up his mace and in the battle crushed the banner, bow, and charioteer of his foe.

**7.164.47**  Unable to bear this, Karṇa fought against Bhīmasena in the encounter with manifold networks of arrows and with weapons of every kind.

**7.164.48**  While the press of battle raged on, the king, the son of Dharma, spoke to the tigers among men of the Pāñcālas and the bulls among men of the Matsyas:

**7.164.49**  "Those who are our very breath, who are our head, our warriors of mighty strength — those bulls among men are now locked in struggle against the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."

**7.164.50**  "Why do you stand here, all of you, like bewildered men robbed of your wits? Go there, where these chariot-warriors of mine are fighting!"

**7.164.51**  "Setting the warrior's duty foremost, every one of you with your fevered fear cast off — whether conquering or slain, you shall attain the destiny you desire."

**7.164.52**  "And conquering, you shall offer many sacrifices with abundant gifts; or slain, having passed into the company of the gods, you shall attain bountiful worlds."

**7.164.53**  Urged on by the king, those heroes, the great chariot-warriors eager to fight, formed their host into four divisions and swiftly advanced upon Droṇa.

**7.164.54**  From one side the Pāñcālas assailed Droṇa with many arrows, and from another those led by Bhīmasena hemmed him in.

**7.164.55**  Among the sons of Pāṇḍu there were three unswerving great chariot-warriors — the twins and Bhīmasena — and they cried out to Dhanaṃjaya:

**7.164.56**  "Charge swiftly, Arjuna! Drive the Kurus away from Droṇa, and then the Pāñcālas will slay him, his protector removed."

**7.164.57**  Then Pārtha rushed suddenly upon the Kauravas, while Droṇa fell upon the Pāñcālas led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

**7.164.58**  Then Droṇa too wrought great slaughter among the Pāñcālas, as Śakra in his wrath had once wrought the destruction of the Dānavas in battle.

**7.164.59**  Though slaughtered by Droṇa's weapon in the fight, O great king, those great chariot-warriors of resolute spirit did not flinch from Droṇa in the battle.

**7.164.60**  Though being slaughtered, O great king, the Pāñcālas and the Sṛñjayas pressed on against Droṇa in the fight, bewildering that great chariot-warrior.

**7.164.61**  As those Pāñcālas were being cut down on every side, slain by arrows and lances, a fearful cry arose among them.

**7.164.62**  As the Pāñcālas were being slaughtered in the battle by that great soul, and as Droṇa's weapon raged on, fear entered into the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.164.63**  Seeing the vast destruction of their hosts of horses and men in the fight, the Pāṇḍavas, O great king, then despaired of victory.

**7.164.64**  "Will not Droṇa, master of the supreme weapons, destroy us all — like a blazing fire at winter's end consuming dry brushwood?"

**7.164.65**  "None in battle is able even to look him in the face, nor would Arjuna, who knows what is right, ever fight against him."

**7.164.66**  Seeing the sons of Kuntī terrified and tormented by Droṇa's arrows, the wise Keśava, intent upon their welfare, spoke to Arjuna:

**7.164.67**  "This commander of the leaders of chariot-bands can in no way be conquered in open battle, not even by the Slayer of Vṛtra himself."

**7.164.68**  "For the sake of victory, O Pāṇḍava, let some stratagem be employed, setting aside strict righteousness, so that he of the golden chariot may not slay you all in the encounter."

**7.164.69**  "It is my belief that, were Aśvatthāman slain, he would fight no more. Let some man announce to him that his son has been slain in battle."

**7.164.70**  This did not please the son of Kuntī, Dhanaṃjaya, O king; but all the others approved of it, and Yudhiṣṭhira only with great reluctance.

**7.164.71**  Then mighty-armed Bhīma, within his own ranks, slew with his mace a great elephant named Aśvatthāman, O king.

**7.164.72**  Then Bhīmasena, somewhat abashed, approached Droṇa in the battle and cried aloud, "Aśvatthāman is slain!"

**7.164.73**  It was the elephant known by the name Aśvatthāman that had been slain; keeping that in his mind, Bhīma then spoke falsely.

**7.164.74**  Hearing Bhīmasena's words, that most unwelcome news, Droṇa grew limp in his limbs in spirit, like a bank of sand in water.

**7.164.75**  Suspecting it to be false, for he knew his own son's valor, and hearing "He is slain," he did not waver from his steadfastness.

**7.164.76**  Regaining his composure, Droṇa recovered himself in but a moment, reflecting that his own son was invincible to his foes.

**7.164.77**  Rushing upon the son of Pṛṣata, seeking to slay him who was his own death, he covered him with a thousand sharp heron-feathered arrows.

**7.164.78**  As he ranged thus through the battle, twenty thousand of those bulls among men of the Pāñcālas showered him with arrows from every side.

**7.164.79**  Then Droṇa, scorcher of foes, in his fury brought forth the Brāhma weapon for the destruction of those heroic Pāñcālas.

**7.164.80**  Then Droṇa blazed forth, striking down all the Somakas; in that great battle he made the heads of the Pāñcālas fall, and likewise their arms, shaped like iron clubs and adorned with gold.

**7.164.81**  Those kings, slaughtered in battle by the son of Bharadvāja, were strewn upon the earth like trees felled by the wind.

**7.164.82**  With elephants and floods of horses falling, O descendant of Bharata, the earth, a mire of flesh and blood, became impassable to behold.

**7.164.83**  Having slain twenty thousand bands of Pāñcāla chariot-warriors, Droṇa stood in the battle blazing like a smokeless fire.

**7.164.84**  And so once more the mighty son of Bharadvāja in his wrath struck off the head of Vasudāna from his body with a broad-headed shaft.

**7.164.85**  Again, slaying five hundred Matsyas and six thousand Sṛñjayas and ten thousand elephants, he then slew ten thousand horses as well.

**7.164.86**  Seeing Droṇa set upon the annihilation of the warriors, the seers swiftly drew near, led by the Bearer of Oblations.

**7.164.87**  Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, and Gautama, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, and Atri, desiring to lead him to the world of Brahmā —

**7.164.88**  the Sikatās, the Pṛśnis, the Gargas, the Vālakhilyas, the Marīcipas, the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases, and other subtle great seers —

**7.164.89**  all these said to Droṇa, resplendent in battle: "Unrighteously has this war been waged; the hour of your death has come."

**7.164.90**  "Lay down your weapon in the battle, O Droṇa, and come to join us who stand here. You ought not again to do a deed more cruel than this."

**7.164.91**  "For you who know the Vedas and their auxiliaries, who are devoted to truth and righteousness, and a Brāhmaṇa above all — this is unbecoming."

**7.164.92**  "Lay down your weapon, O you whose shafts never miss; stand upon the eternal path. Your time for dwelling in this human world is now fulfilled."

**7.164.93**  Hearing these words of theirs, and those words of Bhīmasena, and beholding Dhṛṣṭadyumna in the battle, he became downcast in spirit.

**7.164.94**  Burning within and troubled, he asked Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, whether his own son was unslain or slain.

**7.164.95**  For Droṇa was firm in his conviction that Pārtha would not speak a falsehood, not even for the lordship of all three worlds.

**7.164.96**  Therefore he questioned him in particular and no other; for in that Pāṇḍava his hope of truth had rested from boyhood.

**7.164.97**  Then, knowing that Droṇa, that lord of warriors, was about to make the earth bereft of the Pāṇḍavas, Govinda, troubled, spoke to the King of Righteousness:

**7.164.98**  "If Droṇa, possessed by wrath, fights for half a day longer, I tell you truly: your army will go to its destruction."

**7.164.99**  "Therefore save us from Droṇa: a falsehood here may be greater than truth. He who utters an untruth to save a life is not tainted by untruths."

**7.164.100**  As the two were thus speaking together, Bhīmasena, having heard of that device for slaying the great soul, said this, O great king:

**7.164.101**  "As I was plunging into your host, there was an elephant named Aśvatthāman, like unto the elephant of Śakra, belonging to Indravarman the Mālava;"

**7.164.102**  "him I valiantly slew in the fight, and then I said to Droṇa: 'Aśvatthāman is slain, O Brāhmaṇa; withdraw from the battle!'"

**7.164.103**  "Surely this bull among men did not believe my word. So now do you honor the words of Govinda, who desires victory."

**7.164.104**  "Declare to Droṇa, O king, that the son of Śāradvatī is slain. Told so by you, this bull among the twice-born would surely fight no more, O king; for in this world of men you are renowned as truthful, O ruler of peoples."

**7.164.105**  Hearing those words of his, urged on by the words of Kṛṣṇa, and because of what was destined to be, O great king, Yudhiṣṭhira set himself to speak.

**7.164.106**  Sunk in dread of the untruth yet clinging to victory, Yudhiṣṭhira said indistinctly, O king, "He is slain" — and under his breath, "the elephant."

**7.164.107**  Before this his chariot had stood four finger-breadths above the earth; but when he had spoken thus, his horses touched the ground.

**7.164.108**  Hearing those words from Yudhiṣṭhira, Droṇa, the great chariot-warrior, scorched by grief at his son's calamity, lost all hope of life.

**7.164.109**  Deeming himself an offender against the great-souled Pāṇḍavas, and pondering the words of the seers, and having heard his son was slain —

**7.164.110**  bewildered and stricken with the deepest dismay, and looking upon Dhṛṣṭadyumna, he was no longer able to fight as before, O king, O subduer of foes.

**7.164.111**  Seeing him utterly distraught, his mind overwhelmed by grief, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of the Pāñcāla king, rushed upon him.

**7.164.112**  He who, when the lord of men Drupada had sacrificed at the great rite, had been obtained for Droṇa's destruction from the blazing Bearer of Oblations —

**7.164.113**  he, taking up his victorious bow, terrible, roaring like a thundercloud, firm-stringed, undecaying, and divine, and arrows like venomous serpents —

**7.164.114**  the Pāñcāla, seeking to slay Droṇa, fitted to that bow a shaft like a venomous serpent, like a vast-flaming fire.

**7.164.115**  The form of that arrow, set within the circle of the bowstring, shone like the blazing sun ringed with a halo at the breaking of the clouds.

**7.164.116**  When the son of Pṛṣata grasped that bow, it seemed to blaze; and the soldiers, beholding it, deemed that their final hour had come.

**7.164.117**  Seeing that arrow fitted to the string by him, the mighty son of Bharadvāja judged that the appointed turn of his body's end had come.

**7.164.118**  Then, O lord of kings, the teacher set himself to ward off that shaft, yet the celestial weapons of the great-souled one would not come forth.

**7.164.119**  For four days and one night his weapons had served him without fail, but by a third part of that day his winged shafts ran out.

**7.164.120**  His arrows spent, afflicted by grief for his son, and finding the manifold celestial weapons no longer favorable to him—

**7.164.121**  —wishing to lay down his arms, urged on by the words of the brāhmaṇas, yet driven still by his own splendor, he fought on more than mortally.

**7.164.122**  Then, taking up another celestial bow, that of the Aṅgirases, and arrows like the rod of Brahmā, he gave battle to Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

**7.164.123**  Then with a great rain of arrows he overwhelmed him, and the wrathful, unforgiving one beat Dhṛṣṭadyumna back.

**7.164.124**  Droṇa cut that arrow of his into a hundred pieces with his shafts, and with keen darts he felled his banner, his bow, and his charioteer as well.

**7.164.125**  Dhṛṣṭadyumna, laughing, took up another bow and pierced him in return between the breasts with a sharpened arrow.

**7.164.126**  That mighty archer, deeply wounded, as if bewildered in the fray, with a keen-edged broad-headed shaft cut asunder his great bow.

**7.164.127**  And whatever arrow he sent, and his bows besides, O lord of peoples, the unassailable one cut them all to pieces, and his mace and his sword as well.

**7.164.128**  Then the scorcher of foes, enraged, pierced the wrathful-looking Dhṛṣṭadyumna with nine keen arrows that bring life to its end.

**7.164.129**  That great chariot-warrior of measureless soul mingled the horses of Dhṛṣṭadyumna's car with the horses of his own, and loosed the Brāhma weapon.

**7.164.130**  Thus mingled, those swift steeds, fleet as the wind, shone splendidly—some dove-colored, some red, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.164.131**  As thundering clouds charged with lightning at the coming of the rains, so, O great king, they shone, intermingled at the head of the battle.

**7.164.132**  The pole-fastenings, the wheel-fastenings, and likewise the chariot-fastenings of Dhṛṣṭadyumna's car—all these that brāhmaṇa of measureless soul destroyed.

**7.164.133**  His bow severed, his car broken, his horses slain, his charioteer slain, the hero, fallen into the direst straits, laid hold of his mace.

**7.164.134**  As he hurled it, that great chariot-warrior Droṇa, enraged, whose valor was true, struck it down with his keen, barbless arrows.

**7.164.135**  Seeing his mace struck down by Droṇa's arrows, that tiger among men took up a spotless sword and a shining shield marked with a hundred moons.

**7.164.136**  In such a pass the Pāñcāla prince held, beyond doubt, that the time had surely come for slaying the foremost of teachers, that great-souled one.

**7.164.137**  Then, standing in the body of his own car, he advanced along the chariot-pole, raising aloft his sword and the shining shield of a hundred moons.

**7.164.138**  Seeking to accomplish a deed hard to do, the great chariot-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna desired to cleave the breast of the son of Bharadvāja in the fight.

**7.164.139**  He took his stand in the middle of the yoke, and upon the yoke-fastenings, and upon the hindquarters of the red steeds; and the soldiers honored that feat.

**7.164.140**  As he stood upon the yoke-rails and trod even upon the red horses, Droṇa could find no opening in him; and that was as though a marvel.

**7.164.141**  Swift as the wheeling of a hawk that hungers for its prey, even so was the onset of him who sought out Droṇa in the battle.

**7.164.142**  Then the enraged and valiant Droṇa, with the spear of his car, slew his horses—all of them, one by one—those steeds dove-gray in hue.

**7.164.143**  Slain, the horses of Dhṛṣṭadyumna fell to the earth, and the red steeds were loosed from the chariot-harness, O lord of peoples.

**7.164.144**  Seeing those horses slain by the foremost of brāhmaṇas, the son of Pṛṣata, that best of warriors, the son of Yajñasena, the great chariot-warrior, brooked it not.

**7.164.145**  Carless, that best of swordsmen seized his sword and rushed upon Droṇa, O king, as the son of Vinatā swoops upon a serpent.

**7.164.146**  His form, O king, as he sought to slay the son of Bharadvāja, shone like the supreme form of Viṣṇu in the slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu.

**7.164.147**  He moved through manifold paths, the one-and-twenty modes: wheeling, soaring up, weaving, leaping, advancing, gliding,

**7.164.148**  turning about and turning back—and bearing sword and shield, the son of Pṛṣata displayed the swooping strike and the upraised stroke.

**7.164.149**  Then with a thousand arrows that brāhmaṇa struck down, in the press of battle, the hundred-mooned shield, and the sword and buckler of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

**7.164.150**  Those arrows, called vaitastika, a span in length, that strike at close quarters in the grappling fight, belonged to Droṇa alone; none others possessed such shafts—

**7.164.151**  —save for Śāradvata, for Pārtha, for Droṇa's son, and for the son of Vikartana, for Pradyumna and Yuyudhāna, and for Abhimanyu—theirs too were such arrows.

**7.164.152**  Then the teacher fitted to his bow a firm, exceedingly keen arrow, seeking to slay his own pupil, dear to him as a son.

**7.164.153**  That arrow the bull of Śini's line cut through with ten keen shafts, before the very eyes of your son and of the great-souled Karṇa, and freed Dhṛṣṭadyumna, seized by the foremost of teachers.

**7.164.154**  And Sātyaki of true valor, ranging along the chariot-paths, passing between Droṇa and Karṇa and Kṛpa as well, O Bhārata—him the two great-souled ones, Viṣvaksena and Dhanaṃjaya, beheld.

**7.164.155**  They honored the Vārṣṇeya, crying "Well done! Well done!" as the unfaltering one struck down the celestial weapons of all in the fight; then Viṣvaksena and Dhanaṃjaya fell upon the host.

**7.164.156**  Then Dhanaṃjaya said to Kṛṣṇa: "Behold, O Keśava, the scion of the Madhus, sporting in the very midst of the foremost of great teachers!

**7.164.157**  Sātyaki of true valor gladdens me again and again, and the two sons of Mādrī, and Bhīma, and King Yudhiṣṭhira.

**7.164.158**  For by his training Sātyaki, unboastful, ranges through the battle, sporting among the great chariot-warriors—he who magnifies the glory of the Vṛṣṇis."

**7.164.159**  Him the Siddhas and the wondering soldiers acclaimed, beholding the invincible Sātvata in battle, crying "Well done! Well done!"; and the warriors of both sides honored him for his deeds.

**7.165.1**  Saṃjaya said: A cruel slaughter arose at that gathering of kings, like that of an enraged Rudra striking down the beasts.

**7.165.2**  With severed hands and heads, with bows, O Bhārata, with parasols struck down and with yak-tail whisks in the fray,

**7.165.3**  with broken-wheeled chariots, with great banners cast down, and with slain heroic horsemen, the earth was strewn over.

**7.165.4**  The warriors mangled by the fall of arrows, O best of the Kurus, were seen writhing in manifold contortions amid the great battle.

**7.165.5**  As the dreadful battle, like that of gods and demons, went on, the Dharma King Yudhiṣṭhira spoke to the kṣatriyas there: "Charge, you great chariot-warriors, girded for the fight, upon the pitcher-born one!

**7.165.6**  Here is the heroic son of Pṛṣata, joined in combat with the son of Bharadvāja, striving with all his might at the destruction of the son of Bharadvāja.

**7.165.7**  By such portents as we see in this great battle, the son of Pṛṣata, enraged, will today bring Droṇa down in the fight. Be you united, then, and press hard upon the pitcher-born one."

**7.165.8**  Commanded thus by Yudhiṣṭhira, the great chariot-warriors of the Sṛñjayas, girded for battle, rushed upon the son of Bharadvāja, eager to slay him.

**7.165.9**  As they all bore down upon him, the great chariot-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, charged them with speed, resolved that he must die.

**7.165.10**  When the one true to his vow set forth, the earth trembled, and winds blew with crashing thunderclaps, striking terror into the host.

**7.165.11**  And a great meteor fell, as if it had issued from the sun, seeming to set all aflame with its heat, seeming to portend some mighty terror.

**7.165.12**  The weapons of the son of Bharadvāja blazed up, O honored one, his chariots groaned exceedingly, and his horses let fall their tears.

**7.165.13**  The great chariot-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, seemed as one whose vigor had been struck away; and resolving upon the heaven-bound path of the seers who proclaim the Veda, he began, through a worthy fight, to give up his life-breaths.

**7.165.14**  Then, hemmed in on all four sides by Drupada's troops, Droṇa ranged through the battle, consuming the hosts of kṣatriyas.

**7.165.15**  The crusher of foes, having slain twenty thousand kṣatriyas, slew a hundred thousand more with his keen, sharp-pointed barbless shafts.

**7.165.16**  He stood firm in the battle, intent, like a smokeless fire, set upon the destruction of the kṣatriyas, having assumed the form of Brahman within himself.

**7.165.17**  The self-controlled Bhīma hastened toward the Pāñcāla prince, carless, stripped of all his weapons, yet unflinching and great of soul.

**7.165.18**  Then the crusher of foes, taking the Pāñcāla up onto his own car, looked upon Droṇa loosing his shafts close at hand, and spoke:

**7.165.19**  "No other man than you here dares to fight the teacher. Make haste to his slaying; upon you the burden is laid."

**7.165.20**  Thus addressed, the mighty-armed one swiftly seized a fresh and firm weapon, the choicest of arms, able to bear every strain.

**7.165.21**  And in fury, loosing his arrows, eager to hold back the teacher Droṇa, hard to ward off in battle, he overwhelmed him with showers of shafts.

**7.165.22**  Those two foremost warriors, wrathful, the glory of the battlefield, held each other in check, and again and again loosed celestial weapons sprung from Brahmā.

**7.165.23**  With his mighty weapons, O great king, the son of Pṛṣata enveloped Droṇa in the battle, having quelled all the weapons of the son of Bharadvāja.

**7.165.24**  And the unfaltering one scattered the Vasātis and the Śibis, the Bāhlīkas and the Kauravas too, as they sought to shield Droṇa in the fray.

**7.165.25**  Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O king, shone like the sun with its rays, veiling all the quarters about him with nets of arrows on every side.

**7.165.26**  Droṇa cut through his bow and, piercing him with stone-headed arrows, struck again at his vital parts; and he came to the utmost anguish.

**7.165.27**  Then Bhīma, his wrath grown firm, gripping that chariot of Droṇa's, spoke to Droṇa, O lord of kings, slowly and deliberately:

**7.165.28**  "If only these so-called brāhmaṇas, trained for war yet unsatisfied with their own proper duties, did not fight, the kṣatriya order would not be going to ruin.

**7.165.29**  Harmlessness toward all beings the wise hold to be the higher law, and of that law the brāhmaṇa is the root—and you are the foremost knower of the Veda.

**7.165.30**  Like an outcaste dog-cooker, O brāhmaṇa, slaying hordes of barbarians and others of every sort, ignorant men, as a deluded creature might, out of craving for son and wife and wealth—

**7.165.31**  —for the sake of one, your son, slaying many, like one heedless of dharma, you who have strayed from your own calling slay those who keep to theirs: how is it you feel no shame?

**7.165.32**  And he today lies fallen, as the Dharma King declared to you when you asked. That word you ought not to doubt overmuch."

**7.165.33**  Thus addressed by Bhīma, the righteous-souled Droṇa, wishing to cast away that bow and all his weapons, spoke: "Karṇa, Karṇa, great archer! Kṛpa! Duryodhana!

**7.165.34**  Let your utmost effort be made in the battle—this I tell you again and again. Against the Pāṇḍavas may all go well with you. I am laying down my arms."

**7.165.35**  Thus, O great king, he cried out there, and to Droṇa's son as well; and casting away his weapon in the battle and seating himself upon the body of the car, the one yoked in yoga granted safety to all beings.

**7.165.36**  Marking that opening of his, Dhṛṣṭadyumna rose up, sword in hand, and leaping suddenly down from his chariot rushed upon Droṇa.

**7.165.37**  All beings, men and others alike, cried out in horror to see Droṇa brought to such a pass, fallen into Dhṛṣṭadyumna's power.

**7.165.38**  They raised a great wail and cried, "Alas! Shame!" And Droṇa himself, casting aside his weapons, took his stand in the highest equanimity.

**7.165.39**  Having so spoken, the great ascetic took to yoga and, become pure light, the teacher ascended to that heaven hard to attain, together with the holy ones.

**7.165.40**  When he passed on in that manner, our thought was that there were two suns; the sky, filled with radiances, seemed gathered into one, and the son of Bharadvāja, like the moon, took on the splendor of the sun.

**7.165.41**  In the space of an eye's blink that light vanished away; there arose a glad clamor of the rejoicing dwellers of heaven, now that Droṇa had gone to the world of Brahmā and Dhṛṣṭadyumna stood bewildered.

**7.165.42**  We five alone, born of human wombs, beheld the great-souled one, yoked in yoga, going to the supreme goal.

**7.165.43**  I, and Dhanaṃjaya the son of Pṛthā, and Kṛpa the brahmin son of Śaradvat, and Vāsudeva of the Vṛṣṇis, and the Pāṇḍava Yudhiṣṭhira the King of Righteousness.

**7.165.44**  But all the others did not see, O great king, the glory of the wise son of Bharadvāja as, freed by yoga, he departed.

**7.165.45**  Not knowing that he had attained the supreme goal, the human-born ones did not see the teacher going, together with the bulls among sages, taking to yoga toward the world of Brahmā—he, the tamer of foes.

**7.165.46**  His limbs pierced by hundreds of arrows, his weapons laid down, streaming with blood—him the son of Pṛṣata seized, though reproached for it by all beings.

**7.165.47**  Grasping the head of that embodied one whose life had fled and who spoke not a word, he severed the head from the body with his sword.

**7.165.48**  Filled with mighty joy now that the son of Bharadvāja had been struck down, he raised a lion's roar, brandishing his sword upon the field.

**7.165.49**  Gray-haired to the ears, dark of hue, eighty-five years of age, yet for your sake he had ranged the battle like one of sixteen years.

**7.165.50**  And the mighty-armed Dhanaṃjaya, son of Kuntī, had cried out, "Bring the teacher to me alive! Do not slay him, O son of Drupada!"

**7.165.51**  "He must not be slain, he must not be slain!"—so cried the soldiers too, and Arjuna himself, full of compassion, ran toward him.

**7.165.52**  Yet though Arjuna cried out, and all the kings on every side, Dhṛṣṭadyumna slew Droṇa, that bull among men, upon the floor of his chariot.

**7.165.53**  Drenched in blood, that tamer of foes, fallen from chariot to ground, became hard to look upon, like the sun with the body of Mars; and so the host of soldiers beheld him slain in battle.

**7.165.54**  Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna, that great archer, O king, hurled the great head of Bharadvāja's son before the very faces of your men.

**7.165.55**  And when your men, O king, beheld the head of Bharadvāja's son, their whole resolve turned to flight, and they fled in every direction.

**7.165.56**  But Droṇa, taking to the sky, entered the pathway of the stars; I alone, O king, beheld the passing of Droṇa.

**7.165.57**  By the grace of the seer Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, the son of Satyavatī, we beheld him of great splendor mounting and traversing the sky, like a blazing meteor coursing on, smokeless and aflame.

**7.165.58**  When Droṇa was slain, the Pāṇḍavas and Sṛñjayas charged with great fury upon the dispirited Kurus, and thereupon the army was torn asunder.

**7.165.59**  Most of them slain along with their horses in battle by whetted arrows, your men, with Droṇa slain, became as if their breath had fled.

**7.165.60**  Having met with defeat, and with great dread of the world beyond, undone by both alike, they could find no steadiness in themselves.

**7.165.61**  The kings, searching for the body of Bharadvāja's son, could not then find it, O king, in that press thronged with ten thousand headless trunks.

**7.165.62**  But the Pāṇḍavas, having won the victory and great fame in the world beyond, made the twang of bowstrings ring out and raised abundant lion-roars.

**7.165.63**  Then, O king, Bhīmasena and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata danced amid the host, embracing one another.

**7.165.64**  And Bhīma then said to the son of Pṛṣata, the scorcher of foes, "Again I shall embrace you victorious, O son of Pṛṣata, when the wicked son of the charioteer and the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra are slain in battle."

**7.165.65**  Having said only this much, Bhīma the Pāṇḍava, filled with mighty joy, made the earth quake with the clapping of his arms.

**7.165.66**  Terrified by that sound, your men fled in the battle, casting aside the warrior's code and bent wholly upon flight.

**7.165.67**  But the Pāṇḍavas, having won the victory, were glad, O lord of peoples, and through the destruction of their foes in battle they attained happiness.

**7.165.68**  Then, O king, with Droṇa slain, the Kurus, sorely afflicted by weapons, their champions struck down, shattered, were given over utterly to grief.

**7.165.69**  Bereft of sense, their courage broken, their vigor smitten with faintness, with a great cry of anguish they thronged about your son.

**7.165.70**  Covered with dust, trembling, gazing about the ten directions, their throats choked with tears, like the Daityas of old when Hiraṇyākṣa was slain.

**7.165.71**  Surrounded by them, terrified as they were like little beasts, your son the king, unable to hold his ground, withdrew.

**7.165.72**  Worn out by hunger and thirst, those warriors of yours, O Bhārata, and scorched by the sun, became utterly disheartened.

**7.165.73**  It was as though the sun had fallen, as though the ocean had dried up, as though Meru had been overturned, as though Vāsava himself had been vanquished.

**7.165.74**  Beholding that unbearable downfall of Bharadvāja's son, the Kauravas, O king, more terror-stricken still, fled in fear.

**7.165.75**  Śakuni, king of the Gāndhāras, terrified, together with those more terrified still, seeing the lord of the golden chariot slain, fled away with his chariots.

**7.165.76**  Gathering up the swift army in its rout, with its banners, that great host, the son of the charioteer withdrew in fear.

**7.165.77**  Setting before him the army thronged with chariots, elephants, and horses, Śalya, lord of the Madras, gazing about, withdrew in fear.

**7.165.78**  Surrounded by elephants whose champions were mostly slain and by many footmen, the son of Śaradvat went off crying, "Woe, woe!"

**7.165.79**  Surrounded by the remnant of the Bhoja host and by the Kaliṅgas, Āraṭṭas, and Bāhlīkas, Kṛtavarman, O king, went forth on his swift horses.

**7.165.80**  Joined with a band of footmen, terrified and stricken with fear, Ulūka there fled away, O king, on seeing Droṇa struck down.

**7.165.81**  Comely and young, and marked out for his valor, Duḥśāsana, deeply agitated, fled away surrounded by his elephants.

**7.165.82**  Joined with elephants, horses, and chariots, and surrounded by footmen, Duryodhana, O great king, that mighty chariot-warrior, went off from there.

**7.165.83**  Mounting elephants, chariots, and even the horses of another, the men with hair flying loose, shattered, ran—no two together in one place.

**7.165.84**  "This is the end!"—so cried the men, their courage broken, their vigor gone; and others of your folk, casting off their armor, fled away, O lord.

**7.165.85**  The soldiers called out to one another, O bull of the Bhāratas, "Stand! Stand!"—yet they themselves did not stand their ground there.

**7.165.86**  Loosing the well-adorned draught-horses from chariots whose drivers were slain, the warriors mounted them and urged them swiftly on with their heels.

**7.165.87**  As the army thus fled, terror-stricken and stripped of vigor, the son of Droṇa moved against the foe like a crocodile breasting the current.

**7.165.88**  Having slain the manifold army of the Pāṇḍavas, that warrior fierce in battle, with the prowess of a rutting elephant, freed himself only with difficulty from the peril.

**7.165.89**  Seeing the army in flight, with no thought but to flee, the son of Droṇa came up to Duryodhana and spoke these words.

**7.165.90**  "Why does this army flee as though in terror, O Bhārata? And why, O king of kings, do you not halt it in the battle as it flees?

**7.165.91**  You too, O ruler of men, are not as you were before, settled in your nature; and these kings, Karṇa and the rest, do not hold their ground.

**7.165.92**  In other battles too the army never fled like this then. Is all well, O mighty-armed one, with this host of yours, O Bhārata?

**7.165.93**  At the slaying of what lion among chariot-warriors, O king, has this army of yours come to such a plight? Tell me that, O Kaurava."

**7.165.94**  But Duryodhana, hearing this speech of Droṇa's son, that bull among kings, could not bring himself to tell the dread and grievous tidings.

**7.165.95**  Your son, like a shattered boat, was sunk in the sea of grief, his sight veiled with tears as he gazed upon the son of Droṇa standing in his chariot.

**7.165.96**  Then the king said this to the son of Śaradvat, in shame, "Tell here everything—blessings upon you—how it is that this army has fled."

**7.165.97**  Then the son of Śaradvat, O king, sinking again and again into anguish, recounted to the son of Droṇa how Droṇa had been struck down.

**7.165.98**  Kṛpa said: Setting Droṇa before us, the foremost chariot-warrior upon earth, we joined battle with the Pāñcālas alone.

**7.165.99**  Then, when the battle was joined, the Kurus and Somakas, mingling together and roaring at one another, brought down each other's bodies with their weapons.

**7.165.100**  Then Droṇa, that bull among men, wielding the Brāhma weapon, slew his foes with broad-headed shafts by hundreds and by thousands.

**7.165.101**  The Pāṇḍavas, the Kekayas, the Matsyas, and the Pāñcālas above all, coming up against Droṇa's chariot in battle, perished, driven on by fate.

**7.165.102**  A thousand lions among chariot-warriors and two thousand elephants Droṇa, having scorched them with the Brahmā weapon, dispatched to death.

**7.165.103**  Gray-haired to the ears, dark of hue, eighty-five years of age, Droṇa, old as he was, ranged the battle like one of sixteen years.

**7.165.104**  As the armies were sorely afflicted and the kings were being slain, the Pāñcālas, given over to wrath, turned their faces from the fight.

**7.165.105**  When they were somewhat broken and had turned away, the vanquisher of his rivals, wielding a celestial weapon, became like the risen sun.

**7.165.106**  Reaching the midst of the Pāṇḍavas, that majestic one, his arrows for rays, became hard to look upon, like the sun arrived at its zenith—your father did.

**7.165.107**  Burned by Droṇa, who blazed like the sun, their valor scorched away, they grew dispirited and lost their senses.

**7.165.108**  Seeing them tormented by Droṇa's arrows, the Slayer of Madhu, desiring the victory of the sons of Pāṇḍu, spoke these words.

**7.165.109**  "This foremost of weapon-bearers can never be vanquished in battle by his foes, not even by the slayer of Vṛtra—he, the chief of chariot-troop leaders."

**7.165.110**  "Therefore do you, O Pāṇḍavas, set righteousness aside and guard the victory, so that he of the golden car may not slay you all in the battle."

**7.165.111**  "With Aśvatthāman slain, he would fight no more—such is my thought. Let some man falsely tell him that he has been slain in the battle."

**7.165.112**  This counsel found no favor with Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī; but all the others approved it, and Yudhiṣṭhira too, though with difficulty.

**7.165.113**  Then Bhīmasena, in shame, said to your father, "Aśvatthāman is slain!"—and your father came to know of this.

**7.165.114**  Suspecting that this was false, your father, fond of his son, asked the King of Righteousness whether he had been slain or not slain in the fight.

**7.165.115**  Sunk in the dread of speaking untruth, yet bent upon victory, Yudhiṣṭhira said this concerning Aśvatthāman—"the elephant"—that had been slain by Bhīma, the mountain-bodied beast of Indravarman of the Mālavas: "He is slain."

**7.165.116**  Then he drew near to Droṇa and spoke aloud these words: "He for whose sake you take up your weapon, he by looking on whom you go on living, your beloved son Aśvatthāman has been struck down."

**7.165.117**  Hearing that grievous news, the teacher there grew sick at heart, and withholding his celestial weapons he fought no longer as he had before.

**7.165.118**  Seeing him utterly stricken, his mind overwhelmed by grief, the son of the Pāñcāla king, a doer of cruel deeds, rushed upon him.

**7.165.119**  Seeing that his death was ordained, he, skilled in the true nature of the worlds, then cast aside his celestial weapons and sat down upon the field, fasting unto death.

**7.165.120**  Then the son of Pṛṣata, seizing his hair with his left hand, severed his head while the heroes cried out in protest.

**7.165.121**  "He must not be slain, he must not be slain!" they cried out on every side, and Arjuna too, leaping down from his chariot, ran toward him.

**7.165.122**  Raising his arms in haste and crying again and again, that knower of righteousness called out, "Bring the teacher to me alive—do not kill him!"

**7.165.123**  Yet even so, though forbidden by the Kauravas and by Arjuna, your father was slain outright by that ruthless one, O bull among men.

**7.165.124**  Then all the soldiers fled, tormented by fear, and we too were robbed of spirit, O blameless one, when your father had been slain.

**7.165.125**  Saṃjaya said: But when the son of Droṇa heard of his father's death in battle, he gathered a fierce wrath, like a serpent trodden underfoot.

**7.166.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When he heard, Saṃjaya, that his aged father, the brāhmaṇa, had been slain unrighteously by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, what did Aśvatthāman say?

**7.166.2**  He, the mighty one, in whom were ever established the human weapon, those of Varuṇa and Agni, the Brāhma weapon, that of Indra, and the Nārāyaṇa weapon as well—

**7.166.3**  When he heard, Saṃjaya, that the teacher, most righteous of men, had been slain unrighteously by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, what did Aśvatthāman say?

**7.166.4**  He, the great soul, who having gained the science of archery from Rāma, declared its celestial weapons to his son who longed for his teacher's lore—

**7.166.5**  For in this world men desire one thing alone—a son more excellent than themselves; none other, in any way, in all the world.

**7.166.6**  Great-souled teachers do indeed have their secret lore, and this they would impart either to a son or to a devoted disciple.

**7.166.7**  Having received all that craft, and with special favor besides, Saṃjaya, the valiant son of Śāradvatī's lord stood second only to Droṇa in battle.

**7.166.8**  Approved by Rāma in the science of arms, the equal of Purandara in battle, of Kārtavīrya in valor, of Bṛhaspati in wisdom,

**7.166.9**  the equal of a mountain in steadfastness, of Agni in splendor, that youth—deep as the ocean in gravity, and in his wrath like the venom of a serpent.

**7.166.10**  He, the foremost chariot-warrior in the world, of unyielding bow, conqueror of fatigue, swift as the wind upon the field of clamor, ranging like Death enraged—

**7.166.11**  by whose shooting the earth was pressed down hard in battle, that hero of unfailing prowess who never falters in the fight—

**7.166.12**  bathed in the Vedas, bathed in vows, and master to the end of the science of archery, unshakable as the great ocean, like Rāma the son of Daśaratha.

**7.166.13**  When he heard that the teacher, most righteous of men, had been slain unrighteously by Dhṛṣṭadyumna in the encounter, what did Aśvatthāman say?

**7.166.14**  As the Pāñcāla prince, the son of Yajñasena, was made the death ordained for Droṇa by that great soul, so was a death likewise ordained for Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

**7.166.15**  When he heard that the teacher had been slain by that ruthless, wicked, cruel man of meanest vision, what did Aśvatthāman say?

**7.166.16**  Saṃjaya said: Hearing that his father had been slain by treachery by that doer of evil deeds, the son of Droṇa was filled with tears and with fury, O bull among men.

**7.166.17**  As he raged, O lord of kings, his form appeared more than mortal, like that of Death itself, eager to take away all beings at the turning of the age.

**7.166.18**  Then, wiping again and again his eyes that brimmed with tears, sighing in his anger, he spoke these words to Duryodhana:

**7.166.19**  "How my father, having laid down his weapons, was struck down by base men—I know that this sin was wrought by one who flaunts the banner of righteousness; ignoble it was, and I have heard of it from that most ruthless son of Dharma."

**7.166.20**  "For those engaged in battles, victory and defeat are both certain; either of the two may come to pass, O king, and slaying therein is held praiseworthy."

**7.166.21**  "But a slaying that befalls a man fighting in battle by lawful conduct brings no cause for grief; in such wise was that twice-born one seen to fall."

**7.166.22**  "My father has gone to the world of heroes, of that there is no doubt; nor is that tiger among men to be mourned, having met his end in such a way."

**7.166.23**  "But that he, engaged in righteousness, should suffer his hair to be seized in the sight of all the armies—that cuts through my very vitals."

**7.166.24**  "Out of desire, out of wrath, out of contempt, out of pride, or again out of childishness, and out of insolence too, men do deeds contrary to righteousness."

**7.166.25**  "This great unrighteous deed has been done here by the son of Pṛṣata—surely in contempt of me, by that ruthless and evil-souled wretch."

**7.166.26**  "That Dhṛṣṭadyumna shall behold the dire consequence of it, having wrought a most ignoble deed; and the lying Pāṇḍava too shall behold it."

**7.166.27**  "He who by treachery made the teacher lay down his weapon then—the earth shall today drink the blood of that king of righteousness."

**7.166.28**  "By every means I shall strive for the destruction of the Pāñcālas, and in battle I shall slay that doer of evil, Dhṛṣṭadyumna."

**7.166.29**  "By whatever deed it be—gentle or terrible—having wrought the slaughter of the Pāñcālas, I shall win peace, O Kaurava."

**7.166.30**  "That for which men desire a son, O tiger among men—deliverance both hereafter and here from great fear—that has now come to be."

**7.166.31**  "Yet my father came to such a plight, as though he had no kinsman at all, while I, his son and disciple, mountain-like, was living still."

**7.166.32**  "A curse upon my celestial weapons, a curse upon my arms, a curse upon my prowess—that Droṇa, though he had me for a son, should suffer his hair to be seized!"

**7.166.33**  "So shall I act, O best of the Bhāratas, that even toward my father gone to the other world I shall pass free of all debt to him."

**7.166.34**  "A noble man should never speak praise of himself; yet, unable to bear my father's slaying, I shall today proclaim my manhood here."

**7.166.35**  "Let the Pāṇḍavas with Janārdana behold my valor today, as I crush all their armies, working as it were the end of the age."

**7.166.36**  "For neither gods nor gandharvas, neither asuras nor rākṣasas are able today to conquer me in battle, mounted on my chariot, O bull among men."

**7.166.37**  "There is none in this world, save Arjuna, who knows weapons better than I; for I, come into the host, am a wielder of the weapons fashioned by the gods, blazing like the sun among its rays."

**7.166.38**  "For today the offspring of Kṛśāśva, loosed by me in the great fray, displaying their own might, shall crush the Pāṇḍavas."

**7.166.39**  "Today, O king, men shall behold all the quarters thronged, as it were with torrents, covered over with my keen feathered shafts."

**7.166.40**  "Scattering nets of arrows on every side with a fearful roar, I shall lay the enemy low, as a great wind lays low the trees."

**7.166.41**  "Neither Bībhatsu knows that weapon, nor Janārdana, nor Bhīmasena, nor the twins, nor King Yudhiṣṭhira;"

**7.166.42**  "nor that evil-souled son of Pṛṣata, nor Śikhaṇḍin, nor Sātyaki—this art, complete with its means of recall, that lies in me, O Kaurava."

**7.166.43**  "Long ago my father, bowing down to Nārāyaṇa with due rite, offered an oblation when the god appeared in the form of Brahmā."

**7.166.44**  "Then the Blessed One, accepting it in person, granted a boon; and my father thereupon chose the supreme weapon, the Nārāyaṇa."

**7.166.45**  "Then, O king, the Blessed One, best of the gods, said to him: 'There shall be no other man anywhere, ever, equal to you in battle.'"

**7.166.46**  "'But this, O brāhmaṇa, is in no way to be loosed rashly; for this weapon turns not back save by the slaying of the foe.'"

**7.166.47**  "'And it cannot be known, O lord, who shall not be slain by it; indeed it would strike down even one who ought not to be slain—therefore one should not employ it lightly.'"

**7.166.48**  "Slaughter in battle, or flight, or the laying down of weapons, or the foes' suing for mercy, or the seeking of refuge—"

**7.166.49**  "these are the means of quelling the great weapon, O scorcher of foes; for in every way he who, harassing in battle, harms those who ought not to be slain, would himself be afflicted."

**7.166.50**  "My father received it, and the Lord said to him: 'You shall pour down celestial showers of weapons again and again; with this weapon in battle you shall blaze forth in splendor.'"

**7.166.51**  "Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord ascended to heaven; this is the weapon gained from Nārāyaṇa by my kinsman."

**7.166.52**  "With it I shall scatter in battle the Pāṇḍavas, the Pāñcālas, the Matsyas and the Kekayas, as the lord of Śacī scatters the asuras."

**7.166.53**  "In whatever fashion I may wish, in just that fashion my arrows, becoming so, shall fall upon my foes even as they show their prowess, O Bhārata."

**7.166.54**  "Standing in the field, I shall rain down at will a shower of stones, and with iron-beaked birds I shall drive off the great chariot-warriors, and I shall hurl forth manifold battle-axes—of this there is no doubt."

**7.166.55**  "With the mighty Nārāyaṇa weapon, O scorcher of foes, I shall shatter the enemy and bring the Pāṇḍavas to naught."

**7.166.56**  "That hater of friends, of brāhmaṇas, and of teachers, that base and utterly contemptible outcast of the Pāñcālas shall not escape me alive today."

**7.166.57**  Hearing that, the host of the son of Droṇa rallied and turned back, and then all those best of men blew their great conches.

**7.166.58**  In their joy they beat their kettledrums and tabors by the thousand; the earth too resounded, pressed by hooves and wheel-rims, and that tumultuous din made sky, heaven, and earth ring out.

**7.166.59**  Hearing that sound, like the roar of a thundercloud, the Pāṇḍavas, those foremost of chariot-warriors, came together and took counsel as one.

**7.166.60**  And having spoken thus, the son of Droṇa too, having sipped water in due rite, then brought forth that celestial weapon, the Nārāyaṇa, O Bhārata.

**7.167.1**  Saṃjaya said: When that Nārāyaṇa weapon had then appeared, a wind blew laden with raindrops, and thunder rolled in a cloudless sky.

**7.167.2**  The earth too quaked, and the great ocean was stirred, and the rivers that flow to the sea began to run there against their current.

**7.167.3**  The peaks of the mountains split asunder there, O Bhārata, and the beasts kept the sons of Pāṇḍu on their left as an ill omen.

**7.167.4**  All things were strewn over with darkness, and the sun grew dim; and the flesh-eating creatures came flocking together as though delighted.

**7.167.5**  Gods, dānavas, and gandharvas were filled with terror, O lord of peoples, and a sharp dismay arose—"What is this? What is this?"—as they beheld that great turmoil.

**7.167.6**  All the kings then grew distressed and bewildered, beholding the dreadful, terror-bringing weapon of the son of Droṇa.

**7.167.7**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the armies had been turned back in the encounter by the son of Droṇa, sorely scorched by grief and unable to bear his father's slaying,

**7.167.8**  and when the Pāṇḍavas saw the Kurus bearing down upon them, what counsel was there among them for the protection of Dhṛṣṭadyumna? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.

**7.167.9**  Saṃjaya said: Seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who had fled before, and hearing once again the tumultuous din, Yudhiṣṭhira spoke to Arjuna:

**7.167.10**  "Now that the teacher Droṇa has been slain by Dhṛṣṭadyumna in the encounter, even as the great asura Vṛtra was slain by the wielder of the thunderbolt—"

**7.167.11**  No longer did they hope for victory in the battle, O Dhanaṃjaya; their spirits broken, the Kurus, fixing their minds only on saving themselves, fled away as best they could.

**7.167.12**  Some of the princes were swiftly carried off in reeling chariots whose flank-guards and drivers had been slain, their banners, standards, and parasols gone, their chariot-poles shattered.

**7.167.13**  Others, out of their senses, mounted chariots with broken cabs and panic-stricken horses; some in their fear urged the horses on with their own feet from the cars; and others, frantic with terror, fled in chariots whose yokes, wheels, and axles were broken.

**7.167.14**  Some, pinned to the necks of elephants by iron shafts, were dislodged from their seats; and some were borne off in the ten directions by maddened elephants that, tormented by arrows, ran wild.

**7.167.15**  Others, stripped of weapons and armor, fell from their mounts to the ground; some, cut to pieces, were caught beneath the wheel-rims, and others were trampled by horses and elephants.

**7.167.16**  Others fled in fear, crying out 'O father!' and 'O son!'; their vigor smitten by bewilderment, they no longer recognized one another.

**7.167.17**  Some, lifting up sons, fathers, friends, and brothers grievously wounded, loosened their armor and bathed their wounds with water.

**7.167.18**  Reduced to such a state, the army fled when Droṇa was slain; if you know by whom it was made to turn back again, tell me.

**7.167.19**  The neighing of horses, the trumpeting of elephants, and the rumble of chariot-wheels, all mingled together, are heard there as a mighty din.

**7.167.20**  These exceedingly fierce sounds, rising up again and again over the ocean of the Kurus, make my people tremble.

**7.167.21**  This tumultuous, hair-raising sound that is heard could, I think, shatter the three worlds together with Indra himself.

**7.167.22**  I think this terrible roar is the thunder of the wielder of the vajra; surely, now that Droṇa is slain, Vāsava is coming for the sake of the Kauravas.

**7.167.23**  The hairs of our bodies stood erect, and our chariot-warriors and elephants were thrown into panic, O Dhanaṃjaya, on hearing there that deep and most terrible roar.

**7.167.24**  Who is this great chariot-warrior who, having rallied the broken Kauravas, turns them back to battle in the fray, like the lord of the gods himself?

**7.167.25**  Arjuna said: Rousing themselves to a terrible deed and standing firm in resolve, the Kauravas blow their conches, relying on the valor of one man.

**7.167.26**  The one about whom you are in doubt, O king—who, now that the teacher who had laid down his weapons is slain, has rallied the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and roars aloud—

**7.167.27**  that modest one, mighty-armed, who moves with the gait of a rutting elephant, of terrible deeds, the giver of fearlessness to the Kurus—him I shall describe to you.

**7.167.28**  He at whose birth Droṇa gave a thousand cows in wealth to most worthy Brāhmaṇas—that one, Aśvatthāman, is the one who roars.

**7.167.29**  By that hero, the moment he was born, neighing like Uccaiḥśravas, the earth and all three worlds were made to tremble.

**7.167.30**  Hearing this, an unseen being then gave him his name—'Aśvatthāman'; and that hero it is who roars today, O Pāṇḍava.

**7.167.31**  For him who today, as though he had no protector, was thus assailed and slain by the son of Pṛṣata through a most cruel deed, a protector now stands forth.

**7.167.32**  That the prince of the Pāñcālas laid hold of my teacher by the locks of his hair—this the son of Droṇa, knowing his own manhood, will never forgive.

**7.167.33**  By you the teacher was approached with a falsehood for the sake of the kingdom; though called a knower of righteousness, you have committed a most grievous unrighteousness.

**7.167.34**  'This Pāṇḍava is endowed with every virtue and is my pupil; he will not speak a falsehood'—such was the trust he placed in you.

**7.167.35**  And so, with the untruth clad in the garb of truth, he, the teacher, was told by you, 'The elephant is slain.'

**7.167.36**  Then, casting away his weapons, freed of all attachment and bereft of his senses, that lord became overcome, O king, just as you saw him.

**7.167.37**  Filled with grief and turned away from the fight, fond of his son—the teacher, abandoning the eternal law, was struck down by his own pupil.

**7.167.38**  Having unrighteously caused the teacher to be slain when he had laid down his weapons, let your lordship now, with your counselors, protect the son of Pṛṣata if you can.

**7.167.39**  When the son of the teacher, enraged and bereft of his kinsman, has seized the son of Pṛṣata, not all of us together shall be able to save him today.

**7.167.40**  He who shows boundless friendship toward all beings—when he hears today of his father being seized by the hair, he will burn us up in battle.

**7.167.41**  Though I cried out aloud, longing eagerly for the teacher, yet the teacher was slain by his pupil, who cast aside his own duty.

**7.167.42**  When the greater part of his life had passed and but little of ours remains, this monstrous wrong was now done to him—a great unrighteousness.

**7.167.43**  Ever like a father in his affection, and like a father indeed by right—that teacher was slain for the sake of a kingdom that lasts but a little while.

**7.167.44**  By Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O lord of peoples, the whole earth, together with his sons devoted to them, was made over to Bhīṣma and to Droṇa.

**7.167.45**  Yet though he had won such a station and was ever honored by our foes, the teacher always favored me, his pupil, above his own sons.

**7.167.46**  Undiminished in strength, he laid down his weapons at your word and was slain in the fight; while he was fighting, not even the performer of a hundred sacrifices could have slain him.

**7.167.47**  Against that aged teacher, our constant benefactor, this treachery was wrought by us ignoble men of petty understanding, for the sake of a kingdom.

**7.167.48**  The son of Vāsava would give up sons, brothers, fathers, wives, and life itself—everything—out of love for me; this my teacher knew well.

**7.167.49**  And yet, in my desire for a kingdom, I looked on heedless while he was being slain; therefore, O king, head bowed down, I have come, O lord, to hell.

**7.167.50**  Having today caused the slaying of a Brāhmaṇa, aged, a teacher, who had laid down his weapons like a sage—for the sake of a kingdom—death is better for me than life.

**7.168.1**  Saṃjaya said: Hearing the words of Arjuna, the great chariot-warriors there spoke to Dhanaṃjaya nothing, O great king, whether pleasant or unpleasant.

**7.168.2**  Then the mighty-armed Bhīmasena, enraged, as if smiling, addressed the son of Kuntī, Arjuna, O bull of the Bhāratas.

**7.168.3**  You speak words bound up with righteousness, O Pārtha, like a sage gone to the forest, like a Brāhmaṇa of strict vows who has laid down the rod of punishment.

**7.168.4**  A protector from harm, surviving harm, forbearing toward the good of all three orders—such a Kṣatriya swiftly wins the earth, righteousness, fame, and prosperity.

**7.168.5**  You, the upholder of our line, endowed with all the virtues of a Kṣatriya, do not shine today, speaking your words like a man of no understanding.

**7.168.6**  Your prowess, O son of Kuntī, is like that of Śakra, the lord of Śacī; and you do not overstep righteousness, as the great ocean does not overstep its shore.

**7.168.7**  Who indeed would not honor you today, who—putting behind you the wrath of thirteen years—still desire righteousness alone?

**7.168.8**  By good fortune, dear one, your mind today follows your own duty; and by good fortune, O undiminished one, your understanding is ever bent on mercy.

**7.168.9**  But that your kingdom, while you walked in righteousness, was unjustly taken away, and Draupadī was brought into the assembly hall and laid hold of by our foes,

**7.168.10**  and that we were driven into the forest, clad in bark and deerskin, made by our enemies to endure for thirteen years a state we did not deserve—

**7.168.11**  all these occasions for wrath you have borne in patience, O sinless one; devoted to the law of the Kṣatriya, you have endured all this.

**7.168.12**  To undo that wrong I have set out, joined with you; together with their followers I shall slay those base men who seized the kingdom.

**7.168.13**  It was said by you before that we had come for battle; and we strive with all our might—yet today you reproach us.

**7.168.14**  You will not understand your own duty; your words are false. With your speech you cut to the quick of us who are stricken with fear.

**7.168.15**  Like one strewing caustic upon the wounds of the wounded, O scourge of foes, you make my heart split asunder, tormented by the arrow of your words.

**7.168.16**  Righteous though you are, you do not perceive this monstrous wrong—that you praise neither yourself nor us, who are worthy of praise, while you praise one who is not worth a sixteenth part of you.

**7.168.17**  It is not fitting to proclaim one's own virtues with one's own mouth; yet in my wrath I could rend the earth and scatter the mountains.

**7.168.18**  Whirling my heavy, terrible mace garlanded with gold, I could shatter the mountain-like beings born of earth, as the wind shatters trees.

**7.168.19**  You, then, knowing your brother to be of such a kind, O bull among men, ought not, O you of measureless prowess, to make us fear the son of Droṇa.

**7.168.20**  Or else stand aside, O Bībhatsu, with all these bulls among men; mace in hand, I alone shall vanquish him in the great battle.

**7.168.21**  Then the son of the king of the Pāñcālas spoke to Pārtha, as Hari spoke to Hiraṇyakaśipu roaring in his fury.

**7.168.22**  O Bībhatsu, the duties of a Brāhmaṇa are known to the wise: officiating at sacrifices and teaching, giving gifts, and the offering and receiving of sacrifices.

**7.168.23**  The sixth is study; in which of these did the Droṇa stand whom I have slain, that you should blame me, O Pārtha?

**7.168.24**  Fallen away from his own duty and resorting to the duty of a Kṣatriya, that doer of base deeds slew us with a weapon not of human kind.

**7.168.25**  He who employed magic, who was unbearable, a Brāhmaṇa only in name—if one slew him by magic itself, what is unfitting in that, O Pārtha?

**7.168.26**  If, now that he has been slain by me in that manner, the son of Droṇa in his rage makes a terrible roar, what is diminished in me thereby?

**7.168.27**  Nor do I think it any wonder that the son of Droṇa, with mere empty roaring, will get the Kauravas killed, being unable to save them.

**7.168.28**  And whereas you, becoming righteous, call me the slayer of a teacher—for that very purpose was I, the son of the Pāñcāla king, born from the fire.

**7.168.29**  He for whom, when he fights in battle, the proper deed and the improper are all the same—how could you call such a one a Brāhmaṇa, or even a Kṣatriya, O Dhanaṃjaya?

**7.168.30**  He who, frenzied with wrath, would slay with the Brahmā-weapon men ignorant of weapons—how is such a one not to be slain by any means whatever, O best of men?

**7.168.31**  It is declared by those who know the law that, against violators of the law, what is like poison toward them is sanctioned; knowing this, O Arjuna, you who understand the truth of duty and meaning—why do you blame me?

**7.168.32**  That cruel man, assailed by me, was struck down upon his very chariot; for this I deserve your praise, O Bībhatsu—why do you not rejoice?

**7.168.33**  The battle being done, O Pārtha, why do you not praise as praiseworthy the dread cutting-off of Droṇa's head, like blazing fire, the sun, and poison?

**7.168.34**  He who slew in battle the kinsmen of me alone and of none other—even having severed his head, I am not yet rid of my fever.

**7.168.35**  And this cuts me to the quick—that his head was not flung by me into the country of the Niṣādas, as was the head of Jayadratha.

**7.168.36**  To leave one's foes unslain, too, remains an unrighteousness, O Arjuna; for this is the law of the Kṣatriya—he should slay, or in turn be slain.

**7.168.37**  That foe was slain by me in battle by righteous means, O Pāṇḍava, just as the hero Bhagadatta, your father's friend, was slain by you.

**7.168.38**  Having slain the grandsire in battle, you account it your righteousness; then when a wicked foe is slain by me, why do you not account it righteousness?

**7.168.39**  The eldest Pāṇḍava is no liar, nor am I unrighteous, O Arjuna; the wicked betrayer of his teacher has been slain. Fight on—the victory is yours.

**7.169.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: He, the great soul by whom the Vedas with their ancillary sciences had been duly studied, in whom the science of archery was firmly established as in its very seat, restrained by modesty—

**7.169.2**  When that son of the great sage, Droṇa, was thus reviled—reviled by a base-souled, cruel, and contemptible slayer of his own teacher—

**7.169.3**  by whose grace those bulls among men perform feats in battle that are more than human, deeds hard even for the gods to accomplish—

**7.169.4**  when Droṇa was thus reviled before their very eyes by that doer of evil deeds, they showed no resentment. A curse upon the kṣatriya order, and a curse upon their want of indignation!

**7.169.5**  What did all the sons of Pṛthā and the kings of the earth who bear the bow say when they heard the Pāñcāla prince? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.

**7.169.6**  Saṃjaya said: Having heard those words of Drupada's son, that doer of cruel deeds, all the kings fell silent, O lord of peoples.

**7.169.7**  But Arjuna, eyeing the son of Pṛṣata askance with a sidelong glance, sighed with tears in his eyes and said, 'Shame, shame, shame!'

**7.169.8**  Yudhiṣṭhira and Bhīma, the twins, Kṛṣṇa, and the others were sorely abashed, O king, and Sātyaki spoke these words:

**7.169.9**  'Is there here no man who would swiftly strike down this wicked wretch, this vilest of men, as he utters words so unholy?

**7.169.10**  How is it, base one, that your tongue does not split into a hundred pieces and your head burst asunder, when you revile your teacher, and how is it that you are not cast down by your own unrighteousness?

**7.169.11**  You are to be reproached by the sons of Pṛthā and by all the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, for having done so foul a deed you yet boast of it in the assembly of men.

**7.169.12**  Having committed such an undoable deed and now reviling your teacher besides, you deserve death; there is no profit in your living even for a single moment.

**7.169.13**  What noble man other than you, vilest of men, would have resolved upon this—to seize by the hair and slay a teacher, righteous and good?

**7.169.14**  Seven generations of your kinsmen, those before and those to come, have been cast down and forsaken by their renown, having gotten you, the defiler of your line.

**7.169.15**  And as for what you said to Pārtha concerning Bhīṣma, that bull among men—the end of that great-souled one was ordained by his very own self.

**7.169.16**  And of him too the slayer was your own brother, that doer of the worst of deeds; no greater doer of evil than the sons of Pāñcāla is to be found upon the earth.

**7.169.17**  And he too, Śikhaṇḍin, was begotten by your father to be the bringer of Bhīṣma's end; he was guarded by Arjuna, and he became the death of that great-souled one.

**7.169.18**  The Pāñcālas have fallen from righteousness, base traitors to friend and teacher, having gotten you together with your brother, condemned by all good men.

**7.169.19**  If once again you utter such words in my presence, I shall strike off your head with my mace, mighty as the thunderbolt.'

**7.169.20**  Thus assailed by the Sātvata with harsh syllables, the son of Pṛṣata, enraged, spoke to Sātyaki in wrath, yet as though laughing:

**7.169.21**  'It is heard, it is heard—and it is borne, it is borne, O Mādhava. But you, ignoble one, ought not to revile a good and worthy man.

**7.169.22**  Forbearance is praised in the world, but the wicked man does not deserve forbearance; for the evil-souled one thinks of the forbearing man, "This one is beaten."

**7.169.23**  You, of mean conduct, base-souled, and fixed upon evil, deserve to be reproached from the tips of your hair to the tips of your nails—yet you wish to speak.

**7.169.24**  That Bhūriśravas, his arm severed and seated in the vow of fasting to death, was slain by you though you were being restrained—what is more wicked than that?

**7.169.25**  As I shielded Droṇa with a celestial weapon in the fray, he was slain when he had laid down his arms—what cruel ill deed is there in that, you savage?

**7.169.26**  But he who would slay in battle, with another's help, a sage not fighting, seated in the vow of death, his arm already severed—what manner of man is he, O Sātyaki?

**7.169.27**  When that valiant one, having struck you to the ground, was striding upon you, why did you not then slay him, you who would be the best of men?

**7.169.28**  But the heroic son of Somadatta, glorious in might, was first vanquished by Pārtha and then slain by you, ignoble one.

**7.169.29**  Wherever Droṇa, scattering thousands of arrows, put the host of the Pāṇḍavas to flight, thither and thither did I go.

**7.169.30**  Having yourself done such a deed, like an outcaste, why then do you, who deserve reproach, wish to speak harsh words to me?

**7.169.31**  You are the doer of that ghastly deed, not I, O basest of the Vṛṣṇi line; you are the dwelling-place of wicked deeds—speak no more.

**7.169.32**  Hold your peace; you ought not to address me further from here on, for this that you wish to say to me is utter nonsense, the lowest set above the highest.

**7.169.33**  And if out of folly you address such harsh words to me again, I shall send you with my arrows in battle to the abode of Vaivasvata.

**7.169.34**  And not by righteousness alone, you fool, can it be done; hear what manner of unrighteous deeds were wrought even by these.

**7.169.35**  The Pāṇḍava Yudhiṣṭhira was first deceived through unrighteousness, and Draupadī too was tormented likewise through unrighteousness, O Sātyaki.

**7.169.36**  All the Pāṇḍavas were sent into exile in the forest together with Kṛṣṇā, and all their possessions were stripped away likewise through unrighteousness, you simpleton.

**7.169.37**  And the king of the Madras was drawn off from this side by his foes through unrighteousness; and from this side too Bhīṣma, the grandsire of the Kurus, was slain through unrighteousness; and Bhūriśravas was slain through unrighteousness by you, knower of righteousness though you be.

**7.169.38**  Thus was it practiced in battle by your foes and by the Pāṇḍavas alike—by heroes who, though knowers of righteousness, were guarding their victory, O Sātvata.

**7.169.39**  The highest righteousness is hard to know, and so too unrighteousness is most difficult to discern. Fight with the Kauravas; go not to the dwelling of your fathers.'

**7.169.40**  Made to hear these and other words, cruel and harsh, the illustrious Sātyaki became as though shaken.

**7.169.41**  Hearing this, Sātyaki, his eyes copper-red with wrath, took up his mace, hissing like a serpent, having set down his bow upon the chariot.

**7.169.42**  Then rushing upon the Pāñcāla, he said this in his fury: 'I will not speak harsh words to you; I will slay you, who deserve death.'

**7.169.43**  As he fell suddenly upon the Pāñcāla, mighty, impatient of insult, and wrathful, like Death itself against another Death—

**7.169.44**  urged on by Vāsudeva, the mighty Bhīmasena leapt swiftly from his chariot and held him back with both his arms.

**7.169.45**  The strong Pāṇḍava, seizing the wrathful Sātyaki as he rushed and struggled forward, dragged the powerful one back by force.

**7.169.46**  Standing firm and planting his feet, Bhīma held back that bull of Śini's line, the foremost of the strong, by main strength at the sixth step.

**7.169.47**  And Sahadeva, descending from his chariot, spoke to him in gentle words as he was being dragged back by the stronger one, O lord of peoples:

**7.169.48**  'O tiger among men, no other friend higher than the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis and the Pāñcālas is known to us, O Mādhava.

**7.169.49**  And so too for the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, and for you in particular, and for Kṛṣṇa, no other friend than ourselves is known.

**7.169.50**  And for the Pāñcālas too, O scion of Vṛṣṇi, were they to search to the very shores of the ocean, there is no other friend so great as the Pāṇḍavas and Vṛṣṇis are to one another.

**7.169.51**  You regard such a friend even as he regards you; and as you are to us, so are we to you.

**7.169.52**  Therefore, you who know all righteousness, remembering the duty owed to a friend, restrain your wrath against the Pāñcāla and be appeased, O bull of Śini's line.

**7.169.53**  Forgive the son of Pṛṣata, and let the son of Pṛṣata forgive you; we are here to make peace between you—what is there to gain apart from calm?'

**7.169.54**  As the grandson of Śini was being pacified by Sahadeva, O honored one, the son of the Pāñcāla king said this, laughing:

**7.169.55**  'Release, release the grandson of Śini, Bhīma, possessed as he is by the frenzy of battle; let him come at me as the wind comes against a mountain.

**7.169.56**  that with my sharp arrows I may quell his fury, his appetite for battle, and his very hold on life in the fray, O son of Kuntī.

**7.169.57**  But what indeed can I do? A great task is upon the sons of Pāṇḍu, for here the Kauravas are advancing.

**7.169.58**  Or else Phalguna will hold them all back in battle; and I too shall strike off this man's head with my arrows.

**7.169.59**  He thinks me a Bhūriśravas with severed arm in the battle. Let him go—either I shall slay him, or he shall slay me.'

**7.169.60**  Hearing the words of the Pāñcāla, Sātyaki, hissing like a serpent, the mighty one held fast in the clasp of Bhīma's arms, writhed without ceasing.

**7.169.61**  Then in haste Vāsudeva and the Dharma King, O honored one, with great effort held back those two heroes.

**7.169.62**  Having restrained those two great archers, their eyes red with wrath, those bulls among kṣatriyas, eager for combat, advanced against their foes in battle.

**7.170.1**  Saṃjaya said: Then the son of Droṇa wrought havoc among his foes, like Death created by Time at the end of an age to destroy all beings.

**7.170.2**  With banners for its trees and weapons for its peaks, slain elephants for its great boulders, strewn with horses and kiṃpuruṣas, and overgrown with bows for creepers—

**7.170.3**  resounding with pikes and flesh-eating beasts, thronged with hosts of spirits and yakṣas—having slain his enemies with his broad-headed arrows, he heaped up a mountain of corpses.

**7.170.4**  Then with great vehemence that bull among men roared aloud and proclaimed his vow once more to your son:

**7.170.5**  'Because, while my teacher was fighting, Kuntī's son Yudhiṣṭhira, donning righteousness as a coat of mail, said to him, "Lay down your weapon"—

**7.170.6**  therefore, before his very eyes, I shall rout his host; and having routed it, in truth I shall slay that wicked Pāñcāla.

**7.170.7**  I shall slay all of these if they fight me in battle—this I truly vow to you. Turn back your host!'

**7.170.8**  Hearing this, your son turned the host about, dispelling its great fear with a mighty lion's roar.

**7.170.9**  Then, O king, the clash of the Kuru and Pāṇḍava armies arose once more, fierce as that of two full oceans meeting.

**7.170.10**  For the Kauravas, enraged, were made steadfast by the son of Droṇa, while the Pāṇḍavas and Pāñcālas were exultant at the slaying of Droṇa.

**7.170.11**  A mighty onrush arose upon the field of battle from those exceedingly joyful warriors, who, enraged, saw victory already within their grasp.

**7.170.12**  As a mountain might dash against a mountain, or an ocean against an ocean, O lord of kings, so were the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.170.13**  Then the soldiers of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, full of joy, sounded thousands of conches and tens of thousands of kettledrums.

**7.170.14**  Then there arose from that army a tumult, exceedingly great and wondrous, like the roar of an ocean being churned.

**7.170.15**  Then the son of Droṇa brought forth the Nārāyaṇa weapon, aiming it at the host of the Pāṇḍavas and Pāñcālas.

**7.170.16**  Then there appeared in the sky arrows by the thousand, their points ablaze, eager to devour the Pāṇḍavas like serpents with flaming jaws.

**7.170.17**  In that great battle they shrouded the quarters, the sky, and the army in a moment, O king, as the rays of the sun cover the world.

**7.170.18**  And others appeared, blazing like stars in a clear sky, O guardian of the earth—balls wrought of black iron.

**7.170.19**  And on every side appeared wondrous śataghnīs spewing fire, and razor-edged discuses, like the radiant orbs of the sun.

**7.170.20**  Beholding the sky, O bull of the Bhāratas, thickly strewn with shapes of every kind of weapon, the Pāṇḍavas, the Pāñcālas, and the Sṛñjayas were filled with dread.

**7.170.21**  For the more the mighty chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas fought on, the more that weapon swelled in power, O lord of men.

**7.170.22**  Slain by that Nārāyaṇa weapon, scorched as if by fire, they were tormented on every side in the battle.

**7.170.23**  As at winter's end fire consumes the dry grass, so, O lord, that weapon consumed the host of the Pāṇḍavas.

**7.170.24**  As the weapon waxed full and the army dwindled, O mighty one, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, fell into utmost terror.

**7.170.25**  Seeing that army routed and bereft of sense, and Pārtha standing aloof, the son of Dharma spoke these words.

**7.170.26**  "Dhṛṣṭadyumna, flee with the Pāñcāla host; and you, Sātyaki, go home, surrounded by the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.

**7.170.27**  Vāsudeva too, righteous of soul, will do what befits himself; he who is able to counsel the whole world will surely look after his own.

**7.170.28**  Let no battle be waged—this I say to all the troops; for I, with my brothers, shall enter the fire that bears the oblations.

**7.170.29**  Having crossed the battle-ocean of Bhīṣma and Droṇa, that flood impassable to cowards, I shall be left sunk and waterless, with my host, in this cow's-hoofprint pool that is the son of Droṇa.

**7.170.30**  Let this his wish toward me, toward Bībhatsu, be swiftly fulfilled—for it was by me that the preceptor of blameless conduct was struck down in battle.

**7.170.31**  By whose contrivance that boy, the son of Subhadrā, unskilled in warfare, was slain by many ruthless and able warriors, and went unguarded.

**7.170.32**  He who, refusing to answer the question, allowed Kṛṣṇā, dragged into the assembly, to be reduced to bondage, he and his son looking on.

**7.170.33**  And that son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, armored, eager to slay Phalguna when his horses were spent, fought to protect the Saindhava.
