**7.170.34**  He who, knowing the Brahmā weapon, struck down root and branch the Pāñcālas led by Satyajit, even as they strove to overwhelm him.

**7.170.35**  He whom, when we were unjustly driven into exile from our kingdom, we begged to follow us, yet he held us back.

**7.170.36**  He who ever showed us the highest friendship has been slain; for his sake I shall go to my death, together with my kinsmen."

**7.170.37**  As the son of Kuntī spoke thus, the Dāśārha hastily stayed the army with his arms and uttered these words.

**7.170.38**  "Quickly lay down your weapons and dismount from your vehicles; here is the prescribed device, the counter ordained by the great-souled one.

**7.170.39**  Dismount, all of you, to the ground from elephants, horses, and chariots; thus the weapon will not slay you, weaponless upon the earth.

**7.170.40**  For the more the warriors fight against the power of the weapon, the stronger do these Kauravas become.

**7.170.41**  But those men who, dismounting from their vehicles, cast down their weapons—them this weapon will not slay in the battle.

**7.170.42**  Yet whoever shall withstand it, even in thought, all those it will slay, though they had gone down to the nethermost depths."

**7.170.43**  Hearing that speech of Vāsudeva, O Bhārata, they all resolved to lay aside their weapons, in mind and in deed alike.

**7.170.44**  Then, marking them eager to cast aside their weapons, the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena, O king, spoke these words to rouse their spirit.

**7.170.45**  "By no means shall any here lay down his weapons; I will ward off the weapon of Droṇa's son with my swift arrows.

**7.170.46**  Or else, with this heavy mace of golden frame, I shall range over the field like Death itself, shattering the son of Droṇa's weapon.

**7.170.47**  For no man here is the equal of my valor, even as there is no other light to match the light of the Sun.

**7.170.48**  Behold these two firm arms of mine, like the trunks of a king of elephants, able to bring down even Himālaya, the snow-clad mountain.

**7.170.49**  For I alone among men have the strength of ten thousand elephants, even as Śakra is renowned in heaven as the peerless rival among the gods.

**7.170.50**  This day behold the prowess of my thick-shouldered arms in the fray, as I ward off the blazing, flaming weapon of Droṇa's son.

**7.170.51**  If there be none to withstand the Nārāyaṇa weapon, this day I shall withstand it before the eyes of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas."

**7.170.52**  Having spoken thus, Bhīma, the tamer of foes, advanced upon the son of Droṇa in his sun-bright chariot, thundering like a cloud.

**7.170.53**  Swift in his nimbleness, the son of Kuntī reached him in the twinkling of an eye and overwhelmed him with a net of arrows.

**7.170.54**  Then the son of Droṇa, laughing and addressing him with disdain, showered upon him those consecrated arrows with blazing points.

**7.170.55**  As though by flame-mouthed serpents vomiting fire in the battle, Pārtha was covered over, as if with golden sparks.

**7.170.56**  Such, O king, was the aspect of Bhīmasena in the fray—like a mountain wrapped about with fireflies at the close of day.

**7.170.57**  As that weapon of Droṇa's son met him in conflict, it grew greater, O great king, like fire fanned by the wind.

**7.170.58**  Seeing that weapon of terrible power waxing ever greater, a mighty fear seized the Pāṇḍava host, save Bhīma alone.

**7.170.59**  Then they all cast their weapons down upon the earth and dismounted, every one, from their chariots, elephants, and horses.

**7.170.60**  When they had laid down their weapons and quit their vehicles, the vast might of that weapon fell upon the head of Bhīma.

**7.170.61**  All beings cried out in dismay, and the Pāṇḍavas above all, as they beheld Bhīmasena then enveloped in that fiery splendor.

**7.171.1**  Saṃjaya said: Seeing Bhīmasena overspread by the weapon, Dhanaṃjaya, to counter its fiery splendor, enveloped him with the Varuṇa weapon.

**7.171.2**  None could descry him, shrouded by the Varuṇa weapon, by reason of Arjuna's swiftness and of the splendor that enveloped him.

**7.171.3**  Bhīma, with horses, charioteer, and car, shrouded by the weapon of Droṇa's son, garlanded in flame and scarcely to be looked upon, was like fire cast into fire.

**7.171.4**  As at the close of night, O king, the stars sink toward the western mountain, so did the arrows converge upon the chariot of Bhīmasena.

**7.171.5**  For Bhīma, and his chariot, his horses, and his charioteer, O sire, enveloped by Droṇa's son, seemed sunk within the very fire.

**7.171.6**  As the fire, having burned at the appointed time the whole world with all that moves and moves not, passes into the mouth of the Almighty, so did that weapon enwrap Bhīma.

**7.171.7**  As fire might enter the sun, or the sun enter fire, so that splendor entered in, and nothing whatever could be discerned.

**7.171.8**  Seeing that weapon poured forth upon Bhīma's chariot, and the son of Droṇa rising up without a rival in the battle,

**7.171.9**  all the hosts of the Pāṇḍavas, weapons laid aside and senses fled, with Yudhiṣṭhira at their head—those mighty chariot-warriors turned their faces away.

**7.171.10**  Then Arjuna and Vāsudeva, those two heroes of great splendor, leaping in haste from their chariot, ran toward Bhīma.

**7.171.11**  Then those two mighty ones plunged into the splendor of Droṇa's son, born of the weapon's power, and entered it by their magic art.

**7.171.12**  They had laid aside their weapons, and so the fire born of the weapon could not burn them—both by the working of the Varuṇa weapon and by the might of the two Kṛṣṇas.

**7.171.13**  Then Nara and Nārāyaṇa, to quell the Nārāyaṇa weapon, forcibly dragged forth Bhīma and all his weapons.

**7.171.14**  Even as he was being dragged away, the son of Kuntī, that mighty car-warrior, kept roaring on; and the dreadful, scarce-conquerable weapon of Droṇa's son kept growing.

**7.171.15**  Vāsudeva said to him: "What is this, son of Pāṇḍu? Why, O son of Kuntī, though restrained, do you not turn back from battle?

**7.171.16**  Were these sons of the Kurus to be conquered by fighting, we too would fight here, and so would these bulls among men.

**7.171.17**  But all your own people have dismounted from their chariots; therefore you too, O son of Kuntī, withdraw at once from your car."

**7.171.18**  Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa brought him down from the chariot to the ground, hissing like a serpent, his eyes red with wrath.

**7.171.19**  When he had been dragged from the chariot and his weapon laid upon the ground, then that Nārāyaṇa weapon, scorcher of foes, grew still.

**7.171.20**  When that unbearable splendor was thus quelled by the prescribed device, all the quarters and the intermediate quarters became clear.

**7.171.21**  Auspicious breezes blew, the beasts and birds grew calm, and the vehicles and the warriors were filled with cheer, O lord of men.

**7.171.22**  And when that terrible splendor was withdrawn, O Bhārata, the wise Bhīma shone forth like the sun risen at the close of night.

**7.171.23**  There stood the remnant of the Pāṇḍavas' host that the slaughter had spared, rejoicing at the ceasing of the weapon, eager to slay your son.

**7.171.24**  When that army had rallied and the weapon had been thus countered, Duryodhana, O great king, spoke to the son of Droṇa.

**7.171.25**  "Aśvatthāman, loose this weapon again, and swiftly; for the Pāñcālas have rallied once more, hungry for victory."

**7.171.26**  Aśvatthāman, thus addressed by your son, O sire, sighing most piteously, said this to the king.

**7.171.27**  "This weapon does not return, O king; it cannot be employed a second time. He who would call it back, it slays him who wields it—of this there is no doubt.

**7.171.28**  And this Vāsudeva has applied the counter to the weapon; otherwise the slaughter of the foe in battle had been ordained, O lord of men.

**7.171.29**  Defeat or death—death is the better, not so this victory; for these foes, vanquished, are as good as dead, having cast away their weapons."

**7.171.30**  Duryodhana said: "Son of the preceptor, if this weapon may not be loosed twice, then with other weapons let the slayers of the teacher be slain, O best of those who know the arts of war.

**7.171.31**  For in you the celestial weapons abide as they do in the Three-eyed God; should you wish it in your wrath, not even Purandara could escape you."

**7.171.32**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When that weapon had been countered, and Droṇa slain by guile, and the son of Droṇa thus addressed by Duryodhana, what did he do next?

**7.171.33**  And seeing the Pārthas arrayed for battle in the fray, freed from the Nārāyaṇa weapon, ranging at the head of the host—

**7.171.34**  Saṃjaya said: He whose banner bore the lion's tail, knowing the slaying of his father, full of wrath, casting off all fear, rushed upon the son of Pṛṣata.

**7.171.35**  And rushing on, that bull among men pierced that bull among men with twenty small arrows and with five more, in a great fury.

**7.171.36**  Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O king, pierced the son of Droṇa—blazing like fire—with sixty-three feathered shafts, O king.

**7.171.37**  And he pierced his charioteer with twenty gold-feathered, stone-whetted shafts, and his four horses with four sharp arrows.

**7.171.38**  Piercing and piercing again, the son of Droṇa roared, as though making the earth tremble, as though seizing the life-breaths of all the world in that great battle.

**7.171.39**  But the mighty son of Pṛṣata, O king, accomplished in arms and tireless in toil, rushed straight at the son of Droṇa, having made death itself the boundary of his turning back.

**7.171.40**  Then the prince of the Pāñcālas, that immeasurable spirit, the best of chariot-warriors, loosed a rain of arrows upon the head of Droṇa's son.

**7.171.41**  Enraged in the battle, the son of Droṇa veiled him with feathered shafts and pierced him with ten, remembering the slaying of his father.

**7.171.42**  With two well-drawn razor-headed arrows the son of Droṇa cut down the standard and the bow of the Pāñcāla king, and with others he tormented him sorely.

**7.171.43**  In that great battle the son of Droṇa stripped him of horses, charioteer, and car, and in his wrath he overspread all his followers with arrows.

**7.171.44**  Then the army of the Pāñcālas broke and fled, O lord of peoples, bewildered in aspect, anguished, and mangled by the rain of arrows.

**7.171.45**  Seeing the warriors turning away and Dhṛṣṭadyumna hard pressed, the grandson of Śini swiftly urged the fight on toward the chariot of Droṇa's son.

**7.171.46**  With eight whetted arrows he afflicted Aśvatthāman, and striking that unforgiving warrior again with twenty of varied form, he pierced likewise the charioteer with four and the four horses each with one.

**7.171.47**  Deeply pierced by those many-marked shafts of Yuyudhāna, the unforgiving mighty bowman, the son of Droṇa, laughed and spoke these words.

**7.171.48**  "Grandson of Śini, I know your loyalty toward the slayer of my teacher; yet you shall not rescue him from me, who is in my grasp—nor yourself either."

**7.171.49**  So speaking, the son of Droṇa loosed at the Sātvata a peerless, well-jointed arrow bright as a sunbeam, as Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra.

**7.171.50**  That shaft, sped by him, pierced through both the warrior and his armor, and cleaving the earth it entered her, hissing like a serpent entering its hole.

**7.171.51**  His armor shattered, the hero, like an elephant stung by the goad, let fall his bow with its arrow, streaming from many wounds.

**7.171.52**  Sinking and drenched in blood, he sank down upon the floor of his car, and was swiftly borne by his charioteer to another chariot, away from the son of Droṇa.

**7.171.53**  Then with another well-feathered, smooth-jointed arrow that scorcher of foes struck Dhṛṣṭadyumna between the brows.

**7.171.54**  Already deeply pierced before and grievously afflicted thereafter, the Pāñcāla prince sank down in the battle and leaned upon his standard.

**7.171.55**  Upon him—like a rutting elephant tormented by a lion, O king—five heroic chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍava side charged at speed.

**7.171.56**  The Diademed One, Bhīmasena, Vṛddhakṣatra the Paurava, the crown-prince of the Cedis, and Sudarśana the Mālava struck him together from every side, each with five arrows.

**7.171.57**  With twenty serpent-venom-like arrows, and with five more, the son of Droṇa cut down all at once those twenty-five shafts.

**7.171.58**  With seven sharpened arrows the son of Droṇa tormented the Paurava, the Mālava with three, Pārtha with one, and Vṛkodara with six.

**7.171.59**  Then all those great chariot-warriors, O king, pierced the son of Droṇa, together and severally, with arrows gold-feathered and whetted on stone.

**7.171.60**  The crown-prince pierced the son of Droṇa with twenty feathered shafts, Pārtha again with eight, and all the rest each with three.

**7.171.61**  Then the son of Droṇa struck Arjuna with six arrows, Vāsudeva with ten, Bhīma with five, the crown-prince with four; and having cut the prince's bow and standard with two, the son of Droṇa, piercing Pārtha again with a shower of arrows, roared a terrible lion's roar.

**7.171.62**  As the son of Droṇa shot his well-whetted, sharp-edged shafts behind and before, the earth, the air, the heavens, the quarters and the intermediate quarters were covered with arrows of dreadful form.

**7.171.63**  That warrior of fierce splendor, of valor equal to Indra's, with three arrows at once severed the two arms—shining like Indra's banner—and the head of Sudarśana as he sat in his own car.

**7.171.64**  Slaying the Paurava with a chariot-lance, and cutting his car to bits with arrows, he severed his two arms anointed with fine sandal, and with a broad-headed shaft lifted his head from his trunk.

**7.171.65**  Laughing, with swift arrows like blazing fire he pierced the young crown-prince, beloved of the Cedis, dark as a wreath of blue lotuses, and gave him over to death together with his horses and charioteer.

**7.171.66**  Having slain them in battle, the heroic son of Droṇa, that unvanquished lord of warriors, blew his great conch in his joy.

**7.171.67**  Then all the Pāñcālas, and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava, in terror abandoned the chariot of Dhṛṣṭadyumna and fled in every direction.

**7.171.68**  As they broke, the son of Droṇa, scattering arrows upon their backs, bore down with speed upon the host of the Pāṇḍavas like Death himself.

**7.171.69**  As they were slaughtered in the battle by Droṇa's son, those warriors, O king, in their terror saw the son of Droṇa in all the quarters.

**7.172.1**  Saṃjaya said: Seeing that army broken, Dhanaṃjaya the son of Kuntī, that immeasurable spirit, held it back, longing to slay the son of Droṇa.

**7.172.2**  Yet those soldiers, O king, would not stand fast there, though Govinda and Arjuna strove with all their effort to rally them.

**7.172.3**  But Bībhatsu alone, with the remnants of the Somakas, the Matsyas, and others, marshalled his ranks and turned back against the Kauravas.

**7.172.4**  Then Savyasācin, swiftly outstripping him whose banner bore the lion's tail, spoke to the mighty bowman Aśvatthāman.

**7.172.5**  "Whatever is your power, your valor, your knowledge and your manhood, whatever your love for the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and your hatred of us, and whatever splendor still is yours—show me all of it now, to the utmost."

**7.172.6**  "That very son of Pṛṣata, the slayer of Droṇa, will break your pride—he who is like the fire of doom, the ender of foes in battle. Come, then, against the Pāñcāla, and against me too, with Keśava beside me."

**7.172.7**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: The teacher's son is worthy of honor and mighty too, Saṃjaya; he bears love toward Dhanaṃjaya, and dear is he in turn to the son of Vāsava.

**7.172.8**  Never before has such harsh speech come from Bībhatsu; why, then, did the son of Kuntī speak so roughly to his friend?

**7.172.9**  Saṃjaya said: When the crown-prince had been slain, and Vṛddhakṣatra the Paurava, and Sudarśana the Mālava, perfect in the rites of bow and arrow—

**7.172.10**  —and when Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Sātyaki, and Bhīma had been overcome, and Yudhiṣṭhira had been struck to the quick by his words—

**7.172.11**  —and when a rift had opened within them, and remembering his grief, O lord, an unprecedented wrath was born of sorrow in Bībhatsu.

**7.172.12**  Therefore he spoke to the son of Droṇa words undeserved, unseemly, and unkind—to the honorable son of his teacher he spoke harshly, as a base man might.

**7.172.13**  Thus addressed, O king, that foremost of mighty bowmen, hissing with wrath at Pārtha's harsh speech and at words that struck every vital part, the son of Droṇa grew enraged—against Pārtha, and against Kṛṣṇa above all.

**7.172.14**  Standing intent upon his car, the valiant one touched water in purification and took up the fiery weapon, hard to withstand even by the gods.

**7.172.15**  Aiming at the hosts of his foes, both seen and unseen, the teacher's son, that slayer of enemy heroes, charged a blazing arrow with mantras—like smokeless fire—and, filled with wrath on every side, hurled it forth.

**7.172.16**  Then a tumultuous rain of arrows arose in the sky; chill winds blew, and the sun gave no more heat.

**7.172.17**  The Dānavas too cried out frightfully in all the quarters, and raining down blood, they roared amid the rain-clouded sky.

**7.172.18**  Birds, beasts, and cattle, and even the sages of holy vows, though most self-restrained in spirit, could find no peace.

**7.172.19**  All the great elements were thrown into disorder, the maker of day was overturned, and the three worlds were scorched, stricken as if seized by a burning fever.

**7.172.20**  Scorched by the heat of the arrows, the serpents that dwell beneath the earth rose up hissing, eager to discharge their dreadful venom.

**7.172.21**  And the creatures of the waters, scorched, O descendant of Bharata, found no relief, for the very pools that held them were burning.

**7.172.22**  Upon the quarters and the sky, the intermediate quarters and the earth, showers of arrows great and small fell down with the speed of Garuḍa and the wind.

**7.172.23**  By those arrows of Droṇa's son, sped with the force of the thunderbolt, the foes were burned and fell like trees consumed by fire.

**7.172.24**  Great elephants, blazing, fell upon the earth on every side, bellowing fearful cries that rumbled like rain-clouds.

**7.172.25**  Other great elephants there, ablaze, fled away, and yet others trembled, like beasts ringed about by a forest fire in a dreadful wood.

**7.172.26**  Like the crowns of trees seared by a forest blaze, O honored one, the troops of horses and the masses of chariots appeared, O lord; and floods of chariots fell here and there by the thousands.

**7.172.27**  That army the lord Agni burned in the battle, O descendant of Bharata, as the all-dissolving fire consumes every being at the end of an age.

**7.172.28**  But seeing the Pāṇḍava host burning in that great battle, your men, O king, rejoiced and let forth lion-roars.

**7.172.29**  Then your men, O descendant of Bharata, exulting and wearing the look of victory, joyfully struck up a thousand instruments of many kinds at once.

**7.172.30**  As the world was wrapped in darkness, an entire akṣauhiṇī, O king, and Savyasācin the Pāṇḍava, could no longer be seen in that great battle.

**7.172.31**  Never had we seen or even heard, O king, of such a weapon as the unforgiving son of Droṇa let loose.

**7.172.32**  But Arjuna, O great king, raised up the Brāhma weapon, ordained by the Lotus-born to counter every other weapon.

**7.172.33**  Then within a moment that darkness was stilled; a cool wind blew, and the quarters grew clear.

**7.172.34**  There we beheld a marvel: an entire akṣauhiṇī slain, its forms past recognition, burned utterly by the magic of that weapon.

**7.172.35**  Then the two heroes, the mighty bowmen Keśava and Arjuna, delivered unscathed, appeared together like the dispellers of darkness in the sky.

**7.172.36**  With its pennants, standard, and horses, with its axle-pole and its excellent weapons, that delivered chariot shone forth, a terror to your men.

**7.172.37**  Then in an instant a glad uproar arose from the rejoicing Pāṇḍavas, mingled with the blare of conches and drums.

**7.172.38**  "The two are slain"—such had been the thought of both the armies, until they saw Keśava and Arjuna come on swiftly, delivered and unharmed.

**7.172.39**  Unhurt and joyful, the two blew their finest of conches; and seeing the sons of Pṛthā so glad, your men were thrown into distress.

**7.172.40**  Seeing those two great-souled ones delivered, the son of Droṇa, sorely grieved, pondered for a moment, "What is this, then?" O honored one.

**7.172.41**  Having pondered, O lord of kings, given over to brooding and grief, sighing long and hot, he then grew downcast in heart.

**7.172.42**  Then the son of Droṇa laid down his bow and leapt in haste from his car, and crying, "Shame, shame! all this is in vain," he fled from the battle.

**7.172.43**  Then, by the dwelling of Sarasvatī, he beheld Veda-Vyāsa, stainless, with the sheen of a glistening rain-cloud—Vyāsa himself he saw.

**7.172.44**  Seeing him standing before him, O upholder of the Kuru line, the son of Droṇa, his throat choked, saluted him and spoke most piteously.

**7.172.45**  "O sir, O sir, is it illusion, or mere chance? I know not what this may be. How has this weapon of mine come to nothing? And what was my transgression?"

**7.172.46**  "Is this the world turned upside down, or the undoing of the worlds, that these two Kṛṣṇas yet live? For Time, indeed, is hard to overpass."

**7.172.47**  "Not Asuras, gods, or Gandharvas, not Piśācas, not Rākṣasas, not serpents, Yakṣas, or birds, nor men in any wise—"

**7.172.48**  "—are able to make otherwise this weapon launched by me. Yet here it has slain only a single arrayed akṣauhiṇī, blazing as it went."

**7.172.49**  "By what cause did it not slay these two, Keśava and Arjuna, who share the nature of mortals? Declare this to me, O blessed one, asked by me, even as it truly is."

**7.172.50**  Vyāsa said: This is a mighty matter on which, in wonder, you question me. I shall declare it all to you; compose your mind and listen.

**7.172.51**  He who is named Nārāyaṇa, born before even the most ancient ones, was born for a purpose as the son of Dharma, the maker of all the world.

**7.172.52**  He undertook a fierce penance, stationed upon Mount Maināka, his arms raised aloft, of vast splendor, resembling fire and the sun.

**7.172.53**  For sixty thousand years, and as many hundreds besides, the lotus-eyed one, feeding only on air, wasted away his own body.

**7.172.54**  Then, having performed yet another austerity, and twice again another great one, he filled the gulf between heaven and earth with his splendor.

**7.172.55**  When by that penance, my son, he had become one with Brahman, he then beheld the Lord of all, the source of the universe, the master of the whole world —

**7.172.56**  the Lord, exceedingly hard to behold even for all the gods, subtler than the subtlest and vaster than the vast,

**7.172.57**  Rudra the Ruler, the Bull, the all-perceiving, the unborn, the supreme, who whether men move or stand still abides in the heart of every being;

**7.172.58**  irresistible, hard to look upon, fierce in wrath, great of soul, the destroyer of all, the wise; bearing a divine bow and two quivers, clad in golden armor, of boundless valor;

**7.172.59**  wielder of the Pināka bow, of the thunderbolt, of the blazing trident, of the battle-axe, of the mace, of the long sword; fair of brow, crowned with the moon amid a circle of matted locks, clad in a tiger's skin, holding a bludgeon and a staff in his hand;

**7.172.60**  adorned with fair armlets, the sacred thread a serpent across his breast, resplendent with all his hosts, the throngs of spirits; the one made whole, the very repository of austerities, well-praised with chosen words by those who have passed beyond age;

**7.172.61**  whom water, heaven, the sky, the earth, the moon and sun, and wind and fire, and the measured world itself, cannot suffice to behold — the unborn one, whom those of perverse conduct cannot see, slayer of the foes of Brahman, the source of the deathless;

**7.172.62**  whom only Brāhmaṇas of holy conduct behold, who, their sin spent, are free of grief in mind. Devoted to him, through austerity and through love of him — that adorable, righteous one of universal form — he beheld him; and seeing him, with speech and mind and intellect and body, his soul thrilling, he rejoiced in the God of gods,

**7.172.63**  girded with a rosary of beads, the supreme treasure of all lights. Then Nārāyaṇa, beholding him, saluted the source of the universe —

**7.172.64**  the boon-giver, together with Pārvatī of broad and lovely form, the Lord, the unborn, the Ruler, the unperturbed, the very essence of all causes, the imperishable.

**7.172.65**  Then the lotus-eyed one, full of devotion, having paid homage to Rudra, the slayer of Andhaka in an instant, began to praise that god of the strange-set eyes:

**7.172.66**  "From you, O most excellent, sprang the makers of beings, the elder gods who today guard the world, who of old, entering this earth, protected your ancient creation, O God.

**7.172.67**  Gods and demons, Nāgas, Rākṣasas and Piśācas, men, Suparṇas, and Gandharvas and Yakṣas, and all the manifold hosts of beings — we know them all alike sprung from you. The work of Indra and of Yama, of Varuṇa and of the Lord of Wealth, of Mitra and of Tvaṣṭṛ, and of Soma, is yours.

**7.172.68**  Form and light, sound, ether and wind, touch, the tasted, water, scent, the earth, desire, Brahmā, the Veda, and the Brāhmaṇas — all this, the unmoving and the moving, has sprung from you.

**7.172.69**  As drops issue forth from the waters into separateness, and at dissolution return again into oneness with them, so the wise one, knowing both the origin and the passing of beings, leaves them behind and attains union there with you.

**7.172.70**  The two birds, mind-born, wrapped in divine concealment; the pippala tree whose branches turn downward; the seven herdsmen, and the ten others who sustain the body's city — these were created by you, and beyond them all are you. What was, what shall be, and what is to come, unassailable — all the worlds here have sprung from you.

**7.172.71**  Cherish me, your devotee who cherishes you; harm me not by anything unfriendly. He who knows you as his very self, in undivided being, thus attains the radiant Brahman.

**7.172.72**  I have praised you, longing for your favor, seeking you out together with your bull, O best of gods. Grant me the boons I cherish, hard though they are to win; and, thus extolled, turn me not away."

**7.172.73**  To him, the worthy chief of gods, the blue-throated wielder of the Pināka, whose nature is beyond thought, praised by sages, he granted boons:

**7.172.74**  The blue-throated one said: By my grace, O Nārāyaṇa, among men and in the wombs of gods and Gandharvas, you shall be of immeasurable strength of soul.

**7.172.75**  Neither gods nor demons nor great serpents shall prevail against you, nor Piśācas, nor Gandharvas, nor men, nor Rākṣasas,

**7.172.76**  nor Suparṇas, nor Nāgas, nor any of the misbegotten creatures of the world; not even a god shall ever vanquish you in battle.

**7.172.77**  Not by weapon, not by the thunderbolt, not by fire, nor by wind, not by the wet nor by the dry, not by the moving nor by the unmoving,

**7.172.78**  shall anyone, by my grace, ever do you injury in any way; and should you go to battle, you shall be greater even than I.

**7.172.79**  Vyāsa said: Know that these boons were thus won of old by the heroic one. This same god walks abroad by his māyā, bewildering the world.

**7.172.80**  Born of that same one's austerity was the great sage named Nara, the equal of this god; know that one to be ever Arjuna.

**7.172.81**  These two sages, most exalted among the elder gods, are born age after age to order the course of the worlds.

**7.172.82**  And likewise, O wise and great-minded one, from the whole of that great work and austerity were you born, fierce in splendor and in wrath, a very form of Rudra.

**7.172.83**  You, godlike and wise, knowing the world to be pervaded by Bhava, drew yourself inward through self-restraints, longing to win his favor.

**7.172.84**  Fashioning a fair and fresh image of the Great Person in the manner of Ūrva, you worshipped him, O giver of honor, with prayers, oblations, and offerings.

**7.172.85**  That elder god, so worshipped by you, was well pleased, and granted you, O wise one, the abundant boons that dwelt within your heart.

**7.172.86**  The birth, the deeds, the austerity, and the discipline of those two and of you are alike abundant; by those two the god is worshipped in the liṅga, and by you in the image, age after age.

**7.172.87**  Whoever, knowing Bhava to be of all forms, worships the Lord in the liṅga, in him are everlasting union of the self and union prescribed by scripture.

**7.172.88**  Thus the gods and the Siddhas and the supreme sages, by sacrificing, seek the highest and everlasting station in the world.

**7.172.89**  This very Keśava is both a devotee of Rudra and sprung from Rudra; Kṛṣṇa indeed is the one to be worshipped, and he is the eternal one to be honored with sacrifices.

**7.172.90**  To him who, knowing Bhava as the source of all beings, worships the Lord in the liṅga, the bull-bannered god shows surpassing favor.

**7.172.91**  Saṃjaya said: Hearing that speech of his, the son of Droṇa, the mighty car-warrior, made obeisance to Rudra and held Keśava in high honor.

**7.172.92**  His hair bristling with joy, his soul subdued, having bowed to the great sage, he turned toward the army and ordered the withdrawal.

**7.172.93**  Then there was a withdrawal of the Pāṇḍavas, O lord of peoples, and of the stricken Kauravas, now that Droṇa had fallen in the fight.

**7.172.94**  Having waged war for five days and destroyed many a host, Droṇa, the Brāhmaṇa who had crossed to the far shore of the Vedas, went to the world of Brahmā, O king.

**7.173.1**  Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When that surpassing car-warrior Droṇa had been slain there, O Saṃjaya, what did my men and the Pāṇḍavas do thereafter?

**7.173.2**  Saṃjaya said: When that surpassing car-warrior Droṇa had been slain by the son of Pṛṣata, and the Kauravas were broken, Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī,

**7.173.3**  having beheld a very great marvel that brought him victory, questioned Vyāsa, who had come by chance, O bull of the Bhāratas:

**7.173.4**  "As I slew my foes in battle with floods of gleaming arrows, I marked before me a Person moving on, with the radiance of fire,

**7.173.5**  holding aloft a blazing trident; and in whatever quarter he advanced, in that quarter my foes fell shattered, O great sage.

**7.173.6**  His feet touched not the ground, nor did he ever cast his trident; yet from that trident, by his splendor, thousands of tridents shot forth.

**7.173.7**  All the foes broken by him the people deem broken by me; the armies consumed by him I do but burn over again from behind.

**7.173.8**  Tell me this, O blessed one: who is that supreme Person, the great trident-bearer, dark of hue, in splendor like the sun?"

**7.173.9**  Vyāsa said: It was the first of the Lords of Creatures, the Person of fiery splendor, the all-pervading, the very abode of being, earth and atmosphere, the god, the Lord and master of all the worlds —

**7.173.10**  the Ruler, the boon-giver, Śaṃkara, whom you have seen, O Pārtha. Go for refuge to that god, the origin of all, the Lord of the world —

**7.173.11**  Mahādeva, the great of soul, the Ruler, the matted-haired, the auspicious Śiva, the three-eyed, the mighty-armed Rudra, crested, clad in rags, the giver to his devotees of boons granted in his grace.

**7.173.12**  The divine attendants of that pervading Lord are of forms manifold and various — dwarfish, matted-haired, shaven, short of neck, huge of belly,

**7.173.13**  and others vast of body, of great vigor, great of ear, with distorted faces and feet, O Pārtha, and with monstrous garbs.

**7.173.14**  Worshipped by such as these, that Mahādeva, the Great Lord, that splendid Śiva, my son, moves of his grace before you, O Pārtha, in that dreadful, hair-raising battle.

**7.173.15**  That army, guarded by Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa, mighty bowmen and smiters — who then, O Pārtha, could even in thought assail it, save the gods and the great bowman of many forms, the Great Lord?

**7.173.16**  None dares to stand his ground when that one stands before him; for no being is found equal to him in all the three worlds.

**7.173.17**  In battle, at the very scent of him when he is enraged, his foes, swooning and all but slain, tremble and fall.

**7.173.18**  Doing him homage, the gods abide in heaven, and so do other men in the world, and those mortals who have conquered heaven.

**7.173.19**  Those who are devoted to the boon-giving god, the auspicious Rudra, the lord of Umā, having won happiness in this world, go to the supreme goal.

**7.173.20**  Pay homage, O son of Kuntī, to him, ever serene — to Rudra, the white-throated, the youngest, the radiant,

**7.173.21**  to the one of braided locks, the terrible, the tawny-eyed, the boon-giver, the kin of Yama, the one of unkempt hair, and to Śaṃkara of good conduct;

**7.173.22**  to the lovely one, the green-eyed, the Pillar, the Person, the golden-haired, the shaven, the lean, and the deliverer;

**7.173.23**  to the radiant as the sun, the holy ford, the God of gods, the swift, the one of many forms, Śarva, the beloved, the one in dear raiment;

**7.173.24**  to the turbaned, the fair-faced, the thousand-eyed, the bountiful, the dweller on the mountain, the wholly tranquil, the Lord clad in rags;

**7.173.25**  to the golden-armed, to the fierce, to the Lord of the quarters, to the Lord of the rain-cloud, and to the Lord of beings — homage!

**7.173.26**  To the Lord of trees, and likewise to the Lord of the waters, to the one whose body is veiled by trees, to the army's leader, to the one in the midst;

**7.173.27**  to the god with the sacrificial ladle in hand, the bowman, the kinsman of Bhṛgu, the one of many forms, the Lord of all, clad in rags;

**7.173.28**  to the thousand-headed, and to the thousand-eyed, to the thousand-armed, and to the thousand-footed.

**7.173.29**  Take refuge, O son of Kuntī, in the boon-giving Lord of the world, the lord of Umā, the strange-eyed, the destroyer of Dakṣa's sacrifice, the unperturbed Lord of creatures, the imperishable Lord of beings;

**7.173.30**  the braided-haired, whose course is the bull, whose navel is the bull, whose banner is the bull, the bull's own pride, the lord of the bull, the bull-horned, the bull among bulls;

**7.173.31**  the bull-marked, exalted as a bull, the bull itself, bull-eyed, whose weapon is the bull, whose arrow is the bull, who has become the bull, the Great Lord;

**7.173.32**  the vast-bellied, the great-bodied, clad in a panther's skin, the Lord of the world, the boon-giver, the shaven, the friend of holiness, dear to the Brāhmaṇas;

**7.173.33**  the trident-handed, the boon-giver, the Lord who bears sword and shield, the wielder of the Pināka, the one of the broken axe, the Lord and Master of the worlds — to that god, the refuge of all, clad in rags, I go for shelter.

**7.173.34**  Homage to that Lord of the gods, whose friend is Vaiśravaṇa; to the well-clad, ever homage, to the one of holy vows, the bearer of the goodly bow;

**7.173.35**  to the god with the sacrificial ladle in hand, the one of the gladdening bow, the bowman, the one in the bow's interval, the bow itself, the master of archery, the archer.

**7.173.36**  Homage to the god of dreadful weapons, and to the best of the gods; homage be to him of manifold forms, and homage to him who wields many bows.

**7.173.37**  Homage forever to Sthāṇu, the firm of vows, the bearer of the goodly bow; homage to the slayer of Tripura, and homage indeed to him who struck down Bhaga.

**7.173.38**  Homage to the lord of the forest trees, to the lord of men; homage forever to the lord of the waters, and homage to the lord of sacrifices.

**7.173.39**  Homage to the destroyer of Pūṣan's teeth, to the three-eyed boon-giver, to the blue-throated, the tawny, the golden-haired indeed.

**7.173.40**  And the divine deeds of the wise Mahādeva — these I shall recount to you, as far as my understanding reaches and as I have heard them.

**7.173.41**  When he is angered, neither gods nor demons in the world, neither Gandharvas nor Rākṣasas, prosper in happiness — not even those who have hidden themselves in a cave.

**7.173.42**  Enraged, Bhava, the fearless, then pierced the sacrifice, and loosing an arrow from his bow he roared aloud with a great cry.

**7.173.43**  Then the gods found no shelter, much less peace, when the sacrifice scattered all at once and Maheśvara was wroth.

**7.173.44**  At that sound of the bowstring and the palm striking it, all the worlds were thrown into turmoil, O Pārtha, and gods and demons alike, overmastered, fell down.

**7.173.45**  All the waters were stirred up, the earth trembled, the mountains were shattered, and the quarters of the sky and the Nāgas were stupefied.

**7.173.46**  And the worlds, blinded by darkness and shrouded over, gave no light, for he had stricken away, along with the Sun, the radiance of all the luminaries.

**7.173.47**  And the seers, terror-stricken, cried out, and likewise performed rites of appeasement, desiring the welfare of all beings and of themselves.

**7.173.48**  Śaṃkara, as if laughing, rushed upon Pūṣan and dashed out the teeth of the god as he was eating the sacrificial cake.

**7.173.49**  Then the gods went forth, trembling and bowing low to him; and once more he fitted to the string his blazing, sharpened arrow aimed at the gods.

**7.173.50**  And out of fear the gods then assigned to Rudra a distinguished share in the sacrifice, O king, and took refuge with him.

**7.173.51**  And by that very excess of his wrath the sacrifice was then restored; the gods grew watchful of him, and watchful they remain toward him even to this day.

**7.173.52**  The mighty Asuras had three great cities in the sky: one of iron, one of silver, and another, the greatest, of gold.

**7.173.53**  The iron city was Tārakākṣa's, the silver Kamalākṣa's, and the supreme golden one belonged to Vidyunmālin.

**7.173.54**  Maghavan was unable to break those cities even with all his weapons; then all the immortals, sorely afflicted, went to Rudra for refuge.

**7.173.55**  All the gods, with Vāsava at their head, spoke to that great one: 'Rudra, beasts shall become the offering in all sacred rites; lay low these Asuras, O lord of the worlds.'

**7.173.56**  Thus addressed, he said 'So be it,' and out of desire for the gods' welfare he stood motionless as a post for a thousand full years.

**7.173.57**  When at last the three cities came together in the firmament, he pierced them with that three-jointed, three-barbed shaft.

**7.173.58**  And the Dānavas of those cities could not so much as look upon that arrow, joined with the fire of doom and conjoined with Viṣṇu and Soma.

**7.173.59**  Making himself a child with five tufts of hair seated in her lap, Umā, wishing to test the gods, asked them, 'Who is this?'

**7.173.60**  The Lord paralyzed the thunderbolt-bearing arm of the angered Śakra — he, this very god, the blessed one, sovereign of all the worlds.

**7.173.61**  Yet the gods, together with the Prajāpatis, all failed to recognize him, the lord of the worlds, whose radiance was like the newly risen sun.

**7.173.62**  Then Brahmā, drawing near and beholding that Maheśvara, knew 'This is the highest,' and the Grandfather paid him homage.

**7.173.63**  Thereupon those gods propitiated Umā and Rudra, and the arm of the thunderbolt-wielder became once more as it had been by nature.

**7.173.64**  The Lord, with his consort, the bull-bannered, best of the Thirty among gods, the destroyer of Dakṣa's sacrifice, was gracious to them.

**7.173.65**  He indeed is Rudra, and he is Śiva; he is Agni, he is Śarva, he the all-knowing; he is both Indra and Vāyu, he the Aśvins, and he the lightnings.

**7.173.66**  He is Bhava, and he is Parjanya; he is Mahādeva, and he the sinless; he is the moon, he is Īśāna, he is the Sun, and he is Varuṇa.

**7.173.67**  He is Time, he is the Ender, he is Death; he is Yama, and the nights and days; the months, the fortnights, the seasons, the twilights, and the year — that is he.

**7.173.68**  He is both Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, the soul of all, the doer of every work; and he, the formless, bears the form of all the deities.

**7.173.69**  Praised by all the gods, the god is one and yet manifold — a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and so a hundred-thousandfold.

**7.173.70**  Such is that Mahādeva, and yet more is the blessed unborn one; for not all the virtues of the Lord can be told by me.

**7.173.71**  Those seized by every malign planet and beset with every sin — them, well pleased, he sets free, the refuge of those who come to him for refuge.

**7.173.72**  Long life, health, lordship, wealth, and abundant desires he grants to men; and he too snatches them away again.

**7.173.73**  His sovereignty is proclaimed over the gods, Indra and the rest; and it is he who ordains in the world the good and the ill of men.

**7.173.74**  Because of his lordship over all desires he is again called the Lord; and he is Maheśvara, the great lord of beings, the lord of the mighty ones.

**7.173.75**  With many forms in many ways he pervades the whole universe; and that mouth of this god abides within the ocean.

**7.173.76**  And this god dwells perpetually in the cremation grounds; there men worship him, the Lord, by the name 'Abode of Heroes.'

**7.173.77**  His forms are blazing and terrible and many; those which men make and speak of in the world are his.

**7.173.78**  His names in the worlds are many, and here they are fittingly derived, according to his greatness, his pervading power, and his deeds.

**7.173.79**  And in the Veda the supreme Śatarudrīya is handed down concerning him, and by the name 'Endless Rudra' the worship of the great-souled one is performed.

**7.173.80**  That god is lord of all desires, the heavenly and the human alike; he is the all-pervading, he the sovereign god who fills the whole great universe.

**7.173.81**  The Brāhmaṇas and the sages call him the eldest of beings; for he is the first of the gods, and from his mouth the fire arose.

**7.173.82**  Because in every way he protects the creatures and again takes his delight in them, and because he is their overlord, he is therefore called Paśupati.

**7.173.83**  Because by his perpetual chastity his liṅga stands erect, and because the worlds magnify him, he is remembered as Maheśvara.

**7.173.84**  The seers and the gods, and likewise the Gandharvas and Apsarases, worship his liṅga, and it too stands upraised.

**7.173.85**  When that liṅga is worshipped, Maheśvara rejoices; Śaṃkara becomes happy and pleased and well delighted.

**7.173.86**  Because his form is manifold, abiding in past, future, and present, both unmoving and moving, he is therefore remembered as Bahurūpa, of many forms.

**7.173.87**  He sits blazing as the one-eyed, or else made all of eyes on every side; and because in wrath he entered into the worlds, he is therefore remembered as Śarva.

**7.173.88**  Because his form is smoke-grey he is called Dhūrjaṭi; and because all the gods abide in him, he is therefore remembered as Viśvarūpa.

**7.173.89**  And because the lord of the worlds embraces the three goddesses — heaven, the waters, and the earth — he is therefore remembered as Tryambaka.

**7.173.90**  Because he ever furthers all ends in all undertakings, desiring the welfare of men, he is therefore remembered as Śiva, the auspicious.

**7.173.91**  Thousand-eyed, or ten-thousand-eyed, or made all of eyes on every side, and because he protects this whole great universe, he is therefore remembered as Mahādeva.

**7.173.92**  Because, standing upright, he burns, and because he abides at the source of the life-breaths, and because his liṅga ever stands fixed, he is therefore remembered as Sthāṇu, the pillar.

**7.173.93**  Dwelling unevenly in bodies, yet equal in all living beings here, he is the Vāyu coursing unevenly within the bodies as the in-breath and the out-breath.

**7.173.94**  Whoever worships his image, or duly honors his liṅga — he who ever worships the liṅga attains great prosperity.

**7.173.95**  From the thighs upward, half his auspicious body is of fire and half of the moon; one half of himself is said to be Agni, and again the other half is Soma.

**7.173.96**  Toward the gods his auspicious body is fiery, vast, and blazing; among men this radiant body of his is called the dreadful fire.

**7.173.97**  With that body of his which is auspicious he practices chastity; but with that more terrible form of his the Lord devours all things.

**7.173.98**  Because he burns all utterly, because he is sharp, fierce, and full of scorching might, and because he is the devourer of flesh, blood, and marrow, he is therefore called Rudra.

**7.173.99**  This god is Mahādeva, he whom you, O Pārtha, beheld before you in battle, smiting down your foes — the bearer of the Pināka.

**7.173.100**  It is this blessed god who goes before you in battle — he by whom your weapons were given, and by which you slew the Dānavas.

**7.173.101**  The Śatarudriya of the god of gods — bestowing fortune, fame, and long life, holy, and named in the Vedas — has now been expounded to you, O Pārtha.

**7.173.102**  It accomplishes all ends, it is holy, it destroys all defilements, it stills all sins, and it takes away all sorrow and fear.

**7.173.103**  The man who ever hears this fourfold hymn of praise conquers all his enemies and is exalted in the world of Rudra.

**7.173.104**  This auspicious, divine, warlike deed of the great-souled one — reciting the Śatarudrīya and hearing it, ever diligent —

**7.173.105**  the man who among mortals is ever devoted to the god Viśveśvara obtains the boons of his desire when Tryambaka is well pleased.

**7.173.106**  Go, fight, O son of Kuntī; there is no defeat for you, for at your side, as counselor and protector, stands Janārdana.

**7.173.107**  Saṃjaya said: Having spoken thus to Arjuna on the field of battle, the son of Parāśara then departed, O best of the Bhāratas, scourge of foes, by the way he had come.
